text: Disclosure in criminal proceedings Context The prosecution duty of disclosure is fundamental to the integrity of the criminal justice system. It is enshrined in and governed by common law and the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (the Act) to ensure every accused person receives a fair trial. The obligation to disclose is ongoing and extends from the material upon which the prosecution intends to rely, to all other material in the organisation’s possession which is relevant, or possibly relevant, to the case against an accused person. The obligation to disclose all relevant material to the court must always involve careful assessment for appropriate exceptions and redactions to balance privacy considerations and to ensure the disclosure of only what is relevant to the proceeding. Compliance with disclosure obligations promotes fairness and efficiency, prevents miscarriages of justice and increases public confidence in the criminal justice system and Victoria Police. As a public authority under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006, employees must act compatibly with, and give proper consideration to, relevant human rights in the course of their duties. Appropriate disclosure practices in criminal proceedings will ensure employees fulfill these obligations by: enabling an accused person to understand the nature and reason for a charge, while providing the information necessary to prepare their defence ensuring appropriate protection is afforded to members of the public who provide information and assistance to police. Policy at a glance This policy includes guidance on: the assessment of relevance, categorisation and disclosure of material collected during an investigation developing an investigation plan to assist in managing disclosure obligations the requirement to complete a disclosure certificate when a brief of evidence is served the process to comply with disclosure obligations in both the summary and indictable jurisdictions exceptions to the obligation to disclose material, including: material relevant to the credibility of a prosecution witness third-party material. Responsibilities and procedures Duty of disclosure Legal obligation The prosecution’s duty of disclosure is an obligation that is owed to the court to promote the fundamental principle that every accused person has a right to a fair trial. The common law obligation to disclose provides an ongoing positive obligation. This means the obligation exists regardless of whether the accused person makes a specific request for material. The Act imposes statutory requirements in relation to disclosure that complement, but do not replace, the positive obligation imposed by common law. Section 415A, the Act requires the informant to disclose all relevant material to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP). The allocated solicitor at the OPP must be notified if material has been withheld. The member does not need to provide withheld material to the OPP in the first instance, but the OPP can call for its production. If the member thinks there is a reason they should not inform the OPP of the material, or produce it when called for, they must notify the Disclosure Support Unit (DSU). The obligation to provide relevant material also applies to criminal proceedings where the CDPP is the prosecuting agency. Prosecution’s duty of disclosure To comply with the common law obligation of disclosure and statutory provisions of the Act, and subject to the exceptions provided for at section 4 of this policy, the prosecution must ensure disclosure of all material that is: relevant or possibly relevant to an issue in the case raises or possibly raises a new issue to which its existence is not apparent from the evidence the prosecution proposes to use holds out a real prospect of providing a line of inquiry in relation to the two criteria above exculpatory or possibly exculpatory. Refer to the Policy of the DPP – Chapter 2 for further detail. To effectively meet this obligation, all material collected during an investigation must be assessed for relevance, categorised and considered for disclosure. For further instructions on categorisation see section 1.4 of this policy. The duty of disclosure extends beyond the evidence on which the prosecution relies. The informant must assess all material in their possession or that they have knowledge of. This includes: material gathered solely for intelligence purposes material held by covert areas within Victoria Police. The informant's obligation extends to making reasonable enquiries to determine whether other areas of Victoria Police hold relevant material (see section 2.3 of this policy and the Disclosure Due Diligence Process in the Practice Guide – Disclosure in criminal proceedings). The duty applies to material regardless of whether the accused person, the prosecution or the

title: Disclosure_VPM_Disclosure_final
text: they have knowledge of. This includes: material gathered solely for intelligence purposes material held by covert areas within Victoria Police. The informant's obligation extends to making reasonable enquiries to determine whether other areas of Victoria Police hold relevant material (see section 2.3 of this policy and the Disclosure Due Diligence Process in the Practice Guide – Disclosure in criminal proceedings). The duty applies to material regardless of whether the accused person, the prosecution or the court has asked for the material or whether the material is likely to be admitted into evidence. The prosecution’s duty to disclose does not extend to material: relevant only to the credibility of defence (as distinct from prosecution) witnesses relevant only to the credibility of the accused person relevant only because it might deter an accused person from giving false evidence or providing a false version of events for the purpose of preventing an accused person from creating a trap for themselves, if at the time the prosecution became aware of the material it was not a relevant issue at trial. Refer to the Policy of the DPP on the DPP website for further details. Contact a police prosecutor, Prosecutions Frontline Support Unit, or the DSU where advice is required to confirm whether material meets the criteria set out in section 1.3 of this policy. Where an accused person raises a new issue or if facts change, consideration must be given as to whether there might be additional material in the possession of Vitctoria Police that might be relevant or possibly relevant to that issue and might therefore need to be disclosed to the accused person, DPP or CDPP in accordance with the ongoing duty of disclosure. The prosecutor should be made aware of the existence of this material or provided with a copy of it so they can determine if it needs to be disclosed at a later time. If the material cannot be disclosed to the prosecutor the member should seek assistance from the DSU. Assessing relevance All material collected, identified or created during an investigation, including contemporaneous notes, must be assessed for relevance. The relevance of material must be assessed on a case-by-case basis and should continue to be re-assessed as the investigation (and prosecution) progresses. The determination of relevance must be based on a thorough assessment of: the issues or likely issues in the case any defence available, or likely to be available, to the accused person any credibility issues associated with prosecution witnesses. Material will be deemed relevant or possibly relevant if it: can be seen to undermine the prosecution case might reasonably be expected to assist or strengthen the accused person’s case is relevant to the credibility of a

text: determination of relevance must be based on a thorough assessment of: the issues or likely issues in the case any defence available, or likely to be available, to the accused person any credibility issues associated with prosecution witnesses. Material will be deemed relevant or possibly relevant if it: can be seen to undermine the prosecution case might reasonably be expected to assist or strengthen the accused person’s case is relevant to the credibility of a prosecution witness lends weight to a reasonable hypothesis consistent with the accused person’s innocence suggests the existence of an alternate suspect opens a line of enquiry going to any of these factors. For further assistance with the assessment of relevance refer to the Practice Guide – Disclosure in criminal proceedings. Categorisation and storage of material In the course of an investigation, once an informant or investigator has possession or knowledge of material, that material must be categorised. There are four distinct categories which must be used: material relied upon unused material withheld material material that is not relevant. Once the material has been categorised, it must be stored electronically in a location accessible to the work unit manager. Further guidance on categorising material collected during the investigation is provided in the Practice Guide – Disclosure in criminal proceedings. Complying with the duty Overview Disclosure of the prosecution case is initiated when Victoria Police commences proceedings i.e., filing a charge sheet. The obligation to disclose is ongoing and continues even after criminal proceedings are finalised. The work unit manager is responsible for embedding robust administrative and supervision processes to ensure compliance with disclosure obligations. Work unit managers must also comply with VPM Workplace standards and management. Disclosure obligations apply to all material that is in the possession or knowledge of the prosecution regardless of admissibility or evidentiary considerations. The informant must consider whether there may be relevant material held within other areas of Victoria Police. If so, the informant must make reasonable enquiries to obtain that material. Sensitive material must be assessed to determine whether it may be subject to an exception and should be withheld pending a public interest immunity (PII) or statutory secrecy claim or application for a non-disclosure order. The informant must consult with a supervisor from the area within which the sensitive material originates e.g., Intelligence and Covert Support Command. Disclosure to the accused person must be made as soon as reasonably practicable and in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Act. Informants must not provide any material which is subject to a claim of PII to the DPP unless it has been specifically requested by the DPP in accordance with s.415A(5), the Act and/or the Protocol for engagement and resolution

text: area within which the sensitive material originates e.g., Intelligence and Covert Support Command. Disclosure to the accused person must be made as soon as reasonably practicable and in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Act. Informants must not provide any material which is subject to a claim of PII to the DPP unless it has been specifically requested by the DPP in accordance with s.415A(5), the Act and/or the Protocol for engagement and resolution of complex issues arising from disclosure obligations and public interest immunity claims (available on the OPP website) and advice has been sought from the DSU. Investigation plans An investigation plan must be developed and enacted by the investigator once an investigation has commenced. The purpose of the investigation plan is to determine in advance, the actions, objectives, strategies, resources required and associated risks to achieve case resolution. For serious offences, a comprehensive investigation plan must be recorded in Interpose. The investigation plan should include a disclosure task where required. For less complex investigations, the investigation plan (consisting of short dot points) must be created in Interpose or in the AIM file [Form 1313]. The investigation plan should include a disclosure task where required. An investigation plan is not required for minor traffic matters, such as certain offences against the Road Safety Act 1986 and Road Rules, where no follow up investigation is required. Disclosure certificates The Act requires the relevant officer to complete a disclosure certificate in proceedings where: a full brief is served in the summary jurisdiction (s.41A, the Act) a hand-up brief is served in the indictable jurisdiction (s.110A, the Act). The disclosure certificate is an acknowledgement that the relevant officer understands: they have a duty under the Act, and at common law, to disclose to the accused person all material relevant to the alleged offence and that this duty may be subject to exceptions they are aware of their continuing obligation under the Act, and at common law, to disclose to the accused person any relevant material that comes into their possession or notice after service of the hand-up brief they are aware of their obligation under s.415A, the Act to provide to the DPP any material that they possess or have knowledge of, or that the law enforcement agency they represent possesses or has knowledge of, that is relevant to the alleged offence, subject to the provisions in s.415A that the information they have given in this certificate is true, to the best of their knowledge and belief, and has been reviewed by a supervisor that the certificate discloses the existence of withheld material and the reason it has not been provided. Withheld material listed on the disclosure certificate must be

text: law enforcement agency they represent possesses or has knowledge of, that is relevant to the alleged offence, subject to the provisions in s.415A that the information they have given in this certificate is true, to the best of their knowledge and belief, and has been reviewed by a supervisor that the certificate discloses the existence of withheld material and the reason it has not been provided. Withheld material listed on the disclosure certificate must be described in accordance with the guidance provided in the Practice Guide – Disclosure in criminal proceedings. In certain limited circumstances, withheld material may be omitted from the disclosure certificate, see section 2.4 of this policy for details regarding non-disclosure orders Advice should be sought from the DSU in these situations. A supervisor must review and sign the completed disclosure certificate before it is signed by the relevant officer. In summary matters a copy of the Form 1517 must be included with the full brief for forwarding to the appropriate prosecutions unit. The disclosure certificate must be provided to the accused person, the court and the DPP/prosecutions unit as follows: Non-disclosure orders An application for a non-disclosure order must be made pursuant to section 416A(1), the Act when the relevant officer considers that withheld material is of a sensitive nature. In indictable proceedings: the application for a non-disclosure order must commence prior to the completion of the disclosure certificate any information not included in the disclosure certificate must be included in the case direction notice unless otherwise ordered by a court. In summary proceedings, the Form 1517 should not be completed until the application or the claim causing the material to be withheld is resolved or directions are given by the court. Where information is provided by a person with an expectation of confidentiality (including a human source), an application for a non-disclosure order must be made as soon as possible after criminal proceedings commence. This must involve seeking direction from the court regarding the omission of the material from the certificate. For the relevant officer to meet their disclosure obligations in respect to withheld material not included on the disclosure certificate, a court must assess the application and may make certain orders or determine the claim. Contact the DSU where advice is required in respect of non-disclosure orders. Disclosure process To comply with disclosure obligations, refer to: Table 1: Disclosure process in criminal proceedings (summary jurisdiction) Table 2: Disclosure process in criminal proceedings (indictable jurisdiction/hand-up brief) Note: the member preparing the brief must redact the address or phone number of any person in any material disclosed in accordance with ss.48 (summary proceedings), 114 (indictable proceedings pre-committal) and 186 (indictable proceedings post-committal), the Act unless relevant to prove an element of a charge. Material relevant to the credibility of a prosecution witness Both common law and the Act require the disclosure of material relevant to the credibility of a prosecution witness. Subject to any exception (e.g., PII or other statutory exceptions) this material must be included, as part of a full brief (s.41(1)(e)(viii), the Act) or hand-up brief (s.41(e)(viii), the Act). This includes (but is not limited to) the following material: relevant criminal history recorded on LEAP information where a witness has been charged, or charges are pending for a relevant criminal offence the provision of a letter of assistance or similar to the witness the reduction of criminal charges against the witness or other favourable treatment in a criminal proceeding any payment, reward or benefit provided as a result of the witness’ co-operation with police, but not limited to witness letters of support and any drafts, discussions or communications about the provision of the witness letter of support and/or its content expert witness statements or scientific evidence which contradicts or calls into question the credibility of any prosecution witness any prior inconsistent statements (including Victim Impact Statements and overt and covert recordings) findings by or evidence given in any court or tribunal (criminal and non-criminal) relevant information about a physical or mental condition which is of central importance to the case and which may affect the reliability of a prosecution witness. The DSU should be consulted, and members may be advised to contact the VGSO for advice, where: a witness has previously received a reward, benefit or favourable treatment as a result of their co-operation with police the disclosure of an ongoing prosecution may result in it being prejudiced a witness' personal health information may be required. The relevant officer must consider the exception to disclosing evidence of confidential communications between a victim of sexual offending and a medical practitioner or counsellor under s.32C, Evidence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1958. The prosecution must be consulted in these circumstances. Material held by PSC or within Victoria Police or VPS personnel/employment files will not be relevant in the majority of cases. Proactive enquiries do not have to be made in the absence of any particular reason or basis upon which the material might

title: Disclosure_VPM_Disclosure_final
text: disclosing evidence of confidential communications between a victim of sexual offending and a medical practitioner or counsellor under s.32C, Evidence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1958. The prosecution must be consulted in these circumstances. Material held by PSC or within Victoria Police or VPS personnel/employment files will not be relevant in the majority of cases. Proactive enquiries do not have to be made in the absence of any particular reason or basis upon which the material might substantially affect the credibility of a prosecution witness. In these circumstances advice must be sought from the DSU. Exceptions to disclosure - withheld material There are exceptions to the duty of disclosure. These include but are not limited to: a claim of privilege (such as Client Legal Privilege) or PII (such as application for PII to protect information received from a human source or to protect confidential police methodology) immunity conferred by statute (such as under the Witness Protection Act 1991 or the Major Crimes (Investigative Powers) Act 2004) a prohibition or restriction provided by statute that has the effect of precluding disclosure to the prosecution or defence (such as s.48, the Act – prohibition on disclosing the address and telephone of any person) a non-disclosure order (s.416A, the Act) s.464JA Crimes Act 1958 (Offences in relation to possession of a record of interview). An application to the court must be made to claim PII or request a non-disclosure order. The DSU should be consulted prior to commencing an application. If an application for PII or a non-disclosure order is made to the court, all information and documents must be provided to the legal practitioners acting for the Chief Commissioner of Police without redactions. Advice should be sought from the DSU where the disclosure of information about a witness could prejudice the safety and welfare of any person. Members must describe the nature and the basis of the claim in as much detail as possible. In exceptional cases, that information may be provided only to the court. Where statutory secrecy provisions and/or other safety or operational considerations apply, specialist areas may seek legal advice and initiate an application for a non-disclosure order or PII without the informant’s knowledge if necessary. Disclosure of third-party material Third-party material is material provided to Victoria Police to assist with a criminal investigation by another agency (a third-party). This may be subject to intelligence sharing agreements, statutory exceptions or a Memorandum of Understanding. A third-party who provides material to Victoria Police may wish to claim PII or invoke statutory protections that limit disclosure of that material. If material has been provided by a third-party and it is categorised as either material relied upon or unused material, contact that third-party to

title: Disclosure_VPM_Disclosure_final
text: Victoria Police to assist with a criminal investigation by another agency (a third-party). This may be subject to intelligence sharing agreements, statutory exceptions or a Memorandum of Understanding. A third-party who provides material to Victoria Police may wish to claim PII or invoke statutory protections that limit disclosure of that material. If material has been provided by a third-party and it is categorised as either material relied upon or unused material, contact that third-party to determine whether the material can be disclosed or should be withheld, including the basis on which it should be withheld. An informant must not disclose the material to the accused person, the DPP or CDPP if the third-party advises Victoria Police that a claim for PII will be made regarding the material. Before communicating any information to the accused person or DPP about the existence and nature of the third-party material, the informant must confirm with the third-party whether there are any issues in doing so. A PII application may be made by either Victoria Police or the relevant third-party regardless of which organisation owns the third-party material. The DSU should be contacted and the VGSO engaged where a PII application is contemplated by either party. text: The Victoria Police Manual is issued under the authority of the Chief Commissioner of Police in s.60, Victoria Police Act 2013. Non-compliance with or a departure from the Victoria Police Manual may be subject to management or disciplinary action. Employees must use VPM Professional and ethical standards to inform the decisions they make to support compliance. Bail and remand Context The Bail Act 1977 provides the legislative framework for deciding whether a person should be granted bail and includes guiding principles for bail decision makers, clarifying the matters which must guide their decision making and the application of the legislation. The key principle is: The overarching importance of maximizing, to the greatest extent possible, the safety of the community and persons affected by crime The other principles are: taking account of the presumption of innocence and the right to liberty promoting fairness, transparency and consistency in bail decision making promoting public understanding of bail practices and procedures. Police bail decision makers have the power to grant bail to a person, especially Aboriginal people, children and vulnerable adults. Bail decision makers must apply specific provisions applicable to Aboriginal people, children and vulnerable groups as outlined in ss.3A-3B, Bail Act. As a public authority under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (the Charter), all members must act compatibly with, and give proper consideration to, relevant human rights in the course of their duties. This means genuinely considering the power to grant bail when it is available, in order to give effect to the right to liberty. It also means taking into account the particular vulnerability of Aboriginal people in custody to give effect to the right to equality and cultural rights under the Charter. Each matter must be considered case-by-case and assessed on individual merits. Though there will be occasions where it will be appropriate to oppose an application for bail, this does not create an obligation to oppose bail where a person’s circumstances establish exceptional circumstances or compelling reasons to grant bail, when the person does not present an unacceptable risk. Scope and application This policy applies to all members and PCOs, particularly: police bail decision makers informants in bail and remand applications. Responsibilities and procedures Prima facie entitlement to bail Section 4, Bail Act recognises the prima facie right that a person is entitled to be granted bail. Enforcement options Police are responsible for identifying the most appropriate enforcement action to take against a person. As detailed in VPM Disposition the options, from least to most severe are: caution/official warning infringement notice charge and summons charge and bail charge and remand - this is the most severe action that can be taken and should only happen where no other options are appropriate. Bail decision makers General The Bail Act specifies that bail decision makers are empowered to grant bail, extend bail, vary the amount or the conditions of bail or revoke bail. As stated at section 9 of this policy, the Bail Act includes three schedules of offences, which require applications for bail to be considered by specific bail decision makers. Bail decision makers must genuinely consider the power to grant bail when it is available, noting the prima facie right that a person is entitled to be granted bail. Each matter must be considered case-by-case and assessed on individual merits. When making any determination under the Bail Act, bail decision makers must: take into account any issues that arise due to the person’s Aboriginality (see s.3A, Bail Act and section 5 of this policy) comply with the requirements of s.3B, Bail Act if the person is a child (see section 6 of this policy). Police as the bail decision maker Section 10, Bail Act provides that a police officer of or above the rank of sergeant, or for the time being in charge of a police station, must, without delay consider whether to grant bail to the person in accordance with the Bail Act in either of the following circumstances: where it is impractical to bring a person before a court immediately after the person is taken into custody if questioning, or an investigation under s.464A(2), Crimes Act 1958 has commenced, immediately on the expiration of the reasonable time provided by

Police bail proceedings Overview of the decision making process Police bail decision makers must fulfil their obligations in accordance with the Bail Act. This includes consideration of bail for an Aboriginal person, a child or a vulnerable adult subject to the exceptional circumstances test on occasions when empowered to do so. The following tables provide an overview of the decision-making process which must occur when determining whether a police bail decision maker may grant an application for bail. For further considerations which apply where the accused is an Aboriginal person, a child or a vulnerable adult, see sections 5 and 6 of this policy. Refer to the Bail Act 1977 and the PFSU Bail & Remand Hub intranet page for the relevant Schedules. Prohibition on refusing bail Accused on two or more undertakings of bail for indictable offences Exceptional circumstances Show compelling reason Unacceptable risk Terrorism considerations Imposing conditions As stated at section 9.3 of this policy, when considering the release of someone on bail, the bail decision maker must impose any condition that, in their opinion, will reduce any unacceptable risk posed by the accused (s.5AAA(1), Bail Act). If conditions are imposed, the police bail decision maker must ensure that they are: no more onerous than is required to reduce the likelihood that the accused may pose an unacceptable risk reasonable, having regard to the nature of the alleged offence and circumstances of the accused consistent with each condition of any family violence intervention order (FVIO), family violence safety notice (FVSN) or recognised domestic violence order (DVO) which applies to the person (s.5AAA(2), Bail Act). A bail decision maker may impose a condition in order to reduce the likelihood that the accused may: commit a Schedule 1 offence or Schedule 2 offence endanger the safety or welfare of any other person, whether by committing an offence that has that effect or by any other means interfere with a witness or otherwise obstruct the course of justice in any matter fail to surrender into custody in accordance with the bail undertaking For example, a bail decision maker may impose a condition to reduce the likelihood that the accused may: drive dangerously, e.g., driving at high speeds in built up areas or filming themselves whilst

In addition, where a bail decision maker is considering the release on bail of an accused charged with a family violence offence, they must consider whether the accused poses a risk of committing family violence and whether that risk could be reduced by the: imposition of condition(s); or making of a FVIO (s.5AAAA), Bail Act). Where a police bail decision maker imposes a condition that is inconsistent with a condition of an existing FVIO, FVSN or recognised DVO, they must be satisfied the bail condition better protects: the safety or welfare of the alleged victim of the offence for which the accused is charged, or a protected person (s.5AAA(3), Bail Act). Should such conditions be made, the informant must apply to vary the original order to ensure the civil action is consistent with the bail conditions and must inform the protected person(s) about the bail conditions. Consideration should be given to any referral options in consultation with local court services. Granting bail Police bail decision makers must genuinely consider the power to grant bail when it is available, in order to give effect to a person’s right to liberty under the Charter. Each matter must be considered case-by-case and assessed on individual merits. Police bail decision makers must record the decision for granting bail using Preliminary Brief - Statement made by Informant including Remand/Bail Application [Form 1372] or the Remand/Bail Application [Form 286]. For any Schedule 2 offence members must complete a Statement of Reasons for Granting Bail [Form 497]. The ‘Record of police bail decision’ should also be completed in circumstances where a person is taken before a court and bail is not granted or refused. When granting bail, a police bail decision maker must consider whether to release the accused: on bail with conduct condition(s) on bail without conduct conditions with a bail guarantee for a specified amount or deposit of money, with or without conduct condition(s). Bail proceedings in relation to an Aboriginal person General All bail decision makers must ask the person applying for bail if they are an Aboriginal person. A person’s Aboriginality must be referenced in the remand summary of the Form 1372 or Form 286. When considering whether to grant bail to an Aboriginal person for a criminal matter, the police bail decision maker must take into account any issues that arise from that person’s Aboriginality including (s.3A, Bail Act): the historical and ongoing discriminatory systemic factors that have resulted in Aboriginal people being over-represented in the criminal justice system, including on remand the risk of harm and trauma that being in custody poses to Aboriginal people the importance of maintaining and supporting the development of the person's connection to culture, kinship, family, Elders, country and community any issues that arise in relation to the person's history, culture or circumstances, including the following: the impact of any experience of trauma and intergenerational trauma, including abuse, neglect, loss and family violence any experience of out of home care, including foster care and residential care any experience of social or economic disadvantage, including homelessness and unstable housing any ill health the person experiences, including mental illness any disability the person has, including physical disability, intellectual disability and cognitive impairment any caring responsibilities the person has, including as the sole or primary parent of an Aboriginal child any other relevant cultural issue or obligation. A person’s Aboriginality must be considered regardless of whether their connection to their Aboriginality and culture has been intermittent, recently connected to or discovered. When determining whether to grant bail or remand an Aboriginal person, consider: what ties

When determining whether to grant bail or remand an Aboriginal person, consider: what ties the person currently has to family, place and culture whether the person currently has cultural obligations related to their Aboriginality will remanding the person disrupt their cultural ties or obligations? i.e., the opportunity to access culturally sensitive services such as drug and alcohol rehabilitation and/or participation in cultural events or ceremonies. Note: police bail decision makers should use the Guide to bail considerations for Aboriginal people available on the Prosecutions Frontline Support Unit (PFSU) Bail and Remand Hub. If the Aboriginal person is also a child, the bail decision maker must also take into account the matters set out in s.3B(1), Bail Act (see section 6 of this policy). When considering bail for an Aboriginal person charged with a Commonwealth offence, a bail decision maker must have regard to section 15AB(1)(b), Crimes Act 1914 (Cth). Ensuring opportunity to exercise rights In addition to the rights available to any person in custody in accordance with the Crimes Act, members must ensure that an Aboriginal person under arrest has a meaningful opportunity to make an informed decision about whether to accept an offer to communicate with the Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service (VALS) Custody Notification Officer, including providing the person with information about the purpose of that contact and what assistance the Custody Notification Officer may be able to provide. The person in custody must be advised that purpose of the notification is for VALS to both: perform a welfare and wellbeing assessment on the person including identification of any medical, physical and mental health concerns, disability or impairment (including due to substance use) communicate any identified risks to the person’s safety while in custody to police so that appropriate management and care is provided. Note: under s.464FA, Crimes Act, investigating officials must notify VALS if a person is taken into custody and either the person states that they are an Aboriginal person, or the investigating official knows or is of the opinion the person is an Aboriginal person. Members must offer the person a copy of the VALS Custody Information Sheet. Ensure an Aboriginal person under caution has a meaningful opportunity to both: consider whether to exercise their rights to communicate with a friend or relative and a legal practitioner exercise those rights. Considerations regarding the exceptional circumstances test The Bail Act allows a police bail decision maker to grant bail to an Aboriginal person subject to the exceptional circumstances test but only when s.4AA(2)(c) or (d), Bail Act applies. See the table at section 4.1 of this policy for further guidance. Oversight of Aboriginal children in police custody In addition to requirements contained within section 6 of this policy, where the police bail decision maker is considering denying bail for an Aboriginal child, they must seek advice from: during business hours - the Youth Law Group (YLG), PROS-YOUTH-LAW- UNIT-MGR (ph. 8533 1002) after hours – PFSU via Police Communications (ph. 1300 385 885). Any decision to grant or refuse bail remains the responsibility of the police bail decision maker. The YLG or PFSU can assist bail decision makers’ understanding of applicable legislative considerations to ensure that bail decisions are appropriate. The custody supervisor, who may also act as the police bail decision maker, with oversight from the on-duty senior sergeant, is responsible for decisions and actions taken during the custody process and for recording if YLG or PFSU were engaged on the Attendance Module. For further resources regarding processing children in custody, refer to the YLG intranet page. Bail proceedings in relation to a child General The minimum age of criminal responsibility is 12 years. A child who is under 12 years of age must not be charged. Prior to charging a child aged 12 or 13 years, members must have regard to whether it appears that there is admissible evidence to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the child knew, at the time of committing the alleged offence, that the conduct was seriously wrong. Refer to VPMP Briefs of evidence for applicable processes and factors that must be considered prior to authorising a brief where the accused is aged 12 or 13 years. These processes must be followed prior to charging any child and before considering bail or remand. Section 346(2), Children Youth and Families Act 2005, states that within a reasonable time of being taken into custody, but no later than 24 hours after being taken into custody, a child must be: released unconditionally released on bail by a police bail

Section 346(2), Children Youth and Families Act 2005, states that within a reasonable time of being taken into custody, but no later than 24 hours after being taken into custody, a child must be: released unconditionally released on bail by a police bail decision maker brought before the court brought before a bail justice if the court is not sitting. Once 24 hours has expired, the child must be released unconditionally or on bail. When considering whether to grant bail to a child for a criminal matter, a parent or guardian of the child or an independent person must be present during the bail proceeding. The parent, guardian or independent person may take steps to facilitate the granting of bail (ss.10A(3)-(4) Bail Act). When making any determination, the police bail decision maker must take into account the following as required by s.3B, Bail Act: the child's age, maturity and stage of development at the time of the alleged offence the need to impose on the child the minimum intervention required in the circumstances the presumption at common law that a child who is 12 years of age or over but under 14 years of age cannot commit an offence the need to preserve and strengthen the child's relationships with both: the child's parents, guardian and carers other significant people in the child's life the importance of supporting the child to live at home or in safe, stable and secure living arrangements in the community the importance of both: supporting the child to engage in education, or in training or work ensuring engagement is subject only to minimal interruption or disturbance the need to minimise the stigma to the child resulting from being remanded the fact that time in custody has been shown to pose criminogenic and other risks for children, including: risk that the child will become further involved in the criminal justice system risk of harm the need to ensure that the conditions of bail: are no more onerous than is necessary do not constitute unfair management of the child the fact that some cohorts of children, including the following cohorts, experience discrimination resulting in that cohort's over-representation in the criminal justice system: Aboriginal children children involved with child protection children from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds whether, if the child were found guilty of the offence charged, it is likely that both: the child would be sentenced to a term of imprisonment the time the child would spend remanded in custody if bail is refused would

Bail must not be refused to a child on the sole grounds that the child does not have any, or any adequate accommodation. Children without capacity to enter an undertaking of bail If the police bail decision maker believes the child does not have the capacity or understanding to enter into an undertaking, the child may be released on bail if the child’s parent or some other person enters into an undertaking to produce the child at the court to hear the charge. Depending on the circumstances, it may be sufficient for the parent, guardian or other person to sign (including by electronic signature in accordance with s.17B, Bail Act) the bail. Generally, unless there are circumstances that justify the taking of a bail guarantee/security from the parent or guardian, no monetary amount should be considered. PCOs or custody staff are responsible for facilitating communication between the person and their legal representative e.g., by phone, in person or AVL technology. The informant and prosecutor must attend the hearing via AVL technology, separate to the person. Refer to the Children’s Court WORC Intranet page for further information. First remand hearings For a first remand hearing (even if no application for bail is lodged), the court can direct the person to appear by AVL instead of physically on: its own initiative an application by the person, the prosecution or police. The court can make the direction if it is satisfied that appearance by AVL is consistent with the interests of justice, and either of the following apply: the person consents to appear by AVL the court is satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist e.g., a state of emergency is in place. Where the person has consented to appear via AVL, the informant must record consent by ticking the appropriate box on Form 1372 or Form 286. This should be raised by the informant before the person seeks legal advice and after having had the opportunity, the informant must ask if the person consents to appear via AVL. Remote bail justice hearings via audio visual link technology The following

text: e.g., a state of emergency is in place. Where the person has consented to appear via AVL, the informant must record consent by ticking the appropriate box on Form 1372 or Form 286. This should be raised by the informant before the person seeks legal advice and after having had the opportunity, the informant must ask if the person consents to appear via AVL. Remote bail justice hearings via audio visual link technology The following criteria must be met to commence a remote bail justice hearing: BaRC or WORC are unavailable or are unsuitable; refer to sections 7.5 and 7.6 of this policy a bail justice is required where the person is a child, consent has been obtained from all parties (child, parent / guardian or Independent Person) or a bail justice has determined appearance by AVL is necessary the hearing is being held at a police station with an AVL room an appropriate risk assessment of the person has been completed to ensure the hearing can be conducted safely there are no extenuating circumstances that prevent the hearing from being held remotely. Examples of extenuating circumstances are included in the Conducting remote bail justice hearings Practice Guide. Where consent is not obtained by all parties to conduct a hearing via AVL for a child, the bail justice may determine appearance by AVL is necessary if either of the following apply: exceptional circumstances exist it is consistent with the interests of justice and is reasonably practicable in the circumstances. The person may be transported to a police station with an AVL room when it is safe and practical to do so for the purpose of conducting a remote bail justice hearing. All bail justice hearings will be recorded by the bail justice and securely stored by the Department of Justice and Community Safety (DJCS). For in-person hearings, a risk assessment must be conducted. Information security guidelines must be applied. Refer to the Conducting a remote bail justice hearings Practice Guide for further instruction on remote bail justice hearings. Procedure for bailing Bail dates The informant should coordinate bail dates with: pending charges recorded on LEAP another upcoming court date, or where co-accused(s) or other associated or relevant charges are to be heard. People should be bailed to a court within one month of being charged unless: the matter is unusually complicated, or exceptional circumstances exist. People required to attend court for a bail or remand hearing All people required to attend court for a bail or remand hearing should first be processed at a police station. PCOs or custody staff may then either: transport the person to court when the hearing may be held in person escort the person to/from

text: bailed to a court within one month of being charged unless: the matter is unusually complicated, or exceptional circumstances exist. People required to attend court for a bail or remand hearing All people required to attend court for a bail or remand hearing should first be processed at a police station. PCOs or custody staff may then either: transport the person to court when the hearing may be held in person escort the person to/from the AVL room during BaRC and WORC operating hours arrange for the person to be seen by a bail decision maker. Responsibilities when a person is granted bail Where a person is granted bail the following responsibilities apply: Application to vary bail conduct conditions Once bail conduct conditions are imposed, they can only be varied upon application to the court. Members must not grant permission to a person to fail to comply with any conduct conditions, including reporting obligations and curfews. Members must instead instruct a person to make a formal application to vary bail at the relevant court. Responsibilities when a person fails to report on bail When a person fails to report on bail the following responsibilities apply: Exceptions to entitlement to bail Overview The Bail Act recognises certain circumstances where the prima facie entitlement to bail does not apply. In summary, these are when: there is an unacceptable risk posed if the person is released on bail the person is charged with a Schedule 1 offence and they cannot demonstrate exceptional circumstances that justify bail being granted the person is charged with a Schedule 2 offence which is alleged to have been committed while they were on bail, summons, at large awaiting trial, subject to a CCO, parole order or otherwise serving a sentence for any Schedule 1 or 2 offence and they cannot demonstrate exceptional circumstances that justify bail being granted the person is charged with a Schedule 2 offence and they cannot show compelling reason that justifies the granting of bail the person has a terrorism record, or the court (as the bail decision maker) determines that there is a risk that the person will commit a terrorism or foreign incursion offence and they cannot demonstrate exceptional circumstances or show compelling reasons that justify bail being granted. Flow Chart 1- Terrorism Record or Terrorism Risk (Appendix 1) and Flow Chart 2 - Which tests apply generally? (Appendix 2) show the process for determining which tests must be applied in deciding whether to grant bail. Whether these circumstances apply depends on the alleged offence and this in turn determines whether the person may apply to the court, a bail justice or a police officer for bail. Police and bail justices cannot

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Bail_and_remand_final
text: being granted. Flow Chart 1- Terrorism Record or Terrorism Risk (Appendix 1) and Flow Chart 2 - Which tests apply generally? (Appendix 2) show the process for determining which tests must be applied in deciding whether to grant bail. Whether these circumstances apply depends on the alleged offence and this in turn determines whether the person may apply to the court, a bail justice or a police officer for bail. Police and bail justices cannot grant bail where the following applies: a person is accused of treason - only the Supreme Court may grant bail a person is accused of murder - only the Supreme Court or the Magistrates’ Court, on committing the person for trial, may grant bail a person has a terrorism record – only a court may grant bail, irrespective of the offence the person is accused of a person is accused of a Schedule 1 offence – only a court may grant bail any other circumstances where a person is otherwise required to demonstrate exceptional circumstances as set out in section 9.4 of this policy – only a court may grant bail, unless the person is an Aboriginal person, a child or a vulnerable adult (s.13(4) of the Bail Act) a person (other than an Aboriginal person, a child or a vulnerable adult) accused of a Schedule 2 offence and is already on two undertakings of bail in relation to other indictable offences. Surrounding circumstances The bail decision maker must take in to account the surrounding circumstances that are relevant to the matter when considering whether to grant bail. Surrounding circumstances are defined at s.3AAA, Bail Act as including: whether, if the person was found guilty of the offence they have been charged with, it is likely that: they would be sentenced to a term of imprisonment and the time they would spend remanded in custody if bail is refused, would exceed that term of imprisonment the nature and seriousness of the alleged offence, including whether it is a serious example of the offence the strength of the prosecution case the person’s criminal history if the person has complied with the conditions of earlier grants of bail whether, at the time of alleged offending, the person was subject to any of the following: on bail for another offence a summons to answer to a charge for another offence at large awaiting trial for another offence on remand for another offence at large awaiting sentence for another offence released under a parole order a CCO made in respect of, or was otherwise serving a sentence for, another offence whether there is in force: a FVIO made against the person a FVSN issued against the person a recognised

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Bail_and_remand_final
text: the following: on bail for another offence a summons to answer to a charge for another offence at large awaiting trial for another offence on remand for another offence at large awaiting sentence for another offence released under a parole order a CCO made in respect of, or was otherwise serving a sentence for, another offence whether there is in force: a FVIO made against the person a FVSN issued against the person a recognised DVO made against the person the person’s personal circumstances, , including the caring responsibilities that the accused has (if any) and the accused’s associations, home environment and background any special vulnerability of the person, including being a child (see s.3B for specific matters) or an Aboriginal person (see s.3A for specific matters), experiencing any ill health, mental illness or having a disability, including physical or intellectual disability, or cognitive impairment or being pregnant. the availability of treatment or bail support services any known view or likely view of an alleged victim of the offending on the granting of bail, the amount of bail or conditions of bail the length of time the person is likely to spend in custody if bail is refused the likely sentence to be imposed should the person be found guilty of the offence with which the person is charged whether the person has expressed support for any of the below: the doing of a terrorist act a terrorist organisation (defined in Division 102, Criminal Code of the Commonwealth) the provision of resources to a terrorist organisation whether the person knowingly (to the satisfaction of the bail decision maker) has, or has had, an association with any of the below: another person or group that has expressed support of the kind referred to in the previous point another person or a group that is directly or indirectly engaged in preparing for, planning, assisting in or fostering the doing of a terrorist act a terrorist organisation. Unacceptable risk – any offence Section 4E, Bail Act provides that the bail decision maker must refuse bail if they are satisfied: there is a risk that the person, if released on bail, would: commit a Schedule 1 or a Schedule 2 offence otherwise endanger the safety or welfare of any other person, whether by committing an offence that has that effect or by other means interfere with witnesses or otherwise obstruct the course of justice or fail to surrender themselves into custody in answer to their bail and the risk is unacceptable. For example, an unacceptable risk that the accused, if released, would: drive dangerously, e.g., driving at high speeds in built up areas or filming themselves whilst driving at high speeds commit a family

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Bail_and_remand_final
text: other person, whether by committing an offence that has that effect or by other means interfere with witnesses or otherwise obstruct the course of justice or fail to surrender themselves into custody in answer to their bail and the risk is unacceptable. For example, an unacceptable risk that the accused, if released, would: drive dangerously, e.g., driving at high speeds in built up areas or filming themselves whilst driving at high speeds commit a family violence offence commit an aggravated burglary commit an armed robbery commit a carjacking or commit a home invasion. The prosecutor or informant bears the burden of satisfying the bail decision maker of the existence of the risks listed above and that the risk is an unacceptable risk. Members must seek remand in relation to an application for bail, if appropriate in all the circumstances, where: the alleged offending involves high risk / high harm conduct, which includes but is not limited to conduct such as driving dangerously (e.g., driving at high speeds in built up areas or filming themselves whilst driving at high speeds) or committing a family violence offence, an aggravated burglary, a carjacking or a home invasion and they consider there is an unacceptable risk of the accused committing further high risk/ high harm conduct if released on bail that is likely to endanger the safety or welfare of the community. When considering whether a risk is an unacceptable risk, the bail decision maker must do both of the following: take in to account the surrounding circumstances consider whether there are any conditions that may be imposed to mitigate the risk so that it is not an unacceptable risk. High Degree of Probability Test – Unacceptable risk The High Degree of Probability Test forms part of the unacceptable risk framework and will apply whenever a person is charged with committing one of six specified Schedule 1 offences whilst already on bail in relation to one those offences. The specified Schedule 1 offences that apply to the High Degree of Probability Test are: - armed robbery - aggravated burglary - home invasion - aggravated home invasion - carjacking - aggravated carjacking When the High Degree of Probability Test applies, the accused is considered an unacceptable risk to commit a Schedule 1 or Schedule 2 offence unless the bail decision maker is satisfied there is a high degree of probability that the person would not commit one of the specified offences. The prosecution (and informant) bears the responsibility of satisfying the bail decision maker that the accused is an unacceptable risk due to the High Degree of Probability Test. As police bail decision makers and bail justices are not empowered to consider bail for an

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Bail_and_remand_final
text: Schedule 1 or Schedule 2 offence unless the bail decision maker is satisfied there is a high degree of probability that the person would not commit one of the specified offences. The prosecution (and informant) bears the responsibility of satisfying the bail decision maker that the accused is an unacceptable risk due to the High Degree of Probability Test. As police bail decision makers and bail justices are not empowered to consider bail for an accused charged with a Schedule 1 offence, the High Degree of Probability Test will only be considered by the Court and limited to occasions where the accused has firstly demonstrated exceptional circumstances exist. Exceptional circumstances test The Bail Act provides that bail must be refused where the person is charged with certain offences unless the bail decision maker is satisfied exceptional circumstances exist that justify the granting of bail (s.4A(1A)). The exceptional circumstances test applies where the person is charged with a: Schedule 1 offence Schedule 2 offence and: the person has a terrorism record the court (as the bail decision maker) determines under s.8AA, Bail Act, that there is a risk that the person will commit a terrorism or foreign incursion offence. Schedule 2 offence which is alleged to have been committed while on bail, summons, at large awaiting trial, subject to a CCO, parole order or otherwise serving a sentence for any Schedule 1 or 2 offence (or an offence of conspiracy, incitement or attempting to commit an offence in these circumstances). For these offences: police prosecutors will be responsible for bail applications, which will be heard in the Magistrates’ Court police bail decision makers may consider granting bail in certain circumstances. The person has the burden of satisfying the bail decision maker as to the existence of exceptional circumstances (s.4A(2)). The bail decision maker must take in to account the surrounding circumstances (as described at section 9.2 of this policy) when considering whether exceptional circumstances exist (s.4A(3)). Show compelling reason test A bail decision maker must refuse bail for certain offences unless the person satisfies the bail decision maker that there is a compelling reason that justifies the granting of bail (s.4C(1A), Bail Act). The show compelling reason test applies where the person is charged with a Schedule 2 offence and the ‘exceptional circumstances’ test does not apply. The show compelling reason test also applies where the person is charged with an offence that is not a Schedule 1 or Schedule 2 offence and: the person has a terrorism record the court (as the bail decision maker) determines under s.8AA, Bail Act, that there is a risk that the person will commit a terrorism or foreign incursion offence (s.4AA(4)). The person has

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Bail_and_remand_final
text: Schedule 2 offence and the ‘exceptional circumstances’ test does not apply. The show compelling reason test also applies where the person is charged with an offence that is not a Schedule 1 or Schedule 2 offence and: the person has a terrorism record the court (as the bail decision maker) determines under s.8AA, Bail Act, that there is a risk that the person will commit a terrorism or foreign incursion offence (s.4AA(4)). The person has the burden of satisfying the bail decision maker as to the existence of a compelling reason (s.4C(2)). In considering whether there is a compelling reason, the bail decision maker must take into account the surrounding circumstances (s.4C(3)). If the bail decision maker is satisfied that compelling reasons exist, they must determine if there is an unacceptable risk as required at section 9.4 of this policy (s.4C(4)). Grounds for refusing bail or adjourning the bail application hearing in the first instance Separate to the above considerations, the bail decision maker may also do any of the following: refuse bail for a person accused of any offence if satisfied that it has not been practicable to obtain sufficient information to decide the matter because of the shortness of time since the commencement of the bail application hearing and the offence (s.8A) refuse bail if a person is accused of an offence of causing injury to another person and it is uncertain whether the person injured will die or recover from injury (s.8B) adjourn the hearing of a matter for up to four hours if satisfied the person appears to be seriously affected by alcohol and/or other drug(s) and remand the person in custody until the further hearing. If the person is still substance affected at the further hearing, the bail decision maker may adjourn the hearing for one further period of up to four hours and remand the person in custody until the next hearing (ss.8(3)-(6)). Remand of a person in custody Procedure for remand applications A remand warrant is issued by a court or bail justice so that a person may be held in custody until further dealt with at court. The informant must: prepare a Form 1372 or Form 286 in accordance with VPMP Briefs of evidence obtain any other supporting documentation where the remand application involves a child, ensure a parent, guardian or an independent person is present be in a position to provide relevant supporting evidence obtain the services of a bail justice if required prior to court attend any later hearings if bail and/or any conditions are to be opposed (a suitably briefed member may attend in place of the informant). The completed Form 1372 or Form 286 and remand warrant are

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Bail_and_remand_final
text: supporting documentation where the remand application involves a child, ensure a parent, guardian or an independent person is present be in a position to provide relevant supporting evidence obtain the services of a bail justice if required prior to court attend any later hearings if bail and/or any conditions are to be opposed (a suitably briefed member may attend in place of the informant). The completed Form 1372 or Form 286 and remand warrant are to remain at the same location as the detainee. A bail justice who refuses bail can only remand a person to appear before a court on the next working day, or if the next working day is not practicable, within two working days (s.10A(6), Bail Act). All provisions of the remand warrant must be complied with. Remanding children A parent or guardian or an independent person must be present at any application for bail in respect to a child. If a child is remanded on a weekend or public holiday (excluding Christmas Day and New Year’s Day), then the child must be presented before the WORC. Children on remand must be held in either a remand centre or police gaol and may only be remanded to a police gaol in a prescribed region if the remand period is for no more than two working days (Schedule 3, Children Youth and Families Regulations 2017). When a child is on remand at a police gaol, DJCS must be notified and the child must be: given access to DJCS held in particular conditions in police cells, see VPM Management of people in police care or custody. Appeals against the granting of bail or insufficient bail conditions A decision to grant bail may be appealed by the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) within one month of that decision (s.18A, Bail Act). An appeal in relation to the granting of bail may be made where the DPP is satisfied that either the conditions of bail are insufficient or the decision to grant bail contravenes the Bail Act, and it is in the public interest to do so. Where the prosecutor, in consultation with the informant, believes that an appeal is necessary pursuant to s.18A the: prosecutor must immediately discuss the matter with a supervisor to consider whether there exists a reasonable prospect of an appeal being successful prosecutor should seek approval to consider an appeal from the informant’s divisional superintendent prosecutor must notify the Manager, Legal Training and Development Unit - Appeals and Advice Team via ph: (03 8628 3667) or email (LSD-RTU-APPEALS- MGR) who will provide instructions in relation to the materials required Manager, Appeals and Advice Team will assess the materials and determine if an appeal should be recommended for consideration by the DPP. Contravention of a bail conduct condition Offence to contravene conduct condition (s. 49F, Summary Offences Act 1966) A person on bail has committed this offence if they without reasonable excuse, contravene a conduct condition imposed on them. This does not apply to a child or to an imposed condition to attend or participate in bail support services. ‘Conduct condition’ means a condition of bail imposed under s. 5AAA, Bail Act. Members must consider disposition options when deciding whether to charge the person with the offence under s.49F, Summary Offences Act, or issue an infringement notice in accordance with s.60AA, Summary Offences Act (see section 12.2 of this policy). Where the breach of conduct condition is also a contravention of an intervention order, members must lay charges: pursuant to the Family Violence Protection Act 2008 or the Personal Safety Intervention Orders Act 2010 for the breach of the conduct condition. Issuing an infringement notice An infringement notice may only be issued for an offence committed under s.49F, Summary Offences Act in the following limited circumstances: the offence is a minor contravention of a single conduct condition it is the first infringement notice

Commit indictable offence while on bail Section 30B, Bail Act creates an offence when an accused commits an indictable offence while on bail. Rather than laying multiple charges against s. 30B for each indictable offence, only one charge should be laid on occasions where more than one indictable offence is committed during a single incident (e.g. an offender on bail that drives a stolen vehicle and commits various other indictable offences such as reckless conduct endangering life). An offender that is on multiple counts of bail should only receive one charge against s. 30B in relation to indictable offences arising from the one incident. Revocation of bail Application process An informant or the DPP may apply to revoke bail granted to a person to the court which the person is required to appear, or to the Supreme Court if the person is charged with murder or treason. Without limiting the informant’s general power to apply to revoke a grant of bail under s 18AE(1), Bail Act, they may also make an application to revoke bail if they believe on reasonable grounds that the person: has committed an offence since bail was granted is likely to commit an offence whilst on bail has breached a condition of bail or is likely to breach a condition of bail or the bail undertaking. The informant must complete and file an Application for Revocation of Bail [VP Form 1105] at the at the relevant court. Arrest of person released on bail (s. 24, Bail Act) Pursuant to s. 24, Bail Act, if a police officer or PSO member believes on reasonable grounds a person is likely to breach a condition of bail or has suspicion on reasonable grounds the person is breaching or has breached a condition, they may arrest the person. A PSO must hand the person into the custody of a police officer as soon as practicable. If the arrested person is required to appear at court in accordance with their bail undertaking within 24-hours from their arrest, they must be presented to that court in accordance with the bail undertaking. For any other occasion, a police officer must present the person as soon as practicable and within 24-hours before: if it is within ordinary court sitting hours, a court; or if it is outside ordinary court sitting hours, a bail justice. Where the person is brought before a bail justice or the court, the bail justice or court may revoke bail and remand the person or release the person on the same undertaking or a new undertaking with or without conditions. text: Cautions Context Police have discretion in determining what enforcement action may be taken against a person found committing or reasonably suspected of committing an offence. As stated in VPM Disposition: In deciding what enforcement action is to be taken against a person, members must: balance the need to: enforce the law and take appropriate, reasonable and proportionate action (or no action) regarding a person where there is sufficient evidence that they have committed an offence and that recognises their individual circumstances and the circumstances of the offence. choose the least severe action that achieves the purpose of taking that action against the offender. Victoria Police supports the appropriate use of cautions, with the aim of redirecting eligible persons, both adult and child, away from contact with the formal criminal justice system. Police may exercise discretion by issuing a caution to a person as an alternative to laying charges where relevant eligibility criteria are met. This policy provides direction to police when it is appropriate to exercise discretion regarding the use of cautions, considering all relevant factors including the human rights enshrined in the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (the Charter). Victoria Police employees must consider human rights under the Charter, including the desirability of promoting rehabilitation for children and young people (s.25(3)) and the best interests of the child (s.17(2)). Policy at a glance This policy includes: guidance around the different types of cautions, criteria for eligibility and limitations on cautions instructions for issuing and cancelling cautions details regarding drug cautions (excluding cannabis) (referred to throughout the policy as drug diversions), including requirements, notifications and steps if an offender fails to complete diversion considerations for an offender as a prosecution witness. title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Disposition_final
text: Disposition Context At law, members have discretion as to whether enforcement action is taken against persons found committing an offence. However, members also have a duty to enforce the law, keep the peace, protect life and property and prevent offences. Generally, members have broad discretion in relation to what enforcement action (caution, infringement notice, prosecution etc.) is taken against a person found committing or reasonably suspected of committing an offence. The Bail Act 1977 provides direction on the circumstances where police may grant or refuse bail and the factors that must be taken into consideration in that decision-making process. The Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 (CYFA) provides similar direction for children in custody. The purpose of this instruction is to provide members with direction on how to appropriately exercise their discretion in order to ensure: compliance with legal duties and responsibilities an appropriate level of accountability recognition of the human rights of individuals appropriate and effective enforcement action is taken against people who break the law. In deciding what enforcement action is to be taken against a person, members must: balance the need to: enforce the law and take appropriate, reasonable and proportionate action (or no action) regarding a person where: there is sufficient evidence that they have contravened the law and that recognises their individual circumstances and the circumstances of the alleged offence. Members must choose the least severe action that achieves the purpose of taking that action against the person. This policy includes: guidance regarding the enforcement options available to members and the Enforcement Action Framework factors to consider when determining appropriate action to be taken against an accused person guidance regarding informant’s responsibilities. Contents Context 1 Policy at a glance 1 Contents 2 Scope and application 2 Responsibilities and procedures 2 1. Enforcement options 2 2. Enforcement action framework 3 3. Informant’s responsibilities 5 Related documents 5 Further advice and information 6 Update history 6 Scope and application In addition to the requirements of this policy, specific legislative requirements must be complied with where they apply, e.g. family violence, liquor licensing, road safety, transport offences, double jeopardy direct indictments. Where action must be taken against a Victoria Police employee, also comply with VPM Complaints. Responsibilities and procedures Enforcement options Access to a range of enforcement options has been shown to support compliance with the law. It is based on the principle that compliance will be enhanced by dealing with a person in the most effective but least severe way. This framework also supports the accused being dealt with fairly, appropriately and efficiently. The enforcement options available are: no action caution official warning infringement notice charge and summons charge and bail/remand. The eligibility criteria and limitations of

This framework also supports the accused being dealt with fairly, appropriately and efficiently. The enforcement options available are: no action caution official warning infringement notice charge and summons charge and bail/remand. The eligibility criteria and limitations of each option is detailed in the following instructions: VPM Cautions VPM Infringement notices and official warnings VPM Laying charges VPM Bail and remand. These options can also be represented in the form of a pyramid to demonstrate the hierarchy of severity (see the following diagram). The top of the pyramid represents the most severe action available (deprivation of liberty) and the bottom of the pyramid represents the less severe actions. In deciding what action is to be taken against a person, the minimum (least severe) action must be chosen that achieves the purposes of taking that action against the accused. Enforcement action framework Initial considerations Before taking enforcement action against a person: determine whether an offence has been committed verify the identity of the accused ensure there is sufficient admissible evidence where practicable, consult with a supervisor or member approved to authorise prosecutions to review proposed action. Factors to consider when determining appropriate action for an adult accused When determining the appropriate enforcement action, members must consider the overall circumstances of the offending. This includes considering the factors below and the requirements that apply to the specific enforcement action; see VPM Cautions, VPM Infringement notices and official warnings, VPM Laying charges and VPM Bail and remand. Factors to consider when determining appropriate action for a child The minimum age of criminal responsibility is 12 years. Enforcement action must not be taken against a child who is under 12 years of age. Special considerations apply to the type of enforcement action to be taken against children of or above the age of 12 years and under 18 years. Available evidence suggests that the later a young person enters the criminal justice system, the less likely they are to have continued involvement. Therefore, prosecution of a child should always be regarded as a severe step, unless the seriousness of the offence or extenuating factors dictate otherwise. Ordinarily the public interest will not require the prosecution of a child for offences that are not serious and an alternative option is considered more appropriate. For information on issuing cautions to children refer to VPM Cautions. When deciding whether to prosecute a child, members must assess the below factors and consider: the seriousness of the offence the age and apparent

text: a severe step, unless the seriousness of the offence or extenuating factors dictate otherwise. Ordinarily the public interest will not require the prosecution of a child for offences that are not serious and an alternative option is considered more appropriate. For information on issuing cautions to children refer to VPM Cautions. When deciding whether to prosecute a child, members must assess the below factors and consider: the seriousness of the offence the age and apparent maturity (including cognitive, social or emotional development) the mental capacity of the child if the child has a disability or mental illness available alternatives to prosecution, such as a caution or diversion whether a prosecution would be likely to be harmful to the child or be inappropriate, having regard to drivers to offending behaviour and family/environmental factors. any previous decisions by a court or person that suggests the child could be held criminally responsible for any other conduct Prior to charging a child aged 12 or 13 years, members must have regard to whether it appears that there is admissible evidence to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the child knew, at the time of committing the alleged offence, that the conduct was seriously wrong. Where charges must be laid against a child, there is a legislated presumption in favour of proceeding by summons (s.345, CYFA). Police must have regard to this presumption (s.345(2), CYFA) and proceed against a child by summons unless there are reasonable grounds for believing that charge and bail or charge and remand is necessary. Where there are factors contributing to the risk of offending, a referral must be made to a relevant agency. Consulting the local Youth Resource Officer may assist with this process. If the offence took place in a residential care unit, consideration should be given to guidance contained within the Framework to Reduce Criminalisation of Young People in Residential Care, which aims to reduce unnecessary and inappropriate contact of young people in residential care with the criminal justice system. title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Diversion_final
text: Diversion Context Diversion is governed by the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (for adults) and the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 (for children) and allows an accused person to avoid a criminal record if they successfully participate in and complete a court ordered diversion program. A diversion cannot be granted without the consent of both the prosecution and the accused. The purpose of this policy is to provide guidance to employees as to when it is appropriate to exercise discretion regarding recommending diversion, taking into account all relevant considerations including the human rights enshrined in the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006. This policy includes: eligibility criteria for adult and child diversion the process for requesting and consenting to diversion special considerations regarding diversion processes following a decision regarding diversion.
