Child – a person under the age of 18 years but of or above the age of 12 years. Children’s Court Youth Diversion Service - an opportunity for a child appearing before the criminal division of the Children’s Court to complete a diversion plan. Criminal Justice Diversion Program - an opportunity for an accused adult appearing before the criminal division of the Magistrates’ Court to complete a diversion plan. Qualified prosecutor - a prosecutor who has successfully completed the Graduate Certificate in Police Prosecution. Scope and application These instructions apply to police officers and prosecutors. Responsibilities and procedures Objectives of diversion Magistrates’ Court The Criminal Justice Diversion Program for adults is governed by Division 2 of Part 3.3 of the Criminal Procedure Act with the main purposes of: diverting adult accused persons away from the criminal justice system where possible and appropriate reducing the likelihood of reoffending through participation in support services which address the underlying cause of the offending behaviour. Children’s Court The Children’s Court Youth Diversion Service is governed by Division 3A of Part 5.2 of the Children, Youth and Families Act with the purposes of: diverting children away from the criminal justice system where possible and appropriate reducing the risk of stigma caused to children by contact with the criminal justice system encouraging children to

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Diversion_final
text: the likelihood of reoffending through participation in support services which address the underlying cause of the offending behaviour. Children’s Court The Children’s Court Youth Diversion Service is governed by Division 3A of Part 5.2 of the Children, Youth and Families Act with the purposes of: diverting children away from the criminal justice system where possible and appropriate reducing the risk of stigma caused to children by contact with the criminal justice system encouraging children to accept responsibility for unlawful behaviour responding to offending in a manner that acknowledges the child's needs and assists with rehabilitation providing children with opportunities to strengthen and preserve relationships with family and other persons of importance in the child's life providing children with ongoing pathways to connect with education, training, and employment. Pre-charge programs Where the circumstances meet the criteria for pre-charge programs, such as the police cautioning program or drug cautioning program, those programs should be considered as a first option. Refer to VPM Cautions for further information. Eligibility for diversion Before the court can adjourn a proceeding for an accused to complete a diversion program, the following legislative pre-conditions must all be met: the accused acknowledges to the court responsibility for the offence both the prosecution and the accused consent to diversion it appears appropriate to the court, which may inform itself in any way it considers appropriate, that the accused should participate in a diversion program. The following offences make an accused ineligible for diversion: an indictable offence that is not triable summarily (for adult accused only) offences punishable by a minimum or fixed sentence/penalty (including cancellation or suspension of a driver’s licence/permit under the Road Safety Act 1986 or Sentencing Act 1991) any offence against s.49(1) of the Road Safety Act not captured under the above. Recommending, requesting and consenting to diversion Recommending diversion (informants, sub-officer or work unit manager) Informants, sub-officers or work unit managers authorising the brief of evidence may recommend a matter be considered for diversion at the brief authorisation stage. The prosecution and accused must consent to the court adjourning the matter for the accused to complete the diversion program. Prior to authorising a brief of evidence for a child aged 12 or 13 years, members must have regard to whether it appears that there is admissible evidence to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the child knew, at the time of committing the alleged offence, that the conduct was seriously wrong. Refer to VPMP Briefs of evidence for applicable processes and factors that must be considered prior to authorising a brief where the accused is aged 12 or 13 years at the time of the alleged offence. Informants, sub-officers, and work unit managers should apply the relevant

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Diversion_final
text: appears that there is admissible evidence to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the child knew, at the time of committing the alleged offence, that the conduct was seriously wrong. Refer to VPMP Briefs of evidence for applicable processes and factors that must be considered prior to authorising a brief where the accused is aged 12 or 13 years at the time of the alleged offence. Informants, sub-officers, and work unit managers should apply the relevant considerations of suitability at section 4 of this policy when deciding whether to recommend a matter for diversion. See section 4.2 for children and section 4.3 for adults. The decision to recommend or not recommend a matter for diversion must be noted on the Brief Head [VP Form 208A] and should take into account the relevant considerations of suitability. If the matter is not eligible for diversion due to the nature of the charge, there is no requirement to consider the considerations of suitability. See section 5.1 of this policy for the process to be followed when diversion is recommended. Consenting to diversion (prosecutors) The prosecution must consent to the matter being adjourned for the accused to complete a diversion program (s.59(2)(c), Criminal Procedure Act and s.356D(3)(a), Children, Youth and Families Act). Prosecutors must apply the considerations of suitability guidance at section 4 of this policy when considering a matter for diversion. The prosecutor should consider the recommendation of the informant, sub-officer, or work unit manager on the Form 208A. In Children’s Court proceedings, a prosecutor must also consider the matters specified in s.356F, Children, Youth and Families Act when determining whether to consent to an adjournment under s.356D(1) of that Act. The prosecutor should consider the availability of suitable diversion programs in accordance with s.356F(a), Children, Youth and Families Act. Prosecutors cannot prescribe the duration or conditions to be attached to a diversion program; this is for the court to determine. Considerations of suitability Diversion should be considered on a case-by-case basis. Police and prosecutors must use the considerations of suitability guidance tables at sections 4.1 (special considerations), 4.2 (children) and 4.3 (adults) of this policy to substantiate their decision making when deciding whether to recommend or consent to diversion. Special considerations for adults and children Firearm offences For any firearm offence, a diversion or withdrawal of charges must not be offered to the accused or their legal representative without first consulting with an Inspector or above at the Licencing and Regulation Division. Family violence offences For any family violence offence, a diversion and any resulting withdrawal of charges must not be offered to the accused or their legal representative without prior approval from an Officer in Charge (OIC) at the relevant Prosecution Unit.

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Diversion_final
text: any firearm offence, a diversion or withdrawal of charges must not be offered to the accused or their legal representative without first consulting with an Inspector or above at the Licencing and Regulation Division. Family violence offences For any family violence offence, a diversion and any resulting withdrawal of charges must not be offered to the accused or their legal representative without prior approval from an Officer in Charge (OIC) at the relevant Prosecution Unit. After reviewing all relevant information regarding the nature and seriousness of the offending, careful consideration must be given to the accused’s background in relation to family violence, future risk of family violence and any other relevant information. Special consideration must be given where it is alleged that a child has committed adolescent family violence. Children and young people who commit adolescent family violence have often experienced it themselves, therefore, it may be considered a trauma response. Victoria Police employee Where the accused is a Victoria Police employee, in addition to the eligibility for diversion set out in section 2 of this policy, the Assistant Commissioner of Professional Standards Command must also agree to diversion. Sexual offences For any sexual offence, a diversion and any resulting withdrawal of charges must not be offered to the accused or their legal representative without prior approval from the OIC of the Specialist Sexual Offences Prosecution Unit (SSOPU), Legal Services Department. A diversion must be appropriate in the circumstances, taking into account the following considerations: Adult diversion – considerations for suitability This section applies to adult accused aged 18 years or older. For accused persons aged 18 – 24 years, additional consideration should be given to their personal circumstances and prospects of rehabilitation. Procedure for recommending and consenting to diversion Recommending diversion (informants, sub-officer or work unit manager) Where a brief of evidence is recommended to be considered for diversion by an informant, sub-officer or work unit manager, an employee qualified to authorise a brief or criminal charge: ensure the Diversion Notice [Form 948] is completed and where there is a victim, the Victim Contact Details [Form 948B] are also completed ensure all copies of the Form 948B are attached to the police copy of the brief of evidence. For the filing of charges, refer to VPM Laying charges. For information about who is qualified to authorise a brief, refer to VPMP Briefs of evidence. Victim notification The victim must be advised by the informant that a diversion is being recommended and that their details will be given to a court diversion coordinator who may subsequently contact them. The victim’s details must not be given to the

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Diversion_final
text: police copy of the brief of evidence. For the filing of charges, refer to VPM Laying charges. For information about who is qualified to authorise a brief, refer to VPMP Briefs of evidence. Victim notification The victim must be advised by the informant that a diversion is being recommended and that their details will be given to a court diversion coordinator who may subsequently contact them. The victim’s details must not be given to the accused. The victim should be notified that the prosecution will determine whether the matter proceeds to diversion. If diversion was not recommended by the informant, sub-officer or work unit manager, but is being considered by the prosecutor, the prosecutor must facilitate contact with the victim to advise that a diversion is being recommended. Consenting to diversion – prosecutor A qualified prosecutor or a prosecutor of the rank of sergeant or VPS 4 or above can decide whether to consent to a diversion. The court may adjourn the proceedings for a period not exceeding 12 months in the Magistrates’ Court, and not exceeding 4 months in the Children’s Court, to enable the accused to complete the diversion program. When consenting to a diversion, the prosecutor should consider the appropriate duration and make relevant submissions as required. If the prosecutor consents to diversion, they must: ensure Form 948 and 948B are completed and filed with the diversion co-ordinator at the relevant court who will obtain the victim’s views provide the accused or their legal representative a copy of the Form 948, notifying them that diversion has been consented to by the prosecution attach a copy of the endorsed Form 948 to the brief notify the informant of the prosecution’s consent to diversion. Review process Review of diversion - Children’s Court Where the prosecutor has refused to consent to the diversion, the accused or their legal representative may request a review of the decision by the OIC of the applicable Prosecutions Unit for the relevant court. The Prosecutions Unit OIC must notify the accused or their legal representative of the outcome and reasons for the decision in writing. If the accused or their legal representative is not satisfied with the outcome of the initial OIC review, they may submit a further request for review to the relevant Prosecutions Group Inspector via the Prosecutions Unit OIC. The inspector must notify the accused or their legal representative of the outcome and reasons for their decision in writing. Withdrawal of charges Commencement of diversion When prosecutors consent to a diversion, they must withdraw charges if: there is no reasonable prospect of a conviction or a prosecution is not in the public interest. text: review to the relevant Prosecutions Group Inspector via the Prosecutions Unit OIC. The inspector must notify the accused or their legal representative of the outcome and reasons for their decision in writing. Withdrawal of charges Commencement of diversion When prosecutors consent to a diversion, they must withdraw charges if: there is no reasonable prospect of a conviction or a prosecution is not in the public interest. Completion of diversion If an accused adult and/or child completes a diversion program to the satisfaction of the court: prosecutors must withdraw charges that are a lesser alternative to a more serious charge and no plea to the remaining charge/s is to be taken and the court must discharge the accused without any finding of guilt. Forfeiture, restitution and other ancillary orders Prosecution At the time the accused enters a diversion program the prosecutor should make any applications for restitution, compensation or other ancillary orders (where it is appropriate to do so) under the appropriate Act (s.59, Criminal Procedure Act for adults or s.356I, Children, Youth and Families Act for children). A copy of the diversion plan and any orders granted by the court are to be attached to the brief and forwarded to the informant’s work unit. Informant Treat exhibits as detailed in VPM Property and exhibit management. Treat all orders for restitution as detailed in the VPM Confiscation Act. Brief movement pending completion of diversion program Briefs pending the completion of a diversion program listed in the Magistrates’ Court should be treated as finalised and returned by the Prosecutions Unit to the informant’s work unit for retention. If notified the matter has been adjourned to open court, the brief must be returned to the relevant Prosecutions Unit at least seven days prior to the adjourned mention hearing date. Briefs pending the completion of a diversion program listed in the Children’s Court should be retained by the Prosecutions Unit until the diversion program is completed and the matter finalised by the court. After the matter is finalised at court, the brief should be returned to the informant’s work unit for retention. Commission of further offences If the informant becomes aware that the accused has committed further offences while undergoing a diversion program, they must provide details, in writing, to the Diversion Coordinator of the court at the adjourned diversion hearing. title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Infringement_notices_and_official_warnings_final
text: Infringement notices and official warnings Context Members have discretion in determining what enforcement action may be taken against a person found committing or reasonably suspected of committing an offence. Members have extensive powers to protect the community and uphold the law. Members must consider the human rights of all people they interact with, including acting in a way that is compatible with the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (the Charter). Members must ensure their actions and decisions are proportionate, lawful, accountable and necessary to support community trust and confidence in police. Refer to the VPM Human rights standards for further information. As stated in VPM Disposition: In deciding what enforcement action is to be taken against a person, members must: balance the need to: enforce the law to its full extent; and take appropriate action (or no action) in relation to a person who has broken the law that recognises their individual circumstances and the circumstances of the offence. choose the least severe action that achieves the purposes of taking that action against the offender. Where legislation specifies an offence is an infringement offence and therefore subject to an infringement penalty, police may determine that an infringement notice or official warning is the most appropriate enforcement action in the circumstances. Policy at a glance This policy includes: information on infringement notices and official warnings, and the general criteria that should be met for members to issue them list of offences for which a person may be issued an infringement notice or an official warning, along with particular limitations and associated age requirements guidelines for issuing a notice, including completing the relevant forms, serving the notice, finalising after service documentation, and recording of notices instructions on how to withdraw served and unserved notices information on reviewing a decision to issue an infringement notice considerations for issuing infringement notices to children. Scope and application The procedures in this policy do not apply to the Road Policing Enforcement Division (RPED). Policy Police may issue infringement notices for offences listed in the current Infringement Notice Codes and Penalties Guide [Form 508A] (the Code Book). Responsibilities and procedures Infringement notices General criteria A person must be 14 years or over to receive an infringement notice. Specific offences may require the person to be of a greater age to be eligible for an infringement notice; see below at section 2 of this policy. The maximum number of infringement notices that may be issued on one occasion is three. On all occasions where more than one notice is to be issued, they are to be issued by the same member. Infringement notices must only be issued where there is a verified address. If no verified address, then members must consider alternative process. An infringement notice must not be issued: until the member has spoken to the recipient in person, except in the case of parking infringements where a brief is to be submitted for offences arising from the same set of circumstances. If an infringement notice is not served within one month of the offence, members should seek an alternative approach to address the behaviour. Specific criteria for certain road policing offences In relation to careless driving (s.65, Road Safety Act 1986), an infringement notice can only be issued if the following apply: the driver has been interviewed and enquiries made to discount other causes for the offending driving the driver holds a full and current licence where a collision was involved, there are no injuries and the damage is minor. An infringement notice must not be issued in the following road policing circumstances: where the offence arises from a fatal collision for drink driving infringements unless under 0.15% blood alcohol concentration (BAC) and either a first offence or no previous drink driving convictions or findings of guilt in the last 10 years for drug impaired driving offences for ‘accompanying driver’ alcohol and drug impaired in charge of a vehicle offences to a learner driver under the age of 18 years for a loss of licence infringement to an unlicensed driver for a loss (suspension or cancellation) of licence infringement. Victoria Police employees Where the person is a Victoria Police employee no further authority is required to issue an infringement notice. The issuing member must notify Professional Standards Command (PSC), except in the case of parking

The issuing member must notify Professional Standards Command (PSC), except in the case of parking infringements. Diplomatic or consular staff Infringement notices may be issued to diplomatic/consular staff and their families for traffic and other minor offences. Any diplomatic privilege and immunity available will be recorded on their Diplomatic Consular identity card, however these will not extend to driving offences. Offences eligible for an official warning or infringement notice Official warnings For certain offences and in specific circumstances (see section 2.2 of this policy), an official warning may be served in lieu of an infringement notice where the member: believes on reasonable grounds that a person has committed an infringement offence is of the opinion that it is appropriate to serve an official warning believes there is enough admissible evidence to prosecute the matter at court. In addition to the general requirements in section 1.1 of this policy, the following criteria apply to these offences: charging the person would have been justified the person admits the offence and consents to the official warning the victim, if applicable, has been consulted to determine the extent of the offending there are no aggravating circumstances, such as an assault. Legislation with specific conditions The Official Warning [Form 1333] and Infringement Notice – Crime [Form 508G] must be used for the offences listed in this section. Only the RPED may issue an official warning on review of an infringement notice offence in other circumstances. In addition to the age restrictions and notice limits specified in the table above, the following limitations apply when determining whether to issue either type of notice (i.e. an official warning or infringement notice): if the person is intoxicated, the notice must be issued at a later time if the offence was committed in the course of a lawful assembly or other form of legitimate public protest, a notice cannot be issued offensive behaviour or language – if the offensive behaviour or language is directed at a member of Victoria Police, the

Issuing the notice Completing the notice Members must use the Infringement Notice [Form 508], except where the Code Book specifies that Form 508G and/or Form 1333 must be used. All infringement notices should be marked with a specified due date for payment set at 28 days from the date of issue. That is, on the same day of the week 4 weeks from the day of issue. A ready reckoner is available on the VP Forms intranet site to assist in calculating the specified due date. Service of notices Members should serve infringement notices within one month of the date of the offence to ensure timelines in the legislation can be met. An infringement notice may be served: personally on the offender by posting in the case of a parking offence, by attaching the notice to the windscreen of the motor vehicle. A notice returned undelivered is deemed to be served where a verified address has been used. If a notice cannot be served, the notice should be cancelled and the matter should be dealt with by an alternative process. Drink and drug driving infringements When an infringement notice is issued, the driver must also be served with the breath certificate. In blood test cases, follow the guidelines issued by Road Policing Drug and Alcohol Section (RPDAS). Informants must ensure that the duplicate certificate and any notes relating to the offence are retained at station level, in case a notice of objection is lodged. If advice of an objection is not received from Fines Victoria (FV) within three months, the duplicate certificate and notes should be filed as a completed brief. Also see the VPM Road policing - enforcement. After service Immediately after service of the duplicate, complete the description of the infringement on the original and triplicate copies and submit the original to a supervisor at the end of the shift. On receipt of the completed original notice, the Work Unit Manager or checking supervisor must check its content and: if satisfied that the notice is valid – include initials and registered

After service Immediately after service of the duplicate, complete the description of the infringement on the original and triplicate copies and submit the original to a supervisor at the end of the shift. On receipt of the completed original notice, the Work Unit Manager or checking supervisor must check its content and: if satisfied that the notice is valid – include initials and registered number in the ‘checked box’ if not satisfied as to the validity of the notice - serve a withdrawal notice and issue a new notice. Recording of notices A copy of the notice is retained in the Infringement Notice or Official Warning book. No other register for recording infringement notices or official warnings is required. LEAP forms have been incorporated into the following notice books and are to be faxed to the Central Data Entry Bureau (CDEB): Form 508G Form 1333. Withdrawal of an unserved notice Where a mistake has been made, the infringement notice should be cancelled prior to service: write “Cancelled” across all copies of the notice complete a Request for Cancellation of Infringement or Official Warning Notice [Form 508E] and have both copies signed by a sub-Officer attach a copy of the completed Form 508E to the notice book forward a copy of the completed Form 508E to FV with all copies of the infringement notice. FV does not record official warnings fax a copy of the completed Form 508E to CDEB (if required). Withdrawal of a served notice When an infringement notice that has been served is to be withdrawn: write “Cancelled” across all available copies of the notice complete an Infringement Notice or Official Warning Withdrawal Notice [Form 508C] and Form 508E and have both copies signed by a sub-Officer serve the appropriate copy of Form 508C on the original recipient, together with the reissued notice (if applicable) attach a copy of the completed Form 508E to the notice book forward a copy of the completed Form 508E to FV with all available copies of the infringement notice (the cancelled notice and reissued notice) fax a copy of the completed Form 508E to CDEB (if required). Internal review Criteria An individual served with an infringement notice may apply to the RPED for a review of the decision to serve the notice if they believe that: the decision was contrary to the law or involved a mistake of identity special circumstances (as defined in the Infringements Act) apply to them the relevant conduct should be excused having regard to exceptional circumstances relating to the infringement notice. Infringements issued under the following provisions are ineligible to be the subject of an internal review: ss. 89A-89D, Road Safety Act 1986 ss.61A and 61BA, Marine (Drug, Alcohol and Pollution Control) Act 1988. Application An application for review may be made at any time before: the infringement penalty is registered with the Director, FV for an infringement offence if the infringement notice was served on a child, at any time before the infringement penalty is registered with the Children’s Court for a non-registrable offence, the expiry of the period for bringing a proceeding in relation to the offence to which the infringement notice relates. An application for review is to: be made in writing state the grounds on which the decision should be reviewed provide the applicant’s current address for service of the outcome of the review only be made once in relation to any given infringement offence. Action Where there are grounds to do so, the RPED may do any of the following: seek an explanation or advice from the informant or their supervisor require the informant to issue another notice and forward it to the offender together with a prepared letter explaining the reason for the second notice instruct the informant to submit a brief issue an official warning withdraw the notice direct that no further action be taken. Outcome After reviewing a decision to issue an infringement notice the RPED may: confirm the decision to issue the notice withdraw the notice withdraw the notice and issue an official warning withdraw the notice and refer the matter to court waive all or any prescribed costs. RPED will make a determination on an internal review within 90 days and notify the applicant in writing within 14 days of the decision being finalised. Unpaid infringement notices In general, unpaid infringement notices are dealt with through FV or the Children and Young Persons Infringement Notice System (CAYPINS). Both are automated systems; see section 6 of this policy for further information on CAYPINS. The system recognises an individual as eligible to proceed through CAYPINS only where the individual’s date of birth is recorded. Where a date of birth is not recorded the unpaid infringement notice will proceed through FV. Where the notice is contested and the issuing member wishes to pursue the matter, Victoria Police retains responsibility for processing the brief and

Infringement notices issued against children Legislation Section 581 and Schedule 3, Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 regulates the CAYPINS procedure. Infringement notices should be issued to children in accordance with the process detailed in s.581 and Schedule 3, Children, Youth and Families Act. Members should personally serve the notice and explain what it means in a way the child will understand. Review of Registrar’s determination Under CAYPINS, the child may elect to be dealt with by the Children’s Court Registrar, who may order a range of outcomes – see Schedule 3, Children, Youth and Families Act. Where the Registrar orders that payment of the fine should not be enforced, based on the information to be supplied by the child under Schedule 3 Children, Youth and Families Act, the issuing member will be supplied with a copy of the order and the child’s information. If a member believes that the Registrar’s decision should be reviewed by the Children’s Court, they should notify the Court in writing within 14 days of the date of the order. A review of the Registrar’s decision should only be sought where there are reasonable grounds for doing so, for example, where the issuing member is aware, or believes that, the evidence supplied to the Registrar, by the child, is inaccurate. The Registrar notifies the child and issuing member of the time and place of the hearing. Summary Offences Act 1966 – infringement notices Disorderly conduct Section 17A, Summary Offences Act provides that any person who behaves in a disorderly manner in a public place is guilty of an offence. An infringement notice can be issued for this offence. The types of behaviour that may amount to disorderly conduct are not detailed in the Act. However, the term “disorderly” conduct is already subject of case law. For example, in Meiser v Police [1967] NZLR 437 (CA) the court said “it is conduct which, while sufficiently ill-mannered, or in bad taste, to meet with the disapproval of well conducted and reasonable men and women, is also something more – it must, in my opinion, tend to annoy or insult such persons as are faced with it - and sufficiently deeply or seriously to warrant the interference of

text: already subject of case law. For example, in Meiser v Police [1967] NZLR 437 (CA) the court said “it is conduct which, while sufficiently ill-mannered, or in bad taste, to meet with the disapproval of well conducted and reasonable men and women, is also something more – it must, in my opinion, tend to annoy or insult such persons as are faced with it - and sufficiently deeply or seriously to warrant the interference of the criminal law”. Move on power Section 6, Summary Offences Act provides members with a power to direct people to move on from a certain area where there is a fear there will be a breach of the peace. A person who ignores a move on direction may be given an infringement notice for contravening the direction. For further information refer VPM Arrests and warrants to arrest and VPM Breach of the peace and move on powers. Process for issuing infringement notices In relation to the above infringements, only the Form 508G may be used to issue notices. The codes for the infringements in the Code Book under ‘Crime – Extra’ are: Disorderly conduct (s.17A, Summary Offences Act) – 9104 Contravention of a direction to move on (s.6(4), Summary Offences Act) – 9101. Additional requirements for children Where an infringement notice for any of the above offences is issued to a child (aged between 14 years and under 18 years), a parent or guardian must be informed in writing of this fact Notice to Parent - Advice Regarding Your Child Receiving an Infringement Notice [Form 508H]. This action must be recorded on the notes section of the infringement notice if delivered in person. If sent by mail, this correspondence is to be recorded in the correspondence register. A supervisor is to ensure that Form 508H is submitted with the infringement notice by the issuing member prior to entering their supervisor number on the infringement notice. Work unit managers must ensure that the Form 508H is forwarded (by mail or by hand) to their nominated last known address. title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Laying_charges_final
text: Laying charges Context Police have discretion in determining what enforcement action may be taken against a person found committing or reasonably suspected of committing an offence. As stated in VPM Disposition: In deciding what enforcement action is to be taken against a person, members must: balance the need to: enforce the law and take appropriate, reasonable and proportionate action (or no action) regarding a person where: there is sufficient evidence that they have contravened the law and that recognises their individual circumstances and the circumstances of the offence. Members must choose the least severe action that achieves the purpose of taking that action against the person. Where it is determined that laying charges is the appropriate way of dealing with the person accused of an offence, police must then assess the most appropriate action from the following options: charge by way of summons consider recommending a court diversion charge and bail charge and remand. This policy provides direction on issuing charges by summons and the process for recommending court diversions; refer to VPM Bail and remand for instruction for the alternative methods for laying charges. This policy includes: guidance and requirements for laying charges the process for charge and summons, including issuing, recording and reporting, brief preparation, service and notification of offences the process for bringing an accused to court. Responsibilities and procedures Requirements for laying charges General A person may be charged with an offence where there is sufficient admissible evidence to cover all points of proof relevant to each charge and there is a reasonable prospect of a conviction being secured. Depending on the circumstances, charges may be issued by way of: charge and summons charge and bail/remand (see VPM Bail and remand) A court diversion may also be considered in appropriate circumstances (see section 3). The laying and filing of charges must comply with Part 2, Criminal Procedure Act 2009 or Part 5.1A, Children Youth and Families Act 2005 (CYFA), including the relevant time limits. Informants should consult the OPP– Historical Sex Offences Ready Reckoner when laying historical sex offence charges or seek prosecution advice early, when required, to ensure charges are laid as soon as practicable. Have regard to s.464K(2), Crimes Act 1958 which requires fingerprints to be destroyed within six months if charge or summons has not been issued. Refer to VPM Fingerprinting for further obligations when taking fingerprints. Also refer to VPM DNA Profile samples where applicable. For multiple charges founded on the same facts or that form a series of offences of the same or similar character use the Continuation of Charges [Form 404]. Ensure the person served with a charge is also given the information sheets: ‘Going to the Magistrates’ Court’ or ‘Going to the Children’s Court’ as appropriate. Nominate the informant’s details for service of documents, include business address fax number email address (as per local arrangements). For speeding and drink driving charges include the alleged speed, see VPM Road policing - enforcement. Children The minimum age of criminal responsibility is 12 years. A child who is under 12 must not be charged. If the accused is a child, and VPM Cautions does not apply, there is a presumption in favour of proceeding by summons (s.345, CYFA). Police must have regard to this presumption (s.345(2), CYFA) and proceed against a child by summons, unless there are reasonable grounds for believing that charge and bail or charge and remand is necessary; see VPM Disposition and VPM Bail and remand for factors that must be considered. Please refer to the ‘Guide to Processing Young People’ suite of materials accessible via the Youth Law Group intranet page, for further information. Prior to charging a child aged 12 or 13 years, members must have regard to whether it appears that there is admissible evidence to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the child knew, at the time of committing the alleged offence, that the conduct was seriously wrong (doli incapax). Refer to VPMP Briefs of evidence for applicable processes and factors that must be considered prior to authorising a brief where the accused is aged 12 or 13 years at the time of the alleged offence. However, a charge and summons must be issued within two months of interview unless not practicable. text: Charge and Summons General requirements A proceeding for an offence must be commenced not later than the time provided by the appropriate legislation. However, a charge and summons must be issued within two months of interview unless not practicable. A charge sheet and summons directs the accused to attend the mention court nearest to either: the place where the offence is alleged to have been committed the place of residence of the accused Court dates should be allocated according to local instructions. A charge sheet and summons can be issued by a registrar or a police member. Only the informant may issue a summons to answer a charge. A summons may not be issued on behalf of another member. Ensure that the accused contact details included on the summons are current. Where it is not appropriate to issue a summons and it is necessary to proceed by charge and remand or bail, refer to VPM Bail and remand for the applicable processes. Initial action when issuing a summons Where a member will proceed by way of summons for a matter involving at least one criminal charge, they are to: interview the accused in accordance with VPM Interviews and statements determine that the summons will be issued after the accused has been released from custody and obtain approval from a sub-officer or member approved to authorise prosecutions complete Intent to Summons [Form L14A] and other appropriate LEAP forms, ensuring that: the Form L14A lists the sub-incidents for which the suspect is interviewed, not the charges that could be laid the Printer ID at which the Intent to Summons Report [Form LAZ02A] will be printed is accurate. submit the brief head [Form 208A] with contemporaneous notes attached to their supervisor (as required by VPMP Briefs of evidence) and fax completed LEAP forms to CDEB by the end of that shift. Procedure for recording the matter on LEAP The Form L14A provides a means of creating a record on LEAP that connects a person who has been interviewed for a criminal offence with a sub-incident. This information is then used to create the Form LAZ02A which is required by the supervisor when authorising the brief of evidence. This initial record also provides early information which may have important intelligence value. Also refer to VPM Sexual offence investigations. Where a summons is issued by a court, the above does not apply except for submitting Form 1320 or 1321 if relevant offences apply. Service of summons The informant is responsible for ensuring service of the summons on the accused within a reasonable period and within legislative timeframes (where applicable). Service and filing of charge sheets and summons must comply with Part 2, Criminal Procedure Act. After service, file the execution copy of Form 402 and Form LFR02A at the court to enable the matter to be listed. Where a summons is unable to be served, the informant should consider proceeding by Charge Sheet and Warrant to Arrest [Form 403]; see VPM Arrests and warrants to arrest. Notification of offences Informants may consider it in the public interest to notify the employer or regulatory authority of a person coming under their notice. VPM Notification of offences provides guidance on the circumstances and requirements for members who may need to make such notifications. Charge and recommendation for post-charge court diversion Where the circumstances meet the criteria for pre-charge programs, such as police cautioning or drug diversion program, those programs should be used before a recommendation for diversion is considered. If pre-charge enforcement action is considered to be clearly inappropriate, then consideration should be given to a recommendation for diversion, particularly where the accused is a child. Refer to VPM Diversion for further information, including eligibility criteria, suitability guidance and procedures for recommending diversion. Notice to appear Notice to appear (NTA) is a process for bringing the accused to court. Section 21 of the CPA provides that an NTA may

text: recommendation for diversion is considered. If pre-charge enforcement action is considered to be clearly inappropriate, then consideration should be given to a recommendation for diversion, particularly where the accused is a child. Refer to VPM Diversion for further information, including eligibility criteria, suitability guidance and procedures for recommending diversion. Notice to appear Notice to appear (NTA) is a process for bringing the accused to court. Section 21 of the CPA provides that an NTA may be used when a member reasonably suspects that an adult has committed: a summary offence; or an indictable offence that may be heard and determined summarily (IOTS). Service of an NTA must be in person (s.21(3)), using the Notice to Appear Booklet [Form 406]. The mention date must be at least 49 days after the service date of the notice. Due to the prescribed timeframe for listing the mention hearing and serving the documents, when considering whether an NTA is appropriate, members must have regard to: the complexity of the investigation the likely date of charge authorisation leave commitments likely delays in obtaining statements/exhibits where it is inappropriate to issue an NTA, members must proceed by summons or alternative process. When an NTA is served by a member, a Brief Head [Form 208A] and a copy of the member’s contemporaneous notes must be submitted to their supervisor by the end of the shift. If the NTA is related to at least one criminal offence, all relevant crime reports must be submitted as normal, including the Form L14A. The Form L14A must be faxed to CDEB by the end of the shift. Completing the Form L14A will produce an NTA Report, which must be attached to the brief (refer to section 2, above, for specific instructions relating to the Form L14A). Once the NTA has been served, the member must prepare a preliminary brief (see VPMG Brief preparation and management for the procedure for instructions relating to preliminary briefs). Once the preliminary brief has been authorised, the charge must then be filed at the appropriate court within 14 days of serving the notice (s.22). Where the charge is not filed at court within 14 days, the NTA lapses (s.22). Where this occurs, the member must within seven days of the notice lapsing: give written notice, using Notification of Lapse of Notice to Appear [Form 407], to the person on whom the NTA was served (s.23) file the Court Copy of the NTA together with Form 407 at the court prior to the first mention fax the endorsed NTA Report to CDEB. Failing to notify the person on whom the NTA was served that the NTA has lapsed (as described above) may result in costs being awarded

text: Notification of offences Context When a person is suspected of or charged with an offence, police members must consider whether it is necessary to notify a person’s employer or relevant regulatory authority to prevent or lessen a serious threat to public safety, public health or public welfare. For similar reasons the Department of Families, Fairness and Housing (DFFH) may be notified where unlawful activity in or around public housing is suspected or known. In both circumstances, there is a need to balance the privacy of individuals with the public interest. This policy outlines these considerations and the processes for approving and making notifications. This policy supports compliance with the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (PDPA). Policy at a glance This policy includes: considerations for the release of personal information procedures for notifying employers, regulatory authorities, and government agencies that a person has been charged, or is the subject of a criminal investigation mandatory notification obligations that apply regarding registered teachers and medical professionals the procedure for making a notification. Contents Context 1 Policy at a glance 1 Contents 1 Definitions 1 Scope and application 2 Responsibilities and procedures 2 1. General considerations 2 2. Notification procedures 4 3. Procedures for persons in specific professions 5 4. Notifying Homes Victoria (Department of Families, Fairness and Housing) 7 Related documents 9 Further advice and information 9 Update history 9 Definitions Charged includes when a person is charged and bailed, charged and remanded or charges are listed with a court and a summons issued. Not charged refers to a person who is under investigation but has not been charged. Regulatory authority includes government departments, industry regulators, sport governing bodies and workplace and training regulators. Scope and application This policy applies to all employees. Responsibilities and procedures General considerations In certain circumstances, investigating members must notify employers, government agencies or regulatory authorities of a person coming under their notice. Where notification is not mandated, members must assess whether it is appropriate to notify the employer or regulatory authority, taking into consideration the legislative authority and privacy principles outlined in sections 1.1 and 1.2 of this policy. Legislative authority In accordance with Information Privacy Principle 2.1(a), (d), (e) and (f), Schedule 1 of the PDPA, Victoria Police may only disclose personal information if it: reasonably believes that the disclosure is necessary to lessen or prevent either: a serious threat to an individual’s life, health, safety or welfare a serious threat to public health, public safety, or public welfare or suspects that unlawful activity has been, is being or may be engaged in, and discloses personal information as a necessary part of its investigation or in reporting its concerns to relevant persons or authorities or

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Notification_of_offences_final
text: disclose personal information if it: reasonably believes that the disclosure is necessary to lessen or prevent either: a serious threat to an individual’s life, health, safety or welfare a serious threat to public health, public safety, or public welfare or suspects that unlawful activity has been, is being or may be engaged in, and discloses personal information as a necessary part of its investigation or in reporting its concerns to relevant persons or authorities or is required or authorised by or under law or discloses the information for a related secondary purpose and the person who is the subject of the notification would reasonably expect Victoria Police to disclose the information for that purpose. In these circumstances, the secondary purpose must be related to the primary purpose for which the information was collected. For example, to alert a regulator of criminal offending so that they can prevent the commission of further offences by suspending a person’s registration to work in a particular field. Privacy considerations Due to the personal impact that a notification may have on a person, care should be taken to ensure that the notification is: supported by legislation in the public interest based on details that are factual not to be used as a form of penalty confirmed in writing. In reference to Information Privacy Principle 2.1(a), (d), (e) or (f) of Schedule 1 of the PDPA, additional considerations for notification include the: nature and seriousness of the charge; the mere fact that the person has been charged is not enough to justify notification duties performed by the person nature of the charge as it relates to the business of the employer or regulatory authority relationship of the person and the victim to the employer or regulatory authority potential of exposing the public to further offending if the person returns to their role ability of any recipient regulator to act on or use the information to lessen or prevent any relevant threat potential for the notification to harm the interests of the person. Only in exceptional circumstances, members should consider notifying a person’s employer or regulatory authority where they have not been charged. Where a person’s employer or regulatory authority has been notified, the investigating member must also notify the employer/regulatory authority of the outcome when the investigation or matter is finalised. See Privacy Information Sharing Guide for assistance in providing information to external agencies. Making and recording the notification The member making the notification must inform the recipient of their responsibilities regarding security of the information. This includes advising and maintaining the privacy of the individual and confidentiality of information. Work unit managers are to maintain a record of all notifications considered for release on their

text: of the outcome when the investigation or matter is finalised. See Privacy Information Sharing Guide for assistance in providing information to external agencies. Making and recording the notification The member making the notification must inform the recipient of their responsibilities regarding security of the information. This includes advising and maintaining the privacy of the individual and confidentiality of information. Work unit managers are to maintain a record of all notifications considered for release on their correspondence register. For audit purposes, the correspondence register should capture sufficient information that identifies the: details of the organisation to which the notification was made details of who authorised the release of the relevant data/information time, date, and format in which the notification was made. Continuous police record checks The continuous checking service identifies people who are the subject of relevant police involvements such as active or ongoing investigations, pending charges and court results and notifies their respective accrediting agency. The Police Information Liaison Office (PILO) of the Police Enquiry and Data Sharing Department undertakes both legislative and consensual continuous police record checking for a number of government agencies. The agencies include: Working with Children Check Victoria Victorian Institute of Teaching National Disability Insurance Scheme Victorian Gambling and Casino Control Commission Safe Transport Victoria. Provision of this information to these agencies may prompt requests to investigating members for further information. Informants can contact the Privacy Unit, Security, Information and Privacy Division, Digital Services and Security Department (DSSD) for guidance if required. Notification procedures Investigating member responsibilities Investigating members must make relevant inquiries about the employment duties of the person charged/under investigation in order to assess whether the charge/investigation brings into question their ability or capacity to properly perform the role in their employment or under a regulatory authority. Members should consider their responsibility to prevent offences in this assessment. To assess whether a notification is appropriate, the investigating member should refer to the privacy considerations outlined in section 1.2 of this policy. Procedures for when the person is charged The work unit manager is required to authorise the notification regarding a person who is charged. The work unit manager is responsible for assessing whether a notification is appropriate under section 1.1 of this policy, and must refer to the privacy considerations outlined in section 1.2 of this policy. Unless there is a likelihood that notification would interfere with the effective conduct of a pending prosecution, the investigating member should advise the person being charged that their employer and/or regulatory authority will be notified before making the notification. Where necessary, the investigating member should make enquiries with the employer or regulatory authority to ascertain the appropriate person to be notified, (e.g. Manager, Human Resources). Members must

Unless there is a likelihood that notification would interfere with the effective conduct of a pending prosecution, the investigating member should advise the person being charged that their employer and/or regulatory authority will be notified before making the notification. Where necessary, the investigating member should make enquiries with the employer or regulatory authority to ascertain the appropriate person to be notified, (e.g. Manager, Human Resources). Members must ensure that the privacy of the charged person is protected to the extent reasonably practicable when conducting these enquiries. The investigating member or in their absence, their supervisor, must notify the appropriate person in writing (i.e. email) of the circumstances, marked ‘Sensitive: Personal’. See section 3 of this policy regarding specific occupations – medical and health practitioners, teachers, DFFH employees. Procedures for when the person is not charged A member at the rank of inspector or above is required to authorise the notification regarding a person who is not charged. The authorising member is responsible for assessing whether a notification is appropriate under section 1.1 of this policy and must refer to the privacy considerations outlined in section 1.2 of this policy. Any decision to notify requires careful: balancing between a serious breach of personal privacy against the likelihood of significant risk to the public interest/welfare consideration of the possibility that civil action may be taken against all persons involved in the disclosure and Victoria Police. Sex Offenders For information concerning the disclosure of a person’s sex offender status, refer to VPM Registered Sex Offender management. Members should also consult the Sex Offenders Registry. Reportable Conduct Scheme and Child Safe Standards Members should notify the Commission for Children and Young People of matters that come under the Reportable Conduct Scheme or Child Safe Standards. For guidance, refer to VPM Reportable Conduct Scheme and Child Safe Standards. Procedures for persons in specific professions Medical and health practitioners Where the person is charged, the investigating member must notify the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) in line with section 2.2 of this policy. Where there are concerns about the person’s suitability to practice, the investigating member must notify AHPRA in writing. Registered teachers Victorian Institute of Teaching The Victorian Institute of Teaching (VIT) is the independent statutory authority for the teaching profession. All teachers working in Victorian schools (including public, independent and Catholic schools) and early childhood services must be registered with the VIT in order to practice. Registered teachers are listed publicly on the VIT Register of Teachers, which is published on the VIT website. A person listed on the register is registered and permitted to teach, unless their registration status shows otherwise. The register may

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Notification_of_offences_final
text: (VIT) is the independent statutory authority for the teaching profession. All teachers working in Victorian schools (including public, independent and Catholic schools) and early childhood services must be registered with the VIT in order to practice. Registered teachers are listed publicly on the VIT Register of Teachers, which is published on the VIT website. A person listed on the register is registered and permitted to teach, unless their registration status shows otherwise. The register may provide police with additional information for their investigation. The Professional Conduct Unit, VIT can also be contacted for further advice and support. When a teacher is charged The investigating member must immediately notify the VIT if a registered teacher has been charged with, found guilty of, or committed for trial for a sexual, violent or drug offence. This notification triggers a preliminary assessment by the VIT to determine whether to conduct an investigation; see s. 2.6.31 (4), Education and Training Reform Act 2006 for further details. Notification may be by e-mail or phone; phone notifications must be confirmed in writing. Notifications must include the following information: a brief summary of the alleged conduct of the teacher details of the educational setting the teacher is/was employed in whether the teacher’s employer is aware of the conviction, including whether the employer has taken any action against the teacher whether the teacher is still registered. If a student is involved in the offending, notifications must also include: when and in what circumstances the student was taught by the teacher (include details regarding the setting (e.g., classroom, religious instructions, coaching) the age and gender of the student. Liaison during criminal investigation To avoid compromising any criminal investigation, the VIT will advise Victoria Police of the progress of their disciplinary investigation. The investigating member should also notify the VIT of developments in any ongoing criminal investigation so that the VIT may adjust or cease their disciplinary investigation. Improper conduct of a teacher – not charged Victoria Police may refer allegations of improper conduct between teachers and/or children/students that have not resulted in any criminal charges, convictions and/or findings of guilt against them to the VIT. Improper conduct is conduct that may impact their fitness to teach, as defined in the Education and Training Reform Act. Members need to consider the implications for the teacher, as well as protective concerns for the children/students. Refer to sections 1 and 2.3 of this policy for guidance. Teachers who were registered at the time of the offence, but are no longer registered, can also be referred to the VIT (i.e. historical offences). DFFH staff or any outside organisation engaged to conduct an internal review are not ‘investigating officials’ under s.464, Crimes Act 1958 and as such are not immediately authorised to conduct a criminal investigation. Their role is to facilitate an internal administrative inquiry relating to employment. They are expected to notify the Station Commander before commencing any internal departmental process. Where Victoria Police is aware of an internal review, the investigating member should notify DFFH of emerging developments in any ongoing criminal investigation so that DFFH may adjust their internal inquiry accordingly, or cease if necessary. The Station Commander is responsible for liaison with the DFFH contact during any further investigation or hearing phase. For guidance on information exchange, see VPMP Information sharing or contact the Local Area Commander for advice. The Privacy Unit, Security, Information and Privacy Division, DSSD may also refer DFFH to the appropriate regional contact. Victoria Police or other Victoria Police personnel Refer to VPMG Offences by or service of process on employees. Notifying Homes Victoria (Department of Families, Fairness and Housing) Purpose of making a notification Members can notify Homes Victoria when there is reason to suspect that illegal activity has occurred in a Homes Victoria owned or managed premises or on a common area of a DFFH housing estate. The notification of subject information is made with the aim of preventing or lessening the serious threat to public safety, public health or public welfare. Subject information ‘Subject information’ is information linking the alleged illegal activity to Homes Victoria premises or common area within a public housing property and may include: name of the tenant and any other persons present address of the premises the tenant’s role in the household (e.g., mother of alleged offender, son of alleged offender) name and address of any other Homes Victoria tenant present when a search warrant has been executed (only in circumstances where Victoria Police has evidence to indicate that the tenant has knowledge or is aware of the alleged illegal activity) charges laid summary of alleged offences committed which

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Notification_of_offences_final
text: of the tenant and any other persons present address of the premises the tenant’s role in the household (e.g., mother of alleged offender, son of alleged offender) name and address of any other Homes Victoria tenant present when a search warrant has been executed (only in circumstances where Victoria Police has evidence to indicate that the tenant has knowledge or is aware of the alleged illegal activity) charges laid summary of alleged offences committed which should include the location of the tenant inside the premises when a search warrant has been executed (e.g. tenant located in bathroom, tenant located in kitchen) a brief summary of the relevant evidence linking the alleged illegal activity to the premises, which should include location of where the alleged illegal activity is situated within the premises (e.g., traffickable quantity of drugs found in kitchen, selling a traffickable amount of drugs on a common area of an estate, selling/dealing stolen goods from inside the premises) investigating member’s details. Where a tenant has not used the rented premises themselves for the alleged illegal activity, subject information may include information which shows the tenant: had knowledge or should have known the offending was occurring and had the power to prevent the offending. Legislative authority The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 allows Homes Victoria to give a public housing tenant notice to vacate if the tenant has, within a private or common area of a public housing property: engaged in specific drug-related conduct (s.91ZR, Residential Tenancies Act) as outlined in section 4.5 of this policy committed prescribed indictable offences, for which the person has been convicted or found guilty (s.91ZS, Residential Tenancies Act). In line with Information Privacy Principle 2.1(e) Schedule 1 of the PDPA, members may notify Homes Victoria, when they become aware of a tenant that has engaged in or permitted the use of a DFFH premises for an offence, including specific drug-related conduct, as outlined in section 4.4 of this policy. Members may also make a notification of subject information under Information Privacy Principle 2.1(d) Schedule 1 of the PDPA when there is enough evidence demonstrating that there is a serious threat to public health, public safety or public welfare because: a tenant or another person present has been charged or convicted with an offence that has occurred inside a DFFH premises or where the premises has been used for the commission of the offence a tenant has knowledge or has allowed a DFFH premises to be used for an offence. Drug-related conduct in public housing Members may also make a notification of subject information when a warrant under the Drug, Poisons and Controlled Substance Act 1981 has been executed on a DFFH premises or DFFH housing

title: Disposition_of_offenders_VPM_Notification_of_offences_final
text: with an offence that has occurred inside a DFFH premises or where the premises has been used for the commission of the offence a tenant has knowledge or has allowed a DFFH premises to be used for an offence. Drug-related conduct in public housing Members may also make a notification of subject information when a warrant under the Drug, Poisons and Controlled Substance Act 1981 has been executed on a DFFH premises or DFFH housing estate common area, which has resulted in charges laid or a conviction for the following offences: trafficked or attempted to traffic a drug of dependence supplied a drug of dependence to a person under 18 possessed a preparatory item with the intention of using the item for the purpose of trafficking a drug of dependence possessed without lawful excuse, a tablet press or precursor chemical, or cultivated or attempted to cultivate a narcotic plant on the rented premises or in a common area (see s.91ZR, Residential Tenancies Act). Approval and making a notification Complete Notification of Illegal Activity [Form 1423] and forward to the work unit manager for approval. If the notification of subject information is approved the work unit manager is to forward the completed Form 1423 to the appropriate Homes Victoria Regional Manager in one communication by mail. The summary of charges form and/or LEAP reports are not to be included. The investigating member may be contacted by DFFH to have further discussions about the subject information already provided. New subject information or documentation (e.g., briefs, summary of charges forms) can only be provided to DHHS by way of a subpoena. Refer to VPM Court processes for further information on requirements relating to subpoena requests. Members may be subject to a subpoena to provide evidence in a Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal hearing. Notification should occur when a charge has been laid, however if this did not occur, a notification may also be made when a conviction has been recorded. Recording the notification Work unit managers are to maintain a record on their correspondence register of all notifications as detailed in section 1.3 of this policy. For further information refer to VPMP Information sharing. text: Donations and sponsorships Context The effective and efficient use of donation and sponsorship arrangements provides opportunities to communicate the work Victoria Police does, engage with relevant audiences within the community and enhance Victoria Police’s image. While effective arrangements can bring many benefits, poorly managed arrangements can have negative consequences on the work and reputation of Victoria Police. This policy is underpinned by the following overarching principles: ensuring probity achieving efficiency and effectiveness maintaining accountability implementing effective risk management. To meet these requirements, it is necessary to give careful thought to the individuals and organisations Victoria Police makes arrangements with, to ensure that there is no actual, potential or perceived conflict of interest with VPM Professional and ethical standards or the organisation’s regulatory responsibilities. This policy provides guidance for employees assessing whether a donation or sponsorship is appropriate and to ensure that a clear audit trail is maintained. Policy at a glance This policy includes: criteria for meeting an appropriate donation or sponsorship activity information on substantial sponsorship arrangements considerations for employees when assessing applications for donations or sponsorships exclusions from accepting or providing donations and sponsorships approvals, authorisations and documentation requirements for managing donations and sponsorships. Evaluation of sponsorships 8 Related documents 9 Further advice and information 9 Update history 9 Definitions Approver is the Victoria Police employee responsible for approving and providing oversight over the proposed arrangement and/or agreement who holds the relevant financial delegation. Donation is the voluntary provision of money, goods and/or services where the donor does not seek or expect to receive a commercial benefit. This includes both incoming and outgoing donations. Where a reciprocal benefit is sought or offered, it is a sponsorship. Requesting employee is the Victoria Police employee responsible for seeking and managing the proposed arrangement and/or agreement. Sponsorship is the purchase of rights or benefits, including naming rights, delivered through association with the sponsored organisation’s name, products, services or activities. The rights or benefits typically relate to the sponsor's reputation, brand, management or communication objectives. The sponsor provides money, goods and/or services in return for certain specified benefits, such as logo placement, public acknowledgement, etc. This includes both incoming and outgoing sponsorships. Considering donation and sponsorship arrangements 2.1 Appropriate activity assessment All potential or proposed donations and sponsorship arrangements must comply with the Victorian Government Sponsorship Policy and the below standards for an appropriate activity. An appropriate activity: aligns with Victoria Police strategies and objectives satisfies a substantiated business need is not a delivery or replacement of core services does not conflict with Victorian Government or Victoria Police policy would not be reasonably seen to compromise the public interest or affect Victoria Police’s ability to perform its duties impartially. If a proposal is assessed as meeting the appropriate activity criteria, employees must ensure that the proposal is not excluded under section 2.2 of this policy and that it meets the general criteria under section 2.3 of this policy before arranging the donation/sponsorship. 2.2 Exclusions In line with the appropriate activity assessment, donations or sponsorships must not be accepted or provided where: there is an actual, potential or perceived conflict of interest between the donor or sponsor and Victoria Police. Refer to VPM Conflict of interest for further guidance the recipient or sponsor is a political party or individual politician Victoria Police directly or indirectly regulates or inspects the donor or sponsor industry. Refer to VPM Conflict of interest for the full list of prohibited industries the proposed donation or sponsorship is for an activity that: amounts to a delivery or replacement of core Victoria Police services conflicts with Victorian Government or Victoria Police policy. the donation or sponsorship fee will be passed on to a third party in the form of a sponsorship or grant. text: Emergency management response Context Police must be able to take charge and effectively and efficiently manage incidents or emergencies that may arise as part of their duties, regardless of the size or intensity, and whether planned or unplanned. This policy covers the police response to either an incident or an emergency, and applies to planned and unplanned events. As they are managed in the same way, all incidents are considered emergencies. The response to these emergencies is referred to as the emergency management response. Victoria Police uses the Incident Command and Control System (ICCS) in response to all emergencies. ICCS is a functions-based incident management system, aligned to the ICCS+ guidelines released by Australia New Zealand Policing Advisory Agency (ANZPAA). It is made up of a number of functions which the Police Forward Commander is responsible for when responding to an emergency. The use of ICCS aligns Victoria Police with other jurisdictional arrangements, and with emergency services agencies to provide a standardised approach to an emergency. Under the Emergency Management Act 1986 and the Emergency Management Act 2013 (EM Act 2013), which operate concurrently, police have specific responsibilities reinforced by the State Emergency Management Plan (SEMP). For any interpretation, application or definitions relating to this policy refer to the Victoria Police Emergencies Handbook (VPEH) and other reference documents contained on the State Emergency Response Coordination Division (SECRD) intranet pages. Policy at a glance This policy includes: responsibilities of the Police Commander and Police Forward Commander coordination function at incident, regional and state tiers guidance on the ICCS for police and requirements for how it is used for emergencies responsibilities for Victoria Police specific roles i.e., managing evacuations and traffic establishment of Police Operations Centres (POCs) at incident, regional and state tiers considerations for activating the Protracted Emergency Resource Management Model (PERMM) deployment of Protective Services Officers (PSOs) Victoria Police’s role in managing critical infrastructure. Critical infrastructure 34 Related documents 35 Further advice and information 35 Update history 35 Definitions Emergency – the EM Act 2013 defines an emergency as: an emergency due to the actual or imminent occurrence of an event which in any way endangers or threatens to endanger the safety or health of any person in Victoria or which destroys or damages, or threatens to destroy or damage, any property in Victoria or endangers or threatens to endanger the environment or an element of the environment in Victoria, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing – an earthquake, flood, wind-storm or other natural event; and a fire; and an explosion; and a road accident or any other accident; and a plague or an epidemic or contamination; and a warlike act, or act of terrorism, whether directed at Victoria or a part of Victoria or at any other State or Territory of the Commonwealth; and a hi-jack, siege or riot; and a disruption to an essential service. Major emergency – the EM Act 2013 defines a major emergency as: a large or complex emergency (however caused) which - has the potential to cause or is causing loss of life and extensive damage to property, infrastructure or the environment; or has the potential to have or is having significant adverse consequences for the Victorian community or a part of the Victorian community; or requires the involvement of two or more agencies to respond to the emergency; or a Class 1 emergency; or a Class 2 emergency. Class 1 emergency – the EM Act 2013 defines a Class 1 emergency as: a major fire; or any other major emergency for which Fire Rescue Victoria, the Country Fire Authority or the Victoria State Emergency Service Authority is the control agency under the state emergency management plan. Class 2 emergency – the EM Act 2013 defines a Class 2 emergency as a major emergency which is not— (a) a Class 1 emergency; or (b) a warlike act or act of terrorism, whether directed at Victoria or a part of Victoria or at any other State or Territory of the Commonwealth; or (c) a hi-jack, siege or riot. For example, a Class 2 emergency includes a heatwave. Class 3 emergency – for the purpose of the SEMP a Class 3 emergency means: a warlike act or act of terrorism, whether directed at Victoria or a part of Victoria or at any other State or Territory of the Commonwealth; or a hi-jack, siege

title: Emergency_management_VPM_Emergency_management_response_final
text: a part of Victoria or at any other State or Territory of the Commonwealth; or (c) a hi-jack, siege or riot. For example, a Class 2 emergency includes a heatwave. Class 3 emergency – for the purpose of the SEMP a Class 3 emergency means: a warlike act or act of terrorism, whether directed at Victoria or a part of Victoria or at any other State or Territory of the Commonwealth; or a hi-jack, siege or riot. Class 3 emergencies may also be referred to as security emergencies. Class 3 emergencies are not defined in legislation. Refer to Victoria Police Class 3 Sub-plan for more information. Effective control – for the purpose of the SEMP is when all three of the following apply: a control structure appropriate to the emergency is in place controllers are working to their relevant role statement all response decisions are consistent with the State Emergency Management Priorities. Critical risk means – an incident presenting serious risk requiring immediate police attention, or an investigation, or other police activity, where there is a significant escalation of risk which requires a heightened level of police response and/or command. Significant Protracted Emergency Event (SPEE) – is a significant, protracted event that necessitates a state-wide resourcing commitment to provide both an appropriate police response and mitigate the risk of fatigue on local resources. A SPEE may also include operational events as determined by Executive Command. Significant Security Event (SSE) – is an emergency or event that has the potential for significant loss of life or threat to life. An SSE includes but is not limited to: active shooter/active armed offender suicide bomber chemical, radiological or biological threat hostile vehicle threat/attack. Scope and application This policy applies to all members. The table in section 9.1 of this policy outlines when and where PSOs may be deployed. In addition, PSOs should refer to VPM Protective services officers – duties and responsibilities for further information specific to their powers. Responsibilities and procedures Overview Guiding principles This policy applies to all emergencies, from minor incidents through to major emergencies. The response is designed to be consistent, regardless of the size of the emergency or the number of agencies responding. The arrangements under this policy are designed to permit the response to escalate or de-escalate as necessary. There are three tiers of emergency management response: incident regional/area of operations state. It is not necessary for all tiers to be activated for every emergency response. The structure at every tier of emergency management response is the same and includes: an Incident Controller (where Victoria Police is not the control agency) a Police Forward Commander a Police Commander an Emergency Response Coordinator (ERC) all functions of ICCS;
