It is not necessary for all tiers to be activated for every emergency response. The structure at every tier of emergency management response is the same and includes: an Incident Controller (where Victoria Police is not the control agency) a Police Forward Commander a Police Commander an Emergency Response Coordinator (ERC) all functions of ICCS; these roles can be performed by one person or several people, depending on the scale of the emergency an Incident Management Team (IMT) an Emergency Management Team (EMT) (if multi-agency response). Using the ICCS at all tiers of emergency management response (including the implementation of a command structure and activation of a Police Operation Centre) must be considered by the Police Forward Commander in response to an escalating risk within the operating environment. ICCS will contribute to the effective management of an on-going or expanding emergency. Police roles at emergencies Victoria Police undertakes three predominant emergency management functions (command, control and coordination) at emergencies. When applying these functions to police activity at emergencies, they may be different in context to the traditional understanding of Victoria Police’s command and control role. Refer to the VPEH for further information (Part A – Introduction and Foundations). Under the SEMP and multi-agency guidelines, police are also responsible for the following specific roles which should be undertaken by those appropriately trained: Evacuation Manager (in consultation with the control agency and other expert advice) Traffic Management Manager (in consultation with the control agency and other expert advice), and Emergency Management Liaison Officer (EMLO). Preparedness and assurance by divisional commanders Each year the Chief Commissioner of Police (CCP) requires assurance from each police region that they: are in a state of preparedness to respond to any emergency, including exercising the functions of command, control and coordination, and have developed, implemented, maintained, reviewed and tested their business continuity planning processes. To provide this assurance, every work unit, function or police operation centre must complete a ‘Business continuity and emergency management preparedness and annual assurance report’ in Police Emergency and Event Command (PEEC) annually. The State Emergency Response Coordination Division (SERCD) is responsible for reviewing the effectiveness of the assurance reports and where necessary, making changes and enhancements. Each region must undertake broad liaison with other agencies to ensure appropriate plans, procedures and resources are in place, suitable personnel have been appointed and awareness training has been undertaken. Regional Traffic Management Plans, high risk location evacuation plans (such as for fire and flood emergencies) and other relevant emergency response plans should be reviewed, updated and tested annually. In addition, appropriate ICCS structures and command,

Each region must undertake broad liaison with other agencies to ensure appropriate plans, procedures and resources are in place, suitable personnel have been appointed and awareness training has been undertaken. Regional Traffic Management Plans, high risk location evacuation plans (such as for fire and flood emergencies) and other relevant emergency response plans should be reviewed, updated and tested annually. In addition, appropriate ICCS structures and command, control and coordination facilities should be identified, tested and maintained in a state of readiness. Command Overview Command is the direction of response activities internally within an agency to use its people, resources, governance, systems and processes to discharge its responsibilities in line with relevant legislation, policy or agreed organisational processes. Under the ICCS+ Guidelines and within the ICCS structure for Victoria Police, in line with the scope of an emergency, two key Command Leadership Levels are identified: Strategic – Police Commander; the police officer undertaking this role has overall strategic command of police resources in responding to an incident and provides direction, oversight and support to the Police Forward Commander. Operational – Police Forward Commander; the police officer undertaking this role is accountable and responsible for field/forward operations. During incidents where there is no appointed Police Commander, the Police Forward Commander may also assume strategic level responsibilities. The application of these Command Leadership Levels is most likely at the operational level and is a typical initial response to an emergency. They should not detract from the role of an executive/policy level of leadership. Victoria Police has a clearly defined command structure for general policing which must include a Police Forward Commander and, where required, a Police Commander. Other specific emergency management arrangements are outlined in the ICCS. In the initial stages of an emergency, the first member in attendance or senior member of a police response unit will assume the role of Police Forward Commander. A supervisor must monitor the initial response and decide whether the incident command level is appropriate or whether they need to take command as either the Police Commander or as the Police Forward Commander, depending on the scale of the emergency. If they need to take command, they must notify the next level supervisor, who in turn monitors the situation. The command structure may continue to escalate depending on the nature and size of the emergency. Complex or disparate emergencies/operations may require multiple Police Forward Commanders, Police Commanders and Police Forward Command Posts or Police Operation Centres. In this instance they will all directly report to a singular Regional/Area of Operations Police Commander, or State Police Commander. Coordination operates: vertically within an agency as a function of command, and horizontally across agencies as a function of the authority to control. Emergency response coordination ensures: effective control arrangements are established and maintained information is shared effectively across agencies, and the resources required to support the response are accessed. ICCS – a common approach to incident management Overview ICCS is the sole term to refer to the Victoria Police incident management system. ICCS+ identifies 10 main functions, with these functions considered at each tier of decision making (incident/regional or area of operations/state) by the Police Commander or Police Forward Commander. Note: not all functions within ICCS+ are enacted within the Victoria Police ICCS. The 10 functions of ICCS+ are: command, control and coordination (already undertaken at each level of police response) planning operations logistics investigations intelligence public information safety communications (already occurs across all levels of each function, internally and externally) recovery (undertaken and coordinated by ERV, DFFH or municipal councils – refer to SEMP tables 12-15. Victoria Police has adopted the principles and functions of ICCS+, however there are minor amendments which are reflective of Victoria Police activities, i.e., the functions of Communications and Recovery are not dedicated functions within the Victoria Police ICCS model. Incident Command and Control System guiding principles Underpinning ICCS are a number of guiding principles which assist with application of the framework and support the functions within ICCS. These are: Management by objectives** This is a process of management that determines objectives and associated priorities which are communicated to ensure a common understanding and must be constantly reviewed, re-assessed and amended where necessary, normally through consultation with the IMT and EMT, to determine the desired outcomes of the emergency: objectives are then communicated so everyone involved in the emergency understands the direction being taken during the operation for that tier. What must be achieved now, who is doing it, in what time frames and what are the risks and mitigation strategies? there will only ever be one set of objectives and one overarching Incident Action Plan to ensure that all personnel are working towards the same set of objectives. Functional management** This involves applying the ICCS functions (or any combination of these) to achieve the Police Commanders’ intent. Victoria Police utilises eight specific ICCS functions (command/control/coordination, planning, operations, logistics, intelligence, investigations, public information and safety). Depending on the size and complexity of the emergency, the Police Commander may elect to delegate one or more of the functions. At any one time, there will only be one commander per attending agency managing their agency’s response – a Police Forward Commander and an Incident Controller. Span of control** This is the number of functions and resources that can be managed by one person to prevent overwhelming an individual having regard to the number of groups, individuals or tasks that can be successfully supervised by one person. Where the span of control is exceeded, the Police Forward Commander or ICCS functional manager should consider delegating responsibility for some functions to others, or notify their next line supervisor to attend and assume command. Span of control recognises the need to delegate functions, which is often necessary in order to resolve a large-scale emergency and can work in both directions, meaning that functions may be regained by a supervisor as tasks become fewer in number. ** Key principles utilised by other emergency management agencies within Victoria under their respective incident management systems. Safety Operational and community safety is the primary objective of police in the management of emergencies and involves the continuous assessment and control of risks and threats as circumstances change. Where risks cannot be controlled, they should be mitigated. Safety is a shared responsibility. Victoria Police incorporates this as a dedicated function rather than a principle, to more holistically consider safety aspects of the emergency or event. text: Flexibility The functions outlined in ICCS are scalable and flexible according to the size, nature and complexity of the emergency. They can be adapted and integrated to suit relevant jurisdictional arrangements. This is linked with the principle of Functional Management. Leadership Leadership includes taking command and being proactive and adaptive to changing circumstances: command decisions are often required in an environment of pressure, uncertainty and limited information; delaying or avoiding a decision can lead to additional or elevated risk, and leadership requires a collaborative approach with other agencies. This is linked with the Police Command function and occurs across all capabilities. Communication Any communications should be clear, timely and succinct. Victoria Police incorporates this into each of the functions. Incident tier roles and responsibilities Initial response The first member in attendance or the subsequent senior member must ensure that the roles of Police Forward Commander and IERC are undertaken. As stated in section 1.1 of this policy, it is not necessary for all tiers to be activated for every emergency response, however, early consideration to any breach of the span of control which may cause escalation to a higher tier should be undertaken. Victoria Police ERCs operate at incident, municipal and regional levels for all emergencies: IERC MERC RERC. State tier emergencies – Class 1 and Class 2 emergencies – the EMC Class 3 emergencies – the CCP or delegate. As an example, the below structures for Victoria police may apply. Support agencies may have similar structures as follows. (ICC = Incident Control Centre, RCC = Regional Control Centre, SCC = State Control Centre). Regional/area of operations tier A regional/area of operations tier may be activated when, within that region or across municipalities within that region any one or more of the following occur: there is a forecast of extreme weather there is intelligence or information of any anticipated large scale, extreme activity affecting life or property there is an emergency that involves or is likely to involve one or more of the following: multiple emergency sites depletion of agency resources a significant impact to life, property or the environment interstate deployment of resources an emergency of significant complexity or consequence. State tier The state tier may be activated if any one or more of the following occur: a forecast of extreme weather there is intelligence or information of any anticipated large scale, extreme activity affecting life or property an emergency that involves or is likely to involve one or more of the below where activation is deemed necessary by the State Police Commander (where Victoria Police is the control agency) or State Response Controller: multiple emergency sites depletion of agency resources a significant impact to life, property or the

title: Emergency_management_VPM_Emergency_management_response_final
text: the following occur: a forecast of extreme weather there is intelligence or information of any anticipated large scale, extreme activity affecting life or property an emergency that involves or is likely to involve one or more of the below where activation is deemed necessary by the State Police Commander (where Victoria Police is the control agency) or State Response Controller: multiple emergency sites depletion of agency resources a significant impact to life, property or the environment interstate deployment of resources an emergency of significant complexity or consequence Emergency Management Liaison Officer An EMLO represents an agency and is empowered to commit, or to arrange the commitment of, agency resources in the response to or recovery from emergencies, and to provide a communication link with the agency. This role largely involves provision of a conduit for real time information to be relayed to and from local, regional and state emergency management structures. When Victoria Police is a support agency, control is exercised from a location maintained by the control agency. This may include an ICC, RCC or the SCC. In these circumstances, a Victoria Police EMLO may be deployed to facilitate information exchange between agencies. A police officer appointed as an EMLO should be experienced, authorised to make decisions and be able to exercise sound judgement around when information is required or should be sent to the POC and/or Police Commander A MERC/RERC should not perform the role of an EMLO (although in initial stages of an emergency multiple roles may be performed by the same member) The role of an EMLO includes: providing appropriate representation and expertise, based on authority to speak on behalf of their agency and ensuring regular situation reports are provided to and from their agency operations centre providing specialist advice to the Police Forward Commander or Incident Controller on the roles and capabilities and any limitations of their agency resources using the PEEC Activity Log (where applicable) to convey relevant and timely information to the Police Forward Commander and Police Commander familiarisation of with the current situation and maintaining ongoing situational awareness, and ensuring that adequate handover briefing is provided to incoming EMLOs. Senior Police Liaison Officer In accordance with s.40B, EM Act 2013, the CCP must appoint a SPLO. The role of the SPLO is performed by the Assistant Commissioner, SESC or their delegate. Instrument of delegation EM1 provides for superintendents and inspectors attached to SESC to perform the role of the SPLO if required. The role of the SPLO is to provide advice to the EMC and to facilitate requests to and from RERCs and MERCs. It is not the role of the SPLO to undertake coordination responsibilities. Significant Security Event Member and supervisor responsibilities Once an emergency is considered an SSE, the police officers who made the assessment and are on scene must immediately advise Police Communications for the information of all members and supervisors. Once the emergency is confirmed as an SSE, a supervision unit (251, 265 or 150) must advise Police Communications for information of all local units and managers. Police Communications responsibilities When notified by a supervision unit that an emergency is a confirmed SSE, Police Communications must immediately activate the audible SSE alert tone and broadcast the emergency details to all other units on the channel as per the pre-determined message. Police Communications must subsequently activate the audible SSE alert tone on all other channels and broadcast the pre-determined message on all other channels. Access and use of Emergency Alert Overview In an emergency, a Police Forward Commander or an Incident Controller (as appropriate) at the relevant tier must authorise the provision of public information and warnings. Emergency Alert is the national telephone-based public warning system for delivering emergency warnings via landline and mobile telephones. It is capable of sending up to 800 voice messages to landlines in one minute and 500 text messages to mobile telephones each second. The decision to use Emergency Alert will depend on the nature of the emergency (refer to the criteria listed at section 8.2 of this policy). In most cases the Emergency Alert will relate to a significant risk to the community not an individual and deliver a ‘specific call to action’. The area targeted should be as small as possible to achieve the necessary aim. The system should not be used as the preferred warning method where either: an evacuation is required, or a protracted emergency requiring several instructions to recipients is required. Note: in these situations, information sources may include radio, television, social media and VicEmergency. Emergency Alert is a warning system and cannot be used as an investigative tool. In exceptional

In exceptional circumstances, i.e., missing person investigations, when the use of Emergency Alert is outside the criteria, the initiating police officer must seek advice, support and approval from the SPLO prior to contacting the EMV Warnings Duty Officer (WDO) (see section 8.3 of this policy). Considerations for Emergency Alert When considering the use of Emergency Alert, regard should be given to the following documents accessible on the intranet: National Telephony Warning System Guidelines Victorian Warning Arrangements, and Victoria Police Emergency Incident/Threat Warning [Form 1375]. Emergency Alert can be used when one or more of the following apply: there is an actual or imminent threat to life it is deemed the best way of warning the community in the event of an actual or likely emergency circumstances exist that a reasonable person would consider exceptional alternative mediums have been considered and alone may not achieve objective(s) time is critical and specific action following receipt of the warning is required (e.g., stay indoors) there is a justifiable and permissible reason to access the Integrated Public Number Database data there is a defined geographical area its’ use is lawful, proportionate and necessary based upon the information the agency knows or reasonably believes is true. Where Victoria Police is the control agency, a Police Forward Commander may consider the use of Emergency Alert inclusive of but not limited to the following types of emergencies: a terrorist event a mass casualty event a natural disaster an industrial accident an imminent risk to life. Note: when the emergency has de-escalated or is moving from response to relief/recovery, consideration should be given to how best inform the public. A follow up message using Emergency Alert will usually be appropriate. Legislative requirements for using Emergency Alert Any person who has been granted access to Emergency Alert and the telecommunications data it contains is bound by the Telecommunications Act 1997 (Cth). The data may only be used for either of the following purposes: a purpose connected with persons being alerted to an emergency or a likely emergency the purpose of reasonable testing. Any person who uses or discloses system data for any reason other than the permitted purpose commits an offence (ss.295Z-295ZA, Telecommunications Act 1997 (Cth)). Any person who has been granted access to Emergency Alert

Who can authorise the use of Emergency Alert All Victoria Police initiated Emergency Alert messages must be authorised by an Inspector or above. The use of Emergency Alert during a police emergency should be initiated by the Police Forward Commander and if required in consultation with the SPLO or EMV WDO. Where a Police Forward Commander is satisfied that an Emergency Alert is required which meets the criteria, the Form 1375 must be completed. Form 1375 must be authorised by an Inspector or above. If the Police Forward Commander is not an Inspector, then approval should be sought from the duty 150. Once approved, requests to send a message on the Emergency Alert system must be sent to the EMV WDO and contain all of the following information: name and contact details of the Victoria Police authorising officer issuing the message identification of which template is to be used variables to be added to the template (i.e., location, call to action for recipients) message area designated by street boundaries or via distance from the emergency message delivery timeframe message delivery timeframe. The Emergency Alert will be prepared and disseminated by the EMV WDO based on the information contained in the Form 1375. Contact with the EMV WDO can be made 24/7 via phone: 1300 877 990 or via EMV at the SCC on phone: 1300 368 722. Alternatively, the EMV Duty Officer can be contacted via the SPLO or Police Communications. Where there is doubt over the use of Emergency Alert, staff from Media Communications and Engagement Department may be able to provide additional advice. Alternatively, contact the SPLO for assistance. Requests for Emergency Alert by an external control agency Victoria Police may be requested by another emergency services control agency to use Emergency Alert where that agency is unable to issue the warning. Such requests should be directed to the EMV WDO to facilitate messaging and issue of the Emergency Alert. For further advice on Emergency Alerts, contact the SPLO or the EMV WDO. Notification protocols for foreign nationals in mass casualty incidents Mass casualty incidents A mass casualty incident is an event which involves the death of or serious injury to a significant number of people. The event may occur during a Class 1, 2 or 3 emergency or any other major emergency as defined in the EM Act 2013. Activation of notification protocol The notification protocols between Victoria Police and the Australian Federal Police regarding foreign nationals involved in mass casualty incidents may be activated in response to a mass casualty incident by either: The Police Forward Commander or Police Commander, or the SPLO. What information should be provided When making a notification, all of the following information should be provided: nationalities of people involved or suspected of being involved identification of the foreign nationals health status of those involved being: stable critical deceased. current location of the foreign national, such as hospital, medical facility, police station or prison (police officers must also comply with VPM interviews and statements for suspects and accused) next of kin details. Evacuations Overview The decision to recommend evacuation rests with the control agency, in consultation with police and other expert advice, unless time constraints prevent this consultation. Victoria Police is responsible for managing evacuations on behalf of the control agency including: the appointment of an Evacuation Manager (see section 11.2 of this policy) the registration of affected people monitoring the status and location of affected people carrying out the evacuation process, and returning affected people to their homes. Note registration of affected people during large scale evacuations may be supported by Red Cross personnel who manage the Register.Find.Reunite (RFR) system. RFR kits are located at most police stations. The control agency should consider activating the RFR system where evacuees are able to self-register via an online platform. Contact the SPLO for activation. Evacuation Manager When an evacuation is being considered, a Victoria Police officer must be appointed as an Evacuation Manager. If the emergency: is at the incident tier and Victoria Police is the control agency, the Police Forward Commander may undertake the role escalates and time permits, the Police Forward Commander should appoint an Evacuation Manager. The Evacuation Manager must: maintain constant liaison with the Police Forward Commander and Incident Controller assist in the decision and warning stages co-locate at the same location where control is being exercised e.g. an ICC. Note: a Deputy Evacuation Manager may be located at a separate location such as the POC, where they would sit within the ICCS Operations function. The Evacuation Manager should also maintain ongoing liaison with the Health Commander (if appointed), municipalities, the Department of Health and DFFH in both the planning and execution phases. When managing an evacuation, the Evacuation Manager must particularly consider facilities that house vulnerable people such as aged care facilities, hospitals, schools and child care centres. The Vulnerable Person’s Register lists vulnerable people in the community who are cared for by funded agencies. The funded agencies manage client records and councils coordinate the Registers. When managing an evacuation, this database must be accessed to obtain the list of vulnerable people in the affected area for the attention of the Evacuation Manager. Traffic Management Points Overview The Police Forward Commander or Incident Controller (depending on the emergency) is responsible for developing, implementing and monitoring a Traffic Management Plan, which may include establishing TMPs to restrict and/or facilitate access. Victoria Police is responsible for coordinating implementation of the plan. Use of the Traffic Management Points board within PEEC may assist this function. TMPs are established to facilitate the flow of approved traffic into an area where either: an emergency has occurred, is presently occurring, or has the potential to occur police deem it necessary to cordon off an area for security reasons. In all cases, the safety of all people is paramount and members at TMPs must contact a supervisor for direction or clarification where possible before permitting or denying access. The police supervisor must seek advice from the Police Forward Commander or Incident Controller or their delegate though the Traffic Management Manager (TMM) at the ICC regarding the entry or refusal of entry of any person. Further information and guidance can be found in the Guidelines for the Operation of Traffic Management Points during Emergencies and also within JSOP 03.10 – Traffic Management at Emergencies. A TMM must co-locate at the same location where control is being exercised, e.g., an ICC. Strategic Emergency Management Assurance Team Overview The Strategic Emergency Management Assurance Team (SEMAT) represents the SPLO and provides assurance to Victoria Police Executive Command, Regional Commanders and the EMC. Where required, SEMAT will attend and undertake an independent assessment of the effectiveness of the control and coordination of an emergency or emergencies. The SEMAT assessments may review all control and coordination points at any tier of the emergency management structure. Three primary checklists are used to assess effective control and the operation of an EMT. Refer to the SEMAT intranet page for these checklists and documents relating to Standard Operating Procedures and the practices of SEMAT. Criteria for Strategic Emergency Management Assurance Team deployment for Victoria Police operations The CCP or Deputy Commissioner, Regional Operations may authorise deployment of a SEMAT. They should be deployed if one or more of the following applies: police operations attracting large scale deployment of police personnel and resources involving a heightened risk to life or risk of serious injury police operations attracting large scale media, political or public attention and potentially poses a reputational risk to Victoria Police the emergency/operation is likely to be prolonged and requires community reassurance and confidence strategies during and post the emergency any large scale emergency (e.g. bushfire) where an IPOC requires activation and full implementation of the ICCS structure. Critical infrastructure Overview Critical infrastructure are physical facilities, supply chains, information technologies and communication networks which, if destroyed, degraded or rendered unavailable for an extended period, would significantly impact on the social or economic wellbeing of the nation or affect Australia's ability to conduct national defence and ensure national security. Some examples of critical infrastructure are gas production facilities, bulk storage, pipelines and refineries of petroleum fuels, electricity generators and substations, dams, pumping stations and sewerage treatment plants, airports, sea lanes and shipping container facilities, health facilities, food supply, key government services and national icons. Victoria Police role Where critical infrastructure is damaged or there is a disruption to essential services reliant on critical infrastructure, Victoria Police is the control agency as per the SEMP. Where the control agency is unclear, an ERC will determine the control agency e.g., Department of Transport and Planning is the control agency for critical infrastructure disruptions involving public transport. Victoria Police does not have open access to the Critical Infrastructure Register, which is held by EMV. Should there be a requirement for police officers (usually station commanders, Local Area Commanders, or RERCs) to have access to the register, this can be facilitated by staff at SERCD. MERCs will normally have some oversight of critical infrastructure assets within their respective municipalities, as these would be subject to a Community Emergency Risk Assessment for inclusion in the Municipal Emergency Management Plan. Attendance by members at sites of critical infrastructure for an emergency are to be initially managed per any other emergency event, as it may be unlikely that first responders are unaware of the criticality of the site. Likely sites that may be critical in nature due to their essentiality to the State of Victoria are as follows: banking and finance communications emergency services and government energy food supply health transport water. Where there is any doubt as to whether the site is a critical infrastructure location, advice should be sought from the MERC or RERC. Where appropriate, ensure Field Contact Reports or Information Reports are submitted for all suspicious contacts or incidents relating to critical

Response services Communications services Police Communications is responsible for allocating all call signs, operators, channels and colour codes required for all operations and special events and will assist in the planning of all communication requirements. The Manager, SPOC should be consulted for advice and assistance on the maintenance and readiness of the SPOC. The Tactical Vision Unit (TVU) is responsible for allocating and deploying CCTV and Helivision equipment for use in planned events and operations and will assist in the planning of deploying and using CCTV and Helivision equipment. For planned events and operations requiring CCTV and/or Helivision equipment, members must complete a request for Tactical Vision Support via the ICT & Facilities Portal. Senior Police Command Cadre Senior Police Command Cadre deployment criteria The Senior Police Command Cadre (SPCC) consists of a cadre of Police Commanders and Police Forward Commanders. The SPCC will deploy in the following circumstances: critical incidents, where the level of expertise required to manage an unplanned incident is within the scope of the SPCC members events of state significance. When authorised or requested, the SPCC will deploy through one of the following pathways: state level Risk Evaluation Meeting (REM) Counter Terrorism Advisory Group (CTAG) meeting process unplanned activation of the SPOC, when no other specific SPOC Commander has been identified via the duty commissioner direct request of Special Operations Group (SOG) Tactical Commander, via the Security Services Division (SSD) Superintendent (business hours) or via the Transit and Public Safety Command (TPSC) Duty Superintendent (After hours). If the SPCC is deployed, the SPCC Police Commander must, at the first opportunity, engage with the relevant Police Commander/Police Forward Commander to obtain a situation report and provide direction on command functions including: proposed strategic and operational command structure where command will be exercised when command will be transitioned. Special Operations Group Special Operations Group deployment criteria The SOG responds to unplanned operational critical incidents such as sieges and siege hostage situations and armed offender tasks. The unit also assists operational police in planned operations involving apprehension of dangerous suspects. SOG assistance must be requested in the following circumstances: high risk operations or incidents where there is a probability of confrontation with a person who is armed or reasonably suspected to be armed with a firearm or other lethal weapon, including planned operations, sieges and searches for offenders armed with firearms level three searches of properties, as the entry team (see VPM Searches of property) ‘active’ clandestine laboratories, as determined by a risk assessment conducted by the Clandestine Laboratory Squad a terrorist incident, hostile vehicle or significant politically motivated violence all hostage incidents covert surveillance, reconnaissance or other tasks beyond the scope, expertise, skill level or capability of general duties members or other operational areas. When deploying to Aboriginal communities or in response to Aboriginal persons, any known cultural sensitivities of that community must be considered in determining appropriate action. For more information refer to the Aboriginal Communities Factsheets on the Priority and Safer Communities Division (PSCD) Community Safety Hub intranet page. Deployment Deployment of the SOG must be authorised by either: the SOG Tactical Advisor the Quick Reaction Force (QRF) Tactical Advisor (SOG senior sergeant) or a suitably experienced QRF team leader. The SOG QRF Tactical Advisor must notify the SOG Tactical Advisor of any deployment at the first opportunity. If the QRF deploy to an incident, the SOG QRF Tactical Advisor will assume the role of QRF Tactical Commander. If the SOG Tactical Advisor deploys in support of the QRF, a handover with the QRF Tactical Commander must occur and the SOG Tactical Advisor must then identify as the SOG Tactical Commander via Police Communications. Notification of deployment If the SOG is deployed, the Police Commander/Police Forward Commander must notify the relevant duty officer and 265 of the area where the operation is being conducted. The 265 is required to ensure notifications and deployment approval occur in line with sections 3.3 and 3.4 of this policy. The Police Commander/Police Forward Commander must be of inspector rank or above. Roles, responsibilities and command interaction The SOG must operate within the structure of the Incident Management System (IMS) - Incident Command and Control System (ICCS). The SOG Tactical Advisor is a SOG inspector who has completed the Australian New Zealand Counter Terrorism Committee (ANZCTC) Police Tactical Commanders course. They form part of the 24-hour SOG response and can provide advice on: SOG deployment criteria SOG capacity and capability the necessary authority to approve deployment for the SOG. The SOG Tactical Advisor can be contacted through Police Communications 24 hours a day. The SOG Tactical Commander is a SOG inspector or SOG senior sergeant who has completed the ANZCTC Police Tactical Commanders course. The SOG Tactical Commander must: Provide briefings and be available to the Police Commander/Police Forward Commander throughout the operation or incident. Where it is not practical to obtain approval, the SOG Tactical Commander may take EA to resolve the incident, provided that the above criteria are met. Bomb Response Unit Bomb Response Unit deployment criteria The Bomb Response Unit (BRU) provides 24-hour advice or on-site attendance in response to any explosive device related incident or issue, including fireworks and military ordinance. BRU assistance or advice must be requested in the following circumstances: assessment and resolution of situations involving: suspicious packages/items that are suspected to be improvised explosive devices (IEDs) suspicious packages/items that are suspected of containing chemical, biological or radiological hazardous material where the dispersal system is mechanically, electrically or explosively initiated clandestine explosive laboratories or home-made explosives the presence or location of commercial explosives, pyrotechnics, detonators or military ordinance within the community where an explosive detector dog (EDD) is required for operational support post blast site attendance to conduct a site safety assessment, locate unexploded IEDs or explosive material bomb threat incidents incidents involving or where intelligence indicates the presence of man-traps or booby traps searches for explosive ordinance reconnaissance where hazardous or precursor explosive materials are located which are unsafe to manually handle, requiring the use of BRU skills, tactics and equipment any critical incident where BRU skills, tactics and equipment may increase the likelihood of a safe resolution to the incident. Requests for deployment - planned operations Contact the BRU Bomb Commander (BRU sergeant) to discuss the nature of the planned operation and proposed role of the BRU. The BRU Bomb Commander will assess the request. Requests for deployment – unplanned operations The Police Commander/Police Forward Commander must, as soon as practicable: request BRU advice or deployment, via Police Communications notify the 265 of the request for BRU. Requests for deployment – explosive detector dog The BRU Bomb Commander or Bomb Team Leader will assess EDD deployment requests and must approve any deployment of an EDD. The BRU EDD Operative must retain control of the dog and is responsible for any decisions on the use of the dog. The BRU EDD may be deployed independently of full BRU deployment upon assessment and approval by the BRU Bomb Commander or Bomb Team Leader. Considerations for deployment include, but are not limited to: searches for any suspect package, device or substance reasonably suspected of containing explosives searches of premises searches of vehicles/vessels. Critical Incident Response Team Critical Incident Response Team deployment criteria The CIRT provide 24 hours a day, 7 days a week response (including a negotiator capability) to incidents that are beyond the scope, experience and skill level of general duties members, but that do not meet the criteria of the SOG. CIRT assistance must be requested in the following circumstances: A high-risk incident where there is a probability of a violent confrontation with a person, or it is reasonably suspected that a person is armed with a weapon (including sieges, barricade incidents, and searches for armed or violent people). If a firearm is involved, the SOG must also be notified. Mental health related incidents where a person is threatening or attempting suicide or self-harm and/or intervention is beyond the scope, expertise and capability of general duties police Incidents that meet the SOG deployment criteria, pending the arrival of the SOG Other tasks including planned operations approved by the CIRT Duty Officer in which the deployment of CIRT specialist skills or equipment is likely to provide the most appropriate level of response. text: The CIRT Tactical Advisor role must be performed by a senior sergeant or suitably experienced sergeant or team leader who has completed the CIRT Team Leaders course. The CIRT Tactical Advisor forms part of the 24-hour CIRT response. The senior sergeant assumes the role of the CIRT Tactical Advisor when not physically at the scene of an incident. The CIRT Tactical Advisor will monitor and support all CIRT deployments in line with the CIRT deployment criteria. The role of the CIRT Tactical Advisor includes but is not limited to: monitoring relevant radio channels for all CIRT requests when requested, monitoring the task and its status monitoring the local incident channel as well as the CIRT operational channel ensuring they are available for the CIRT Tactical Commander as required ensuring CIRT personnel have capacity and capability in line with the Police Forward Commander’s requirements providing tactical advice to the Police Forward Commander and Tactical Commander deployment to the incident scene as required and assumption of the role of the CIRT Tactical Commander via police radio. The CIRT Tactical Commander role should be performed by a CIRT member who arrives at the scene first and declares themselves as the CIRT Tactical Commander via police radio. A more senior CIRT member subsequently attending the incident may assume the role of CIRT Tactical Commander by declaring this via police radio. The position of the CIRT Tactical Commander can be subject to ongoing change and should be communicated via the police radio where that occurs. In situations where the circumstances are sufficiently complex, the CIRT Duty Officer may deploy to the scene and perform the role of CIRT Tactical Commander. The CIRT Tactical Commander must: where the scene is static, be available to the Police Commander/Police Forward Commander conduct a risk assessment and discuss the tactical options with the Police Commander/Police Forward Commander, to determine appropriate action to be taken to manage or resolve the incident as far as practicable, be available to the Police Commander/Police Forward Commander during the resolution phase of the operation or incident. unless exceptional circumstances exist, form part of the IMT and attend scheduled IMT meetings. If unable to attend IMT meetings, the capability for a direct line of communication must be established and maintained. If the incident meets the SOG deployment criteria, assistance from the SOG must be requested by the Police Commander/Police Forward Commander. Where CIRT’s attendance involves a death or serious injury, notifications to Professional Standards Command (PSC) will be conducted by the Police Forward Commander in line with VPM Death or serious injury/illness incidents involving police. CIRT must preserve and handle evidence in accordance with VPM Scene management and VPM Seized property and special property types.

Public Order Response Team Public Order Response Team deployment criteria The Public Order Response Team (PORT) provides a highly visible police response to assist with priority organisational issues, public safety incidents and emergency situations. PORT deploys their specialist resources in accordance with VPM Crowd control and public order incidents. Deployment can be requested where the response is beyond the capability and capacity of the local resources, including: public order and community safety incidents, including but not limited to: planned operations; such as protests, demonstrations, sporting events where there is a high potential for violence or a need for crowd management or public order capabilities unplanned operations; such as riots, affrays or brawls, which require a need for crowd management or public order capabilities enforcement or monitoring of high-risk groups; such as outlaw motorcycle gangs. emergency management incidents requiring significant policing resources, such as large-scale state-wide emergencies organisational priorities relating to crime or road policing. Requests for deployment – planned operations Requests for PORT resources are to be made at the earliest opportunity through line management, using the State T&C application process.

Requests for deployment – planned operations Requests for PORT resources are to be made at the earliest opportunity through line management, using the State T&C application process. Requesting members should contact the PORT T&C Manager at the earliest opportunity for advice regarding the preparation of the application. State T&C applications will be assessed at a weekly command-level meeting chaired by the Operations Support Division (OSD) Superintendent, or out-of-sessions, and the decision communicated back to the requesting area via the relevant regional Operational Support superintendent. Requests for deployment – unplanned operations Requests for PORT resources, submitted within 48 hrs of the operation occurring, are considered unplanned operations or ‘hot tasks’ and involve a redeployment of PORT resources across regional or divisional boundaries. Any request must still satisfy the PORT deployment criteria. Requests must not be delayed so that they fall within the unplanned operation definition. Requesting members should contact the PORT at the earliest opportunity to discuss the request and resourcing options. Requests regarding unplanned operations are to be evidenced with sufficient information and intelligence and will be progressed via email or telephone (dependent upon circumstances) to the PORT duty sergeant (Sunday to Thursday night shift) or the PORT duty senior sergeant (all other times) for initial assessment. Re-deployment of PORT resources The redeployment of PORT resources must be assessed against their current tasking and proposed redeployment must demonstrate a higher organisational priority. The Police Commander/Police Forward Commander must consider the operational need and determine if the incident requires additional resources (in particular, specialist capability) which are not available within the impacted region/command. Redeployment for an unplanned operation (‘hot task’) must be in consultation initially with the PORT duty sergeant (Sunday to Thursday night shift) or the PORT duty senior sergeant (all other times) who will engage with the PORT duty inspector. Redeployment from planned tasking requires approval of the regional duty inspector in consultation with the PORT duty inspector (for tasks within the requesting region) or agreement between the requesting region’s Operational Support superintendent and the TPSC duty superintendents (for tasks external to the requesting region). The approver will assess the request and notify the requesting Police Commander/Police Forward Commander of the approval for PORT resources to be redeployed. Deployment authorisation In circumstances requiring an urgent response the PORT supervisor may redeploy PORT resources and seek approval immediately following the allocation of resources. Mounted Branch Mounted Branch deployment criteria The Mounted Branch (MTB) provides a state-wide response and support capability for public order management, search and rescue, planned and targeted patrols, community reassurance and ceremonial duties. The MTB is a highly visible policing resource that promotes public confidence and safety. The MTB can be deployed for: public order management and community safety incidents, including but not limited to planned operations such as protests, demonstrations and sporting events where intelligence indicates that there is a high potential need for crowd management or public order capabilities search and rescue for rural or urban locations, for planned or unplanned operations targeted patrols for local crime or public order operations community reassurance patrols following significant events ceremonial duties (limited to police funerals, police graduations, Governors’ escorts and large-scale events such as Remembrance Day). Requests for service – planned events Requests for MTB services for planned events must be made at the earliest opportunity through line management as follows: for state level events (involving multiple TPSC resources) – request via the State T&C process (template available from TPSC intranet) all other requests – by completion of a Transit and Public Safety Command – Request for Services from Mounted Branch [Form VP1298]. Requests for service – unplanned operations Requests for MTB resources that are submitted within 72 hours of the operation occurring are considered unplanned operations or ‘hot tasks’. Requesting members must contact the MTB at the earliest opportunity to discuss the request and resourcing options. Requests for unplanned operations must be evidenced with enough information and intelligence and must progress via: the State T&C process where multiple TPSC units are requested initial email or telephone consultations, followed by a VP1298 where only MTB resources are requested. Deployment authorisation All deployments for unplanned operations must be approved by the OIC MTB or the Unit Commander, Mounted Branch/Dog Squad. Urgent deployments after hours or on weekends must be made via the on-call Specialist Response Division 265. In the case of event escalation, the management and tactics utilised by the MTB at public order management events will be at the direction of the Police Commander/Police Forward Commander in consultation with the PORT Tactical Commander and the MTB Tactical Advisor. text: COVID-19 vaccination requirements Context The Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 (OHS Act) requires that employers ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, that they provide and maintain a working environment for their employees that is safe and without risks to health and that other people are not exposed to health and safety risks arising from the employer's activities. The following principles apply to this policy regarding vaccination requirements: Victoria Police is responsible for providing a safe working environment, consistent with the duties of employers under the OHS Act. Both infection and serious illness resulting from COVID-19 are workplace health and safety risks. Vaccination is a practicable measure that assists to control the risk of transmission of COVID-19 in the working environment of Victoria Police. To ensure that Victoria Police discharges its obligations under the OHS Act, employees and other workplace participants are to attend the workplace only when they have up-to-date vaccination status against COVID-19. This policy outlines the vaccination requirements for employees and other workplace participants attending a workplace, to ensure a safe workplace for all employees, workplace participants and visitors. This policy does not apply to members of the general public who require the assistance of Victoria Police or who are required to attend Victoria Police facilities, such as victims of crime, offenders and persons in custody. Contents Context 1 Contents 1 Definitions 2 Scope and application 3 Responsibilities and procedures 3 1. Vaccination requirements 3 2. Compliance with this policy 4 3. Review 5 Related documents 5 Further advice and information 5 Update history 6 Definitions Acceptable certification for the purpose of determining an employee’s status as an excepted person is: In any case: a current COVID-19 digital certificate issued by Services Australia that states that the person is unable to receive a dose, or a further dose, of any COVID-19 vaccine that is available in Australia; or a printed version of the COVID-19 digital certificate referred to in subclause (a)(i) above; or a current Immunisation History Statement displayed through the Medicare App, that states that a person is unable to receive a booster dose that is available in Australia; or a printed version of the Immunisation History Statement referred to in subclause (a)(iii) above. Booster dose means: a second dose of a COVID-19 vaccine after receiving one dose of a one dose COVID-19 vaccine; or a third dose of a COVID-19 vaccine after receiving two doses of a two dose COVID-19 vaccine, including different types of two dose COVID-19 vaccines; or any additional booster doses as may be required to maintain up-to-date vaccination status as recommended by the Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (ATAGI) from time to time. Excepted person means an employee who

title: Employee_wellbeing_VPM_COVID_19_Vaccination_final
text: of a COVID-19 vaccine after receiving one dose of a one dose COVID-19 vaccine; or a third dose of a COVID-19 vaccine after receiving two doses of a two dose COVID-19 vaccine, including different types of two dose COVID-19 vaccines; or any additional booster doses as may be required to maintain up-to-date vaccination status as recommended by the Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (ATAGI) from time to time. Excepted person means an employee who holds acceptable certification that they are unable to receive a dose, or a further dose, of any COVID-19 vaccine that is available in Australia due to a medical contraindication or acute medical illness in accordance with current ATAGI guidance. Primary course means that a person has received a primary course of a Therapeutic Goods Association (TGA) approved or recognised vaccine if they have received one dose of a one dose COVID-19 vaccine, or two doses of a two dose COVID-19 vaccine but have not yet received a booster dose. Vaccination evidence means any evidence relating to a person’s vaccination status and includes: any information that is derived from a record of information that was made under, or in accordance with the Australian Immunisation Register Act 2015 (Cth); and the name or type of any dose of an approved COVID-19 Vaccine received by the person; and the date on which the person received any dose of an approved COVID-19 vaccine. Vaccination status means one of the following: Up-to-date Under-vaccinated Excepted person. Under-vaccinated is the vaccination status of an employee whose vaccination status is not up-to-date or they are an excepted person. Up-to-date means, for the purposes of vaccination status, vaccination in line with ATAGI guidance, as updated from time to time, including the maintenance of vaccination status currency through booster doses. Current ATAGI guidance as at 10 February 2022 confirms that up-to-date means: For individuals aged 16 years and over: having completed an appropriate primary course of a TGA approved or recognised vaccine; and if six months has passed since the completion of that course, having received a booster dose. For individuals who have had prior COVID-19 (including asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2) infection: having completed an appropriate primary course of a TGA approved or recognised vaccine; and if both six months have passed since the completion of that course and four months have passed following their infection, having received a booster dose. All employees and other workplace participants must provide this information as soon as reasonably practicable after the commencement of this policy or as otherwise instructed by Victoria Police. For employees, information pertaining to vaccination status will be recorded in HR Assist and maintained in accordance with the Health Records Act 2001 and be accessible to authorised persons only for the purposes of implementing and ensuring compliance with this policy. Employees and other workplace participants are encouraged to redact healthcare

text: workplace participants must provide this information as soon as reasonably practicable after the commencement of this policy or as otherwise instructed by Victoria Police. For employees, information pertaining to vaccination status will be recorded in HR Assist and maintained in accordance with the Health Records Act 2001 and be accessible to authorised persons only for the purposes of implementing and ensuring compliance with this policy. Employees and other workplace participants are encouraged to redact healthcare identifiers, where relevant, from their current COVID-19 digital certificate or other document before providing vaccination evidence to Victoria Police. Exceptions An employee or other workplace participant may be permitted to work outside their ordinary place of residence for Victoria Police if the employee is an excepted person and has produced acceptable certification to Victoria Police to substantiate that they are an excepted person. Prior to granting such permission, Victoria Police will carry out a risk assessment and determine measures to ensure a safe working environment. An employee or other workplace participant whose evidence of an acceptable certification has expired, meaning that they are no longer considered to be an excepted person, will be subject to the following requirements: to obtain and maintain up-to-date vaccination status in accordance with primary course and booster dose timeframes as set out in current ATAGI guidelines to provide vaccination evidence confirming their vaccination status to only work outside of their ordinary place of residence if they have an up-to-date vaccination status. Compliance with this policy Employees who do not comply with the directions outlined in this policy may be subject to one or more of the following: disciplinary action as described within the VPMP Complaints and discipline misconduct as described within clause 25, Victorian Public Service Enterprise Agreement 2020 an assessment as to their capability to meet the inherent requirements of their role, which may result in termination of employment. Workplace participants may have their contract for the provision of services with Victoria Police terminated. Any employee who falsifies and/or knowingly and intentionally misleads Victoria Police in relation to their vaccination status or their status as an excepted person will be subject to disciplinary action and may face sanctions up to and including termination of employment. Review This policy will be subject to review every 12 months from the date of issue, or upon update of ATAGI guidance i.e., for employees to receive additional booster doses to maintain ‘up-to-date’ vaccination status to align with any changes to ATAGI guidance. title: Employee_wellbeing_VPM_Employee_health_final
text: Employee health Context Victoria Police aims to promote safe work practices, provide a safe workplace for its employees and a professional, ethical, high performing service to the community. This aim is underpinned by having employees who are fit for duty in the workplace. Victoria Police is committed to ensuring the health and wellbeing of its employees and preventing illness and injury in the workplace. The organisation supports this commitment through the implementation of comprehensive employee health and safety programs and initiatives, and the provision of exercise facilities for use by employees. This policy applies to all employees of Victoria Police. Contents Context 1 Contents 1 Definitions 1 Responsibilities and procedures 2 1. Victoria Police exercise facilities 2 2. Sharps and infection control 2 3. Alcohol and other drugs 5 4. Eyesight screening 5 5. Managing epilepsy 7 6. Pandemic preparedness and management 9 Related documents 12 Further advice and information 12 Update history 12 Definitions Epidemic: a sudden increase in the incidence of a disease affecting a large number of people and spreading over a large area. Influenza: a viral disease that causes high fever, sore throat, cough, and muscle aches. It usually affects the respiratory system but sometimes affects other organs. It is spread by infectious droplets that are coughed or sneezed into the air. These droplets can land on the mucous membranes of the eyes or mouth or be inhaled into the lungs of another person. Infection can also occur from contact with surfaces contaminated with infectious droplets and respiratory secretions. Pandemic: world-wide epidemic of an infectious disease and is generally associated with an influenza strain. Pandemic Influenza: a global outbreak of a new strain of human influenza spreading rapidly from person-to-person when few if any people have immunity to the new strain. Seasonal Influenza: the annual outbreak experienced in most countries during the winter months. Work Area: A work area is decided upon by senior management and may refer to a range of options including but not limited to: region, station; police service area (PSA); department; unit; branch; cluster. Responsibilities and procedures Victoria Police exercise facilities General conditions of use Employees using Victoria Police exercise facilities are to do so in their own time and at their own risk, except for recruits and specialist areas that have rostered fitness activities. There is no requirement for employees to use Victoria Police exercise facilities to maintain a level of fitness to meet the 'Fitness Qualifications' introduced in July 2010. Employee requirements To use Victoria Police exercise facilities, employees must: use equipment correctly and within your limitations within the exercise facility complete the attendance register maintained at each facility not use faulty equipment and report faults to the local Work

title: Employee_wellbeing_VPM_Employee_health_final
text: and specialist areas that have rostered fitness activities. There is no requirement for employees to use Victoria Police exercise facilities to maintain a level of fitness to meet the 'Fitness Qualifications' introduced in July 2010. Employee requirements To use Victoria Police exercise facilities, employees must: use equipment correctly and within your limitations within the exercise facility complete the attendance register maintained at each facility not use faulty equipment and report faults to the local Work Unit Manager at the earliest opportunity. The Work Unit Manager must report the fault to the local elected Health and Safety Representative report any injuries to the Work Unit Manager immediately and, if the injury is a result of a rostered fitness activity, make relevant entries on HR Assist. Sharps and infection control Managers' responsibilities Work Unit Managers must ensure that their employees: have access to personal protective equipment that is required for that workplace as outlined in VPM OHS Hazard and risk management are aware of the methods for preventing contamination and handling exposure to contaminants as outlined below. Employees' responsibilities Employees must be mindful that all persons and property may be a source of infection or contamination. Therefore, they must ensure that control measures are used to prevent transmission of bodily fluids, including use of personal protective equipment and hygiene measures. Biological hazards and contaminated waste Employees who come in to contact with biological hazards while conducting their duties should take appropriate precautions and, if exposed, apply appropriate first aid. Biological hazards which employees may come into contact include: blood or body fluids that may be infectious (for example infectious diseases such as Hepatitis, HIV or tuberculosis) mould or fungi, including mouldy hay, that may contain organisms that can cause respiratory sensitisation if inhaled cannabis parasites such as scabies and fleas animal faeces. Contaminated waste may include objects soiled with blood, body fluids, faeces, insects, viruses, bacteria and other infectious material. Precautions General Employees should be mindful that all persons and property may be a source of contamination, therefore, employees should ensure: that control measures are used to prevent transmission of bodily fluids, such as personal protective equipment (e.g. gloves and protective eyewear) and measures such as regular hand washing that immunisations for Hepatitis B and Tetanus are current all cuts and abrasions are covered with a waterproof dressing and changed if they become soiled or unsealed. Personal protective equipment Approved protective equipment, such as gloves and protective eye wear, (refer to VPM OHS Hazard and risk management for more information) should be used as appropriate when: attending incidents involving: drug or alcohol affected persons persons suffering from a mental disorder, particularly when involving a mental disorder transfer or hospital attendance conducting searches

Handling sharps Use tongs and sharps resistant gloves to handle sharps; avoid handling directly. Place sharps or contaminated materials in an appropriate container. Exercise caution when handling sharps containers. Inspect the container for protruding sharps before handling. Dispose of sharps containers by contacting the local council or hospital. Employees are not responsible for the collection of sharps in public places, (for example toilets, parks, etc.). This is the responsibility of the local council or Needle Exchange service. Handling contaminated items Where possible, seal contaminated waste in a sealable plastic bag. Arrange for disposal of the bag/s by Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) or EPA approved company. Employee’s clothing – Remove as soon as practicable, seal in plastic bag, label as contaminated, and wash separately to other clothing. Some clothing items may require cleaning by specialist dry cleaning services. Person in custody clothing – Ask them to remove clothing and seal in plastic bag. Provide disposable overalls. Give clothing to next of kin or similar and advise of cleaning procedure as described above. Bedding or towels – Place in sealable plastic bag and arrange for laundering or dry cleaning. Personal issue equipment – Using gloves, wash items using hot or warm water and detergent. If soiled with blood or bodily fluids that potentially contain a transmittable disease, first disinfect item using a hospital grade bleach or similar product and obtain advice from the Medical Advice Line on 1800 004 464. Wound (e.g. needle stick or cut) - flush the wound with running water and apply first aid as necessary. Eye – rinse the open eye with tap water or saline solution and apply first aid. Mouth – spit any blood or bodily fluid out and thoroughly rinse with

Eyesight screening Employees who undertake work involving screen based equipment and are experiencing eyesight fatigue, may be eligible for reimbursement of expenses for eyesight testing and corrective eyewear. Purpose This policy has been developed to reduce visual fatigue for employees as far as is practicable, by identifying and correcting pre-existing eyesight problems that may cause discomfort as a result of the visual concentration needed for many Screen Based Equipment (SBE) tasks. Eligibility Eligibility for reimbursement of expenses for eyesight testing and corrective eyewear may apply to any employee who: operates SBE for an aggregate of two hours or more, inclusive of rest breaks, in any day or shift on a regular basis (more than three days per week); or has experienced

Eligibility Eligibility for reimbursement of expenses for eyesight testing and corrective eyewear may apply to any employee who: operates SBE for an aggregate of two hours or more, inclusive of rest breaks, in any day or shift on a regular basis (more than three days per week); or has experienced or is experiencing visual discomfort as a result of using SBE; or may be required to use SBE intensively but not every day. Screen based equipment and visual fatigue Current literature suggests that there is no significant link between SBE usage and long-term vision problems. There is however, some evidence that persons using SBE for long periods may suffer temporary visual fatigue. Visual fatigue eyestrain symptoms can be experienced as: sore, tired, itchy, dry or burning eyes throbbing or aching eyes difficulties in focusing including blurred and/or double vision headaches and tiredness. It is due to the visually demanding nature of screen based work and considered to be temporary discomfort with no long lasting ill effects. Eyesight screening tests Eyesight screening by a qualified optometrist is offered on a voluntary basis to eligible SBE operators: on commencement of employment or transfer to a position which requires the use of SBE and baseline screening results are not available or have not been undertaken previously; and every two years thereafter; or where physical symptoms identified by the employee may indicate that a problem may exist. Employee responsibilities Employees are to: make an appointment with the optometrist of their choice for an eyesight screening test complete the Request for Eyesight Screening Reimbursement [Form 1420] and give this to the Work Unit Manager for assessment and authorisation prior to their eyesight screening test provide the optometrist with the Request for Eyesight Screening Reimbursement form at appointment, have the form completed and return to the Work Unit Manager for appropriate action pay for eyesight screening test/s and spectacles where prescribed and provide original account and receipts to their Work Unit Manager for reimbursement, along with a general claim form [Form 135]. Employer responsibilities Work Unit Managers are to: assess requests for initial eyesight screening in accordance with these guidelines assess requests for reimbursement treat eyesight test results as confidential and include on personal file. Managing epilepsy Background Epilepsy is a chronic disorder characterised by paroxysmal brain dysfunction due to excessive neuronal discharge. The clinical manifestations may vary from complex abnormalities of behaviour including generalised focal convulsions to short periods of impaired consciousness. Disclosure All police members who are diagnosed with epilepsy must advise their Work Unit Manager immediately. VPS employees are encouraged to advise their Work Unit Manager for health and safety purposes and in particular if they drive work vehicles. The Work Unit Manager must then advise and refer the employee to the Police Medical Officer (PMO). In the case of a VPS or Forensic Officer employee, contact Workplace Relations Division for advice. Employees who have been diagnosed with epilepsy must provide authorisation for the PMO to consult with their treating doctor or neurologist in regard to the on-going management of their condition. Following the initial disclosure of their condition, employees will be restricted from undertaking certain duties or activities as applicable to their role. These duties or activities may be reinstated once the PMO has consulted with the employee’s treating doctor or neurologist. Action following disclosure Police members Following disclosure in accordance with this policy, the police member’s departmental driving authority and OSTT qualifications are to be suspended immediately. This is a preliminary action pending further assessment. Police members, in whom epilepsy has been recently diagnosed, must not wear a police uniform outside police premises or perform the following duties, until their treating neurologist has certified that the condition is well controlled on medication and the neurologist’s

This is a preliminary action pending further assessment. Police members, in whom epilepsy has been recently diagnosed, must not wear a police uniform outside police premises or perform the following duties, until their treating neurologist has certified that the condition is well controlled on medication and the neurologist’s certification has been endorsed by the PMO: driving police vehicles, boats, helicopters and/ or operating other machinery any duties involving the carrying or use of operational safety equipment equipment issue duties working anywhere alone. Duties that may continue to be performed include: detainee management (but never alone) clerical duties answering telephone enquiries information management, for example DIMU, RIMU reception office public enquiries, for example in a police station with separate reception and counter areas file enquiries performed at the police station rostering duties property office Proactive Unit attendance at functions / schools etc. following a risk assessment by the Work Unit Manager other identified duties which do not conflict with prescribed duties listed above. On receipt of the treating neurologist’s certification that the police member's epilepsy is optimally controlled, the PMO will determine when it is appropriate for the member to return to performing the full duties of their substantive position. VPS employees Following disclosure, the PMO will, in consultation with the VPS employee’s medical practitioner, provide advice and assistance, where necessary, in the ongoing management of the employee’s condition. Driving police vehicles Restrictions on departmental driving authority Due to the consequences of a seizure occurring while driving departmental vehicles and community expectation that drivers of police vehicles must meet a higher standard than the general driving population, employees who have epilepsy will not be permitted to drive departmental vehicles until the risk of seizure is minimal and of the same order as that of any member of the general population. Prior to certification by a treating neurologist and full reinstatement of the employee’s departmental driving authority, the PMO may certify an employee fit to hold a restricted white class driving authority depending upon the particular circumstances of the individual case. Reinstating departmental driving authority Employees who, after an appropriate period of time, are certified by their treating neurologist as being seizure free will be permitted to drive departmental vehicles provided that the certification by the treating neurologist specifically states that the condition "is so well controlled that the risk of seizure is minimal and of the same order as that of any member of the general population" and subject to the agreement of the PMO. Upon receipt of such certification, and with the endorsement

Changes in circumstance An employee who has been diagnosed with epilepsy must immediately inform the PMO of any change of their status such as the occurrence of a seizure, a change to or cessation of medication or any other factor that may adversely affect their fitness for duty. text: Deployment (members) Context Victoria Police has a police officer and protective services officer (PSO) base of over 17,000 members and operates across all areas of Victoria. Police members move between work locations for a variety of reasons including promotion, transfers (officer initiated and directed), secondment, higher duties or at level assignment — collectively called 'deployment'. Scope and application This policy applies to all members (Police Officers, Protective Services Officers, Police Reservists and Police Recruits) described in section 2.1 of the Agreement, unless otherwise stated. This policy does not apply to the mobility and redeployment process of members, which are governed by VPM Mobility (members) and VPM Redeployment (members). Policy The filling of positions must be managed in accordance with the Act, the Regulations, and the Agreement. The placement and movement of police officers up to the rank of senior sergeant and PSOs must be managed in accordance with the Agreement. All activities associated with selecting members for transfer or promotion must be consistent with the Act and Regulations, and the principles of equality and diversity, natural justice, and procedural fairness. All information and activities associated with positions must be managed in accordance with relevant privacy and confidentiality legislation and information management and security policies. Procedures prescribed in the Agreement must be followed on every occasion before advertising a vacant position through transfer, promotion, change of work location or redeployment to regions/departments/commands. Only the Chief Commissioner (CCP) or the Chief Commissioner of Police (CCP’s) delegate may approve or reject a recommendation relating to the deployment of a member. Transfer and promotion to advertised positions General provisions This system provides for the filling of vacancies on transfer or promotion for police members, not including reservists. All promotions, except for promotion to senior constable general duties positions, will be made based on merit. Transfers and promotions will occur in accordance with timelines outlined in this policy. Adherence to the selection process, timelines and record keeping for transfer and promotion to advertised positions detailed in this policy, is the responsibility of the relevant region, command, or department head. Transfer or promotion to regions/commands/departments, change of work location and redeployment procedures as prescribed in VPM Redeployment (members) must be followed before advertising vacancies. Except for minimum time-in-position, all qualifications, eligibility criteria and any maximum time-in-position requirements will be contained in the position description. The TPU is responsible for managing the advertisement of positions in accordance with the Act, the Regulations, and the Agreement. Positions other than those subject to an EOI process will be advertised in the Gazette and filled on merit provided there are no suitably qualified members available for redeployment. A position may be advertised prior to a position being vacant, however the appointed member may only take up the position once it is vacant. Transfer and promotion selections will be published in the Gazette, other than positions identified and approved by the CCP or his delegate to be held from publishing for example: intelligence or covert positions. The Deployment Portfolio Manager, RDD, HRC in consultation with the Superintendent RDD, HRC, may withdraw a selection process prior to the selection being gazetted. Eligibility to apply for an advertised position Members must meet the qualifications and eligibility requirements detailed in the relevant position description to be eligible to apply for an advertised position. For members who are not qualified at OSTT, it is accepted that the member will qualify unless there have been previous failures at OSTT or where the member has received final advice of no operational capacity from the PMO. Where a member who is not qualified at OSTT is selected for a position, they must obtain the qualification within 28 days from the date of the selection panel's recommendation unless subject section 7 of VPM Operational safety and tactics training qualifications.
