Review of actions Registrar The Registrar is the nominated person within the Recruitment, Deployment and Workplace Relations Division (RDWRD) responsible for facilitating the formal resolution process (FRP) and providing information and advice to employees and managers on the processes under this policy and how best to resolve review of actions. In performing their functions under this policy, the Registrar must: treat review of actions sensitively, promptly and fairly take all reasonable steps to respect the confidentiality of the people involved observe the rules of natural justice outlined in this policy. Review of actions Registrars will receive diversity and inclusion awareness training pertaining to LGBTQ employees, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, Culturally and Linguistically Diverse people and people with disability. Review of actions review officer The review officer is the appointed independent person who conducts a formal review of the review of actions and makes findings and recommendations to the Registrar. In performing their functions under this policy, the review officer must: treat review of actions sensitively, promptly and fairly take all reasonable steps to respect the confidentiality of the people involved observe the rules of natural justice outlined in this policy conduct the review in an independent and objective manner. The review officer is by appointment, by the Registrar. The appointed independent person will generally be an external party, independent of Victoria Police. The review officer ideally should be able to demonstrate they have received diversity and inclusion awareness training and have active professional memberships in national employer support programs for workplace inclusion, such as Pride in Diversity or the Australian Network on Disability. Informal resolution process General review of actions How to raise a general review of actions If an employee wishes to raise a general review of actions, they must do so by first raising it with their direct manager in writing. In doing so, the employee is to inform the manager that the review of actions is being raised under this policy so that relevant applicable timeframes can be managed. If the employee is unable to raise their general review of actions with their direct manager, the employee should report the matter to their next line manager. If the employee considers it inappropriate to raise their general review of actions with their next line manager, the employee should seek advice from the Registrar. The Registrar will provide information and guidance as to how the review of actions can be resolved, to both the employee and the relevant manager. How to resolve a general review of actions at the local level If the IRP does not resolve the review of actions or is not an appropriate process to resolve the review of actions, the employee and/or their manager/s should contact the Registrar for advice on how to proceed. In some circumstances, the Registrar may suggest that the matter proceed directly to the FRP. Once an employee raises a general review of actions with their direct manager or line manager, they should have an initial meeting with the employee to discuss the review of actions within 10 working days of the employee raising the matter. See the Management Intervention Model – Guide to Assist for the steps to resolution. At the initial meeting, the manager will give the employee a reasonable opportunity to explain: the review of actions how it affects them why they believe the decision or action (or inaction) is unfair or unreasonable in the circumstances the outcome they are seeking. The meeting is to be used to discuss and explore appropriate strategies to resolve the review of actions. Such strategies may include but are not limited to: holding an informal conciliation, the manager having a private conference with the persons named in the employee’s review of actions or a combination of both. During any meeting or conciliation held with employees named in the review of actions, those employees will have an opportunity to respond to the review of actions. During any meeting or conciliation held at any stage of this process, employees and managers may have a support person present. Formal resolution process Delegations The decision-making power with respect to review of actions that are progressed under the FRP is vested in the Chief Commissioner. The Chief Commissioner has delegated certain powers to the Director, RDWRD, to ensure the integrity of the process, this includes the power to accept, reject or vary recommendations made in a review of actions review report issued by a review officer under section 17.2. In accordance with that authority, the Director, RDWRD, has delegated authority to the Registrar to appoint a review officer to conduct a review of actions under section 17. All review of actions are confidential and are subject to the provisions of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 and the Public Records Act 1973. This may include, but is not limited to, copies of policies used to make decisions, witness statements, copies of diary notes from discussions and emails. Assessing the review of actions The Registrar is responsible for assessing the review of actions and determining whether it will be accepted or not. Acceptance of review of actions The Registrar may accept a review of actions application if it is lodged within the prescribed timeframe. The Registrar has discretion to accept a review of actions lodged outside the prescribed timeframe if the Registrar is satisfied the circumstances justify the acceptance of a late application. If the Registrar accepts the application, the review of actions will be managed in accordance with section 16 and the employee will be advised in writing of their decision and, if relevant, the identity of any review officer appointed. Non-acceptance of review of actions The Registrar cannot accept a review of actions application in circumstances including, but not limited to, when: the review of actions relates to a matter listed in section 4 the review of actions is frivolous, vexatious or lacking in substance the employee does not have a sufficient personal interest in the resolution of the review of actions the employee has not specified all the details required to be set out in the Review of Actions Form (see section 14) the matter is the subject of a complaint under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 or a proceeding in any court, commission or tribunal initiated by the applicant the matter could more appropriately be the subject of a complaint under the Equal Opportunity Act or a proceeding in any court, commission or tribunal. If the Registrar does not accept the application, they will inform the employee in writing of that decision and the reasons for that decision within five working days of conducting the assessment. Options for managing the review of actions To progress the review of actions, the Registrar may do any or all of the following, including but not limited to: referring the review of actions to senior management, in the division or department/command, to attempt local resolution of the concerns under the IRP. This will only occur if, in the opinion of the Registrar, reasonable attempts at local resolution have not yet been made and would be appropriate in the circumstances to have been made with the agreement of the parties, appointing an appropriately trained and experienced mediator to mediate a resolution or facilitate a discussion with the relevant parties progressing the matter for review under section 17. Review If the Registrar accepts a review of actions application under this policy and determines that it is a review of actions that should be progressed for review under this part, the review should be conducted with as little formality as a proper consideration of the matter allows. In doing so, the Registrar will: seek management’s response to the review of actions appoint a review officer notify the employee and the manager in writing of the identity of the appointed review officer. If any party has concerns about the identity of the review officer, they must declare those concerns in writing to the Registrar within five working days of receiving advice of the identity of the review officer. The Registrar will only assign a different review officer if the Registrar is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for doing so, including a potential conflict of interest or bias, real or perceived provide the review officer with the employee’s application and supporting documentation, management’s response and any relevant legislation, policies and/or procedures where a formal hearing is deemed appropriate by the review officer, schedule and coordinate the hearing. Review process The review officer must commence the review within 28 calendar days from receipt of the review of actions file from the Registrar. The review officer should advise the employee and the manager of anticipated timelines for completion prior to commencing the review. The review officer may seek further written submissions, background material or other documents from the subject employee and/or manager to assist them in reviewing the review of actions. The review officer may, in order to comply with the rules of natural justice, invite parties subject to a review of actions process to provide a response to any materials submitted by the other party. Once the review officer is satisfied that they have received written submissions and supporting evidence and, if appropriate, responses to those submissions and evidence, the review officer will complete a paper-based assessment of the review of actions. Alternatively, the review officer may deem it appropriate to conduct a formal hearing. In this case, the review officer will seek written submissions through the Registrar from both parties prior to the hearing. Review report At the conclusion of the review process, the review officer must document their findings and recommendations as to the most appropriate resolution of the review of actions in a report to the Registrar. The report must include the: nature of the review of actions findings recommendation(s) rationale for the findings and recommendation(s). The recommendation(s) of the review officer may include recommendations to: confirm the validity of the decision/action vary, reverse or revoke the decision/action request that a decision/action be reconsidered resolve the review of actions in a manner that the review officer considers appropriate amend/update the Victoria Police manual policies and procedures recommence the selection process with an entirely new selection panel (VPS employees only in relation to selection-based review of actions). Review outcome The Registrar must consider the review officer’s report to ensure the review officer has complied with the processes set out in this policy in making their recommendation, and the report contains all necessary information to enable a decision to be made by the delegate as to whether to accept, reject or vary the recommendations made by the review officer. Provided the Registrar is satisfied that the review officer’s report meets the requirements as set out in this policy, the Registrar will provide the report to the Director, RDWRD, to consider the recommendations of the review officer and decide whether to accept, reject or vary the recommendations. All relevant parties, including a management representative (where applicable), will be notified in writing within 14 calendar days of receipt of the report: the recommendations contained in the review officer’s report whether the recommendations have been accepted, rejected or varied a copy of the review officer’s report. Within five working days after receiving confirmation of the outcome from the Registrar, the relevant management representative is expected to: arrange to meet with the employee to plan the way forward, consistent with the recommendation(s) in the review officer’s report implement the recommendations as soon as practicable. If there is an unreasonable delay in implementing the accepted recommendations, the employee should raise this with the relevant management representative in the first instance but may contact the Registrar if the explanation for the delay appears unreasonable. Recommendations rejected or varied If the recommendations from the review report are not to be adopted,

text: to plan the way forward, consistent with the recommendation(s) in the review officer’s report implement the recommendations as soon as practicable. If there is an unreasonable delay in implementing the accepted recommendations, the employee should raise this with the relevant management representative in the first instance but may contact the Registrar if the explanation for the delay appears unreasonable. Recommendations rejected or varied If the recommendations from the review report are not to be adopted, the Director, RDWRD, will provide confirmation of this outcome in writing to the employee and their management, including the Director’s reasons for rejecting or varying the recommendations, together with a copy of the Review Officer’s report. The Director, RDWRD, may only reject or vary a recommendation if they reasonably consider that there are exceptional circumstances justifying that course of action, including but not limited to: where the review officer did not afford natural justice to either party to the review where the review officer’s recommendations are unreasonably burdensome on any party where the Review Officer’s recommendations bear no relation to the review of actions lodged or would otherwise not resolve the review of actions either alone or in combination with other recommendations. Within five working days after receiving confirmation of the outcome, the relevant management representative is expected to: arrange to meet with the employee to plan the way forward, consistent with any of the recommendations as varied implement the varied recommendations as soon as practicable. If there is an unreasonable delay in implementing the varied recommendations, the employee should raise this with the relevant management representative in the first instance but may contact the Registrar if the explanation for the delay appears unreasonable. Further actions Review of the outcome of the review of actions process VPS employee referral A VPS employee may apply to the VPSC for a review of the review of actions process, if the employee considers that the review process: was unfair failed to comply with the Public Administration Act failed to comply with the Public Administration (Review of Actions) Regulations failed to comply with the standards for applying the employment principles. Timelines for applications to the VPSC All applications for review by the VPSC must be lodged in writing within: seven calendar days; after receiving notice of the decision from the Registrar, if the Review of Actions is related to an appointment or promotion 28 calendar days; after receiving notice of the decision from the Registrar, for all other matters. The VPSC may consider applications outside of the above timeframes where circumstances justify acceptance. If an employee lodges a review of actions and Victoria Police fails to commence the initial review process within 30 calendar days from the date of

title: Grievances_VPM_ReviewofactionsGrievance_final
text: notice of the decision from the Registrar, if the Review of Actions is related to an appointment or promotion 28 calendar days; after receiving notice of the decision from the Registrar, for all other matters. The VPSC may consider applications outside of the above timeframes where circumstances justify acceptance. If an employee lodges a review of actions and Victoria Police fails to commence the initial review process within 30 calendar days from the date of receipt of the review of actions application, an employee may apply to the VPSC for a review of that decision review (section 8(1), Public Administration (Review of Actions) Regulations). An employee must lodge their application with the VPSC no later than 70 calendar days from the date of lodgement of the review of actions form with the Registrar. If an employee applies to the VPSC for a review of the internal review of actions process, the employee must provide notice to the Registrar within seven calendar days of submitting the application to the VPSC. Police member referral Police members cannot seek a review of the process by the VPSC. In accordance with clause 11 of the Victoria Police (Police Officers, Protective Services Officers, Police Reservists and Police Recruits) Enterprise Agreement 2019 the PRSB may act as an independent arbitrator for some matters. Rules of natural justice The Registrar and any review officer appointed with the responsibility of assessing or reviewing a review of actions are required to observe the rules of natural justice. Elements of natural justice include: decision makers act fairly and without bias the process and outcome must be as timely as reasonably possible all persons should be informed of the reasons for the decision which affects them all parties to the matter should have the opportunity to present their case, and have the opportunity to respond to any materials submitted all parties should be made aware of all claims made against them and have an opportunity to challenge or contradict such claims all relevant information/evidence provided will be taken into consideration before a decision is made. Employee wellbeing Managers must take responsibility for employee wellbeing and offer assistance to all parties as required and where relevant. Assistance may include the offer of welfare services and counselling and representation as appropriate. text: Honours and awards Context Victoria Police recognises and values outstanding acts and service by employees. A variety of internal and external medals and other awards may be conferred on Victoria Police employees in recognition of special acts, service to the community and to the organisation. Victoria Police may seek to name a physical feature of Victoria Police premises after an individual, individuals or family, or hold memorial events in honour of former employees to recognise and value the distinguished service of an individual, individuals or family, which is significant in the history and development of the organisation. Victoria Police also has a series of awards available to members of the community for assistance in relation to a specific act or service in support of Victoria Police. Policy at a glance This policy includes: nomination and authorisation processes for police members and employees to obtain an honour or award, overseen and maintained by the Honours and Awards Committee minimum criteria, nomination and approval processes for the Public Service Medal (PSM), Australian Police Medal (APM) and National Emergency Medal (NEM) recognitions of service and contributions to community for police members and employees at national and state level information on wearing medals, the processes to replace medals and procedures for naming buildings, facilities or features in honour or recognition procedures for planning memorial events at both the local level and organisation wide. Nomination and authorisation processes - to be granted an honour or award: the employee is either identified or nominated, as required for the specific honour or award the employee must meet the specific eligibility requirements the nomination must be endorsed by the relevant authorised delegate. Nominations and determinations to grant an award or otherwise must be undertaken in a manner consistent with the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and the Victorian Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (the Charter). Recognition of outstanding service (Public Service Medal) Purpose The PSM is awarded in recognition of outstanding public service. In terms of the Australian order of precedence of honours and awards, the PSM is positioned above the APM and the Medal of the Order of Australia. The medal is awarded on Australia Day and the King’s Birthday each year. No more than 17 PSMs are awarded in Victoria each year. Minimum criteria The medal recognises those who have given outstanding public service demonstrated by: service excellence to the public, or to external/internal clients innovation in developing a program, project or policy leadership, including as a member of a team achieving more efficient processes, cost savings, improved products or better service delivery. Nomination and approval process Recognition of distinguished service (Australian Police Medal) Purpose The APM is awarded in recognition of distinguished service by a member of any Australian police force. The APM is part of a collection of meritorious awards created for people providing services for the community, particularly in times of emergency or disaster. The occupations recognised are inherently more hazardous than others, and the awards were established to recognise the meritorious service of people serving in these roles. These medals are solely intended for people whose normal duties require exposure to hazards. The medal is awarded on Australia Day and the King’s Birthday each year. Each Australian police force may award one APM for every 1000 members or part of 1000 members, plus one additional medal for each calendar year. Minimum criteria The medal recognises those who have given distinguished service. This

text: to recognise the meritorious service of people serving in these roles. These medals are solely intended for people whose normal duties require exposure to hazards. The medal is awarded on Australia Day and the King’s Birthday each year. Each Australian police force may award one APM for every 1000 members or part of 1000 members, plus one additional medal for each calendar year. Minimum criteria The medal recognises those who have given distinguished service. This can include: service above and beyond the normal requirements of their position distinguished service on a large-scale investigation demonstration of high integrity outstanding police service to the community contribution to the development and future of policing success in the performance of duty in difficult or unusual circumstances Nomination and approval process National Emergency Medal (Sustained or Significant Service) Purpose The NEM was established to recognise service to others during a national emergency. There are two components – sustained service, and significant service. The Federal Government will formally declare when there is a nationally significant emergency. For example, the bushfires in Victoria in 2009, the 2010-11 Queensland floods and Cyclone Yasi were declared nationally significant emergencies. A list of declared nationally significant emergencies and their eligibility criteria is contained on the Honours and Awards NEM intranet page. Their criteria will need to be considered in conjunction with this policy to determine an employee’s eligibility. Eligibility criteria Sustained service Sustained service must be: in the protection of lives and property in the service of interests that are not their own or in direct response to a nationally significant emergency including support that enables or facilitates the emergency response. This includes action during and/or immediately after an emergency to ensure that its effects are minimised, and that people affected are given immediate relief and support. Refer to NEM Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) on the intranet for the exact eligibility criteria for each declared nationally significant emergency. Significant service Employees may be considered for significant service in response to such emergencies when it appears that they do not meet the sustained service criteria. Significant service may be outside the geographical area established for the declared emergency but should be in the duration period established for the declared emergency. Applications will be presented to the NEM Committee in Canberra for consideration. The Committee will consider whether the person’s service meets all of the following criteria: was part of the response efforts to the nationally significant emergency assisted with the protection of lives and property was extraordinary – service that would be considered above and beyond exceptional, unusual or remarkable in a particular way. Application process Current and former employees Employees should apply for the NEM on either the sustained or significant service application form (see the Honours and Awards intranet site). The application with the Committee’s decision regarding endorsement is forwarded to the region/command/department head. Where the application is not endorsed, the application will still be referred to the Honours and Awards Unit. Region/command/department heads will also notify the applicant of the reasons. Each region, command and department is also responsible for identifying additional employees who may be eligible to be awarded the NEM. Recognition of ethical and diligent service (National Police Service Medal) Purpose The National Police Service Medal (NPSM) is awarded by the Governor General to recognise the special status police members have because of their role in protecting the community. The Letters Patent establishing the NPSM state that the purpose of the medal is to ‘accord recognition for the unique contribution and significant commitment of those persons who have given ethical and diligent service as a sworn police member of an Australian police service’. Minimum criteria Length of service The NPSM may be awarded to police members who have served Victoria Police or other Australian police jurisdictions for a period of 15 years or for periods that, in aggregate, amount to at least 15 years. To be eligible employees must have been serving on or after 14 February 1975. Employees serving on or after 30 October 2008 will automatically be considered for the NPSM (Initial Qualifying Group). Ex-employees who left prior to 30 October 2008 must apply for the NPSM by completing the NPSM Application form available from www.pmc.gov.au/honours-and-symbols/list-australian-honours/national-police-service-medal While a minimum of 15 years’ service is required to qualify for the NPSM, the award represents an employee’s past and future commitment to give ethical and diligent service. It does not represent a distinct period of service. Calculating length of service Service is calculated from

It does not represent a distinct period of service. Calculating length of service Service is calculated from the date an employee is sworn in as a police member. All periods of leave without pay must be deducted from total service accumulated, the only exceptions being: parental leave without pay (up to 52 weeks) if the employee can demonstrate that any leave without pay had a significant link to their position, duties and/or a significant formal study of police related duties. Part time service is treated as full time service. Service with other organisations Service with another organisation will not count as service unless the employee: served as a sworn police member in another Australia Police service continued to serve with Victoria Police whilst at another organisation was on paid leave from Victoria Police or received salary for the period which was ultimately paid by Victoria Police undertook the service at another organisation as a Victoria Police management initiative to further the employee’s professional development served for the period at an organisation within Australia under a staffing interchange agreement between Victoria Police and the other organisation served for the period at an organisation within Australia under an agreement to supply personnel to the other organisation on a temporary rotational basis, to undertake policing or policing related services served at another organisation for the purpose of providing policing or security services in another country e.g., International Deployment undertook the services at another organisation which has otherwise been approved by the CCP as service which may be counted towards the medal. Diligence criteria An employee’s diligence will be assessed by their supervisor and/or other senior manager with regard to their work performance. This assessment involves an objective observation, evaluation and consideration of the employee’s diligent service. Where this assessment identifies performance below an acceptable standard, the issue must be referred to the region/command/department head or Professional Standards Committee who may assess the employee ineligible to receive a medal. Ethical criteria Where any type of offence (criminal or disciplinary) other than those that lead to the employee being dismissed is found proven, the period of ineligibility will be one year. These provisions apply regardless of whether the proven offence was committed while the member was on or off duty. Any employee who is dismissed is permanently ineligible to receive the medal. Impact of incomplete investigation In the case of unresolved or incomplete investigations the matter can be referred to the Honours and Awards Committee for determination on a case-by-case basis. Where an employee retires or resigns whilst under investigation, the employee is deemed permanently ineligible. Impact of suspension Where an employee is currently suspended from duty either with or without pay, the matter can be referred to the Honours and Awards Committee to determine whether to award the NPSM. Consideration of an employee’s eligibility is determined on a case-by-case basis. Where a suspension from duty is rescinded with or without pay, the period of suspension counts towards the total period of service. Periods of service terminated by death, injury or disability The NPSM regulations allow the CCP or delegate to treat periods of service less than 15 years as qualifying for the NPSM under certain conditions. Those conditions are: where a person dies while a member of an Australian police force and, in the opinion of the Commissioner of that police force, the person died as a result of their police service where a person’s service as a police member comes to an end because of an injury or disability sustained, in the Commissioner’s opinion, as a result of their police service. In all cases, the employee must have been serving on or after 14 February 1975 and their service must be assessed as having been ethical and diligent. Nomination and approval process Major Incident Citation Purpose The Major Incident Citation (the Citation) is recognition by the CCP of an employee’s response to a declared major incident. It also acknowledges the unique and unpredictable nature of policing and highlights the significant roles that Victoria Police employees are required to undertake responding to a major incident. Determination of a major incident The CCP, on advice from the Honours and Awards Committee, can declare an incident as being eligible for the Citation by utilising the instrument for declaring a major incident. This can be found on the Honours and Awards intranet site. To assist in determining whether to declare a “major incident”, assessment can be made against a combination of the following: the scale or magnitude of an unplanned event or situation that is beyond the scope of business as usual and involved serious harm, damage, disruption and/or have a significant loss of human life an unplanned event or situation that leads to a significant deployment of Victoria Police resources in responding and that is likely to attract significant media and public interest. The following incidents are a guide only as to the type of incidents that may be considered for the Citation, such

title: Honours_and_Awards_VPM_Honours_and_Awards_final
text: event or situation that is beyond the scope of business as usual and involved serious harm, damage, disruption and/or have a significant loss of human life an unplanned event or situation that leads to a significant deployment of Victoria Police resources in responding and that is likely to attract significant media and public interest. The following incidents are a guide only as to the type of incidents that may be considered for the Citation, such as: a counter terrorism incident mass casualty event such as a significant road or rail disaster. The decision to declare a major incident as being eligible for the Citation will always be an operational decision made by either the Honours and Awards Committee or the CCP on an assessment against the above guide and the intent of the Citation, there are no precise thresholds or triggers. Existing recognition such as the NEM will be utilised in cases of natural disasters such as bushfires. The CCP and Honours and Awards Committee have considered all incidents up to 4 December 2019 to determine which are eligible for the Citation. There will be no retrospectivity for other incidents that occurred prior to 4 December 2019. A list of eligible incidents can be found on the Honours and Awards intranet site. text: Hostile vehicles Context The threat posed to the community by hostile vehicles ranges greatly, from an intentional or reckless criminal act committed by an individual, to a sophisticated, planned multi-mode attack by an individual or group with the intent to cause mass casualties. Any person or group could use a vehicle as a weapon if it suits their objectives of killing or seriously injuring multiple people. It is imperative to the safety of our community that police are able to quickly identify hostile vehicle threats or attacks and respond at the earliest opportunity, while being supported by legislation and policy which recognises that in certain circumstances, extreme action may be required to protect life. That action is supported by the role and general functions of Victoria Police outlined in sections 8 and 9 of the Victoria Police Act 2013. The role of Victoria Police is to serve the Victorian community and uphold the law so as to promote a safe, secure and orderly society (s.8). The functions of Victoria Police include the following: preserving the peace protecting life and property preventing the commission of offences detecting and apprehending offenders helping those in need of assistance (s.9). Contents Context 1 Contents 1 Scope and application 1 Policy 2 Responsibilities and procedures 2 1. Use of force 2 2. Hostile vehicles 2 3. Stopping a hostile vehicle threat / attack 3 4. When does a hostile vehicle threat / attack stop 4 Related documents 5 Further advice and information 5 Update history 5 Scope and application This policy applies to all police officers and protective services officers referred to in this policy instrument as members. It does not apply to pursuits, which must be conducted in line with VPM Pursuits. Policy Hostile vehicles present a significant risk to the safety of both the public and police. In responding to hostile vehicles, members may be required to rapidly assess a threat/attack and act quickly to prevent serious injury and/or death. The intent of this policy is to prevent or minimise the death and serious injury associated with hostile vehicle attacks. This policy sets the criteria for responding to hostile vehicles and how members are to manage the risks involved in order to protect the public and themselves. Any decision that aims to limit the risks to the public, will be viewed as a decision that displays sound professional judgment. Responsibilities and procedures Use of force The use of force, including the use of operational safety equipment or other tactical options, must be in line with VPM Operational safety and the use of force. In accordance with section 462A, Crimes Act 1958 members have the legislative authority to use reasonable force as outlined below:

title: Hostile_vehicles_VPM_Hostile_vehicles_final
text: decision that aims to limit the risks to the public, will be viewed as a decision that displays sound professional judgment. Responsibilities and procedures Use of force The use of force, including the use of operational safety equipment or other tactical options, must be in line with VPM Operational safety and the use of force. In accordance with section 462A, Crimes Act 1958 members have the legislative authority to use reasonable force as outlined below: A person may use such force not disproportionate to the objective as he believes on reasonable grounds to be necessary to prevent the commission, continuance or completion of an indictable offence or to effect or assist in effecting the lawful arrest of a person committing or suspected of committing any offence. Example A police officer or protective services officer uses lethal force on a person to prevent that person from committing an indictable offence that involves causing really serious injury or death because the officer believes on reasonable grounds that it is necessary to use that force for that purpose. The police officer or protective services officer may do so before that offence is committed. Hostile vehicles What is a hostile vehicle threat A hostile vehicle threat occurs where the driver of a vehicle uses it to access or encroach upon an area where the circumstances indicate an intention or recklessness to cause really serious injury and/or death, or additional information about a hostile vehicle indicates an impending attack including: emerging information or intelligence overt acts by the driver/occupants at the time statements of intent (pre-recorded videos, social media posts, texts or phone calls). What is a hostile vehicle attack A hostile vehicle attack occurs when a hostile vehicle is being used or controlled as a primary weapon in a deliberate or reckless attack to cause really serious injury and/or death and continues while there is access to victims. Most likely targets of an attack The most likely targets of hostile vehicle attacks are: spaces occupied by a large group of people at a particular time, (termed crowded places), where the aim of an attack is to intentionally or recklessly cause really serious injury and/or death to large numbers of people infrastructure that is of high significance for social, political or economic reasons and which may be structurally affected or destroyed by a vehicle attack. This is not an exhaustive list. Members must be aware that an attack could occur anytime/anywhere. Significant security event A hostile vehicle attack meets the criteria of a Significant Security Event (SSE) and notification of the incident must be in line with section 7 VPM Emergency management response. Any use of the Emergency Alert public warning system must be in

title: Hostile_vehicles_VPM_Hostile_vehicles_final
text: or economic reasons and which may be structurally affected or destroyed by a vehicle attack. This is not an exhaustive list. Members must be aware that an attack could occur anytime/anywhere. Significant security event A hostile vehicle attack meets the criteria of a Significant Security Event (SSE) and notification of the incident must be in line with section 7 VPM Emergency management response. Any use of the Emergency Alert public warning system must be in line with section 8 VPM Emergency management response. Stopping a hostile vehicle threat / attack Primary objective The primary objective when responding to a hostile vehicle threat or attack is to stop the vehicle/stop the attack. Interdiction Vehicle interdiction is the intentional stopping of a hostile vehicle through the use of force or other means. For further information about vehicle interdiction tactical options see section 3.5. Responding to a hostile vehicle threat At the threat stage, members must identify and assess the threat against the risk to the public. Once identified as a hostile vehicle threat, immediate action must be taken to prevent the incident from progressing to an attack. The operational response to a hostile vehicle threat must be proportionate to the threat and if time permits, planned with the assistance of a supervisor, other members or specialist police resources. If time does not permit a planned response, members must take immediate action. Members should consider the interdiction tactical options. Responding to a hostile vehicle attack Similar to the response to an Active Armed Offender (AAO), members must respond immediately and decisively to an active hostile vehicle attack in order to bring the incident to a rapid conclusion by: taking charge. Regardless of rank, the senior member must take charge as police forward commander, manage the incident and provide leadership until relieved immediately moving available resources towards the vehicle to stop the attack responding with action which is rapid, not reckless. Members must consider: the possibility of a multi-mode attack (initial vehicle attack, transitioning to knife or gun attack on foot). The attack may not stop when the vehicle does the possibility of multiple offenders and/or multiple attacks/incidents which could be co-ordinated that the attack may be well planned and could involve a planned action in response to police action. notifying Police Communications: identify the incident as a hostile vehicle attack request back up, supervisor, additional and specialist resources provide any known details of the incident. reducing the area of operations by positioning back up units, but not at the expense of intercepting and stopping the hostile vehicle attack isolating the vehicle/offender from potential victims. Move civilians away from the threat with direct instructions starting to formulate a plan. An Incident Action Plan should

text: action. notifying Police Communications: identify the incident as a hostile vehicle attack request back up, supervisor, additional and specialist resources provide any known details of the incident. reducing the area of operations by positioning back up units, but not at the expense of intercepting and stopping the hostile vehicle attack isolating the vehicle/offender from potential victims. Move civilians away from the threat with direct instructions starting to formulate a plan. An Incident Action Plan should be used if the situation allows providing active leadership during and after a hostile vehicle attack. Vehicle interdiction tactical options All tactical options considered or used must be in line with s.462A, the operational response principles of Service, Safety and Harm Minimisation, and VPM Operational safety and the use of force. Interdiction tactical options may involve the use of a police vehicle (stationary or mobile), other objects or vehicle(s) to stop the hostile vehicle. Damage to vehicles caused during interdiction is a secondary consideration to the safety of the public. If the circumstances warrant the action, members may use lethal force against the driver of a hostile vehicle in order to stop an attack. See VPM Operational safety and the use of force for further information in relation to the tactical options model. When does a hostile vehicle threat / attack stop The hostile vehicle threat/attack may not stop when the vehicle stops. Depending upon the operational circumstances, a hostile vehicle threat/attack can be a continuing and/or evolving event, which may not necessarily conclude when the known threat/attack has been stopped. Members must maintain their situational awareness as a hostile vehicle attack may not be an isolated or final incident. It is the responsibility of the Police Forward Commander to declare the completion of the hostile vehicle threat/attack, once sufficient information is known/after consultation with specialist resources. text: Information categorisation, collection and recording Context Public confidence in the ability of Victoria Police to collect and manage all information effectively, including personal, sensitive and classified material, requires the application of the highest standards in information management practices which govern information confidentiality, integrity and availability. The key to Victoria Police’s ability to comply with the myriad of legislative and regulatory information requirements, as well as the ability to achieve operational goals, is how information is collected and recorded. This affects the organisation’s ability to effectively use, share, review, retain and dispose of information, as well as the ability to protect this information from unauthorised access or misuse. The primary legal source of Victoria Police’s information management obligations is the Public Records Office of Victoria (PROV) Standards. The standards and supporting specifications developed by PROV apply to all Victoria Police information and detail requirements for the creation, maintenance and security of public records including the selection and disposal of public records not worthy of preservation. Records include all law enforcement data systems, corporate or other data repositories, archives and computer systems and the term is not limited to hardcopy records. The primary legal source of Victoria Police’s information security obligations is the Commissioner for Privacy and Data Protection (CPDP) Standards for law enforcement data security (SLEDS)(2014). The Standards developed by CPDP outline necessary controls for the secure management of law enforcement data systems and the information they contain. Law enforcement data systems include all relevant data repositories and the term is not limited to computer systems. All information collected or created by Victoria Police employees is an organisational resource that must be appropriately managed, regardless of the format (electronic or hardcopy) or media (notebook, DVD, USB, intranet/internet, file). This information is referred to as Law Enforcement Data or Victoria Police information. This policy provides the Victoria Police rules for the appropriate management of information, in line with the Victoria Police Information Management Principles, the Australian Government Protective Security Policy Framework (PSPF) and the Australian Government Information security manual (ISM), for the first two stages of the information management lifecycle. Responsibilities and procedures Information categories All information developed, received or collected by or on behalf of Victoria Police must be assessed for confidentiality and security controls. Victoria Police information is categorised as either: public domain information, or official information. 1.1 Public domain informantion Public domain information is official Victoria Police information that has been authorised for unlimited public release and circulation in accordance with VPMP Information sharing. 1.2 Official information Official information is material that has not been authorised for release into the public domain. Official information deemed personal and/or health related, must be managed in accordance with relevant legislation, including the Information Privacy Principles of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 and Health Privacy Principles of the Health Records Act 2001. Refer to VPMG Information privacy. Even if an individual's personal and/or health information has been disclosed into the public domain, either by another party or by Victoria Police for a permitted purpose, Victoria Police must still manage the information it holds. Any further disclosure of this information must be in accordance with the Privacy and Data Protection Act and/or Health Records Act. The Victoria Police Privacy Information Sharing Guide provides guidance on appropriate sharing of personal and health information. 1.3 Unofficial information Information that is not related to Victoria Police activities, such as a personal email, is categorised as unofficial information. This information should be removed from the workplace, destroyed or stored separately to official information. Use of Victoria Police resources for unofficial information is only permitted in accordance with Code of Conduct - Professional and ethical standards and VPMP Appropriate use of information. The five levels are as follows: 0) INSIGNIFICANT – Negligent or nil risk 1) LIMITED – Low-medium impact 2) MAJOR – High level of harm or disruption 3) SERIOUS – Impacts on national and state security 4) EXCEPTIONALLY GRAVE – Catastrophic damage to the national interest. 2.2 Guide The Protective Security guide – G200 – Assessment and handling of Victoria Police Information provides guidance on using the BIL table and identifies the appropriate level of impact which informs the appropriate PM. The following is an overview of PMs relative to the BIL table. Protective markings Definition PMs are labels which must be placed on all Victoria Police documents and assets. The PM to be applied is determined as a result of business impact level assessment. PMs are assigned to each item of information to outline the method of handling that is required in order to protect against unauthorised use. Use of a PMs enables information sharing and ensures compliance. Types of Protective Markings include UNCLASSIFIED, Dissemination Limiting Markers (DLM) and Security Classifications (SC) and Caveats. Compliance with security conditions Adherence to VPM policy rules, associated guidelines and procedures will ensure that normal operational and business activities comply with requirements provided in the SLEDS, PSPF and ISM. Protective Security guides and factsheets (see Protective Security guide – G200 – Assessment and handling of Victoria Police Information in the first instance) detail the standard security controls or handling requirements for the relevant PMs. After a risk assessment is conducted regarding the circumstances of particular document or assest, additional controls or controls applicable to a higher or lower PM may be necessary. Advice should be sought from Protective Security for any new or unusual process or situation. However, variations to the controls may be required in certain circumstances, such as: Managing identified risk. text: Victoria Police Manual – Policy Rules Information review, retention and disposal Context Public confidence in the ability of the Victoria Police to collect and manage all information effectively, including personal, sensitive and classified material, requires the application of the highest standards in information management practices which govern information confidentiality, integrity and availability. The retention, transfer or destruction of Victoria Police information in line with legislative and regulatory requirements is complex and can create significant risks and liabilities for Victoria Police and individuals. The primary legal source of Victoria Police’s information management obligations is the Public Records Office of Victoria (PROV) Standards. The standards and supporting specifications developed by PROV apply to all Victoria Police information and detail requirements for the creation, maintenance and security of public records including the selection and disposal of public records not worthy of preservation. Records include all law enforcement data systems, corporate or other data repositories, archives and computer systems and are not limited to hardcopy records. The primary legal source of Victoria Police’s information security obligations is the Commissioner for Privacy and Data Protection (CPDP) Standards for law enforcement data security (2007). The 43 Standards developed by CPDP outline necessary controls for the secure management of law enforcement data systems and the information they contain. Law enforcement data systems include all relevant data repositories and are not limited to computer systems. It is an offence under the Crimes Act 1958 for individuals or organisations to destroy documents that they know are reasonably likely to be required in a future legal proceeding, with the intention of keeping the documents out of evidence. It is also an offence under the Public Records Act 1973, to unlawfully destroy a public record. This policy provides the Victoria Police rules for the appropriate retention, destruction or transfer of information, in line with the Victoria Police Information Management Principles, the Public Records Office of Victoria (PROV) Standards the Australian Government protective security policy framework (PSPF), the Australian Government Information security manual (ISM) and the Standards for Law Enforcement Data Security (SLEDS). Application Policy Rules are mandatory and provide the minimum standards that an employee must apply. Non-compliance with or a departure from a Policy Rule may be subject to management or disciplinary action. Employees must use the Professional and Ethical Standards to inform the decisions they make to support compliance with Policy Rules. These Policy Rules apply to all Authorised Users of Victoria Police information. Rules and Responsibilities Review All information must be reviewed and assessed regularly to facilitate ongoing use, retention and disposal requirements. These Policy Rules apply to all Authorised Users of Victoria Police information. Rules and Responsibilities Review All information must be reviewed and assessed regularly to facilitate ongoing use, retention and disposal requirements. Review of security classification The originator (or originating unit) of any Victoria Police security classified information must review its classification regularly and consider declassification of the information. This can occur at: a date nominated by the information originator (when appropriate) a suitable milestone, such as the completion of an operation, investigation, project or prosecution regular set dates as per local instructions when the material is being accessed or used, yet is still marked with a legacy classification (as per the old Protective Security Manual). Refer to Protective Security Guide – G200 – Assessment and handling of Victoria Police Information for further advice. At a minimum, security classified information must be assessed for declassification every 10 years. Under no circumstances can a security classification or caveat be altered or removed without the authority of the originator (or originating unit). If an Authorised User believes that material is marked inappropriately, they are encouraged to contact the originator to discuss the security classification. If the originator or originating unit cannot be located, or is no longer the Information Owner (refer to VPMG Information management and information security roles and responsibilities), the Command position currently responsible for the function or activity related to the information, is responsible for reclassification approval. In accordance with VPMP Information categorisation, collection and recording, all hardcopy records must be retained in hardcopy format until authorised for destruction in accordance with this policy, even if a scanned copy is made. Scanned copies can be deleted as duplicate information. Duplicate information and non-records can be disposed of without authorisation as part of normal administrative practice. Identifying inactive official information Work Unit Managers must ensure that: official information determined to be inactive (information that is no longer being worked on or referred to for current activities) is transferred from the workplace through regular reviews local procedures require all inactive hardcopy information to be either: transferred to VPASC for retention identified for potential destruction. local procedures require inactive digital information on shared drives, any removable media or personal directories to be either: transferred onto DVD (or other suitable archival storage media under advice from Protective Security) and sent to the VPASC for retention printed and incorporated into a hardcopy filing system identified for potential destruction. Retention PROV has set minimum retention timeframes for all public records through Retention and Disposal Authorities (RDAs). The minimum retention periods are based on the content and context of the information, not the format in which it is held. All Victoria Police information, regardless of the format (electronic or hardcopy) or media (notebook, document, database, dvd, usb, intranet/internet, file), must be retained as a public record until it: reaches the minimum retention period and has been authorised for destruction by an appointee under IM 6. Inactive Victoria Police information that has a minimum retention period of seven (7) years or less, can remain under the responsibility of the Work Unit until it is authorised for destruction. Consideration should be given to transferring inactive information material to VPASC where possible. Inactive Victoria Police information that has a minimum retention period of eight (8) years or more must be transferred to VPASC. The only exclusions to this requirement are: information security classified at SECRET or TOP SECRET an external agency’s information. Information in these categories must be retained by the Work Unit until authorised for destruction or returned to the originating agency. System Owners must ensure that information held within official systems is regularly archived or transferred to a format that complies with the PROV Victorian Electronic Records Strategy (VERS) for retention in accordance with the RDAs. Advice on VERS compliance can be obtained from Protective Security. Disposal Disposal of Victoria Police information can occur through two methods – secure destruction or transfer to PROV by VPASC. Additional controls are required around the destruction of protectively marked information, due to the potential for compromise through inappropriate handling or destruction. Any disposal of official information must be conducted in accordance with the Public Records Act 1973. Victoria Police must be able to provide evidence of when and why any records were deleted or destroyed. Work unit manager responsibilities Work Unit Managers are responsible for: arranging a transfer plan with VPASC for any inactive official information (either digital or hardcopy) that is a permanent or long term record under the RDAs (see VPMG Information and information equipment disposal) ensuring the destruction process is completed and authorised ensuring the destruction process meets the minimum requirements for non-public domain or classified material and the type of medium holding the information. Transfer to PROV Victoria Police information must only be transferred to PROV by the VPASC. See VPMG Information and information equipment disposal. Criteria for Destruction Work Unit Managers must confirm that information meets all of the following criteria, prior to seeking approval for destruction of Victoria Police information: it is covered by a current RDA it is not a permanent record under the RDA (see 3.1) the minimum timeframe for retention under the RDA has elapsed it is unlikely to be required as evidence in any future court proceedings it is unlikely to be requested under FOI it does not have any historic significance to Victoria Police or the greater Victorian Community. Authorisation Once the criteria for destruction have been met for digital or hardcopy information, a Record Destruction Request [VP Form 1455] (available from the Protective Security intranet site) must be completed and submitted to an appointee under IM 6 for authorisation. Damage or unauthorised destruction Damage or unplanned destruction can be caused by issues such as, but not limited to, infestation, flood, fire, mould, contamination, vandalism or accident. Should any Victoria Police information suffer damage or be destroyed without authorisation, the Victoria Police Archive Storage Centre (VPASC) must be contacted as soon as possible. Should the damage or unauthorised destruction also be a breach of security (i.e. it was not caused by a natural occurrence) then it must also be reported as a security incident in accordance with VPMP Security incident management and reporting. The VPASC can provide advice on how to handle affected records, possible restoration or recovery, and the process for recording the destruction of records. Should destroyed or damaged information be requested, for example through FOI or legal proceedings, employees must be able to provide a copy of the VPASC record of the unplanned damage or destruction to the requestor. Employees working offsite must ensure that all Victoria Police information is returned to Victoria Police premises for destruction unless they have approved destruction equipment located off-site. text: Victoria Police Manual – Policy Rules Information sharing Context Effective policing relies on Victoria Police to communicate and share information internally and with a wide range of external partners. Information sharing: can help to deliver improved public services leads to an increased openness among partners, which, in turn builds confidence and trust in Victoria Police is a two-way process that enables links to be made between people, objects, location and events that would not be possible otherwise enables partners to make informed decisions about how best to protect the public. However, sharing must always be justified through legislation or a genuine policing requirement and must occur through approved and/or legal avenues to ensure that the disclosure is appropriate and legitimate. Consideration must also be given to the maintenance of broader security and privacy principles when sharing information. Inappropriate sharing could result in serious consequences for Victoria Police and the public including loss of life, denial of access to information sources or failure of prosecutions. Victoria Police regards breaches or violations of this policy and/or the misuse of its information resources and privileges as particularly serious and may lead to disciplinary consequences, and possible charges under sections 227 and 228 of the Victoria Police Act 2013. The Information sharing policy provides the Victoria Police rules for the appropriate release or disclosure of information, in line with the Victoria Police Information Management Principles, the Public Records Office of Victoria (PROV) Standards, the Australian Government Protective Security Policy Framework (PSPF), the Australian Government Information security manual (ISM) and the Standards for Law Enforcement Data Security (SLEDS). A member or former member of Victoria Police personnel has a duty to only access, use, or disclose police information (as defined in the Victoria Police Act), which they have a demonstrable and legitimate need for, and which arises from and is directly related to the performance of their current duties or functions. This is a mandatory duty created in accordance with the Chief Commissioner's powers under the Victoria Police Act. Failure to act in accordance with this duty, breaches or violations of this policy, and/or the misuse of information, resources and privileges are particularly serious and may lead to management or disciplinary action, or charges under ss. 227 and 228 of the Victoria Police Act. Application Policy Rules are mandatory and provide the minimum standards that employees must apply. Non-compliance with or a departure from a Policy Rule may be subject to management or disciplinary action. Employees must use the Professional and Ethical Standards to inform the decisions they make to support compliance with Policy Rules. Audio/Visual recordings of interviews or events may be viewed by participants, but should not be available for download. Reference to showing the footage is to be included as part of the records of the training presentation/content. Where possible, consent is to be obtained for the use of the recordings, or the individual’s image is to be pixelated. text: Freedom of Information (FOI) FOI supports the principles of open and accountable government by providing the public with a right to access information held by the public sector, including the right to access and update their personal information. Limitations are imposed on this right to protect public, personal and commercial interests. The presence or absence of protective markings (in the form of Disseminating Limiting Markers or Security Classifications) does not affect a document’s status under the FOI Act. On receipt of a request from the FOI office, personnel must make a diligent search and supply all documents or information requested within the required timeframe. Information must not be edited before being given to the FOI office. It is the responsibility of the FOI office to apply the various exemption provisions within the FOI Act. The legislated timeframe for processing standard FOI requests is 30 days. Requests for documents will be sent electronically to employees and their Work Unit Manager for actioning. The responding employee must: ensure a response is provided within four calendar days from the date the request was sent send the response, including required documents, electronically to PBEA: FOI-DOCUMENTS-MGR contact the FOI Unit for advice where materials cannot be provided within the required timeframe (for example; where the file cannot be sent electronically or due to rostering constraints or issues with retrieving the documents). The Work Unit Manager is responsible for providing a response, as per the above process, where the employee is not available within the required timeframe. If the responding employee cannot locate any of the requested documents a confirmation email must be sent to the FOI Unit detailing the searches undertaken and any reasons why the document/s cannot be located. Where documents cannot be located due to the unavailability of the responding employee the Work Unit Manager must reply to the FOI Unit detailing why the documents cannot be located and the expected return of the member. If the requested information has been destroyed the employee is to provide a copy of the destruction authorisation in accordance with VPMP Information review, retention and disposal. If the requested information existed but is unable to be located, a security incident should be reported in accordance with VPMP Protective security incident reporting and management. Further guidance on the FOI process for Victoria Police is provided on the FOI intranet pages, which includes FOI Instructions and FOI FAQs. Release of information into the public domain Victoria Police may release information of public interest into the Public Domain. Whilst a significant amount of information held by Victoria Police is not suitable for public release, Information Owners should identify datasets or other information that may be suitable for public access. text: Victoria Police Manual – Policy Rules Information use, handling and storage Context Public confidence in the ability of the Victoria Police to manage all information effectively, including personal, sensitive and classified material, requires the application of the highest standards in information management practices which govern information confidentiality, integrity and availability. The primary legal source of Victoria Police’s information management obligations is the Public Records Office of Victoria (PROV) Standards. The standards and supporting specifications developed by PROV apply to all Victoria Police information and detail requirements for the creation, maintenance and security of public records including the selection and disposal of public records not worthy of preservation. Records include all law enforcement data systems, corporate or other data repositories, archives and computer systems and the term is not limited to hardcopy records. The primary legal source of Victoria Police’s information security obligations is the Commissioner for Privacy and Data Protection (CPDP) Standards for law enforcement data security (2014). The Standards developed by CPDP outline necessary controls for the secure management of law enforcement data systems and the information they contain. Law enforcement data systems include all relevant data repositories and the term is not limited to computer systems. This instrument provides the Victoria Police rules for the appropriate management of information, in line with the above requirements, the Victoria Police Information Management Principles, the Australian Government Protective Security Policy Framework (PSPF) and the Australian Government Information security manual (ISM). Application Policy Rules are mandatory and provide the minimum standards that employees must apply. Non-compliance with or a departure from a Policy Rule may be subject to management or disciplinary action. Employees must use the Professional and Ethical Standards to inform the decisions they make to support compliance with Policy Rules. These Policy Rules apply to Authorised Users of Victoria Police information. Rules and Responsibilities Information Use Principles Victoria Police information use should occur in line with the Victoria Police information Management principles: Use of Victoria Police information supports business processes and functions and must only be used for official purposes. All Authorised Users are responsible for the security of Victoria Police information that they access or hold. Victoria Police information will be analysed and risk assessed for its accuracy, value and sensitivity. This analysis and assessment must: determine actions identify priorities identify links with other Victoria Police information recorded elsewhere identify any inherent risks. Appropriate use of Victoria Police information In accordance with VPMP Appropriate use of information, Authorised Users: must only access and use Victoria Police information where they have a demonstrable, legitimate business need which is directly related to the performance of their current duties with Victoria Police are responsible for the security of Victoria Police information that

Physical and environmental considerations In accordance with VPMP Information access, Authorised Users must ensure that all non public domain information is physically protected from viewing, hearing or access by persons that do not have approval to access the information. Prior to the use of protectively marked Victoria Police information, Authorised Users are to critically assess their work area. This assessment must be based on the minimum security controls for the classification level of the information. The Authorised User should assess if the area is appropriate to: protect Victoria Police information from oversight, or overhearing (audio secure) by other people securely store Victoria Police information within the work area securely store any information communication technology equipment on which Victoria Police information will be accessed and/or contained. As far as practicable within a facility, Work Unit Managers are to ensure that photocopiers, fax machines, shredders, and printers are located in areas where activity cannot be conducted unobserved. Information communication technology (ICT) considerations In accordance with VPMP Appropriate use of information, Authorised Users must not take unacceptable risks in the transfer and storage of information. Victoria Police information must not be stored or transmitted using internet based systems or accounts unless specifically authorised by the Information Management Committee and/or VPM policy. In accordance with VPMP Information categorisation, collection and recording, legacy classified information that is being actively used, should be reclassified against the new classification scheme (which aligns to the PSPF) and marked appropriately. Inactive legacy classified information does not need to be reassessed. There is not a direct correlation between legacy markings and current markings. text: Recording devices, CCTV and digital asset management Context This policy supports Victoria Police compliance with the Victorian Protective Data Security Standards (VPDSS) and the Public Records Office of Victoria standards. This policy also supports Victoria Police’s compliance with the Australian Government Protective Security Policy Framework and the Information Security Manual, which describe the minimum standards for physical and information security for all Federal and State government agencies. A recording device (RD) generates digital assets, such as footage, images and audio files, which are relied on for investigations and public order management. Digital assets can be generated by Victoria Police and lawfully obtained from external sources. Policy at a glance This policy includes: definitions and examples of RDs and digital assets the responsibilities of Victoria Police employees regarding the use of RDs and the handling of digital assets guidance regarding the generation and management of copies of digital assets human rights considerations for the placement of RDs in public places. CCTV 8 Related documents 9 Further advice and information 10 Update history 10 Definitions Closed circuit television (CCTV) - a television system in which broadcasts are not publicly distributed but are monitored for surveillance and/or security purposes. Digital Asset – audio recordings, still images, video and/or audio files that have been generated by a RD. Other types of digital assets are not included in this policy. Non-rewritable media – storage media on which data cannot be overwritten (e.g., CD-/+R, DVD-/+R). Original copy – the first instance in which images and/or audio is recorded on to non-rewritable media, preferably directly generated from the primary source, obtained by police. Recording device – any device capable of, and used to, generate digital assets, such as digital imagery (e.g., footage and still images), audio-visual and/or audio files. RDs include, but are not limited to: mobile phones portable or personal computing devices video or still cameras (tripod/equipment mounted or handheld) audio recorders (digital or analogue) CCTV (including mobile CCTV trailers). Primary source – the system or device that the digital asset was originally generated by. This may be a RD, the physical box containing recording equipment that is installed at a site (such as a business, local council or station) or an email/website that allows Victoria Police to obtain the digital asset. Working copy – any copy produced from the original for the purpose of converting and editing. Scope and application This policy applies to all employees. Some RDs and digital assets managed by Victoria Police are subject to alternative legislation or policy which takes precedence over this policy to the extent of any differences. RDs and digital assets excluded from this policy include: devices used for approved covert police operations or surveillance (refer to VPMP Investigation support and VPMG Surveillance devices) devices used for discreet or covert online investigation and intelligence gathering (refer to VPM Official online activities and VPM Assumed identities and online personas) Victoria Police-issued body worn cameras (BWCs) (refer to VPM Body worn cameras) Victoria Police-issued In-Car Video (refer to VPM Road policing - general) a recording device attached to a conducted energy device (CED) (refer to VPM Conducted energy devices) Digital Evidence Capture (DEC) recording equipment (refer to VPM Interviews and Statements) digitally recorded evidence-in-chief (DREC) captured using BWCs following a family violence incident (refer to VPM Digitally recorded evidence-in-chief (DREC) – family violence) forensic samples taken and any related material and information addressed by the s.464ZG(3), Crimes Act 1958 (refer to VPM Forensic procedures and VPM Fingerprinting) protected information as defined under s.30D, Surveillance Devices Act 1999, restricted records as defined under s.3, Telecommunications (Interception) (State Provisions) Act 1988 and stored communications as defined under s.3, Telecommunications (Interception) (State Provisions) Act 1988 (refer to VPMP Investigation support). Responsibilities and procedures Recording devices Use of Victoria Police-issued recording devices The personal use of a RD is subject to VPM Appropriate use of information and VPMG Portable computing devices. Victoria Police-issued RDs must not be connected to non-Victoria Police networks or information and communications technology (ICT) equipment, unless essential for operational purposes. When connected to a non-Victoria Police network, the RD must be scanned for viruses prior to downloading or accessing any digital assets contained on the RD. Refer to VPMP Information access for further guidance. All Victoria Police-issued RDs must be returned to Digital Services and Security Department (DSSD) at
