Victoria Police-issued RDs must not be connected to non-Victoria Police networks or information and communications technology (ICT) equipment, unless essential for operational purposes. When connected to a non-Victoria Police network, the RD must be scanned for viruses prior to downloading or accessing any digital assets contained on the RD. Refer to VPMP Information access for further guidance. All Victoria Police-issued RDs must be returned to Digital Services and Security Department (DSSD) at the end of their useful life (e.g. if the device is faulty), to ensure that: all digital assets contained on the RD are properly erased the RD is disposed of in accordance with ICT equipment disposal standards. Refer to VPMP Information review, retention and disposal for further guidance. Suspected loss or theft of a recording device If a Victoria Police-issued RD is suspected lost or stolen, employees must immediately notify: their supervisor and the Security Incident Registry, Protective Security, DSSD in line with VPMP Protective security incident reporting and management. Overt use and deployment of recording devices Use of recording devices Only fixed and portable DEC units should be used to record formal interviews with a suspect for an indictable offence in accordance with VPM Interviews and statements. Employees should refer to the Forensic Guides for advice on collection of evidence at a crime scene. RD audio or video recordings of operational activities should commence on deployment to an incident and continue uninterrupted until the incident is concluded. Recording may be stopped: in cases of a sensitive nature when no longer necessary or appropriate. A record must be made of why audio or video recordings were stopped, interrupted, or failed. Employees must use established methods of note taking in accordance with VPM Operational duties and responsibilities and remain mindful of standard evidence gathering procedures at scenes. RDs should not be relied upon for all note taking or evidence as: some aspects of incidents that are vital to the evidence for the offence may occur out of camera view or audio range sound recordings may not be complete other sounds may block significant statements by those present technical failures or operator errors may hinder the production of the recorded evidence. Employees must give caution and rights when appropriate in accordance with VPM Interviews and statements. Employees must advise individuals that recording of their interaction is occurring, unless impractical or unsafe to do so. Placement of recording devices in public places The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities All employees must consider and act compatibly with human rights in their decisions and actions in accordance with the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006. text: VPM Interviews and statements. Employees must advise individuals that recording of their interaction is occurring, unless impractical or unsafe to do so. Placement of recording devices in public places The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities All employees must consider and act compatibly with human rights in their decisions and actions in accordance with the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006. Considerations for the deployment of portable recording devices in public places The deployment of RDs in public places must only occur: using Victoria Police-issued RD equipment and where any human rights impacts are justified and proportionate, regardless of whether CCTV or other RDs are or are reasonably known to have been operating in the same area. Contact information for the responsible person or station must be affixed to the RD if it is left unattended (e.g. a mobile CCTV trailer deployed in a public place). The physical placement of a RD that is to be left unattended should: record only the area that is necessary not record audio not record any part of a person’s private accommodation (e.g., balcony or windows of a private residence or hotel) where doing so can be reasonably avoided. Where the physical placement of a RD is likely to record private activities conducted in a public location, impact on a person’s right to privacy must still be justified and proportionate, regardless of whether other CCTV equipment is operating in the same area. Refer to VPM Human rights standards for further guidance or contact the Human Rights Portfolio Manager, Priority and Safer Communities Division, Capability Department for advice. Covert use and deployment of recording devices RDs must not be used covertly, or to obtain covert recordings unless this is in accordance with VPMP Investigation support and VPMG Surveillance devices. The use of a RD by an employee to covertly record a conversation between themselves and another employee, in a non‐operational context, is not permitted. Handling of Recordings All digital assets generated using RDs are official Victoria Police records and must be handled in accordance with VPMP Information use, handling and storage. Recordings must be uploaded in full. Partial upload, and/or the altering or editing of recordings prior to upload (such as deleting, cropping, or redacting footage) is prohibited. Original copy Obtaining or creating an original copy When an employee obtains or creates a digital asset from a system or other device in support of a crime investigation or as a record of police activities: An exact copy of the information must be obtained or created from the primary source. Wherever possible this should be on Victoria Police-issued non-rewritable media. Note that DVD-/+RW or CD-/+RW are not suitable as they can be overwritten. This

text: Original copy Obtaining or creating an original copy When an employee obtains or creates a digital asset from a system or other device in support of a crime investigation or as a record of police activities: An exact copy of the information must be obtained or created from the primary source. Wherever possible this should be on Victoria Police-issued non-rewritable media. Note that DVD-/+RW or CD-/+RW are not suitable as they can be overwritten. This must be treated as the original copy. When unable to use Victoria Police-issued non-rewritable media, only a Victoria Police-issued Universal Serial Bus (USB) or other appropriate device (see VPMG Obtaining IT equipment and services) may be used. Footage must be transferred to non-rewritable media as soon as possible and deleted from the rewritable device once it has been confirmed that the copy was successful. If the footage is too large to capture on non-rewritable media, contact the Audio Visual Unit (AVU), Forensic Services Department for assistance or advice. If the AVU advises that rewritable media has to be used to create or retain the original copy it is the investigating member’s responsibility to ensure that the media is protected from editing and/or erasure. No conversion or editing is to be conducted on the original copy. The original copy must be suitably labelled. Refer to the Closed Circuit Television Practice Guide for guidance on labelling. Obtaining primary source recording If the primary source records directly onto removable storage media (e.g. Secure Digital (SD) memory card) and this item is obtained by the investigating member: Volunteered Property - this item can be treated in line with the requirements for an original copy, however creation of an original copy on non-rewritable media is recommended Seized Property - an original copy on non-rewritable media must be made and the requirements of VPM Seized property and special property types and VPM Property and exhibit management apply to the seized item. Contact AVU to book their self-serve dubbing rack facility. Categorisation and classification of information The original copy must be assessed by the investigating or creating employee to determine the appropriate protective marking and potential use of the information, having regard to the Information Privacy Principles (Schedule 1 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014) and Health Privacy Principles (Schedule 1 of the Health Records Act 2001). Refer to VPM Information categorisation, collection and recording and VPMG Information privacy. The original copy of the digital asset may be retained as a record of official duty, used as evidence and/or retained for intelligence purposes. It may be determined that the digital asset is to be retained as intelligence when first received/created or when it is no longer required as evidence. Recording

The original copy of the digital asset may be retained as a record of official duty, used as evidence and/or retained for intelligence purposes. It may be determined that the digital asset is to be retained as intelligence when first received/created or when it is no longer required as evidence. Recording and storage All units/stations that handle digital assets must maintain an appropriate register of the digital assets. The original copy must be recorded in the register. Refer to the Closed Circuit Television Practice Guide for guidance on suitable registers. For an incident recorded on LEAP, the existence of the digital asset and the storage location of the original copy should be noted in the LEAP narrative for the incident. If the digital asset is to be retained for intelligence purposes, a record should be made in Interpose. The record should include where the original copy is stored. Video and audio files must not be uploaded into Interpose. Sharing The original copy must always be held securely and must not be shared when a working copy will suffice. Retention and destruction When a digital asset is no longer required, all copies must be archived or disposed. Refer to VPMP Information review, retention and disposal. If the original copy is related to a brief (authorised or unauthorised) or other hardcopy file (such as an AIM or complaint file), it should be attached to the file and managed together with the related information. If the digital asset is not related to any other information (e.g., video footage of traffic stops with no associated briefs or complaints) the original copy must be securely destroyed in accordance with VPMP information review, retention and disposal. Working copies Creating and using the working copy If the information on the original copy is required for further action, a second copy of the digital asset must be made as soon as possible. This becomes the working copy, which is the version that is to be used for reviewing, editing and creating relevant extracts and attaching to the brief of evidence or complaint file. If the digital asset is a record of operational duties, then a working copy only needs to be made if the digital asset is to be accessed for a brief of evidence or a complaint. The working copy must be suitably labelled. Refer to the Closed Circuit Television Practice Guide for guidance on labelling. All working copies must have the same protective marking as the original. Working copies must not be stored on personal drives, portable computing devices, local disk drives (i.e. C:) or local desktops or any non-Victoria Police ICT equipment. A record must be made in the register when copies are shared or provided. Copies of photos may be stored temporarily on approved Victoria Police networks and systems if operationally required for the purpose of collaboration. This must only occur in line with the applicable protective marking handling requirements and any system instructions. Refer to VPMP Information use, handling and storage for information. Where digital assets are to be used in Victoria Police training programs refer to VPMP Information sharing for further requirements. Where the digital asset was obtained under processes listed in VPMG Obtaining information from external organisations, refer to this guideline for advice on releasing information to external parties. Please refer to VPMG Release of information to the media for further guidance on releasing recordings to the Media. For information regarding disclosure obligations in criminal proceedings refer to VPM Disclosure in criminal proceedings. Retention and destruction When a digital asset is identified as inactive all copies must be archived or disposed. Refer to VPMP Information review, retention and disposal. If the working copy is related to a brief (authorised or unauthorised) or other hardcopy file and is significantly different to the original copy it should be attached to the file and managed together with the related information. The working copy may be sent to the Victoria Police Archive Services Centre

If the working copy is related to a brief (authorised or unauthorised) or other hardcopy file and is significantly different to the original copy it should be attached to the file and managed together with the related information. The working copy may be sent to the Victoria Police Archive Services Centre (VPASC) for immediate destruction as part of normal administrative practice if the working copy: is related to a brief (authorised or unauthorised) or other hardcopy file, and is a duplication of the original copy, and the original copy is confirmed as being attached to the file. If a working copy was created but no related brief (authorised or unauthorised), complaint or other related file has been progressed, then the working copy may be destroyed as part of normal administrative practice. It is the work unit manager and/or system administrator’s responsibility to ensure best efforts are made to dispose of copies uploaded into official Victoria Police systems in accordance with VPMP Information review, retention and disposal. CCTV Victoria Police managed CCTV equipment The use of CCTV equipment in public places supports policing functions to manage high crime locations and matters of public order. It also supports frontline policing by providing targeted monitoring and real time intelligence gathering. The installation or placement of Victoria Police-issued CCTV equipment (including mobile CCTV trailers) must be justified as a necessary and appropriate solution to the identified crime problem at the proposed location, having regard to other crime prevention or investigative approaches. Placement of Victoria Police-issued CCTV equipment, excluding Air Wing Downlink, must be in accordance with section 3 of this policy and approved by a senior sergeant or above. Once placed, the use of CCTV equipment should be continuously assessed, taking into consideration the introduction of alternative crime prevention and/or investigative approaches and any human rights impacts. The management of CCTV equipment placed on Victoria Police premises should be in line with VPM Management of people in police care or custody. Externally managed CCTV equipment Station OICs may contribute to the assessment, planning, implementation and placement of local public CCTV monitoring schemes. Before any CCTV equipment is placed on police premises a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) must be entered into with the CCTV operator, incorporating the following conditions for placement of CCTV monitoring equipment: Victoria Police will not undertake to continuously monitor CCTV Victoria Police has responsibility for determining the appropriate level and priority of responses required to incidents identified by the CCTV cameras, according to available resources and existing priorities the CCTV system is not to be connected to

Requests for the development of MOUs must be in line with VPMP Formal arrangements with external organisations and must be submitted to Legal Services Department for assessment and advice. Once obtained, all footage from CCTV equipment is recognised as law enforcement data and is to be managed in accordance with this policy. text: Restrictions on the use of applications on Victoria Police devices Context The Commonwealth Government has increased the scrutiny of potentially malicious social media applications. This has led governments across Australia and overseas to restrict the installation and use of malicious applications on government-issued devices due to significant concerns that malicious applications can potentially: monitor activity and capture data on a user’s device and store that data in a way which can be accessed by foreign intelligence and national security agencies provide a gateway for the covert deployment of malicious software (i.e. viruses) on to a user’s device be exploited for the purpose of social engineering and disinformation campaigns. In line with Commonwealth Government guidance, and in response to the risks posed, there are new limitations for the Victorian Government and associated agencies regarding the use of the restricted high-risk applications on government provided devices. Victoria Police policy strictly controls the use of restricted applications on Victoria Police devices, limiting use of these applications to circumstances where exemptions have been approved (i.e., legitimate business purposes) and mitigating controls are applied. This policy aligns with wider Whole of Victorian Government policy, and provides guidelines on: the limitations in relation to use of restricted applications the circumstances in which restricted applications can be used for law enforcement purposes. Victoria Police employees must exercise care when using social media and engaging in online activities and avoid any actions that might be damaging to the reputation or security of the organisation. Refer to VPM Social media and online engagement. VPM Professional and ethical standards applies whether employees are using social media in an official or a personal capacity. Policy at a glance This policy: describes the applications restricted for use on Victoria Police devices explains the exceptional circumstances restricted applications may be used on Victoria Police devices describes the applications process for accessing and using restricted applications details the system and security requirements for authorised use of restricted applications provides reporting avenues for unauthorised use of restricted applications. Personal device – a piece of IT equipment that is not owned and issued by Victoria Police. Legitimate business reason - means a lawful and valid need to install or access the restricted application on a Victoria Police device to conduct Victoria Police business and/or achieve a work objective of Victoria Police. Personally identifiable information – information that, when used alone or with other relevant information, can identify a person. Restricted applications – web-based and software applications identified by Victoria Police as potentially malicious and should not be accessed, installed or used on a Victoria Police device. Restricted applications are listed in Appendix A. Stand-alone device – refers to a device that does not have the Victoria Police managed image on it and is not connected to the Victoria Police network. Also refer to the general VPM Dictionary for definitions and acronyms. Scope and application This policy applies to all employees, contractors, service providers, consultants, vendors and any other parties who have access to Victoria Police networks, data or devices. Responsibilities and procedures Use of restricted applications Victoria Police prohibits the installation of restricted applications and requires the removal of existing instances of restricted applications on Victoria Police devices, unless a legitimate business reason exists necessitating the installation or ongoing presence of the application. Employees must not access, install or use restricted applications on a Victoria Police device without authorisation as per this policy. Restricted applications must only be accessed or installed where all of the following has occurred: a legitimate business reason has been authorised by the relevant assistant commissioner or executive director, considering any relevant risks the applicant has completed a risk assessment and mitigation strategies have been implemented to reduce associated risks. Contact Digital Services and Security Department (DSSD) via the IT-SECURITY-ADVICE-MGR PBEA for further advice the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) has provided final approval. A legitimate business reason to access a restricted application includes: to carry out regulatory functions including compliance and enforcement activities for authorised crime investigation and intelligence activities that relate directly to duties or functions within Victoria Police, such as surveillance and intelligence gathering for research to be conducted or communications to be sent to assist with a law enforcement purpose to reach key audiences to undertake education, child safety, marketing

title: Info_use_handling_storage_of_info_VPM_Restrictions_on_the_use_of_applications_on_VP_devices_final
text: (CISO) has provided final approval. A legitimate business reason to access a restricted application includes: to carry out regulatory functions including compliance and enforcement activities for authorised crime investigation and intelligence activities that relate directly to duties or functions within Victoria Police, such as surveillance and intelligence gathering for research to be conducted or communications to be sent to assist with a law enforcement purpose to reach key audiences to undertake education, child safety, marketing or public relations activity on behalf of Victoria Police. Employees must not use their personal device to access or use restricted applications for law enforcement purposes. Use for legitimate business reason There are a variety of investigative and intelligence functions that may constitute a legitimate business reason to use a restricted application. Investigations and inquiries using restricted applications are to be conducted according to established policies and guidelines, including the use of online personas; refer to VPM Official online activities and VPM Assumed identities and online personas. For guidance about investigation or intelligence gathering that involves discreet or covert official online activities, refer to VPM Official online activities and VPM Assumed identities and online personas. Where access or use of a restricted application is required for a legitimate business reason, employees must apply to install and use the restricted application using the application form located on the DSSD intranet page. This must include prior endorsement from the appropriate assistant commissioner/executive director and evidence of this provided with the completed application form. Security controls for authorised use of restricted applications The CISO must approve the use of restricted applications on Victoria Police devices only where there is a legitimate business reason. The approval period will be for the duration of the legitimate business reason or for a period not exceeding 12 months and the following security controls must be met: the restricted application must only be installed and/or accessed on a stand-alone device the stand-alone device must be appropriately stored and secured when not in use. This includes the isolation of these devices from sensitive conversations and information (i.e. by switching off the device) metadata must be removed from photos, videos and documents when uploading any content to restricted applications personally identifiable information must not be shared on restricted applications the use of restricted applications must be approved by the assistant commissioner /executive director and CISO all accounts accessing restricted applications must use multi-factor authentication and unique passphrases all devices that access restricted applications must use the latest available operating system to control individual application permissions. The CISO must establish processes to regularly check for and update the application to ensure the latest version is used restricted applications must only be installed from trusted stores, such

The CISO must establish processes to regularly check for and update the application to ensure the latest version is used restricted applications must only be installed from trusted stores, such as the Microsoft Store, Google Play Store and the Apple App Store. Work unit managers must ensure restricted applications are accessed only by authorised users and that access is immediately revoked when there is no longer a business need for that access or use. The CISO must ensure that the terms and conditions of the restricted application are regularly reviewed, as well as application permissions with each update, to ensure appropriate risk management controls can be put in place or adjusted as required. Restricted applications must be deleted from devices when the legitimate business reason no longer exists or authorisation expires. Unauthorised use of restricted applications Where an employee believes on reasonable grounds that another employee is, or has engaged in unauthorised or improper use of restricted applications they must report this behaviour to any one of: the Security Incident Registry a work unit manager sub-officer or above the Police Conduct Unit, Professional Standards Command via submission of a Complaint Form [VP 918] the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) in accordance with either s.167(3), Victoria Police Act 2013 or Part 2 of the Public Interest Disclosure Act 2012. title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: Police interactions with correctional facilities and prisoners Context Police members may be required to visit correctional facilities, including police gaols for a variety of reasons. These include: service of documents including summons, intervention orders and service of briefs conducting forensic procedures interview of prisoners investigation of offences obtaining witness statements. The legislative authority to arrange and conduct the visit may differ depending on the reason. This procedure aims to facilitate smooth entry and operations in this high security environment. Contents 1. Attending a prison 1 2. Prisons intelligence 2 3. Custodial witnesses 4 4. Threats against prisoners 6 5. Warrants to arrest a prisoner 7 6. Investigation of crimes reported in correctional facilities 7 7. Conducting interviews in a prison or police gaol 9 8. Other visits to correctional facilities 15 Responsibilities and procedures Attending a prison General considerations Members will often be required to enter secure prison premises. Entry to these facilities will involve varying levels of security and may include signing a visitor book, showing certificate of identity (no ID, no entry), retinal (eyeball) scanning, metal detector, and air analysing illicit substance detection. To avoid delays members should: contact the relevant correctional facility’s Prison Intelligence Unit and advise them of the nature of the visit ensure that relevant documentation has been signed off prior to visit, if applicable; see sections 5, 7 and 8 for required documentation ensure that items required for interviewing are described on the documentation and that prison staff are aware that you need to bring in items such as micro-recorders, cameras, USB sticks etc. These items will require authority of the General Manager or delegate of the prison leave mobile phones secured in vehicles or in lockers offered in prison foyers as these will not be allowed into the secure area minimise metal items carried such as coins, metal belt buckles, tie pins, jewellery etc. Although these items will mostly be allowed to pass, they will delay the entry process. Any disputes or issues encountered should be brought to the immediate attention of a supervisor, Victoria Police Prisons Intelligence Unit (VPPIU). Prisons intelligence Role of the VPPIU The VPPIU is the liaison point between Victoria Police and Corrections Victoria (CV). The VPPIU can provide advice to members in relation to prison-related issues and can be contacted via the position based email address (PBEA) ICS-PRISONS INTELLIGENCE-OIC. Refer to the Prisons Intelligence Unit – Services and Support intranet page for details of the services provided by the VPPIU. Police service requests The VPPIU has direct access to CV systems – Centurion and PIMS. VPPIU members will, where possible, utilise these systems to respond to requests from Victoria Police members to avoid unnecessary delays. Members wishing to

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: to prison-related issues and can be contacted via the position based email address (PBEA) ICS-PRISONS INTELLIGENCE-OIC. Refer to the Prisons Intelligence Unit – Services and Support intranet page for details of the services provided by the VPPIU. Police service requests The VPPIU has direct access to CV systems – Centurion and PIMS. VPPIU members will, where possible, utilise these systems to respond to requests from Victoria Police members to avoid unnecessary delays. Members wishing to request information from CV are required to forward their request to the VPPIU PBEA ICS-PRISONS INTELLIGENCE-OIC and provide the following details: name of prisoner DOB of prisoner MNI information required reason for the request date range (if applicable). Type of information available The following types of prisoner information are available from CV: long profile – this document provides a summary of information including phone contacts, approved visitors, emergency contacts, next of kin, earliest proposed release dates etc phone contact list – lists approved telephone contacts for a prisoner which includes names and contact phone numbers call activity report – lists call activity for a prisoner for a particular location in a similar manner as a CCR (date range required) visitor list – includes approved/verified visitors for a given prisoner visits list – chronological list of visits to a prisoner. Lists time, date, name of visitor, and address of visitor (date range required) release dates - provides earliest release date (parole eligibility date), and latest possible release date (sentence lapse with no parole). These dates can be the same if the prisoner is not eligible for parole. The earliest release date does not mean that the prisoner will be released on that day, it is merely the date from which the prisoner is eligible for parole. The Adult Parole Board will decide the actual release date. This will be updated on the CV database, but sometimes at short notice following an Adult Parole Board hearing associates list – cumulative historical database for a particular prisoner which details known enemies or friends of a given prisoner. A person may be added to this list through intelligence received from CV (eg. prisoners request to be housed in the same unit) or through prison incidents (eg. fight between prisoners). This list is used by CV to assist in prisoner placement next-of-kin and emergency contact details – lists prisoner next-of-kin/emergency contact. Name, address and phone numbers available. For all other non-standard requests, refer to the Prisons Intelligence Unit – Services and Support intranet page or contact the VPPIU for advice. Access to prison information reports Members requiring intelligence and information from CV are to contact the VPPIU in the first instance. CV staff create an information report for all major

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: CV to assist in prisoner placement next-of-kin and emergency contact details – lists prisoner next-of-kin/emergency contact. Name, address and phone numbers available. For all other non-standard requests, refer to the Prisons Intelligence Unit – Services and Support intranet page or contact the VPPIU for advice. Access to prison information reports Members requiring intelligence and information from CV are to contact the VPPIU in the first instance. CV staff create an information report for all major prison incidents involving a prisoner/s, as well as intelligence received by prison staff. Original reports are not released by CV. VPPIU staff can generate an Intelligence Report (IR) in relation to relevant reports in consultation with the requesting member, however blanket requests for “all Corrections Information Reports” will not be considered. Providing Victoria Police intelligence to Corrections Victoria Members wishing to provide intelligence to CV must complete an IR (sanitised if required) and forward it to the VPPIU. In urgent circumstances (eg. immediate threat/risk to safety or good order of a prison) contact the VPPIU for advice. Locating a prisoner The VPPIU will not conduct checks for members in relation to where a prisoner is located in the first instance. Members should utilise the Person Custody Location Search which is available via the intranet applications page under the attendance module. Instructions on this process are available from the download section of the VPPIU intranet site. Where members still cannot locate a person believed to be in custody, contact the VPPIU for further assistance. Access to prisoner phone calls and prisoner mail Members can access a range of other services such as mail interception and ARUNTA Prisoner Telephone System (PTS) monitoring. Individual detailed instructions are available on the Prisons Intelligence Unit – Services and Support intranet page. CV prisoners have the right to send and receive unopened mail from a number of agencies and bodies, including Victoria Police, without those letters being opened by prison staff (s. 47(1)(M), Corrections Act 1986). If a prisoner sends mail to a police member which is found to have any information pertaining to the safety and security of a prison, CV must be notified immediately. Youth Justice Intelligence Unit The Corrections Victoria, Youth Justice Intelligence Unit (YJIU) is responsible for the management and dissemination of intelligence within Malmsbury and Parkville Youth Justice Centres. Information that is, or may be, relevant or useful to either VPPIU or YJIU should be exchanged at the earliest opportunity. Processes relevant to youths in custody (eg. monitoring of ARUNTA PTS phone calls) and the VPPIU’s ability to access information relating to youths in custody may differ in comparison to offenders in custody at adult prisons. Contact the VPPIU for further information or advice if required.

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: intelligence within Malmsbury and Parkville Youth Justice Centres. Information that is, or may be, relevant or useful to either VPPIU or YJIU should be exchanged at the earliest opportunity. Processes relevant to youths in custody (eg. monitoring of ARUNTA PTS phone calls) and the VPPIU’s ability to access information relating to youths in custody may differ in comparison to offenders in custody at adult prisons. Contact the VPPIU for further information or advice if required. Custodial witnesses Custodial Witness Management Program The Custodial Witness Management Program (CWMP) is a multi-agency program designed to reduce the risks associated with high risk custodial witnesses. The CWMP is coordinated through the VPPIU. When dealing with a prisoner or soon to be incarcerated person, members must be mindful of the risk posed to that person while in custody and consider making an application to the CWMP, where the eligibility requirements are met. Interdepartmental Custodial Witness Committee The Interdepartmental Custodial Witness Committee (ICWC) assesses and determines applications for entry of prisoners to the CWMP. The Committee consists of senior executives of CV, Victoria Police, Australian Federal Police and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission. The committee meets bi-monthly to consider new applications and can be convened urgently if required. Definitions Eligibility Any prisoner in the custody of CV serving a sentence or on remand, who has important and vital evidence in support of a Crown prosecution or investigation and who is at risk and/or has been threatened may be eligible for entry to the CWMP. The ICWC's criteria for determining if a prisoner is formally recognised as a high-risk custodial witness is: the witness evidence or information will assist in the prosecution or investigation of serious and organised crime, and relevant assessments determine that the prisoner is at significant risk of or threat from serious harm or death from other prisoners as a result of their witness evidence or provision of information. Special arrangements for prisoners in other States and Territories of Australia may also apply. Applications Contact the VPPIU in the first instance for advice. A copy of the application form and instructions is available on the VPPIU intranet site. Applications must be submitted to the VPPIU in writing on the application form by the informant or witness manager (case officer). Applications must be endorsed by an Inspector or above. The VPPIU ensures the application meets the requirements for entry and submits the application to the ICWC for approval. Upon approval by the ICWC the case officer will be notified of the decision by the VPPIU and the custodial management regime to be applied. A full and current profile of the custodial witness, including known associates is to be electronically attached to the application. Emergency

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: officer). Applications must be endorsed by an Inspector or above. The VPPIU ensures the application meets the requirements for entry and submits the application to the ICWC for approval. Upon approval by the ICWC the case officer will be notified of the decision by the VPPIU and the custodial management regime to be applied. A full and current profile of the custodial witness, including known associates is to be electronically attached to the application. Emergency notifications In cases of emergency, where a risk or threat develops suddenly during a court hearing or similar situation and a prisoner may be in danger if returned to a normal prison environment, the facts should be verbally reported to the ICWC through the VPPIU as soon as possible. Special arrangements will be made pending a formal application. Additional responsibilities Informants or case managers of prisoners accepted into the CWMP have an on-going responsibility to notify the VPPIU of any relevant information or intelligence which may indicate changes, updates, or further escalations to the prisoner’s risk status whilst on the program. Urgent notifications should be done by telephone, with an IR to the VPPIU to follow. Threats against prisoners Threats to prisoners Members may become aware of a potential threat to a prisoner, or a person whose incarceration is imminent. This threat may be a threat of physical harm, or an attempt to undermine the judicial process (eg. persuade prisoner to recant statement to police etc). Members’ responsibility on receipt of threat information Where a member becomes aware of a threat to a person in custody, they must: identify the potential source of the threat (names of fellow prisoners requiring separation/known crime groups) specify details of the threat if known (locations, date, time and method to be used to carry out threat) create a sanitised IR in relation to the threat in Interpose, ensuring that methodology such as telephone intercepts, listening devices, or the use of human sources is not revealed. The IR needs to be sufficiently detailed to enable CV staff to make an accurate assessment of the prisoner’s placement contact the Human Source Management Unit (HSMU) for advice if the information is from a human source contact the VPPIU by phone to discuss the threat move the sanitised IR to the Prisons Intelligence Unit Interpose security group and email the link to the ICS-PRISONS INTELLIGENCE-OIC PBEA further information received should be the subject of further IRs as per the above instructions. Do not place handwritten notes for CV staff on a prisoner’s file in order to notify prison staff of potential custody issues. These can be lost or handled inappropriately. Role of the VPPIU The VPPIU will assess the IR to ensure sufficient

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: IR to the Prisons Intelligence Unit Interpose security group and email the link to the ICS-PRISONS INTELLIGENCE-OIC PBEA further information received should be the subject of further IRs as per the above instructions. Do not place handwritten notes for CV staff on a prisoner’s file in order to notify prison staff of potential custody issues. These can be lost or handled inappropriately. Role of the VPPIU The VPPIU will assess the IR to ensure sufficient sanitisation, and add comment where possible. The IR will then be forwarded to CV. Role of Corrections Victoria CV will assess the information provided and manage the placement of the prisoner to best ensure the prisoner’s safety within the prison system. Warrants to arrest a prisoner Informant responsibilities Investigation of crimes reported in correctional facilities Reporting and investigation of criminal offences and serious incidents Police may be required to respond to a correctional facility in relation to a non-routine incident (see section 8.5) or where a visitor is found with contraband or a prisoner makes an allegation of a sexual assault. When this happens, CV staff will contact Victoria Police by the emergency telephone number 000. CV will: preserve the crime scene until advised by Victoria Police that the crime scene is able to be used again by the prison preserve evidence (if applicable) and provide it to attending police members provide any information (eg. prisoner files, phone records, intelligence information, photographs etc) that will assist in the criminal investigation or the preparation of a brief of evidence make facilities available for investigating police members to interview staff and prisoners and conduct other on-site inquiries as required. Members must still comply with s.464B, Crimes Act 1958 when interviewing suspects. See section 7. Victoria Police members responding to incidents must: attend and investigate all criminal offences and serious incidents reported to them by CV in accordance with normal incident/investigative guidelines advise the nominated prison staff member or the General Manager, CV Intelligence Unit of the results of any investigations. These instructions do not diminish members’ responsibilities under VPM Crime and event reporting and recording and VPM Crime attendance and investigation. For attendance and management of non-routine incidents see section 8.5 Sexual crimes Where an alleged sexual crime has taken place in a prison, Victoria Police will provide a specialist investigative response, including: attending the prison within 24 hours, including those circumstances where the victim has indicated that they do not wish to proceed with any police investigation advising the victim in person of their options for progressing a complaint where required, and with the informed consent of the victim, arranging for a forensic medical officer to examine the victim. The conduct of the forensic medical examination

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: a prison, Victoria Police will provide a specialist investigative response, including: attending the prison within 24 hours, including those circumstances where the victim has indicated that they do not wish to proceed with any police investigation advising the victim in person of their options for progressing a complaint where required, and with the informed consent of the victim, arranging for a forensic medical officer to examine the victim. The conduct of the forensic medical examination will be undertaken in a forensically secure environment. Victoria Police members need to be mindful that the urgent medical needs and crisis care (through the Centre Against Sexual Assault) of the victim will take precedence over any investigative response. These instructions do not diminish members’ responsibilities under VPM Sexual offence investigations and the Code of Practice for the Investigation of Sexual Crime. Alleged assaults by prison staff Where a prisoner makes an allegation that they have been assaulted by a staff member, CV will refer the matter to Victoria Police for investigation, irrespective of the seriousness or nature of the alleged assault. Minor offences In circumstances where an alleged criminal offence is of a minor nature such as: prisoner located with small quantities (less than traffickable quantity) of contraband drugs (illicit or prescription) and there is no evidence of trafficking, or prisoner assaulting another prisoner where the assault is deemed to be a “minor assault” under the definition at section 4.2, VPM Crime and event reporting and recording, or prisoner assaulting prison staff where the assault is deemed to be a “minor assault” under the definition at section 4.2, VPM Crime and event reporting and recording the member may: investigate the incident, or refer the matter to CV or Youth Justice (YJ) for an internal general manager’s disciplinary hearing. Assaults with bodily fluids Where a prisoner spits or bodily fluids are projected onto the body of the staff member, the incident is to be investigated in line with VPM Crime attendance and investigation. The investigating member should consider the submission of a Person Warning Flag [Form 292] in these circumstances. Conducting interviews in a prison or police gaol Overview Police can interview a person in a prison or a police gaol for a variety of reasons, including interviews for matters the person is currently in custody for or other matters. Depending on the circumstances, the following legislative authorities apply: s.104AC, Corrections Act permits any person to visit a police gaol, subject to conditions. Police can use this section to visit and question a prisoner about the same matter for which that person is already being held, subject to conditions. See section 7.4 s.41, Corrections Act provides that police members may, at the times fixed by

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: the person is currently in custody for or other matters. Depending on the circumstances, the following legislative authorities apply: s.104AC, Corrections Act permits any person to visit a police gaol, subject to conditions. Police can use this section to visit and question a prisoner about the same matter for which that person is already being held, subject to conditions. See section 7.4 s.41, Corrections Act provides that police members may, at the times fixed by the regulations, enter a prison and visit a prisoner. Police can use this section to visit and further question a prisoner about the same matters for which that person is already being held, subject to conditions. See section 7.3 s.464B(1) and 464B(11), Crimes Act allow for police to interview prisoners held in a prison or police gaol for an offence other than the offence for which they are being held. See sections 7.5 and 7.6 where an interstate police member is intending to interview a suspect for an offence committed interstate: a Victoria Police member is to be present to ensure compliance with s.464 the interstate police member must play an active role in the conduct of the interview. This also includes liaising with Victoria Police to advise of and ensure the respective State’s interview legislation is followed and that where there is any conflict, Victorian legislation prevails Note: Section 464B (10), Crimes Act includes a varied definition of investigating official for s.464 interviews. An investigating official in relation to an offence committed outside Victoria includes a person (other than a person who is engaged in covert investigations under the orders of a superior) who is: a member of the Australian Federal Police or a police force for another State or Territory. a person appointed by or under an Act of the Commonwealth or another State or Territory whose functions or duties include functions or duties in respect of the prevention or investigation of offences. Note: Offence for the purpose of s.464B (10) includes an offence against a law of the Commonwealth or another State or Territory. Prisons and youth justice centres – location and availability of prisoner Police seeking to interview a person in a correctional facility should inquire about the person's availability and location through either of the following: adult prison – Victoria Police Prisons Intelligence Unit youth justice centre – Youth Justice Intelligence (yjintelligence@justice.vic.gov.au) Interviews for the same offence – prisons Criteria – s.41, Corrections Act provides that police members may at the times fixed by the regulations, enter a prison and visit a prisoner. Police can use this section to visit and further question a prisoner about the same matters for which that person is already being held, providing the following

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: following: adult prison – Victoria Police Prisons Intelligence Unit youth justice centre – Youth Justice Intelligence (yjintelligence@justice.vic.gov.au) Interviews for the same offence – prisons Criteria – s.41, Corrections Act provides that police members may at the times fixed by the regulations, enter a prison and visit a prisoner. Police can use this section to visit and further question a prisoner about the same matters for which that person is already being held, providing the following criteria is met: the prisoner consents to the interview permission to interview the prisoner has been obtained from the manager of the prison before any interview, ensure the prisoner has been cautioned and informed of their rights removal of a prisoner from the prison is prohibited. Application – police seeking to visit a person in prison or a youth justice centre must first obtain permission from an Officer using the Request to Interview a Person in Custody [Form 478 or 479 – Refer to instructions attached to forms] and then: adult prisons – submit the Form 478 directly to the Corrections Victoria Intelligence Unit (CVIU) at: intel@justice.vic.gov.au. CVIU will process the request and email the completed Form 478 to the member youth justice centre – obtain the consent of the General Manager or delegate of the relevant youth justice centre (Malmsbury YJC or Parkville YJC) using Form 479. Conducting interviews – once permission to interview has been granted: the prisoner may decline to be interviewed at a youth justice centre, the interview may be conducted in the presence of a youth officer interviews in prisons may be conducted in the presence of a prison officer. The full procedure for visits to adult prisons including contact details for all adult correctional facilities is available from the VPPIU intranet page. Interviews for the same offence – police gaols Section 104AC, Corrections Act permits any person to visit a police gaol, subject to conditions. Police can use this section to visit and question a prisoner about the same matter for which that person is already being held, subject to the following conditions: the prisoner consents to the interview permission to interview the prisoner has been obtained from the Officer in Charge of the police gaol before any interview, ensure the prisoner has been cautioned and informed of their rights Interview in prison or police gaol for an offence other than the offence being held – with consent Police may interview a person held in a prison or police gaol for an offence other than the offence for which they are being held with the person’s informed consent. Only adults can give informed consent, so this provision does not apply to children. If police wish to interview a child

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: cautioned and informed of their rights Interview in prison or police gaol for an offence other than the offence being held – with consent Police may interview a person held in a prison or police gaol for an offence other than the offence for which they are being held with the person’s informed consent. Only adults can give informed consent, so this provision does not apply to children. If police wish to interview a child for an offence other than the offence for which they are being held they must make an application under s.464B, Crimes Act; see section 7.6. Obtaining informed consent (s.464B(13)) – a person gives informed consent to be questioned if they consent after the investigating member informs the person, in a language they are likely to understand, of the following: the nature of the offence they are suspected of having committed that they may refuse to be questioned that if they give their informed consent they are still not required to say or do anything that they may withdraw their informed consent to be interviewed at any time that if they refuse to give their consent, an application can still be made to the Magistrates’ Court for an order to interview them that if the Magistrates’ Court makes an order under this section, that they may be delivered into the custody of the police member for the purpose of questioning that the person still has their rights under s.464, Crimes Act, being; they may communicate or attempt to communicate with a friend or relative they may communicate with or attempt to communicate with a legal practitioner if they are not an Australian citizen or permanent resident of Australia they may communicate with or attempt to communicate with the consular office of the country of which they are a citizen. Recording (s.464B(15)) – an audio visual recording must be made of: giving the person the above information any response given by the person to that information any questioning of the person that takes place and anything said by the person any withdrawal of consent to the questioning. Location of interview – police gaol – the member may remove a person being held in a police gaol for the purpose of questioning if - the police gaol is in the same building as a police station; and the person is to be removed to a room in the police station; and the person is not to be taken outside the building; and the person consents to being removed to a room in the police station; and the Officer in Charge of the police gaol gives approval. prisons – the person must not be removed from the prison for

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: - the police gaol is in the same building as a police station; and the person is to be removed to a room in the police station; and the person is not to be taken outside the building; and the person consents to being removed to a room in the police station; and the Officer in Charge of the police gaol gives approval. prisons – the person must not be removed from the prison for the purposes of questioning. Approval – members utilising this provision will still need to apply to: police gaol – Officer in Charge of the police gaol, who may approve the removal of the person to a room in a police station if they are satisfied that the use of the room: is in the best interests of the person to be questioned, having regard to confidentiality and privacy enables an audio visual recording as required by s.464B(15) for any other reason is preferable to conducting the questioning in the police gaol. prison – an Officer and obtain the consent of the General Manager or delegate of the Prison, using a Form 478. Return to police gaol – at the end of questioning, the person must be returned to the police gaol. Interview in prison or police gaol for an offence other than the offence for which the person is being held - s.464B application Criteria – under s 464B(1), Crimes Act a police member must apply to a Magistrates’ Court or Children's Court for an order under s.464B(5), Crimes Act to interview a person held in a prison or police gaol for an offence other than the offence for which they are being held where the person: does not give informed consent; or subsequently withdraws their informed consent; or provides their consent, but the criteria in section 7.5 are not met; or is a child. Application - Submit applications on Application to Transfer Custody of a Person for the Purpose of Questioning or Investigation [Form 482]. A s.464B application must be served on the subject of the application or the person in charge of where the subject person is being held. The person who is the subject of an application under s.464B, must be 'before the court' (see s.464(4A)) by being present, either in person or by way of video conference. See the following table for details of the process: Effect of the order – An order under s.464B has effect as a suspension of a direction in the original warrant. The court will not hear a s.464B application unless the person has legal representation or is satisfied that the person has had, or refused to have legal advice provided in relation to the application

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: being present, either in person or by way of video conference. See the following table for details of the process: Effect of the order – An order under s.464B has effect as a suspension of a direction in the original warrant. The court will not hear a s.464B application unless the person has legal representation or is satisfied that the person has had, or refused to have legal advice provided in relation to the application (s.464B (4B)). The Form 482 should be lodged with time for the prisoner to seek legal advice, prior to the hearing of the application. Under s.464B(5C), the court may order the transfer of custody of the person to the member making the application for the purpose of questioning or investigation. The order will specify a reasonable period of time in which questioning or investigation may take place and any other conditions that may apply (ss.464B(5B) and 464B(8A)). The court will only grant an extension of order or subsequent application, if satisfied that further questioning will assist in determining the involvement of the person in the commission of the offence. If an extension is required, make the request before the initial period of questioning or investigation has expired. Recording the interview – Interviews under s.464B must be audio visually recorded (s.464B(5H)). Before the application hearing, the investigating member should obtain either a portable audio visual recorder from their division, or alternatively the Parkville Youth Justice Centre or Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre may have compatible camera equipment. Contact the facility beforehand if unsure. Location of interview – The interview needs to occur at the place where the person was detained at the time that the order was made, unless the court orders otherwise (s.464B(5B)). In most cases it will be impracticable to conduct interviews in police goals. When making an application, the investigating member should request that the interviews take place in an interview room in the police station or complex. Conducting the interview – Include the full caution (as detailed in VPM Interviews and statements) and the person’s response in the recording. Handling the recording – Include details of the interview in the Attendance Register. File the Station Master in the Master Disc Register at the interviewing member’s station. Copy of the interview to the accused – give a copy of the recording to the person or their legal practitioner within 7 days of the interview (s. 464H(3)(A)). Copies of recorded interview can be made using the disc duplicators provided with the audio visual recording equipment. Follow the normal process for obtaining a transcription; see VPM Interviews and statements. Return of the prisoner – When the period of the order or questioning/investigation is completed, deliver the

title: Interviews_statements_VPM_Interactions_correctional_facilities_final
text: the interview to the accused – give a copy of the recording to the person or their legal practitioner within 7 days of the interview (s. 464H(3)(A)). Copies of recorded interview can be made using the disc duplicators provided with the audio visual recording equipment. Follow the normal process for obtaining a transcription; see VPM Interviews and statements. Return of the prisoner – When the period of the order or questioning/investigation is completed, deliver the person in custody to the place where the person was held at the time of the application for the order. Interviews outside prisons Re-interviews/re-enactments for offences for which the prisoner is in custody are to be conducted under police custody transfer orders (s.56B, Corrections Act). The order: is available for all prisoners authorises the absence of a prisoner from a prison for a specified period up to a 3 day maximum. The applications for an order, made to the Supreme Court by an Assistant Commissioner or above in writing, must include: the grounds on which the application is made a risk assessment the prisoner’s written consent to the making of the proposed order an assessment made by the Secretary, Department of Justice and Community Safety (DJCS) a statement made by the Secretary, DJCS as to the conditions (if any) the Secretary seeks to be imposed on the order. A copy of the application must also be served on the Secretary, DJCS. All applications for this process are required to be made to the VPPIU. Investigators are to contact the VPPIU for further advice and initial assessment of the circumstances. Interviews for other offences – follow the procedure outlined in sections 7.5 and 7.6 above. Notification where a prisoner’s identification is an issue When further charges are pending against a prisoner already in prison, and identification is an issue, notify the general manager of the prison so that no change in the prisoner's appearance may be made which might render identification difficult. When it is desired to have a prisoner in prison identified for a further offence, the investigating member must give the general manager at least 24 hours’ notice of their intention. Other entry arrangements may be arranged to avoid production of forms at front desk of the prison. For discreet visit arrangements, seek advice from the VPPIU prior to submitting Form 478. Attending a correctional facility in response to a non-routine incident CV classifies incidents at correctional facilities in two ways; routine and non-routine. Police may be called to respond to either type of incident, with a different response to each, depending on the nature, complexity and classification of the incident. Routine - A routine incident is one which CV has the resources and capacity to deal with independently. Victoria Police may still be called in response to these incidents, but involvement may be limited to a support or investigative role. Non-routine - A non-routine incident is defined as an incident that affects the normal operation of a prison or transition centre. It can include but is not limited to, a riot, siege, hostage situations, bomb threat, external evacuation or a natural disaster. The General Manager (or delegate) of the correctional facility will determine what constitutes a non-routine incident after assessing the complexity, scale and resource requirements of the incident and will notify Police via 000. The State Correctional Emergency Response Plan (SCERP) outlines the arrangements for how Victoria Police respond and manage non-routine incidents affecting a correctional facility. Managing non-routine incidents at correctional facilities The SCERP clearly defines the roles and responsibilities of Victoria Police and Corrections Victoria to ensure that all activities undertaken are integrated and coordinated and should be referred to by members in charge of an incident declared non-routine. The General Manager (or delegate) of the correctional facility will fulfil the Incident Controller role in the first instance. The correctional facility will maintain control of the incident until a ‘transfer of control’ occurs with Victoria Police, based on the needs of the incident. Victoria Police are required to respond to a request from correctional facilities for assistance during a non-routine incident. As per the MOU concerning the management of non-routine incidents at prisons, Victoria Police will assume the role of the control agency where it considers the incident to be ‘significant’. This determination may occur at the first Emergency Management Team meeting. The correctional facility will assist Victoria Police in relation to that significant emergency, including ensuring that none of the powers Victoria Police may lawfully exercise are interfered with. See SCERP for full details. 8.7 Visiting a correctional facility to serve process Members attending a correctional facility to serve process such as intervention orders, or summonses, do not need

text: Interviews and statements Context Police members should conduct interviews so that they may discover information leading to the truth of a matter under investigation and if necessary, use this information as evidence at court. It should be clear to any court that the content of any admission or confession is voluntary, meaning that any person being interviewed or providing a statement, does so freely and with informed consent. Police members must comply with all relevant legislative requirements including the appropriate cautioning of suspects under s.139, Evidence Act 2008 and address the requirements of s.464 Crimes Act 1958 and Part 3.4, Evidence Act. As a public authority under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (the Charter), all members must act compatibly with, and give proper consideration to, relevant human rights in the course of their duties. This means that any person being interviewed or making a statement is afforded appropriate support to ensure their human rights are respected by providing a fair, accessible and respectful process as outlined in the Charter. This policy includes: the process and member obligations when delivering caution and rights the roles and responsibilities of the investigating member and independent third persons (ITPs) considerations and legislative requirements when recording interviews, admissions, confessions, interstate interviews, and when taking written statements in different settings considerations and risk mitigations in determining whether a person is fit for interview in relation to drugs or alcohol, cognitive impairment and mental health issues guidance regarding the diverse needs of priority communities that should be considered when conducting an interview. Responsibilities and procedures Before interviewing a suspect or accused Caution and rights In all circumstances, a police member who suspects an offence, prior to questioning, must caution a person and make that person aware of their legal rights, which they may exercise before interview. This table helps you decide when to caution and which rights apply. How to advise a person of their caution and rights To give a person their caution and rights, the police member must read aloud from the Form 252A. To confirm that the caution and rights are understood, the police member should ask the person to repeat what has been said, in their own words. If the person has difficulty doing this, consider whether the person has a cognitive impairment or needs an interpreter. See sections 8 and 13 of this policy for more information. Refer to section 2 of this policy for additional considerations relating to Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people. Exercising rights to communicate with a friend, relative or legal practitioner In accordance with s.464C(1), Crimes Act, before any questioning or investigation* under s.464A(2) commences, police members must inform the person in custody that they may communicate with, or attempt to communicate with: a friend or relative to inform that person of their whereabouts a legal practitioner. * An investigation is defined as an objective assessment of an act, omission, situation or event with a view to determining whether any breach of law is involved or to assign responsibility for the occurrence, which depending on the seriousness of the incident or resources required, may be conducted by frontline units and/or Investigation and Response Units. If a person wishes to communicate with a friend, relative or legal practitioner, the police member must do both of the following: as soon as practicable, afford the person reasonable facilities i.e., that provides for privacy, to enable the person to do so allow the person's legal practitioner (or a clerk of the legal practitioner) to communicate with the person in circumstances in which as far as practicable the communication will not be overheard. If a person does not have a lawyer and requests to speak to a lawyer, police members should refer to the contact details provided in the Legal Practitioner Referral Guide (e.g. Victoria Legal Aid, the Law Institute of Victoria and the Victorian

text: do so allow the person's legal practitioner (or a clerk of the legal practitioner) to communicate with the person in circumstances in which as far as practicable the communication will not be overheard. If a person does not have a lawyer and requests to speak to a lawyer, police members should refer to the contact details provided in the Legal Practitioner Referral Guide (e.g. Victoria Legal Aid, the Law Institute of Victoria and the Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service (VALS)). Police members must ensure that questioning and investigation is deferred for a time that is reasonable in the circumstances to enable the person in custody to make, or attempt to make, the communication, unless they believe on reasonable grounds that: communication would result in the escape of an accomplice or the fabrication or destruction of evidence the questioning or investigation is so urgent, having regard to the safety of other people, that it should not be delayed (s.464C(1), Crimes Act). If access to communication is refused, details of the grounds for the refusal should be recorded in the Attendance Module and the investigating member’s notes. If reasonable grounds do not exist to refuse a person an opportunity to exercise their rights, an interview may be ruled inadmissible. Carrying operational safety equipment in an interview Police members should remove and appropriately store firearms before an interview unless exceptional circumstances exist. In those circumstances, police members should consult with the custody supervisor and make an appropriate notation in the Attendance Module. People of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander descent Overview Aboriginal person – means a person to whom all of the following apply: is of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander descent identifies as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander is accepted as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander community (s.3, Bail Act 1977). Caution and rights As stated in VPM Bail and remand, police members must ensure an Aboriginal person under caution has a meaningful opportunity to both: consider whether to exercise their rights to communicate with a friend or relative and a legal practitioner exercise those rights. Note: see section 2.4 of this policy for further considerations when issuing a person their caution and rights. The indication of Aboriginal status within the Attendance module will trigger a notification directly to VALS. text: other support services As soon as practicable and prior to any questioning under s.464A(2), police members must ask the person whether they identify as Aboriginal (s.464AAB, Crimes Act). The indication of Aboriginal status within the Attendance module will trigger a notification directly to VALS. Refer to VPM Attendance and Custody modules and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in police care or custody Practice Guide for more information. Police members must offer a copy of the VALS Custody Information Sheet (available on the Prosecutions Frontline Support Unit Information Sheets intranet site) to an Aboriginal person in custody to inform them that VALS has been notified for the purpose of performing a welfare and wellbeing assessment of the person and provide an opportunity for the person to engage with the service prior to their interview. As stated in VPM Bail and remand, police members must ensure that an Aboriginal person under arrest has a meaningful opportunity to make an informed decision about whether to accept an offer to communicate with the VALS Custody Notification Officer, including providing the person with information about the purpose of that contact and what assistance the Custody Notification Officer may be able to provide. In the case of a person who is in custody in the field, and not entered into the Attendance module, in accordance with s.464FA(2), Crimes Act, police members must notify VALS within one hour or as soon as practicable via phone or using VALS Notification – in field custody [Form 1505]. Once a notification has been made, the person in custody must be informed of that notification as soon as practicable. For victims or witnesses, the identification of Aboriginal status will provide an opportunity to engage with a support service including the Aboriginal Family Violence Prevention and Legal Service (during business hours) or the Aboriginal Community Justice Panel member (where operating) for the provision of legal advice and/or support for the interviewee. Consideration of the Anunga Rules The Anunga Rules are guidelines formulated by the Northern Territory Supreme Court in 1976 for the questioning of Aboriginal people. Although they have been adopted by other state and territory police services, they have not been incorporated into legislation. Police members must consider the principles created by the Anunga Rules, where practicable. In summary, the Anunga Rules state that: unless the Aboriginal person in custody is fluent in English, an interpreter should be present during the interview where practicable, it is desirable for the person to have a friend or support person present during an interview when issuing a person their caution and rights, police members should ask the person in simple terms to tell them what is meant by the caution, phrase-by-phrase; interviews

In summary, the Anunga Rules state that: unless the Aboriginal person in custody is fluent in English, an interpreter should be present during the interview where practicable, it is desirable for the person to have a friend or support person present during an interview when issuing a person their caution and rights, police members should ask the person in simple terms to tell them what is meant by the caution, phrase-by-phrase; interviews should not proceed unless it is clear that the person understands their right to remain silent during interviews, police members should not ask leading questions or ask questions in a manner or tone that might suggest a particular response the prosecution of an offence should only occur where there is sufficient evidence and in the public interest to proceed; this should not rely solely on admissions or confessions police members must ensure that meals, drinks, and toilet breaks are made available whilst a person is in custody a person must not be interviewed if they are impaired by substances or tiredness where a person expressly states they do not wish to answer any (further) questions put to them, questioning should cease, with the remaining allegations put to the person in non-question form and a person must be provided suitable, alternative clothing on any occasion where their clothes have been seized for forensic or medical examination. Victims and witnesses For Aboriginal victims or witnesses, police members should, where possible, consider a culturally appropriate environment in which to take a statement such as a local Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisation or another place. Recording confessions and admissions Legislative requirements In order for confessions and admissions in relation to indictable offences to be admissible in court, s. 464H, Crimes Act requires any admissions made to a police member (other than a police member engaged in authorised covert investigations) to be recorded, either by audio or audio visual. When conducting any questioning, the recording should commence immediately. If a confession or admission was made before questioning commenced or at a place where facilities to conduct an interview were not available, the police member must either: record such evidence at the time, or take notes of everything said at the time and later obtain confirmation of what was said on a recording by getting the suspect to repeat in substance what was said previously. Where forensic evidence forms part of the case against a suspect, or where forensic samples or fingerprints need to be taken from the suspect see VPM Forensic procedures and VPM Fingerprinting. People with disability Under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010, police members must make reasonable adjustments for people with disability. Not doing so constitutes discrimination. Reasonable adjustments in an interviewing situation means providing support, resources and adaptive practices to enable equitable and inclusive access to justice. People with a cognitive impairment How to identify persons with a cognitive impairment Cognitive impairment is a term used to cover a range of conditions which adversely affect a person’s ability to understand and process information. It includes intellectual disability, acquired brain injury, mental illness and neurological disorders. Through observations and by making active enquiries, police members must seek to identify whether a person may have a cognitive impairment. This can be achieved by: observing the person’s words or actions asking the person directly checking police records relating to any previous interactions, or contacting the person’s nearest Medical Health Triage or Disability Service Intake to check whether they are or have been a client of the medical health or disability service. For further guidance on identifying whether a person may have a cognitive impairment, refer to the ready reckoner: Responding to persons who may have cognitive impairment. Use of independent third persons An ITP must be present during the interview of any person with a cognitive impairment, who is fit to be interviewed or have a statement taken as a suspect, an accused, an offender, a victim or a witness. An ITP can be a volunteer from the Office of the Public Advocate (a trained ITP), a parent, guardian, relative or close friend of the person. If the alleged offence occurred within a disability or mental health service, the person’s ITP must be independent of the service provider. It is recommended that police members engage a trained ITP whenever possible due to a trained ITP’s independence, familiarity with police procedures and capacity in helping a person understand their rights, options and consequences. In some circumstances, it may be beneficial to have a trained ITP for communication support and a parent, carer, relative, close friend or other person present for emotional support.
