Patrol responsibilities 3 4. Police escorts 5 5. Recording of duties – overview 5 6. Patrol duty returns 5 7. Contemporaneous notes 7 8. Official diaries 8 9. Incident fact sheets 10 Related documents 13 Further advice and information 13 Update history 13 Definitions 24-hour police station – a station which offers 24/7 counter reception and response capability and may also have police cells. Stations classified as 24-hours are determined by the Deputy Commissioner (DC), Regional Operations, and are listed on the DC, Regional Operations intranet site. Primary response – duties that involve general patrolling, public order management and/or where providing a first response to incidents is likely or expected (e.g. divisional van, patrol car, highway patrol, patrol supervisors (251), members on availability to perform first response to incidents, attendance at sporting or community events). Secondary response – duties where members may be required to provide supervision, back-up or specialist capabilities for incidents but do not provide a primary response other than as back-up to primary response units (e.g., divisional patrol supervisor (265), duty officer (150), PACER units, dog squad, crime scene or other similar specialist or investigative units). Scope and application This policy applies to all employees. Responsibilities and procedures Patrol resource management and supervision Regional assistant commissioners have responsibility to ensure patrol resources are appropriately allocated and supervised, and that Police Communications is advised of available resources. CCI 09/24 Minimum station profiles outlines the minimum number of resources required at police stations to ensure service delivery and member

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_Operational_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: (150), PACER units, dog squad, crime scene or other similar specialist or investigative units). Scope and application This policy applies to all employees. Responsibilities and procedures Patrol resource management and supervision Regional assistant commissioners have responsibility to ensure patrol resources are appropriately allocated and supervised, and that Police Communications is advised of available resources. CCI 09/24 Minimum station profiles outlines the minimum number of resources required at police stations to ensure service delivery and member safety. VPM Operational supervision and incident attendance provides guidelines on how to manage patrol resources. CCI 05/25 Operational readiness and work-related activity provides rostering requirements to maintain service delivery within rostered shift times. Messages and tasks Important messages All members must record important messages received and relay the messages as appropriate. Tasks for mobile units Any telephone calls received at the station and which are to be given to a mobile unit for response must be: recorded relayed to Police Communications. Local management must ensure: a consistent approach is applied to the location of messages messages relating to tasks for mobile units can be audited. Allocation of patrol tasks Police Communications is responsible for the allocation of events to patrol units. Once an event is allocated, members are responsible for the resolution of the task, including priority of attendance, handling of the event and submission of appropriate reports. Patrol supervisors or sub-officers may allocate priorities according to local needs. Patrol responsibilities Undertaking patrol duties Radio is the primary mode of operational communication. Mobile telephones (where provided by Victoria Police) are a secondary mode of communication and must only be used for non-operational, organisational, management or welfare issues. Minimum member requirements The criteria above does not apply where a member believes that they need to immediately respond to a task or incident to prevent the loss of life or serious injury to themselves or another person. In these circumstances, members must consider their safety, conduct a risk assessment, develop appropriate risk mitigation strategies and if possible, notify Police Communications and call for assistance. Responsibilities when on patrol While all members are responsible for their own actions and conduct, the senior member on the patrol is responsible for ensuring: that radio is used wherever available and that Police Communications is notified as required by VPMG Patrol responsibilities and communications that the patrol does not leave its area of patrol except in the circumstances below: in an emergency with authority of a supervisor. Identification of members If a member of the public requests details of a member, including station details, this must be provided unless there is a justifiable reason. Some legislation requires police to give this information in writing or orally, when asked, if police request a

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_Operational_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: required by VPMG Patrol responsibilities and communications that the patrol does not leave its area of patrol except in the circumstances below: in an emergency with authority of a supervisor. Identification of members If a member of the public requests details of a member, including station details, this must be provided unless there is a justifiable reason. Some legislation requires police to give this information in writing or orally, when asked, if police request a person’s name and address in certain circumstances (s.456AA, Crimes Act 1958) or require production of a certificate of identity (e.g., s.150, Firearms Act 1996). Refer to VPM Uniform and appearance standards in relation to general requirements for carrying identification. Securing premises Members attending or locating insecure premises are responsible for the premises until the owner or their representative takes responsibility. Have regard to VPMG Patrol responsibilities and communications to comply with this requirement. Members must not engage, recommend, refer or provide information regarding specific shutter services. Police contact with and requests for a shutter service must only be via Police Communications. Refer to VPMG Patrol responsibilities and communications for details of the notification procedure. Responding to alarms When responding to alarms, members must have regard to VPMG Patrol responsibilities and communications. Police escorts Police may be requested to escort a person or property. The level of assistance is dependent on the type of escort required and the availability of police resources and may be charged for. Refer to VPMG Police escorts when assessing requests for or conducting escorts. Recording of duties – overview Operational duties To ensure appropriate accountability for and oversight of operational duties, members are required to record and report on operational duties in the following ways: Patrol duty return – members must complete a hand-written Patrol Duty Return [Form 501] or electronic Patrol Duty Return (ePDR): every time they are on patrol, including foot or other patrol when directed by a region/command/department head. contemporaneous notes – must be made in accordance with section 7 of this policy Official diary [PB13] – must be maintained by members attached or assigned to the Crime Command or a Crime Investigation Unit (CIU); see further details in section 8 of this policy IFS– must be submitted by operational supervisors after significant or high-profile incidents in accordance with section 9 of this policy. Other duties Inspectors/VPS-5 and above are required to keep appropriate records of their duties. Patrol duty returns Handwritten patrol duty return Completing handwritten patrol duty returns A Form 501 or Initial Action Pad [Form 502] is a record of the duties performed while on patrol. When completing a handwritten Form 501: only enter details of incidents, tasks, person/vehicle checks, searches, and referrals or requests

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_Operational_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: or high-profile incidents in accordance with section 9 of this policy. Other duties Inspectors/VPS-5 and above are required to keep appropriate records of their duties. Patrol duty returns Handwritten patrol duty return Completing handwritten patrol duty returns A Form 501 or Initial Action Pad [Form 502] is a record of the duties performed while on patrol. When completing a handwritten Form 501: only enter details of incidents, tasks, person/vehicle checks, searches, and referrals or requests for service where information is captured on a corporate form, e.g., LEAP, Penalty Infringement Notice (PIN), Traffic Incident System reports, only enter sufficient information to reference the corporate form, and include the registered number of the member submitting it and attach a copy of the form when appropriate all task narratives (including those captured on corporate forms) as a minimum must briefly describe actions taken and briefly explain the recorded disposition. Submitting handwritten patrol duty return Members on patrol – within 24 hours of the completion of that patrol shift, must: read and sign the Form 501 as an acknowledgement of its correctness submit the Form 501 to a supervisor for checking. Supervisors – as soon as practicable, must: check the Form 501 to ensure its completeness, including: all required Form 501s have been submitted all tasks have a recorded disposition the task narratives (and/or associated corporate forms) adequately record the disposition all relevant forms (including LEAP, PIN, Field Contact [Form L19], Use of Force App report are completed and checked for accuracy justification for use of force, searches and field contact submissions are explained. after checking the Form 501: initial the Form 501 to acknowledge its completeness or adequacy note any discrepancies and return to the respective member/s for rectifying or explanation submit to a work unit manager for recording as required by local instructions. Both members on patrol and supervisors – must write their full name, rank, VP number and the date and time of the submission. Regional duty officer – must submit original to the regional assistant commissioner. Divisional patrol supervisor – must submit to the local area commander. Electronic patrol duty returns ePDRs are electronic running sheets that utilise transaction data automatically captured through IRIS-enabled mobile devices. All ePDR entries (LEAP checks, comments etc.) are auditable. Creating ePDRs log on to IRIS-enabled mobile devices at the station prior to commencing patrol duties and create a new ePDR for the patrol shift. This ePDR form will be in ‘draft’ status until submitted to a supervisor for review. log onto the IRIS-enabled mobile devices in the vehicle and access the ePDR created for the relevant patrol. once patrol duties have concluded, members must log off the IRIS-enabled mobile devices. Contemporaneous notes When to take notes The Form 502 must be carried by all members when performing frontline duties and used to record notes for inclusion in the Investigation Case File [Form 1313]. When attending or investigating any incident, take notes of any observations and conversations with people connected with the incident. In some cases, a report or document will be sufficient, e.g., PIN, Form 501, official diary. In the case of investigations, notes must include all relevant facts, information and observations, including details of the incident scene and the questioning of all suspects and witnesses. As notes may be required for evidential purposes, or to confirm any admissions or confessions made on a recording, they must be made contemporaneously, i.e., at the time or while facts are still fresh. Where a person is charged or it is intended to charge a person, notes must be attached to the Brief Head [Form 208A]. Timeframe for taking contemporaneous notes Take notes as close as possible to the actual time of the event being recorded. Where this is not possible, they should be made at least before the end of the shift

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_Operational_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: they must be made contemporaneously, i.e., at the time or while facts are still fresh. Where a person is charged or it is intended to charge a person, notes must be attached to the Brief Head [Form 208A]. Timeframe for taking contemporaneous notes Take notes as close as possible to the actual time of the event being recorded. Where this is not possible, they should be made at least before the end of the shift but no later than 48 hours after the event. The main consideration is that the notes are made while the facts are fresh in the memory of the maker. Manner of recording contemporaneous notes Notes should be compiled in either hard copy or electronic format. The maker or informant must retain the original copy unless it is needed for some other purpose (e.g., a PIN). Retain the notes, including printed, signed copies of electronic notes, in accordance with VPMP Information review, retention and disposal. Any changes or corrections required to original notes should only be added with an explanation as to why the note was required to be amended. If notes are compiled electronically, a hard copy of all notes primarily intended for use in court must be made at the time of recording and dated and signed by the maker. Where previously made electronic notes are altered, a contemporaneous note of the reasons why must be also made. Adopting contemporaneous notes Others who may wish to use the notes should, at the time or while the facts are still fresh in their minds, read, adopt and endorse the notes by dating and signing. Use of initial action pads, daybooks and notebooks Members should record details of their duties performed and contemporaneous notes in the Form 502. The Form 502 remains the property of Victoria Police and should be returned to the work unit manager when completed. Employees issued with a notebook or daybook, are to record their contact details inside. Notebooks and daybooks remain the property of Victoria Police and should be returned to the work unit manager when completed. Work unit managers must comply with VPMP Information review, retention and disposal for completed Form 502s, notebooks and daybooks. Officers and equivalent VPS employees are only required to maintain appropriate records and therefore are not required to keep official diaries unless they wish to. Completing an official diary Make entries as soon as possible after completing the relevant duty An official diary should also be used as a daybook Where it is not practical to complete entries at the time, take other notes and transcribe details into the official diary as soon as possible. Where a record of duties performed is recorded on another corporate report (e.g., Form 501) it is not necessary to repeat the full record in the official diary. However, the entry should include a summary and reference to the corporate report. The following should also be recorded in the diary: rest days and leave. Show rest days, numbered consecutively for each year. Record rest days, leave, accrued time off and expenses in red ink arrests human sources. Reference to human sources should be by their source code. Management and security of official diaries A register of official diaries, which can be maintained at the local or region/command/department level, should include details of the: employee it is issued to, including their work location date of issue number of the diary date returned or disposed. Diary retention periods can be affected by the contents of the diary: diaries must be retained by Victoria Police for at least 10 years from when an employee ceases employment diaries may need to be retained for more than 10 years, based on content and required retention according to VPMP Information review, retention and disposal. Any significant cases or events included in the diary that may affect the retention period are to be

Where possible, an inspection should be planned. If this is not possible, arrange for an inspection while the employee is absent from work to avoid them needing it on the day of inspection. Conducting inspections of official diaries: ensure compliance with this policy ensure entries are up-to-date note any irregularities and any action taken to resolve them sign and date the diary in red ink to acknowledge it has been inspected. Lost or stolen official diaries Where an official diary is lost or stolen, employees must: report it to a supervisor complete appropriate LEAP reports with Victoria Police as the victim send a report to their work unit manager report it to the Security Incident Registry. Incident fact sheets Overview The IFS system is an internal method of communicating summary information regarding a significant or high-profile incident which has occurred in the immediate 24-hour period. Use and disclosure of IFS must occur in accordance with VPMP Appropriate use of information, VPMP Information sharing and VPM Disclosure in criminal proceedings. Supervisor’s responsibilities Supervisors are responsible for ensuring an IFS is submitted after a significant or high-profile incident, such as any matter likely to: attract significant media attention involve a Victoria Police employee as a victim, offender or suspect warrant notification of Victoria Police employees including

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_Operational_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: occurred in the immediate 24-hour period. Use and disclosure of IFS must occur in accordance with VPMP Appropriate use of information, VPMP Information sharing and VPM Disclosure in criminal proceedings. Supervisor’s responsibilities Supervisors are responsible for ensuring an IFS is submitted after a significant or high-profile incident, such as any matter likely to: attract significant media attention involve a Victoria Police employee as a victim, offender or suspect warrant notification of Victoria Police employees including management be assessed as a Category 1 or 2 offence in accordance with the Accountability and Resource Model. Submission of an IFS should occur when appropriate and as soon as possible (ideally by the end of the shift). Supervisors can authorise the submission and content of an IFS after physically checking or otherwise satisfying themselves as to the appropriateness of the report. Supervisors are not to transmit incidents or allegations of a sensitive nature which may be compromised by its inclusion in an IFS. Alternatives such as the telephone or e-mail are to be used to notify the appropriate authority. An authorisation check should not impact on the timeliness of the submission of the report. Where a person in police custody sustains an injury, or police members (on or off duty) sustain an injury during an incident and no allegations of police impropriety are made, PSC must be notified by the 251 via an IFS. The IFS must be assigned the PSC sensitivity classification, and entered as soon as possible, but no later than the completion of the rostered duty. The following information must not be published in an IFS: any information which may lead to the identification of a sexual assault victim incidents or allegations of a sensitive nature against a police member or high-profile individual any information that has been alleged to have been a cause or impediment to an incident where that information has not been verified where a death involves police, see VPM Death or serious injury/illness incidents involving police for more information. Report standards and content IFS content is accountable and may be subject to public scrutiny, therefore information is to be reported in a clear, concise way without using abbreviations. The description of the incident is to be brief, factual, using non-judgemental language and preferably is not to contain details of dialogue. Additional comments should only be added to an IFS where that information is required to correct a misunderstanding conveyed by the wording of the original summary comments, to rectify a critical omission or clarify a system administrative update. Additional comments may only be included in an Executive Command morning briefing where that update was made prior to the daily report run on the day the IFS was

Additional comments may only be included in an Executive Command morning briefing where that update was made prior to the daily report run on the day the IFS was submitted. The Peer Support check box on an IFS is intended as a prompt to remind supervisors of the range of support services available for their members regardless of whether the incident requires the mandatory notification or involvement of the Police Psychology Unit or Wellbeing Services. Supervisors are required to follow established business practice and initiate contact with a Peer Support Officer. In all complaints relating to racial, political or ideological circumstances, an IFS must be compiled as soon as possible and the incident should be brought to the immediate attention of the Manager, Security Intelligence Unit and the Superintendent Community Portfolio, Priority and Safer Communities Division by forwarding correspondence to position based email accounts; CTC-SIU-MGR and OFFICE-OF-CMDR-PSCD-MGR. Sensitivity classifications The IFS sensitivity classifications only relate to the visibility of the report and do not relate to the Victoria Police information security classifications. No security classification information is to be entered into the IFS system. There are three IFS access classifications available to system users: restricted – inspector/VPS 5 and above sensitive – senior sergeant/VPS 4 and above routine – constable/VPS 2 and above. Any employee may apply for an access classification if that level of access is required for the performance of official duties or to obtain, change, suspend or reinstate a user’s access. Requests must be authorised by a superintendent or above and must be submitted via an ICT and Facilities Portal request. Employees may be provided with the level of access that they are entitled to by rank, excluding higher duties, without completing an application form. However, an application form must be completed if the employee has a suspended account. Requests for upgraded access from members performing higher duties as a senior sergeant or inspector must be authorised by a superintendent or above and must be submitted via an ICT and Facilities Portal request. Sensitive – a sensitive classification

text: Operational supervision and incident attendance Context The supervision and management of operational policing resources and responses to incidents is critical for achieving Victoria Police’s operational objectives and providing quality professional and ethical policing services to the community. This policy outlines Victoria Police’s patrol supervision requirements and responsibilities for regional managers and supervisors, and provides guidance on attending, leading and supervising incident responses. Policy at a glance This policy includes: the patrol supervision responsibilities of members in the regions and the Incident Leadership and Attendance Model (ILAM) matrix to determine when and which members are to attend and make notifications for specific operational incidents. Contents Context 1 Policy at a glance 1 Contents 1 Responsibilities and procedures 1 1. Operational principles 1 2. Patrol Supervisor (251) 2 3. Sergeants at police stations 3 4. Divisional Patrol Supervisor (265) 4 5. Senior sergeants at police stations 4 6. Regional Duty Officer (150) 5 7. Local inspector 5 8. Regional Superintendent / Duty Superintendent 6 9. Regional Assistant Commissioner / Duty Assistant Commissioner or Commander 6 10. Incident Leadership and Attendance Model for operational incidents 7 Related documents 7 Further advice and information 7 Update history 7 Appendix A – Incident Leadership and Attendance Model (ILAM) 8 Responsibilities and procedures Operational principles This policy is supported by the following principles, which are critical to achieving Victoria Police’s operational objectives and providing quality professional and ethical policing services to the community: effective, timely and appropriate supervision and leadership will be provided to frontline members at all levels effective, timely and appropriate notifications of operational incidents or events will be made within the organisation through the chain of command effective control structures will be established in a timely manner in response to operational incidents or events. Regional assistant commissioners have overarching responsibility for ensuring that patrol supervision resources are appropriately allocated and that incidents are attended in accordance with the requirements of this policy. It is acknowledged that some of the requirements in this policy may not be practical in rural locations. The policy provides flexibility to address these circumstances as far as possible, but where a situation is not covered, the rostered duty supervisors or managers should engage with local managers to make appropriate supervision arrangements. Patrol Supervisor (251) Rostering A sergeant must be rostered in each police service area (PSA) for each shift to perform Patrol Supervisor (251) duties. In rural PSAs the 251 may be part of a patrol unit (divisional van); a dedicated 251 patrol unit is not mandatory. Patrol responsibilities The 251 must: supervise and provide leadership to all patrol units within the PSAs and conduct a safety briefing at the start of the shift or as soon as practicable

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_Operational_supervision_and_incident_attendance_Final
text: Rostering A sergeant must be rostered in each police service area (PSA) for each shift to perform Patrol Supervisor (251) duties. In rural PSAs the 251 may be part of a patrol unit (divisional van); a dedicated 251 patrol unit is not mandatory. Patrol responsibilities The 251 must: supervise and provide leadership to all patrol units within the PSAs and conduct a safety briefing at the start of the shift or as soon as practicable contact stations at the commencement of each shift to check on any issues with resourcing, custody, security or service delivery contact the Divisional Patrol Supervisor (265) at the start of each shift and carry out any additional duties as directed oversee the allocation and coordination of tasks from Police Communications for the PSA ensure that calls for urgent police assistance are promptly attended to and respond to incidents requiring attendance of a 251 in line with the ILAM; see Appendix A. Incident management The 251 has the following incident management responsibilities: Unless it is impractical or another sergeant is attending, attend planned or unplanned incidents where people are in, or may be taken into custody, or if there is potential for confrontation between the person(s) and police If assuming the Police Commander or Police Forward Commander role, maintain command responsibility to manage all resources at incidents, including resources that contain another sergeant If they cannot meet the needs of the incident or it is not feasible for them to attend (e.g., competing supervision priorities, geographical distance), they must arrange for another sergeant to take charge of the incident in consultation with the Divisional Patrol Supervisor (265) Advise Police Communications and make an entry on the electronic Patrol Duty Return whenever incident management is handed over Seek guidance from the Divisional Patrol Supervisor (265) regarding any confusion over incident management. Sergeants at police stations Section Sergeants The station Section Sergeant must: supervise the station and employees, including employees from other units co-located at the station where no sergeant is on duty allocate tasks and conduct a safety briefing at the start of the shift supervise custody management in locations where a dedicated custody supervisor is not required; refer to section 3.2 of this policy keep abreast of incidents occurring in their PSA and remain available to respond to any significant incident requiring supervision in accordance with the ILAM; see Appendix A. Responsibility for attendance in the first instance remains with the Patrol Supervisor (251). The station section sergeant may attend and assume the role of Police Commander only after engagement and consultation with the Divisional Patrol Supervisor (265). Custody Supervisor A dedicated custody supervisor (sergeant rank or above) must be rostered for all facilities listed in

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_Operational_supervision_and_incident_attendance_Final
text: PSA and remain available to respond to any significant incident requiring supervision in accordance with the ILAM; see Appendix A. Responsibility for attendance in the first instance remains with the Patrol Supervisor (251). The station section sergeant may attend and assume the role of Police Commander only after engagement and consultation with the Divisional Patrol Supervisor (265). Custody Supervisor A dedicated custody supervisor (sergeant rank or above) must be rostered for all facilities listed in the Register of Detention Facilities marked with an asterisk (*). Refer to the Register of Detention Facilities located on the State Event Planning and Custody Management Division tab, State Emergencies and Support Command intranet page for more information. For all other detention facilities, any sergeant may be nominated to fulfill the custody supervisor role alongside other supervisory responsibilities. Unit sergeants Other sergeants, including those from Highway Patrol (HWP) Units, Crime Investigation Units (CIU), Family Violence Investigation Units (FVIUs), Sexual Offence and Child abuse Investigation Teams (SOCIT) etc., should be rostered to supervise the employees and functions of those units to ensure optimum efficiency, accountability and supervision. They must: supervise the employees under their control, allocate tasks and conduct a safety briefing at the start of the shift and undertake other duties as required or directed to meet service delivery requirements. Divisional Patrol Supervisor (265) Rostering A senior sergeant must be rostered in each division for each shift to perform Divisional Patrol Supervisor (265) duties. In some regional divisions a 265 is rostered between two divisions, as the individual divisions do not have the resources to operate a 265 roster independently. Patrol responsibilities The 265 must: manage and provide leadership to supervisors in the field and conduct a safety briefing with all PSA patrol supervisors at the start of the shift, or as soon as practicable actively supervise, provide leadership, and manage the activities of all patrol units within the division/s, including Investigation and Response units, Highway Patrol and Support Services units contact the Regional Duty Officer (150) at the start of each shift and carry out any additional duties as directed ensure that the 251 and rostered Investigation and Response units respond to and attend incidents in accordance with the ILAM; see Appendix A monitor police communications. If an incident occurs that appears to exceed the capacity or authority of a sergeant, coordinate responses and attend the incident respond to and attend incidents where required by the ILAM; see Appendix A brief the 150 at the earliest opportunity regarding any incident likely to create political, media or Executive Command level interest and ensure an Incident Fact Sheet is completed by the member responsible. Refer to VPM Operational duties and responsibilities for further information. Incident management

Regional Duty Officer (150) Rostering An Inspector must be rostered in each region each shift to perform Regional Duty Officer (150) duties. Incident management The 150 must: ensure there is an adequate and appropriate police response to incidents, including supervision provide leadership and support and conduct a safety briefing with all Divisional Patrol Supervisors (265) at the start of the shift, or as soon as practicable attend incidents where required by the ILAM (see Appendix A) or the incident management requirements exceed the capacity of the relevant 265 where the incident requires inspector level management, assume the Police Commander role where the geographical distance of an incident or other exceptional circumstances prevents the timely attendance of the 150, the 150 should contact the: Divisional Superintendent (during business hours); or Duty Superintendent (after hours or when the Divisional Superintendent is unable to be contacted during business hours) to identify a local inspector to attend and assume incident management responsibilities. Local inspector When on duty, the Local Area Commander

text: inspector level management, assume the Police Commander role where the geographical distance of an incident or other exceptional circumstances prevents the timely attendance of the 150, the 150 should contact the: Divisional Superintendent (during business hours); or Duty Superintendent (after hours or when the Divisional Superintendent is unable to be contacted during business hours) to identify a local inspector to attend and assume incident management responsibilities. Local inspector When on duty, the Local Area Commander (LAC) is: responsible for keeping abreast of incidents occurring in respective PSAs and with respective units and resources to remain available to respond to any significant incident requiring supervision in accordance with the ILAM; see Appendix A. Where an incident occurs in their PSA which requires inspector level attendance and management, responsibility for attendance in the first instance remains with the Regional Duty Officer (150). The LAC or another local Inspector may attend and assume the role of Police Commander only after engagement and consultation with the regional Duty officer (150). Regional Superintendent / Duty Superintendent Rostering and response A Regional Duty Superintendent (RDS) must be rostered on duty in each region to respond to and attend relevant incidents and events outside of business hours according to the ILAM; see Appendix A. During business hours, the relevant local Divisional Superintendent must be notified in the first instance of any incident requiring Superintendent level attendance according to the ILAM. If the local Divisional Superintendent cannot be contacted, the Duty Superintendent must be notified. After hours, where the geographical distance of an incident or other exceptional circumstances prevents the timely attendance of the RDS, the RDS should contact the Duty Commander/Assistant Commissioner to determine whether the Divisional Superintendent or another local superintendent should attend. Incident management The local Divisional Superintendent or the RDS must: ensure any major incidents receive the appropriate level of supervision maintain regular liaison with the 150 where required during major incidents engage as necessary to ensure policing priorities are maintained Attend incidents where required by the ILAM (see Appendix A) or the incident management requirements exceed the capacity of the relevant 150 When responding to significant emergency events, the local Divisional Superintendent or RDS should undertake the following actions as required: liaise with the Senior Police Liaison Officer (SPLO) and perform the role of Police Commander If escalation or notification is required, the local superintendent or RDS (whichever takes primacy) must report directly to the: Regional Assistant Commissioner (business hours) Duty Assistant Commissioner/Duty Commander (after hours or if the Regional Assistant Commissioner is unable to be contacted) Brief the Regional Assistant Commissioner or Duty Assistant Commissioner or Commander regarding any incident likely to create political, media or Executive Command level interest and ensure

If unable to contact the Regional Assistant Commissioner, the Duty Assistant Commissioner or Commander must be notified. Provide incident updates to the Deputy Commissioner, Regional Operations as required / requested. title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: Protective services officers – duties and responsibilities Context Protective services officers (PSOs) are responsible for patrolling the public transport network, ensuring Victoria’s public transport system is safe and the community feels safe. PSOs focus on addressing incidents of antisocial behaviour, alcohol and drug-related offences, weapon offences and property damage. PSOs may also provide support and assistance for particular operations and in response to an emergency or state of disaster in Victoria. PSOs are managed and supervised by the Transit Safety Division (TSD), Transit and Public Safety Command (TPSC). This policy details the role and responsibilities of PSOs and details how these responsibilities align with broader Victoria Police policy. Contents 1. Management 3 2. Commencement of duty 3 3. Search and seizure 3 4. Power to request name and address 4 5. Arrests 4 6. Issuing infringement notices 7 7. Taking a person into care and control under the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 8 8. Family violence 8 9. Road policing 9 10. Handling property 10 11. Declaration of a designated place 11 12. Deployment of protective services officers in an emergency 14 13. Reporting contacts and intelligence 14 14. Complaints 15 Scope and application This policy applies to PSOs who are managed by the TSD, TPSC. It does not apply to PSOs managed by the Protective Services Unit (PSU), except for where PSU PSOs are deployed using voluntary duties in accordance with section 11 of this policy. Definitions Authorised Officer (TA) – as defined by the Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act 1983. Designated place – means: as defined by r.27, Victoria Police Regulations 2014, a place on or within any of the following places is a designated place: railway premises, which includes trains and tracks (see r.4 for the full definition); rail premises on or adjoining railway premises including any car parking area on the rail premises; land on or in which a tram stop and any associated tram stop infrastructure is situated (see s.48H of the Road Management Act 2004 for further definition); any rail premises on or adjoining a tram stop including any car parking area on the rail premises; bus premises; any roadway or other thoroughfare giving access to the rail premises or specified bus premises; any area on or adjoining rail premises or specified bus premises used by other modes of transport including taxi ranks; any municipal council controlled car park adjoining rail premises or specified bus premises; any privately owned or managed land used for a car park or other public transport purposes adjoining rail premises or specified bus premises; a road on which a specified bus route or rail replacement bus provides a bus service at the time the service is in

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: adjoining rail premises or specified bus premises used by other modes of transport including taxi ranks; any municipal council controlled car park adjoining rail premises or specified bus premises; any privately owned or managed land used for a car park or other public transport purposes adjoining rail premises or specified bus premises; a road on which a specified bus route or rail replacement bus provides a bus service at the time the service is in operation. a place or area declared to be a designated place in a notice published under s. 3A, Victoria Police Act 2013 (see section 11 of this police for further information). Refer to r. 4, Victoria Police Regulations for further definitions of rail premises, bus premises, bus service, bus stopping point, rail replacement bus, specified bus premises and specified bus route. Also refer to the general VPM Dictionary for definitions and acronyms. Policy PSOs have been given a number of legislative powers in support of their role of keeping the public transport network safe. In addition to these legislated powers, PSOs have a general responsibility to protect and assist members of the public, particularly children and vulnerable people. Tasking of duties: PSOs may only be tasked to undertake duties in a designated place, except in the case of section 12 of this policy. Legislative powers: Except for the general authority to arrest a person without warrant under s.458, Crimes Act 1958 or the deployment of PSOs in a state of emergency or disaster, PSOs can only exercise their legislative powers when on duty at a designated place. General duties when on duty at a designated place: PSOs should provide assistance to members of the public as far as practicable and ensure that available emergency or support services are contacted as required PSOs are responsible for ensuring the safety, security and wellbeing of a person who has been taken into their care or custody (refer to VPM Management of people in police care or custody). Responsibilities and procedures Management PSOs are attached to TSD, TPSC. TSD has overarching responsibility for the management of PSOs in accordance with relevant policies, procedures and guidelines, including: HR and financial processes/responsibilities rostering supervision/performance management and discipline matters health, safety and wellbeing matters. Commencement of duty On commencement of duty, PSOs are required to report to their direct start location and obtain operational safety equipment, necessary forms and all other equipment required to perform their duties. Search and seizure Legislative authority PSOs on duty at a designated place have the authority to conduct searches without a warrant and seize items under the following: common law – search of arrested persons s. 10AA, Control of Weapons Act 1990 – search a person

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: On commencement of duty, PSOs are required to report to their direct start location and obtain operational safety equipment, necessary forms and all other equipment required to perform their duties. Search and seizure Legislative authority PSOs on duty at a designated place have the authority to conduct searches without a warrant and seize items under the following: common law – search of arrested persons s. 10AA, Control of Weapons Act 1990 – search a person and any vehicle or thing in their possession for a controlled or prohibited weapon or dangerous article. However, a PSO is not authorised to conduct a strip search in accordance with clauses 7-10, Schedule 1, Control of Weapons Act ss. 13-16, Graffiti Prevention Act 2007 – search a person and any vehicle, package or thing in their possession for a graffiti implement ss. 60E-60H, Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act 1981 – search a person and any vehicle, package or thing in their possession for a volatile substance or item used to inhale a volatile substance ss. 82-82A, Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act – search a person, vehicle or animal for a drug of dependence. Conduct and recording of search PSOs must conduct the searches and make records of the search in accordance with VPM Searches of a person. Search powers relating to a designated area – Control of Weapons Act Where a designated area has been declared in accordance with ss. 10D or 10E, Control of Weapons Act and any part of that area covers a designated place where PSOs are on duty, PSOs may be utilised to perform the following duties: without warrant stop and search: a person anything in their possession or under their control a vehicle, if there is a person in or on the vehicle that has been found in a public place, within that designated area. The officer in charge (OIC) of the designated area operation can elect to utilise PSOs to perform searches where a designated area and designated place overlap. Where a direction has been given that PSOs will be utilised the following applies: PSOs can only perform these duties where police are present and actively involved in the designated area operation PSOs do not have the authority to conduct a strip search (as defined under the Control of Weapons Act). Refer to VPM Designated areas – conducting searches and issuing directions for specific requirements and procedures regarding these powers. Power to request name and address In accordance with s.456AA, Crimes Act, a PSO on duty at a designated place may request a person provide their name and address if the PSO believes on reasonable grounds either of the following: the person has committed or is

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: strip search (as defined under the Control of Weapons Act). Refer to VPM Designated areas – conducting searches and issuing directions for specific requirements and procedures regarding these powers. Power to request name and address In accordance with s.456AA, Crimes Act, a PSO on duty at a designated place may request a person provide their name and address if the PSO believes on reasonable grounds either of the following: the person has committed or is about to commit an offence (indictable or summary) the person may be able to assist in the investigation of an indictable offence which has, or is suspected of having been committed. In accordance with s. 456AA, PSOs must state their name, rank and place of duty if requested by a person who is subject to the above power. Arrests Legislative authority PSOs on duty at a designated place are authorised to: apprehend offenders without warrant under s.459, Crimes Act arrest without warrant a person released on bail under s.24, Bail Act 1977 arrest a person, under warrant, who has had their parole cancelled under s.77B, Corrections Act 1986 arrest without warrant a person who is in breach of their parole under s.78B, Corrections Act arrest a person who has committed an offence against the Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act and regulations under s.219, Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act apprehend and detain a person who is under 18 years of age in relation to volatile substances, under Part 4, Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act apprehend a child subject to a relevant search warrant under s.598A, Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 execute a warrant to arrest under s.65(1), Magistrates’ Court Act 1989 arrest a person without warrant under s.458, Crimes Act (as PSOs have the authority to arrest for indictable matters under s.459, s.458 will generally apply to summary offences). Arrests by members of the public or Authorised Officers (TA) Where a member of the public or an Authorised Officer (TA) apprehends a person in accordance with s.458, Crimes Act, PSOs must only take custody of the person if they are able to apprehend them on their own authority under an arrest power listed in section 5.1 of this policy. Where an Authorised Officer (TA) apprehends a person in accordance with s.219, Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act the person can only be handed over to the PSO if they are able to form their own belief that there are reasonable grounds to apprehend the person for an offence against that Act or its Regulations. When a PSO cannot arrest a person on their own authority, but they believe there is a continuing power of arrest on the part of the member of the public or

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: with s.219, Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act the person can only be handed over to the PSO if they are able to form their own belief that there are reasonable grounds to apprehend the person for an offence against that Act or its Regulations. When a PSO cannot arrest a person on their own authority, but they believe there is a continuing power of arrest on the part of the member of the public or Authorised Officer (TA), they should: advise the member of the public or Authorised Officer (TA) that the PSO has no legal authority to intervene in the circumstances and the person should be handed to a police member, and ensure that a police member is contacted and apprised of the situation and asked to attend, and remain with the member of the public or Authorised Officer (TA) and provide all lawful assistance reasonably required in the circumstances until a police member does attend. Making the arrest In making the arrest, PSOs must comply with VPM Arrest and warrants to arrest. Where the person is not released immediately and if suitable facilities exist, the arrested person should be placed in an area that enables appropriate privacy and security as far as practicable, until a police member attends in accordance with section 5.4 of this policy. The PSO must not leave the person unattended. The PSO must place any seized property in a Tamper Evident Audit Bag (TEAB) (unless impracticable) and store it is a secure location until it is: handed over to a TSD or regional police member in accordance with sections 5.5, 5.6 or 9.2 of this policy transported to TSD in accordance with sections 5.7 or 6.3 of this police. After arrest After the person is arrested or apprehended, the PSO must hand the person into the custody of a police member as soon as practicable in accordance with section 5.5 of this policy. Exceptions to this requirement are where: the person is released pending process being issued for a summary offence in accordance with s.458(3), Crimes Act or s.219(4), Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act; see section 5.7 of this policy for details on processing these matters an infringement notice is issued for offences; see section 6 of this policy for details a person who is under 18 is detained under s.60L, Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act and they are released or given in to the care of a suitable person or police member (ss.60M(3) and 60BA, respectively). To hand a person into the custody of a police member, the PSO must contact Police Communications and request police attendance. Where possible, a TSD member/unit will be requested to attend and assume the handover/informant responsibilities.

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: for details a person who is under 18 is detained under s.60L, Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act and they are released or given in to the care of a suitable person or police member (ss.60M(3) and 60BA, respectively). To hand a person into the custody of a police member, the PSO must contact Police Communications and request police attendance. Where possible, a TSD member/unit will be requested to attend and assume the handover/informant responsibilities. Whilst TSD has management responsibility for PSOs they do not have sole responsibility for handover of offenders. If a TSD member/unit is unavailable, a police member/unit from the relevant PSA will be required to attend and assume the responsibilities. Requested police members are to attend the relevant location as soon as possible (see VPM Operational duties and responsibilities). Process for handing a person into the custody of a police member The attending police member must be satisfied that the grounds for arrest or apprehension under the relevant Act exist. If satisfied, the police member takes responsibility for the arrest and becomes the informant for the matter. The PSO should follow the below process for handing a person into the custody of a police member: complete a PSO/LEAP Handover Report [Form 1412] where applicable, request for Closed Circuit Television footage using the Public Transport Data Application Form [Form 1306] make a record of the arrest and the handover (including the receiving member’s details) on the electronic Patrol Duty Return (ePDR) or if this is unavailable use the Initial Action Pad [Form 502], and complete a Use of Force form App report if applicable handover the informant copy of the Form 1412 and any seized property to the informant complete a Statement. This should be completed and forwarded to the informant as soon as practicable. After the informant has received their copy of the Form 1412 and any seized property they are then responsible for: taking the arrested person to their station for processing in the usual manner completing all supplementary LEAP reports (the Form 1412 takes the place of an Incident Report [Form L1] for PSO arrests) ensuring the Form 1412 and relevant LEAP forms are faxed to Central Data Entry Bureau (CDEB) at the end of their shift. Processing the arrest where the person has been released Where a person arrested by a PSO is to be processed by way of a summons, and therefore does not need to be handed into the custody of a police member, the following process applies: the PSO must complete Form 1412 where applicable, the PSO should make a request for Closed Circuit Television footage using the Public Transport Data Application Form [Form 1306] the PSO must make a

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: arrest where the person has been released Where a person arrested by a PSO is to be processed by way of a summons, and therefore does not need to be handed into the custody of a police member, the following process applies: the PSO must complete Form 1412 where applicable, the PSO should make a request for Closed Circuit Television footage using the Public Transport Data Application Form [Form 1306] the PSO must make a record of the arrest on ePDR at the end of their shift, the PSO must submit all completed Form 1412s with any seized property to a supervising sergeant at TSD the sergeant is responsible for ensuring that: relevant entries have been made on Form 1412 and it is faxed to CDEB an entry in the Brief Register is made (see VPMG Brief preparation and management) the matter is allocated to a police member, who becomes the informant any seized property is recorded and stored (see VPM Seized property and special property types). the PSO must complete a Statement. This should be completed and forwarded to the informant as soon as practicable after the arrest. Crime reports where an offender is not present A PSO on duty at a designated place may detect or be notified of a crime that has occurred at or in the vicinity of the designated place where there is no offender present (such as property damage, theft from or of a motor vehicle, etc). In these circumstances, the PSO is required to complete and submit all relevant LEAP reports in accordance with VPM Crime and event reporting and recording. They are then to submit the reports at the end of the shift to a supervising Sergeant at TSD. Issuing infringement notices Legislative authority PSOs on duty at a designated place are authorised to issue infringement notices under: Control of Weapons Act for possess, carry or use a controlled weapon without lawful excuse Environmental Protection Act 1970 for littering offences Graffiti Prevention Act for possess a prescribed graffiti implement without lawful excuse Liquor Control Reform Act 1998 for the following offences: s.119(3) – supply liquor to a person under 18 years s.123(1)(b) – possess or consume liquor by a person under 18 years Road Safety Act 1986 for parking infringements that occur at or in the vicinity of the designated place Summary Offences Act, for the following offences: s.6 – contravention of a direction to move on s.17A – disorderly behaviour in a public place s.17(1)(c) – indecent or obscene language s.17(1(d) – behaves in a riotous indecent offensive or insulting manner. Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act and Transport Conduct Regulations for various ticketing or other transport offences. Issuing the infringement notice

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: for parking infringements that occur at or in the vicinity of the designated place Summary Offences Act, for the following offences: s.6 – contravention of a direction to move on s.17A – disorderly behaviour in a public place s.17(1)(c) – indecent or obscene language s.17(1(d) – behaves in a riotous indecent offensive or insulting manner. Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act and Transport Conduct Regulations for various ticketing or other transport offences. Issuing the infringement notice Infringement notices are to be issued in accordance with the relevant acts, VPM Disposition and VPM Infringement notices and official warnings. Seized property Any seized property is to be transported to TSD at the end of the shift. Contested infringement notices If the recipient of an infringement notice elects to contest the notice at court, the PSO is responsible for compiling the brief in accordance with VPMP Briefs of evidence. Taking a person into care and control under the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 Legislative requirements PSOs on duty at a designated place or in the vicinity of a designated place are authorised to take a person in a mental health crisis into care and control, to prevent serious or imminent harm to that person or another person, in accordance with s.232, Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022. PSOs also have the power to a take a person into their care and control if the person is required to be transported under the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act, including if the person is absent without leave from a mental health service. In order to take the person into their care and control, PSOs have the power to enter premises, search the person under certain circumstances and seize any things found during the search. For further information, see VPM Care and control under the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022. When a PSO takes a person into care and control under the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act, they must transfer the care and control of the person to a police member as soon as practicable. This is done by contacting Police Communications to request the attendance of a police member from TSD or the local PSA (whichever is available) and notifying a supervisor. Handover to a police member When handing a person in care and control over to a police member, the PSO: should hold the person in an area that enables appropriate privacy and security as far as practicable must complete the Mental Health Transfer Form [Form L42] as far as possible. Record the details of the police member taking custody of the person in the ‘Circumstances’ field of the Form must record the handover on ePDR. If applicable, a Use of Force App

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: a person in care and control over to a police member, the PSO: should hold the person in an area that enables appropriate privacy and security as far as practicable must complete the Mental Health Transfer Form [Form L42] as far as possible. Record the details of the police member taking custody of the person in the ‘Circumstances’ field of the Form must record the handover on ePDR. If applicable, a Use of Force App report must also be completed. The police member is responsible for apprehending the person and arranging for the person to be taken to an appropriate mental health service or other place in accordance with VPM Care and control under the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022. Family violence Context The primary response of PSOs in reports of family violence is the safety and welfare of the affected family member (AFM) and children and to gather sufficient information for police to respond to the incident in accordance with the Victoria Police Family Violence Response Model (see VPM Family violence). PSO response to family violence incidents Where PSOs are notified of, or identify a possible family violence incident they must: assess the scene and identify all persons, including any children who are present (and consider the welfare of children) organise medical treatment if required consider the level of immediate threat to any person, identify if a criminal offence has occurred and where a power of arrest exists, arrest if appropriate notify the TSD police supervisor separate the parties, confirm what has occurred and conduct LEAP checks contact police to attend via Police Communications. Police must be contacted to attend regardless of the immediacy of the threat. Police have specific powers to detain or direct a person who has committed family violence. PSOs do not have this power. If the respondent has not committed an offence for which they can be arrested, PSOs have no power to detain them whilst waiting for police attendance. If the AFM refuses to wait for police, there is no power to compel them to remain. Immediately notify Police Communications and the police supervisor that the AFM is refusing to remain at the location. Obtain details of all parties as far as possible (including contact telephone numbers). The TSD police sergeant must ensure attending police respond in accordance with VPM Family violence. Note: Contact with a PSO may be the first opportunity an AFM has had to report a family violence incident that has previously occurred. Even if the incident(s) occurred outside of a Designated Place, PSOs must take steps to ensure police have the best opportunity to intervene and protect AFMs, including children. PSOs must undertake an operational assessment of all family

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: TSD police sergeant must ensure attending police respond in accordance with VPM Family violence. Note: Contact with a PSO may be the first opportunity an AFM has had to report a family violence incident that has previously occurred. Even if the incident(s) occurred outside of a Designated Place, PSOs must take steps to ensure police have the best opportunity to intervene and protect AFMs, including children. PSOs must undertake an operational assessment of all family violence incident reports they receive and identify all affected parties, including children and young people. Road policing Preventing a person from driving PSOs on duty at a designated place have powers under the Road Safety Act as follows: they may request a driver of a vehicle that is being driven from or into a car park at or in the vicinity of a designated place to stop the vehicle, produce their licence and state their name and address (s.59A) if they believe on reasonable grounds that a person driving or about to drive a vehicle is incapable of having proper control of the motor vehicle, the PSO may forbid the person to drive the vehicle and require that the driver gives them the keys to the vehicle (s.62(1)). Generally, PSOs will invoke these responsibilities when they intend to use one of the arrest powers outlined at section 5.1 of this policy. In most cases, this will require the attendance and handover of the person to a police member in accordance with section 5.5 of this policy. Vehicle collisions If a vehicle collision occurs at or in the vicinity of a designated place and is reported to a PSO on duty at that place, the PSO is to conduct a preliminary investigation to determine what course of action is appropriate, as follows: if no injury occurred and all property owners can be notified, the PSO should distribute a ‘Collision Information Pamphlet’ and make notes in ePDR (see VPM Road policing – general) if there is an apparent injury to any party or any offences identified, a police member should be requested to attend and to manage and investigate the matter in accordance with VPM Road policing - general. Handling property Lost or abandoned property Members of the public may find lost or abandoned property. If public transport staff and/or lost property facilities are present, they should be advised to hand lost or abandoned property to staff. If these facilities are not available, PSOs should take responsibility for the property. In these cases, the PSO must: complete Notice of Claim or Abandonment for Property [Form 439] ask the finder if they wish their details to be disclosed to the owner if identified and make a notation on

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: or abandoned property. If public transport staff and/or lost property facilities are present, they should be advised to hand lost or abandoned property to staff. If these facilities are not available, PSOs should take responsibility for the property. In these cases, the PSO must: complete Notice of Claim or Abandonment for Property [Form 439] ask the finder if they wish their details to be disclosed to the owner if identified and make a notation on ePDR at the end of the shift, take the property to TSD for storage and recording in accordance with VPM Property and exhibit management. Seized property Any seized property must be handled using either of the below options: handed over to a TSD or Regional police member in accordance with sections 5.5, 5.6 or 9.3 of this policy, for storage and recording at the member’s station taken to TSD in accordance with sections 5.7 or 6.3 of this policy, for storage and recording at TSD. Property seized under the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act must be handed over to a police member and not carried away. When property cannot be safely stored If property is seized by or handed to a PSO which cannot be safely stored, is of high risk or is dangerous, the PSO must handover the property to an available police member as soon as practicable. The police member must take the property to their home police station for recoding and storing in accordance with VPM Property and exhibit management. Declaration of a designated place Overview Section 3A, Victoria Police Act allows for Victoria Police to, in certain circumstances, declare a designated place for the deployment of PSOs for a specific period to provide services for the protection of the general public. The declaration of a designated place may be made: Non-urgent Declaration – for a period not exceeding 12 months; where the deployment of PSOs is necessary or desirable for community safety or reassurance of the public (s.3A(2)) Urgent Declaration – for a period not exceeding 48 hours; where urgent or unforeseen circumstances require the deployment of PSOs (s.3A(4)). Both types of declaration may only be made where: the exercise of powers by PSOs will not unduly limit the human rights of any person PSOs are supervised by police officers. When PSOs are deployed to a designated place declared under s.3A, they have the same powers and duties as when on duty at an otherwise designated place. Declaring a designated place Only an Authorised Officer may approve the declaration of a designated place. An Authorised Officer must be an Assistant Commissioner or above, as enabled by Instrument of Delegation GP 6 for non-urgent matters and s.3A(4) for urgent matters. The

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: are supervised by police officers. When PSOs are deployed to a designated place declared under s.3A, they have the same powers and duties as when on duty at an otherwise designated place. Declaring a designated place Only an Authorised Officer may approve the declaration of a designated place. An Authorised Officer must be an Assistant Commissioner or above, as enabled by Instrument of Delegation GP 6 for non-urgent matters and s.3A(4) for urgent matters. The Authorised Officer must be satisfied that the following criteria are met: Areas that can be declared a designated place In accordance with s.3A(1), the following places or areas can be declared as a designated place: an area that: adjoins a designated place; and adjoins or is a public thoroughfare to a roadway, sporting venue or a place of mass gathering. a public thoroughfare used to access or exit from the public transport network, a sporting venue or a place of mass gathering an area surrounding or adjacent to a sporting venue, a venue of public entertainment or a place of mass gathering any large area, including the central business district of Melbourne or any part of it. Application process – Non-urgent Declaration The Region or Command seeking approval for a Non-urgent Declaration is responsible for confirming resource availability by contacting TPSC Tasking and Coordination (T&C) and submitting an application for resources. Once the resources have been approved by Assistant Commissioner TPSC, a senior sergeant or above from the requesting Region or Command must complete: an Application to Declare a Designated Place [Form 1512] an Operation Order and Risk Assessment [Form 1117] a draft Notice for Declaring the Designated Place (see section 11.6 of this policy for further information on the notice of declaration process). The member completing Form 1512 should consult with TSD T&C for advice. Further guidance on the overall application process, including completing Form 1512 can be found on the TSD Intranet page under TSD T&C. The completed Form 1512 must be endorsed by an inspector before it is progressed, along with Form 1117 and the draft Notice, through the requesting Region or Command’s chain of command to an Authorised Officer for approval. A copy of the approved/not approved Form 1512, Form 1117 and published Notice must then be provided to TSD T&C. Where the Region or Command chooses to utilise PSOs in a voluntary duties’ capacity, the same application process applies except for the requirement to contact TPSC T&C for resources. Application process – Urgent Declaration The Region or Command seeking approval for an Urgent Declaration must first confirm the availability of resources by contacting the TSD duty inspector (TSD 150) by telephone. Where the resources are available, the requesting Region or

title: Operational_duties_responsibilities_VPM_PSO_duties_and_responsibilities_final
text: be provided to TSD T&C. Where the Region or Command chooses to utilise PSOs in a voluntary duties’ capacity, the same application process applies except for the requirement to contact TPSC T&C for resources. Application process – Urgent Declaration The Region or Command seeking approval for an Urgent Declaration must first confirm the availability of resources by contacting the TSD duty inspector (TSD 150) by telephone. Where the resources are available, the requesting Region or Command must submit a formal request for approval of the resources to the TSD duty inspector by email/text message. Requests for resources will be approved/not approved by the Assistant Commissioner TPSC, or afterhours by the duty superintendent TPSC. If the resources are approved the Region or Command Assistant Commissioner/duty superintendent is responsible for ensuring the following are completed: Form 1512 a draft Notice for Declaring the Designated Place (see section 11.6 of this policy for further information on the notice of declaration process). The member completing Form 1512 should consult with TSD T&C for advice. Further guidance on the overall application process, including completing Form 1512 can be found on the TSD Intranet page under TSD T&C. The completed Form 1512 must be endorsed by a superintendent from the requesting Region or Command, before it is progressed, along with the draft Notice, to an Authorised Officer for approval (where possible the Authorised Officer should be from the requesting Region or Command). A copy of the approved/not approved Form 1512 and published Notice must then be provided to TSD T&C. The Region or Command Assistant Commissioner will need to consider if a Non-urgent Declaration is required to replace the Urgent Declaration when it expires. Refer to section 11.4 of this police for the process of requesting a Non-urgent Declaration. Notice of declaration Where a Non-urgent Declaration is approved (s.3A(2)), a Notice must be published both: in the Government Gazette on the Victoria Police website. Where an Urgent Declaration is approved (s.3A(4)), a Notice must be published on the Victoria Police website. The declaration comes into operation on the day on which it is made available to the public on the Victoria Police website. Where a Non-urgent Declaration has been made to replace a revoked or expired Urgent Declaration, the declaration comes into operation on that revocation or expiry date. The Notice must: describe the designated area and provide specific boundaries include a map of the designated area specify the overall period of operation of the declaration.
