title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: Body worn cameras Context A Body Worn Camera (BWC) is a small, overt camera, worn by members and used when they are performing operational duties. The BWC can capture direct and objective audio and video recordings of police interactions with members of the public, as well as real time capture of video evidence at crime scenes and incidents. The use of BWCs is governed by the Surveillance Devices Act 1999. The use of BWCs offers significant benefits to Victoria Police and the community by: improving evidence collection and prosecution outcomes enhancing police and community interactions by promoting transparency, accountability and safety for both members and the community. Contents Context 1 Contents 1 Definitions 1 Scope and application 2 Responsibilities and procedures 2 1. Member responsibilities 2 2. Supervisor responsibilities 2 3. Activation Framework 3 4. Persons in custody 5 5. Critical incidents 5 6. Assigning BWCs 6 7. Kit up/down 6 8. Evidence management 7 9. Use of BWC footage as evidence 9 10. Lost, stolen, damaged or faulted BWCs 10 11. Voluntary duties 11 12. DEMS file sharing – collecting information from the public 11 Related documents 12 Further advice and information 12 Update history 12 Definitions Critical incident – as defined by s.82, Victoria Police Act 2013 Dock – a power board for charging and uploading of BWC DEMS – digital evidence management system – evidence.com Metadata – a set of data that describes and gives information about other data Frontline duties – duties that involve interactions with the public, including general patrolling, traffic management, public order management and/or where responding to an incident is likely or expected Standby – when the BWC is fitted to the member’s uniform and switched on ready to start recording Start – when the event button on the BWC is pressed to commence recording Stop – when the event button on the BWC is pressed to stop recording and return the BWC to standby mode. Scope and application This policy applies to: members who are issued a BWC work unit managers who will manage the devices members responding to or investigating critical incidents in accordance with section 5 of this instruction. Responsibilities and procedures Member responsibilities Requirements for wearing a BWC Once assigned a BWC, members must wear the device when performing frontline duties. When wearing the BWC, members must ensure they are easily identifiable as a member by either: being in uniform displaying a certificate of identity and wearing a ballistic vest with police identification velcro tabs and/or high visibility police safety vest. Members must wear the BWC in a position which is overt and easy for the public to recognise that the member is wearing the device. In circumstances where

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: wear the device when performing frontline duties. When wearing the BWC, members must ensure they are easily identifiable as a member by either: being in uniform displaying a certificate of identity and wearing a ballistic vest with police identification velcro tabs and/or high visibility police safety vest. Members must wear the BWC in a position which is overt and easy for the public to recognise that the member is wearing the device. In circumstances where the criteria above are met, but a member is unable to wear a BWC for any reason, that member must: notify their direct supervisor to provide that reason/explanation note the reason and details of the supervisor notified on their ePDR or VP502 Initial Action Pad. Requirement to comply with activation framework A member is required to advise their supervisor where they have failed to comply with the activation framework. Supervisor responsibilities A supervisor is responsible for monitoring the use of BWC during their shift. Activation Framework General principle While acknowledging there are some technical and practical limitations, the expectation is that a member wearing a BWC will be recording the majority of operational incidents for their shift. The following section provides criteria for starting and stopping a BWC recording. The operational policing environment is dynamic and there will be situations when the decision to start the BWC will be unclear. If doubt exists, a member must start the BWC recording and later categorise the footage in line with BWC Operational guidelines. A member must commence recording once a decision is made that the circumstances meet the criteria below and where practicable before the activity/interaction occurs for example prior to attending an incident when developing operational plans or tactics. When a BWC recording is required A member wearing a BWC must start a recording: when exercising legislated or common law powers – this includes: the arrest/detention of person/s for any offence, including exercising family violence holding powers vehicle interceptions or checkpoint/RBT sites person/property/premises search conducted with or without warrant (for property searches comply with VPM Searches of property; see section 3.5 of this policy for recording limitations) attending private premises to request a preliminary breath test or abate residential noise issuing infringement notices in car briefings process service, e.g. serving a summons, intervention order or Family Violence Safety Notice interactions with the public where a Field Contact Report is required inspections of premises in accordance with the Liquor Control Reform Act 1998, Firearms Act 1996 or Second-hand Dealers Act 1989 to capture an incident occurring, likely to occur or which has occurred – this includes: attendance at a Triple Zero Victoria (TZV) task, eTask, or station task resulting in a public contact a police pursuit or

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: summons, intervention order or Family Violence Safety Notice interactions with the public where a Field Contact Report is required inspections of premises in accordance with the Liquor Control Reform Act 1998, Firearms Act 1996 or Second-hand Dealers Act 1989 to capture an incident occurring, likely to occur or which has occurred – this includes: attendance at a Triple Zero Victoria (TZV) task, eTask, or station task resulting in a public contact a police pursuit or vehicle interdiction where it is safe to do so, or the deployment of vehicle immobilising devices (excludes vehicles fitted with ANPR and ICV system) being approached/hailed by the public in need of police assistance observations of and attendance to the public in need of assistance during public order events as directed by the Police Commander (see BWC Operational guidelines for further details). When a BWC recording is recommended Members should start a BWC recording on any other occasion they believe a recording is necessary and would assist in: providing transparency during a public interaction or police activity collecting evidence, including recording summary offence interviews conducted in police stations, such as evidentiary breath tests or driver impairment assessments. Where it is not possible to make written notes, the BWC may be used to make a digital record of briefings, initial action plans, on air briefings, tactical briefings or safety briefings as directed by the Police Forward Commander or Police Commander. Contemporaneous notes must still be made when practicable. When to stop recording Members should only stop a recording when: an interaction ceases an incident is resolved or otherwise ends directed to stop by a supervisor in accordance with this policy directed to stop by a member in charge of a critical incident response. When not to start a BWC recording Members must not record in the following circumstances: outside their police duties or functions when conducting a formal indictable offence interview irrespective of the location to covertly record conversations with other members of Victoria Police in line with VPM Recording devices, CCTV and digital asset management during a full or intrusive body search (as defined in VPM Searches of a person) when they are engaged in private conversation. Members should not record in the following circumstances: where a reasonable expectation of privacy exists (e.g. changing rooms, toilets) unless the exercise of the police power, duty or function outweighs the privacy/human right being limited within a police station where CCTV is operating, unless the member believes there is a genuine operational need while taking crime reports and/or an admissible written statement from a victim/witness, unless the member believes the report may be false when undertaking community engagement activities unless there is an operational necessity. BWC must not

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: privacy exists (e.g. changing rooms, toilets) unless the exercise of the police power, duty or function outweighs the privacy/human right being limited within a police station where CCTV is operating, unless the member believes there is a genuine operational need while taking crime reports and/or an admissible written statement from a victim/witness, unless the member believes the report may be false when undertaking community engagement activities unless there is an operational necessity. BWC must not be used as an alternative to the appropriate formal interviewing and processing of a suspect in custody for an indictable offence as outlined in VPM Interviews and statements. When asked by a member of the public to start or stop a BWC recording, members should balance that request against the BWC Activation Framework, the context of the incident and involvement of the member of the public. When a recording is not made, stopped or muted When the Activation Framework applies, but a recording is either not made, is stopped prematurely or muted, the member must record the circumstances on either: the unit’s ePDR, VP502 Initial Action Pad or member’s official diary on the recording itself, prior to deactivation or muting. The member’s record must: provide enough detail to later account for the omission identify the supervisor who directed the action (if applicable). If the action was directed by a supervisor, they must record this on: their ePDR, VP502 Initial Action Pad or official diary, or the recording itself, prior to deactivation or muting. When to mute a recording Members should only mute a recording when: directed to mute a recording by a supervisor in accordance with this policy making or receiving a telephone call when not directly communicating with a subject. Persons in custody Where a person is to be taken into custody (as defined by s.464, Crimes Act) or otherwise detained, a recording must be started in line with the Activation Framework. If caution and rights are provided or a confession/admission is made before the BWC recording is started, then the provision of caution and rights or those admissions should be confirmed by the person when the BWC is started. Also see section 9 for formal indictable offence interviews requirements. Except where recordings should be stopped, or not started in accordance with sections 3.4 and 3.5, the arresting member’s BWC must record continuously for the duration of the member’s interaction with the person in custody, until the person is: released from custody transferred to another police member/unit’s custody secured in the pod or cell compartment of a police vehicle formally transferred to a correctional facility or the care of another agency (Ambulance Victoria/Hospital/mental health facility) brought into a police station or premises and placed

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: in accordance with sections 3.4 and 3.5, the arresting member’s BWC must record continuously for the duration of the member’s interaction with the person in custody, until the person is: released from custody transferred to another police member/unit’s custody secured in the pod or cell compartment of a police vehicle formally transferred to a correctional facility or the care of another agency (Ambulance Victoria/Hospital/mental health facility) brought into a police station or premises and placed into an area, room or cell with the intention of conducting a formal interview or otherwise continuing their custody. The requirement above applies to persons required to accompany the member to a police facility or place in accordance with the ss.55 and 55A, Road Safety Act 1986. Critical incidents In the event of a critical incident, unless a member believes there is a genuine operational need, they must continue a BWC recording until directed to stop on the arrival of the member in charge of the incident. The member in charge of the incident must: at the earliest opportunity at the conclusion of the incident, direct a member involved to stop their BWC recording and make a note of that direction in line with section 3.6 take possession of the BWC worn by a member directly involved in the incident, ensuring continuity of the device and recording, until it can be docked as soon as practicable. Dependent upon the circumstances, the handover of a BWC should occur: at the time of the hand-over of all Operational Safety Equipment (OSE) in line with the Initial Action Checklist for Managing Death or Serious Injury/illness Incidents, or at the earliest opportunity, if the hand-over of all OSE is not warranted in the circumstances. The member who takes possession of a BWC must retain the device until such time as it can be: docked as soon as practicable to complete the upload of data, or handed to the member responsible for the investigation of the incident for forensic testing. Upon receipt of a BWC, the investigating member must: provide their details to the work unit manager responsible for the BWC advise the work unit manager if the device is to be retained as a physical exhibit ensure that all footage on the device is uploaded to the evidence management system determine the appropriate title for the footage of the incident under investigation categorise critical incident footage as PSC. If a BWC is handed over or seized, the work unit manager should inform the: Equipment Officer, for recording BWC portfolio holder, to liaise with the investigating member to expedite return of the BWC to the work unit A member involved in a critical incident, either directly or as a witness,

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: uploaded to the evidence management system determine the appropriate title for the footage of the incident under investigation categorise critical incident footage as PSC. If a BWC is handed over or seized, the work unit manager should inform the: Equipment Officer, for recording BWC portfolio holder, to liaise with the investigating member to expedite return of the BWC to the work unit A member involved in a critical incident, either directly or as a witness, will be provided the opportunity to view BWC footage in accordance with section 9.1 of this policy. Assigning BWCs Once deployed to the workplace, a BWC, where available, must be assigned to: each member who ordinarily performs frontline duties a member temporarily performing frontline duties who has an active DEMS account. Only members who have completed the relevant BWC training may be assigned a BWC. The use of privately owned body worn recording devices is prohibited. Kit up/down When receiving a BWC, a member must ensure the BWC is: fully charged and ready for use free from damage, has no obvious fault and is in working order correctly mounted to the member’s uniform using an approved mounting solution positioned in a location and at an angle that optimises the capture of footage switched on and placed into standby mode. The BWC must remain mounted to the member’s uniform for the duration of its use, except when the BWC is: used to record Digitally Recorded Evidence in Chief (DREC) in line with VPM Digitally recorded evidence-in-chief (DREC) - family violence; or hand-held in accordance with the BWC Operational Guidelines. When considering the location and mounting of the BWC, a member must ensure that the BWC is: placed in the designated mounting location on the ballistic vest not placed in a position which interferes with other operational equipment, their carriage systems or may pose an occupational safety risk. Prior to returning the BWC to the station equipment office, members must: ensure that the BWC is switched off identify/report any faults or damage to the device or its peripherals if possible, categorise all footage captured on the BWC. Evidence management Adding metadata and categorisation The BWC has a pre-set 30 second, video only buffer which captures footage, when in standby mode, prior to the device being started. When a recording is made using the BWC, adding metadata of footage occurs when: the device automatically tags the footage with metadata a member tags an image or footage; which will reference the recording to an incident or occurrence and category. Adding additional metadata may occur: in the field at the station, after the footage is uploaded, using the DEMS. BWC must be paired with a Victoria Police issued mobile device

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: the device being started. When a recording is made using the BWC, adding metadata of footage occurs when: the device automatically tags the footage with metadata a member tags an image or footage; which will reference the recording to an incident or occurrence and category. Adding additional metadata may occur: in the field at the station, after the footage is uploaded, using the DEMS. BWC must be paired with a Victoria Police issued mobile device (see CCI 10/17). Members must not pair the BWC with a privately owned device. If categorisation of footage is not completed prior to the return of the BWC, the member must use the DEMS to complete that process, once the footage has been uploaded. Any free text added to an image/footage must avoid discriminatory attributes or descriptions in line with VPM Professional and ethical standards and VPM Human rights standards. Metadata, tagging and categorisation of footage are fully detailed in the BWC Operational guidelines. DEMS BWC footage is automatically uploaded to the DEMS once the BWC is docked. Access to the system is auditable and use of footage requires a legitimate business need, which may include brief compilation, investigative purposes or complaint investigation purposes. The business reason for sharing or accessing the footage must be recorded in the notes section of that file: when the footage is shared; or where the member is not the owner of the footage. During the station evidence management process, members are responsible for: reviewing, categorising and adding metadata to their BWC footage within one month of uploading the footage creating a redacted copy from their original BWC footage providing access to their footage to another member for a legitimate business need. During the station evidence management process, supervisors are responsible for: reviewing and categorising footage if the member wearing the BWC is unable reviewing the appropriate redaction of BWC footage authorising the sharing of another member’s footage for a legitimate business need. During the production or the review of a brief of evidence, BWC footage can be reviewed, edited and redacted from the original copy by any member who has been provided access to and requires the use of that footage. Members must not use a personal device capable of video capture, to record, store, share or disseminate BWC footage being played on a Victoria Police mobile device or computer. The original recording is maintained and cannot be edited. Every alteration/redaction creates a new file copy. DEMS Auto-transcription The following instructions are to be read in conjunction with VPM Interviews and statements. Officers in charge, operational supervisors and detectives have DEMS permission to activate the auto-transcription feature of any evidence file stored within the DEMS. This allows a transcription

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: store, share or disseminate BWC footage being played on a Victoria Police mobile device or computer. The original recording is maintained and cannot be edited. Every alteration/redaction creates a new file copy. DEMS Auto-transcription The following instructions are to be read in conjunction with VPM Interviews and statements. Officers in charge, operational supervisors and detectives have DEMS permission to activate the auto-transcription feature of any evidence file stored within the DEMS. This allows a transcription to be created for the following matters: contested Indictable Offences Triable Summarily (IOTS) matters (‘not guilty’ pleas) when directed by a prosecutor where the matter is subject of committal proceedings or direct indictment to County or Supreme Courts DREC statements otherwise directed by a prosecutor’s Work Unit Manager or the Office of Public Prosecutions. The member who creates an auto-transcription for any DEMS file, must make a note justifying the reason within the notes section of that file. Where a transcription has been created, it is the informant’s responsibility to ensure accuracy by editing and verifying any and all relevant transcripts which must be completed and checked by a supervisor prior to it being provided or disseminated as an aide memoir. Work unit manager responsibilities The work unit manager must ensure: BWCs are correctly assigned, inspected and accounted for, in line with BWC Operational guidelines evidence files are managed in accordance with the BWC Operational guidelines, including ensuring that: the DEMS work unit group is current and up to date uncategorised footage does not exceed one month since its recorded-on date footage incorrectly categorised is identified and remediated members with low numbers of BWC recordings relative to the number of frontline duties performed are identified for workplace guidance as required supervisors log in to the DEMS to conduct monthly reviews of the footage. Use of BWC footage as evidence General BWCs support conventional forms of evidence gathering; they do not replace them. Members must continue to preserve and collect evidence in line with VPM Crime attendance and investigation. In accordance with VPM Witness statements, before compiling a witness statement for all incidents, (or being interviewed for a critical incident), members must document their independent recollection by making contemporaneous notes or commencing a statement prior to viewing their own BWC footage. The point at which the BWC footage is viewed must be recorded within contemporaneous notes and written statements, including the date and time. Where the primary reason for viewing BWC footage is for investigative purposes, members may view their own or any other relevant BWC footage prior to making contemporaneous notes as required in VPM Operational duties and responsibilities. An example of where BWC footage may be viewed for investigative purposes could be when a

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: The point at which the BWC footage is viewed must be recorded within contemporaneous notes and written statements, including the date and time. Where the primary reason for viewing BWC footage is for investigative purposes, members may view their own or any other relevant BWC footage prior to making contemporaneous notes as required in VPM Operational duties and responsibilities. An example of where BWC footage may be viewed for investigative purposes could be when a suspect has fled a scene and viewing the footage will allow the member to compile a clear description to assist in locating the suspect. Members must record the date, time and reason for viewing the footage. Members may also view BWC footage to facilitate evidence management processes (see section 8 of this policy). Provision of BWC footage which records caution, rights or admissions Section 464H, Crimes Act applies where a BWC recording is made of an unplanned confession, admission or provision of caution and/or rights for an indictable offence. This does not replace the need to conduct a formal interview at a police station in accordance with VPM Interviews and statements. In these circumstances, as soon as practicable upon arrival at a police station, the member should initiate the BWC uploading procedure outlined in the BWC Operational guidelines. Prior to the person being released or remanded/further held in custody: access the footage in the DEMs redact (where appropriate) and copy the relevant footage to a DVD provide that DVD to the person by either handing it to them or lodging it in the person’s property. Where the requirements above cannot be met for any reason, the member must provide the person or their legal representative a copy of any relevant footage, which may later be relied upon as evidence, no later than seven days after the recording was made. Failure to provide a copy of the relevant footage may result in the inadmissibility of that footage as evidence at court. Use and disclosure of BWC footage in court BWC footage, as either direct or indirect evidence must be: included in the preparation of the brief of evidence in line with VPMP Briefs of evidence referred to in the Statement of Alleged Facts in the Preliminary Brief [Form 1372] and listed on the Exhibit List, attributable to the police witness who wore the BWC. BWC footage forming part of a brief of evidence must be: reviewed as part of the authorisation process disclosed as part of the normal disclosure procedure outlined in VPMG Brief preparation and management. BWC footage (redacted or otherwise) disclosed by the informant can be further redacted by a prosecutor as part of the management of the prosecution case. All redacted versions of

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: on the Exhibit List, attributable to the police witness who wore the BWC. BWC footage forming part of a brief of evidence must be: reviewed as part of the authorisation process disclosed as part of the normal disclosure procedure outlined in VPMG Brief preparation and management. BWC footage (redacted or otherwise) disclosed by the informant can be further redacted by a prosecutor as part of the management of the prosecution case. All redacted versions of BWC footage used in court proceedings must be retained until after the expiration of the appeal period and then managed in accordance with VPM Court processes. Lost, stolen, damaged or faulted BWCs If a BWC is lost or stolen the member must immediately notify their supervisor of the circumstances and make all reasonable enquiries to locate the device. If the device remains lost or stolen at the completion of the shift: call the Victoria Police Helpdesk on 1300 307 082 for assistance and to order a replacement if lost, complete and submit a Lost Property Report [Form 220D] if stolen, complete and submit a theft report through LEDR MK2 with ‘Victoria Police’ as the victim notify the Security Incident Registry by submission of a T200 SIR Incident Report. If a BWC is damaged or faulted during an operational shift the member must call the Victoria Police Helpdesk on 1300 307 082 to try and rectify the fault and, if possible, return to their station and exchange the BWC for another device. In any of the above circumstances, if the BWC assigned to a member is to be replaced by another device, the work unit manager is responsible for managing that re-assignment process through the DEMs. Voluntary duties Where a member who is ordinarily assigned a BWC is rostered for voluntary duties (VD) and is required to carry a BWC, the following applies; a BWC should be issued to the member prior to commencing the period of leave or rest days the member may take the BWC home on preceding rest or leave days for use exclusively during a rostered VD shift a portable BWC battery charger must also be issued the BWC does not have to be returned for docking between the VD and next work unit rostered shift prior to commencing the next work unit rostered shift, the member must ensure the BWC is fully charged ready for use during that shift. Instruction on tagging and categorisation is outlined at section 8, however for the purposes of this section, tagging must; occur during the rostered VDs shift using the mobile device use the State Event Planning Unit naming conventions for metadata relating to that event. Where a BWC has been used for an extended

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Body_worn_cameras_final
text: to commencing the next work unit rostered shift, the member must ensure the BWC is fully charged ready for use during that shift. Instruction on tagging and categorisation is outlined at section 8, however for the purposes of this section, tagging must; occur during the rostered VDs shift using the mobile device use the State Event Planning Unit naming conventions for metadata relating to that event. Where a BWC has been used for an extended period of VDs, on returning to rostered duty at their work unit, the member must; ensure their BWC is docked as soon as practicable on returning to their work unit to upload stored data on the BWC review the available memory on the BWC through the MT BWC app to ensure they have sufficient storage for the duration of their first frontline response shift where insufficient storage memory exists (<6 hours), the member must consult a supervisor to either alter their duties from frontline response or have another BWC assigned to them for use during that shift. DEMS file sharing – collecting information from the public The DEMS file sharing platform enables members to share a link by email or SMS to a member of the public to facilitate their upload of privately held digital evidence required for a brief of evidence or investigation. The DEMS ‘citizen’ link can be actioned on a Victoria Police desktop computer or within the ‘capture’ application available on members’ mobile devices. All members with an active DEMS account must use this system for the collection of privately held digital evidence. When sending a ‘citizen’ link, members must ensure they: enter the correct email or telephone number for the recipient add relevant metadata to adequately match the requested data to existing digital evidence or other VP reference such as Interpose investigation, LEAP incident or LEDR reference, pertinent to the brief or investigation provide the recipient with their name, rank and contact number and sufficient instruction as to what digital evidence is required instruct the recipient to retain the original digital evidence for production and continuity at any future court process. title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Management_of_VP_issue_firearms_final
text: Management of Victoria Police issue firearms Context Victoria Police members are issued with firearms to carry out their official roles and functions under the Victoria Police Act 2013. The compliance and governance considerations when managing firearms are significant in order to maintain safety, as well as confidence in Victoria Police’s ability to manage firearms to all compliance expectations. The responsibility of safely managing Victoria Police issue firearms falls to all employees who may issue, carry or use them in their daily duties. The focus on safety when handling a firearm in any manner cannot be overstated. This policy reflects the safest standards available to the organisation, in order to ensure the safety of our members and the public. This policy applies to all employees who issue, handle, carry, use or are otherwise involved in the management of Victoria Police issue firearms. Contents Context 1 Contents 1 Definitions 1 Policy and procedures 2 1. Eligibility to be issued with and carry a firearm 2 2. Lost, faulty or stolen Victoria Police issue firearms 4 3. Transportation of firearms 4 4. Workplace Procedures 6 5. Field stripping and cleaning Semi-Automatic Pistols 8 6. Return of personal issue Semi-Automatic Pistols to the Armoury 8 7. Safe load/unload device and SAR Load/Unload Booth 9 8. Specialised firearm equipment 10 9. Armoury responsibilities 12 Related documents 12 Further Advice and Information 12 Update history 12 Definitions Equipment issue officer – employee of Victoria Police who is required, as part of their duties, to issue members or PCOs with OSE. ETMS – Victoria Police maintained equipment tracking management system. ETMS equipment scope – is equipment defined in ETMS Operational Guidelines. ETMS location – a work unit where ETMS has been deployed. Policy and procedures Eligibility to be issued with and carry a firearm General Members who have successfully completed the Semi-Automatic Pistol (SAP) training course may be issued with either: a personal issue firearm a station issue firearm where certain requirements are met (refer to VPM Operational safety equipment). Members who have successfully completed the Semi-Automatic Rifle (SAR) User course and are gazetted to a designated SAR location may be issued with a station issue SAR when performing primary or secondary response duties. Members who have successfully completed the Animal Destruction Rifle Initial Users course and maintain the annual requalification may be issued with and use an animal destruction rifle. All members who are issued with a firearm are responsible for both: the safe handling and lawful use of the firearm ensuring the firearm is kept in a safe manner and a serviceable condition. Department heads have the authority to direct specific work units to access only station issue SAPs and to assign personal issue SAPs

This may be appropriate where members are required to be Operational Safety and Tactics Training (OSTT) qualified but use operational safety equipment (OSE) irregularly. Personal issue To be assigned a personal issue SAP, a member must be appointed to a position that requires them to regularly perform duties requiring the carriage of a firearm. Personal issue SAPs remain the property of Victoria Police at all times. Members can only be issued with one personal issue SAP at any time. Special Operations Group members may be subject to their own local instructions and qualifications. Allocation of a personal issue SAP is to be approved by the new work unit manager. The Armoury will not issue the SAP to the member until an email verifying the member’s OSTT qualification status has been sent to the PBEA by the work unit manager and a check has been done on ETMS. Personal issue - withdrawal A work unit manager may determine that a personal issue SAP should be withdrawn and returned to the Armoury. Refer to section 6 of this policy for guidance. Station issue Semi-Automatic Pistols In addition to storing members’ personal issue SAPs, work units may be issued with additional SAPs known as station issue SAPs. These may be issued to qualified members in any of the following circumstances: a member’s personal issue SAP is faulty and needs to be repaired special events or circumstances where additional staff require OSTT equipment to be issued to outstation members where the requirements of section 3 of VPM Operational safety equipment are met. Overall allocation of station issue SAPs is the responsibility of the work unit manager. The storage and issue of station issue SAPs must only be undertaken by work units that utilise ETMS. Faulty Members must not attempt to fix firearms faults. Upon identifying a fault the member must: immediately notify a supervisor, and tag the firearm with details of the date, member name, rank, VP number, firearm serial number (where applicable) and a summary of the fault, and then return it to the equipment issue officer. The equipment issue officer is to secure the faulty firearm and contact the Armoury to arrange for its repair. If the faulted firearm is a SAP, the work unit manager must arrange for a replacement for the member until their personal issue SAP is replaced by the Armoury and where ETMS is available, ensure the SAP condition is set to faulty. If the faulted firearm is a SAR, the work unit manager must arrange for the SAR to be returned to the Armoury. The Armoury will be responsible for providing a replacement SAR to the work unit. Transportation of firearms General Members are responsible for keeping firearms in their possession in a manner that is safe and secure. When a member is not wearing the firearm as part of their equipment belt, ballistic vest, or equivalent carriage system, and is required to transport the firearm (e.g. for maintenance or transportation to OSTT training), the member must ensure all of the following: the firearm must be locked in a gun safe or gun carry case with the latter being secured using the steel cable and padlocks supplied ammunition must not be carried unless authorised by the work unit manager and, if authorised, kept separate from the firearm the most direct route available should be taken to minimise the time the firearm is in transit. Member transfer When a member transfers to another work location, their personal issue SAP is to be transported to their new station by that member while on duty or in an approved gun carry case by another member. Portable and attractive equipment item registers are to be updated by the work unit managers at both workplaces. Where applicable the SAP should be included in ETMS immediately upon receipt as per ETMS Operational Guidelines. Transportation in vehicles When members are transporting firearms in a vehicle for administrative purposes, the vehicle should not be left unattended. The person in charge of the vehicle is to ensure that all of the following occurs: the firearm is locked in the gun safe or gun carry case issued to each station or work unit for that purpose the

Transportation in vehicles When members are transporting firearms in a vehicle for administrative purposes, the vehicle should not be left unattended. The person in charge of the vehicle is to ensure that all of the following occurs: the firearm is locked in the gun safe or gun carry case issued to each station or work unit for that purpose the carry case is secured to the vehicle using the cable and lock provided, hidden from view and placed in the boot, the cargo carrying area or some other lockable compartment of the vehicle ammunition, if approved to be carried, is placed in a lockable compartment of the vehicle (other than the compartment in which the firearm is placed) or in another locked container secured in or on the motor vehicle. Refer to VPM Police vehicles for further information. Other means of transportation Where there is a need to transport firearms by means other than a vehicle, members are to ensure that all of the following occurs: a gun carry case is used and remains locked at all times the firearm does not leave the possession of the member unless it is secured in accordance with legislation ammunition must not be carried unless the member is fully OSTT equipped and there is a need for such ammunition carriage their work unit manager has given approval for the transportation. Bulk transportation Where a number of firearms need to be transported (e.g. maintenance program, special events) work unit managers should consider the following: should members be present to provide security is the Transport Branch able to assist is a private contractor appropriate given the circumstances. Further advice can be obtained from Licensing and Regulation Services Division and/or the Armoury where required. The authorising employee is to record the movement of all firearms in ETMS where available, otherwise in accordance with current local procedures for signing-in and signing-out of firearms. Members are to be issued with 30 rounds of ammunition when signing-out a SAP (15 rounds per magazine). Members are to be issued with 60 rounds of ammunition when signing-out a SAR (30 rounds per magazine). A member’s personal issue SAP must not be signed-out to another member unless it is authorised by the shift supervisor (refer to section 1.5 of this policy for instructions on the temporary issue of personal issue SAPs). Station issue SAPs must not to be signed-out without the authorisation of the shift

Station issue SAPs must not to be signed-out without the authorisation of the shift supervisor and are only to be issued in accordance with section 1.4 of this policy. Members issuing firearms to themselves Members must not issue a firearm to themselves, unless one or more of the following apply: in exceptional circumstances (urgent/life threatening situations) when the member is the only employee on duty at the time when a firearm is required to be issued (i.e. single member stations, specialist units or 16-hour stations). If a member relies upon one of the above circumstances to issue a firearm to themselves, that member must: make a note of those circumstances in their official diary or ePDR/VP Form 502. Where ETMS is available, it will record that the firearm has been self-issued for a SAP, ensure the loading and unloading of the SAP is performed at a Safe load/unload device (SLUD) or alternate weapon loading and unloading system i.e. action wall in accordance with section 4.3 of this policy for a SAR, ensure the loading and unloading of the SAR is performed at a SAR Load/Unload Booth (where available) or in a safe direction identified by the member in compliance with procedures taught at the SAR User course and in accordance with section 4.3 of this policy. Loading and unloading of firearms In accordance with OSTT, the following process must be followed when loading and unloading an SAP: At a SLUD or alternate weapon loading and unloading system i.e. action wall, where available, and in the manner instructed at OSTT Where a SLUD is not available, members must follow the procedure instructed at OSTT, including safe direction instructions Once the SAP is loaded, it is to be immediately holstered and secured Immediately after the SAP is unloaded and cleared, the chamber safety flag is to be correctly inserted into the chamber and secured by releasing the slide. In compliance with the procedures taught at the SAR User course, the following process must be followed when loading and unloading a SAR: A SAR Load/Unload Booth must be used to clear and inspect the SAR, where available Where a SAR Load/Unload Booth is not available, members must use a safe direction identified by the member Immediately after the SAR is unloaded and cleared, the chamber safety flag must be inserted into the

In compliance with the procedures taught at the SAR User course, the following process must be followed when loading and unloading a SAR: A SAR Load/Unload Booth must be used to clear and inspect the SAR, where available Where a SAR Load/Unload Booth is not available, members must use a safe direction identified by the member Immediately after the SAR is unloaded and cleared, the chamber safety flag must be inserted into the chamber. SAR User qualified members may also use a SAR Load/Unload Booth to load and unload their SAP in compliance with the SAR User course. Signing in firearms Firearms must be returned to the equipment issue officer at the conclusion of the shift. For carriage while off duty/on availability, refer to VPM Operational safety equipment. Firearm storage When not in approved use, firearms and magazines are to be stored in the firearms storage facility provided at stations and work units. A member on temporary assignment from one work location to another may relocate a SAP to their new location for the period of that assignment with the approval of the work unit managers at both locations. Both equipment registers, including ETMS where available must be updated accordingly and the Armoury notified to ensure that the SAP’s current location is recorded. Members off duty or on availability must store all OSE at a local station unless they are able to comply with the requirements outlined in s.121(2), Firearms Act i.e.: in the manner provided for in item 2 of Schedule 4, Firearms Act; or in any other manner which the Chief Commissioner of Police is satisfied is as secure as the manner provided for in item 2 of Schedule 4. Item 2, Schedule 4(2), Firearms Act requires that the firearm must be stored in a steel safe which; is of a thickness that is not easily penetrable; and if it weighs less than 150 kilograms when it is empty, must be bolted to the structure of the premises where the firearm is authorised to be kept; and when any firearm is stored in it, is locked. Note: s.121(2A), Firearms Act states that when not being carried or used, ammunition must be stored: in the manner provided for in item 2 of Schedule 4 (it must be stored in a locked container separate from the safe in which the firearm must

Field stripping and cleaning Semi-Automatic Pistols Field stripping and cleaning of SAPs should be performed as detailed in the OSTT Unit (Semi-Automatic Pistol) Manual and in the allocated safe cleaning area. It is recommended that SAPs are field stripped and cleaned according to the OSTT Unit (Semi-Automatic Pistol) Manual in the following circumstances: after discharge when used in the destruction of an animal before long term storage and when soiled (other than being fired) after being exposed to water, condensation, dirt, dust or other contaminants before and after firearms training. Return of personal issue Semi-Automatic Pistols to the Armoury General Work unit managers are responsible for ensuring that personal issue SAPs that are no longer required are sent directly to the Armoury where they will be serviced, stored and reassigned. Retaining the Semi-Automatic Pistols at the station Where a decision is made not to return a member’s personal issue SAP to the Armoury, the SAP must be placed in a Tamper Evident Audit Bag (TEAB) which is then sealed and placed in the safe. The TEAB is to be labelled ‘Not to be issued unless authorised by shift supervisor’ with the relevant SAP serial number inserted for cross reference. Where the SAP is held at a one person station, the SAP must be transferred to another work location for safe storage. Order a new front funnel from the Property Division as soon as possible where round/s strike other part of the device - assess damage and replace entire device if necessary (access replacement devices through the Property Division where a round strikes a panel of the SAR Load/Unload Booth – cease use, assess the damage and report to the Facilities Manager for rectification. The bar securing the paper in the back of the SLUD should remain locked at all times and should only be opened to inspect paper for damage or to replace paper in the situation where a round is discharged. Tactical light Members are not to remove the tactical light from a SAP. The exception is to change or check the batteries. Members are not permitted to use the tactical light for any reason other than those taught at OSTT. The tactical light is part of the firearm and therefore can only be used in circumstances where it is appropriate to draw the firearm, refer to VPM Operational safety and the use of force. Members are to either use the standard issue SAP hip/thigh holster or the approved standard plain clothes holster, otherwise they must seek approval for any alternative holster (whether with or without a tactical light). The work unit manager should then conduct a risk assessment to determine that concealment needs cannot be met with the standard issue holsters. If it is determined that the need for SAP concealment outweighs other risks (such as tactical light removal) the work unit manager is to seek approval from the Uniform, Appearance and Equipment Committee for the issue of an alternative holster in accordance with VPM Operational safety equipment. Members may be directed to undertake additional SAP and tactical light/torch training. Magazines and ammunition The magazine is an integral part of the firearm system. It is to be treated as part of the firearm and not a separate item. Magazines are to be returned to the Armoury with the firearm as part of maintenance rotations, individual firearm returns and for firearms that have been faulted and require inspection by the Armoury. A firearm is to be issued with two magazines. Magazines may be stored in a loaded condition when not in use. Magazines, when first loaded for storage, must be loaded with new ammunition. Prior to use, the loaded magazine must be inspected to verify the number of rounds and that they have been correctly loaded. text: Operational safety and tactics training qualifications Context Operational Safety and Tactics Training (OSTT) is delivered to all police, Protective Services Officers (police members) and Police Custody Officers (PCOs) biannually through training programs designed by the Centre for Operational Safety (CfOS), People Development Command (PDC). PDC reviews data and information collected from the operational environment and through a variety of internal and external areas to ensure: evolving environmental issues or changes in offender behaviour that may impact on police member, PCO or community safety are reduced through training internal and external reviews that may change operational practice or process (such as Coronial decisions or internal reviews) are understood the most contemporary and safest tactics are understood and implemented across the organisation police members and PCOs are instructed in and qualified to use operational safety equipment (OSE) in the correct manner legislation, including the use of force and human rights, are understood. Police members and PCOs are responsible for maintaining their OSTT qualification and contemporary knowledge of issues impacting the operational environment. Policy at a glance This policy includes: information for police members and PCOs on their responsibilities to ensure that their OSTT qualifications are kept current through biannual training programs work unit manager responsibilities for ensuring compliance of their police members and PCOs OSTT status eligibility criteria and the application process for an OSTT 28-day extension the application process for exemptions from maintaining OSTT qualifications information and processes about any lapse of qualifications and qualification difficulties because of medical or lack of competency criteria to be followed for the suspension of a police member or PCO’s OSTT qualification process to be followed for promotion or transfer of OSTT unqualified police members and PCOs information on Tactical Arrest Options Training (TAOT) and the Semi-Automatic Rifle (SAR) user course. Responsibilities and procedures General All police members and PCOs must successfully complete and maintain an OSTT qualification unless certified medically unfit to do so. Refer to section 7 Qualification difficulties for more information. As indicated by VPM Operational safety equipment, police members and PCOs are required to hold a current OSTT qualification in order to carry OSE that is appropriate for the duties they are performing. The CfOS, Operational Safety Division, PDC is responsible for developing OSTT packages that are delivered through allocated OSTT venues. Line managers are responsible for ensuring all relevant police members and PCOs hold a current OSTT qualification and are booked in to their correct OSTT course. Obtaining and maintaining qualification Police members and PCOs need to be assessed as competent in all assessable components of the course to obtain their OSTT qualification. This includes any pre attendance e-Learning courses. For further details on the course and its competencies, contact the local OSTT venue. OSTT may include an operational readiness assessment to determine the employee’s operational readiness capacity. Remedial training to meet operational readiness standards may involve operational deployment, but unless agreed to by the police member or PCO, such deployment must not exceed two shifts per OSTT qualifying cycle. To maintain an OSTT qualification, police members and PCOs are to successfully complete the OSTT course twice each calendar year within the: January to June and July to December periods, or cycles directed by the Assistant Commissioner, PDC. Unless otherwise directed by the Assistant Commissioner, PDC, all police members and PCOs (excluding members with exemptions or OSTT suspension) must be booked onto an OSTT course by the completion of the second month of each cycle as follows: 28 (or 29) February for the January to June cycle 31 August for the July to December cycle. The booking must occur in the first two months of a cycle and attendance can occur at any time throughout that six-month cycle. Police members and PCOs unable to requalify within the required timeframe should refer to sections 5 and 6 of this policy for more information. Management of qualifications Police members and PCOs should advise their work unit manager when they are due to renew their OSTT qualification. OSTT course qualification results must be recorded on HR Assist within 48 hours of the training course completion by the

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_OSTT_final
text: can occur at any time throughout that six-month cycle. Police members and PCOs unable to requalify within the required timeframe should refer to sections 5 and 6 of this policy for more information. Management of qualifications Police members and PCOs should advise their work unit manager when they are due to renew their OSTT qualification. OSTT course qualification results must be recorded on HR Assist within 48 hours of the training course completion by the OSTT venue manager or delegate responsible for the training at the venue. The work unit manager is responsible for ensuring HR Assist (HR39) OSTT unqualified reports are generated within 48 hours of the end of each calendar month with action taken and reported on where necessary. HR Assist (HR39) generates reports on police members and PCOs supervised by the relevant work unit manager only. OSTT venues and identified work units can utilise the HR Assist (HR73) Operational Status Report to display the status report of any police member or PCO’s OSTT qualification, conducted energy device (CED) qualification, SAR qualification or first aid status. Expiry of qualification OSTT qualifications expire on the last day of the police member or PCO’s next qualifying period. For example, a qualification attained in the January to June period expires on 31 December. Qualification exemptions General Police members and PCOs who are required to maintain an OSTT qualification, but are not able to requalify, may apply for a temporary or permanent exemption. Exemptions may be applied for due to: a medical condition long service leave leave without pay parental leave other long-term absence. title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Operational_safety_and_the_use_of_force_final
text: Operational safety and the use of force Context Victoria Police is responsible under the Victoria Police Act 2013 (VPA) for specific roles and functions that provide a service to the Victorian community. To perform these roles and functions, members and police custody officers (PCOs) are expected to protect themselves and the public while fulfilling their duties. To do this effectively, they may need to use force. Members and PCOs are trained in a range of techniques and a variety of operational safety equipment to enable them to have options when responding to an incident. The level of force required to bring an incident under control may need to increase or decrease depending on the situation, and is determined by a range of factors including: legislative provisions including 322K and 462A, Crimes Act 1958 the type of incident the capability of the responding members and PCOs the responding members’ and PCOs’ assessment of the risk. When it comes to using force, members and PCOs must lead by example, treating everyone with dignity and respect while having regard to the safety of themselves, other police employees, members of the public and any offenders. Policy at a glance This policy includes: the notification requirements for reporting a use of force incident the responsibilities of the duty officer and divisional patrol supervisor following the notification of a use of force incident member and PCO use of force actions that require reporting the operational response principles providing members and PCOs with guidance on organisational expectations, performance and decision making information on the Tactical Options Model (TOM), a visual aid outlining the tactical options available to members and PCOs in situations when use of force is required information on the use of SAFE TACTICS as an operational safety tool for responding to incidents. Operational response principles 3 5. Operational safety tool 4 6. Operational Safety and Tactics Training 5 7. Specialist support 6 8. Recording of rationale 6 9. Notification requirements 6 10. It states: ‘The role of Victoria Police is to serve the Victorian community and uphold the law so as to promote a safe, secure and orderly society.’ Functions of Victoria Police Section 9, VPA outlines the general functions of Victoria Police. text: Update history 9 Scope and application This policy relates to all members and PCOs. Policy and procedures Role of Victoria Police Section 8, VPA outlines the role of Victoria Police. It states: ‘The role of Victoria Police is to serve the Victorian community and uphold the law so as to promote a safe, secure and orderly society.’ Functions of Victoria Police Section 9, VPA outlines the general functions of Victoria Police. It states: ‘The functions of Victoria Police include the following: preserving the peace protecting life and property preventing the commission of offences detecting and apprehending offenders helping those in need of assistance’. Legislative powers Overview The use of force, including the use of operational safety equipment (OSE), must be in accordance with specific legal requirements (e.g. legislative provisions or common law). Two relevant sections of the Crimes Act are addressed within this policy. Additional powers relating to the use force are available to members and PCOs, including under common law and other legislative provisions. Use of force (s.462A, Crimes Act) Any force used by a member or PCO must be in line with legal requirements and the principles of s.462A, Crimes Act, which states: A person may use such force not disproportionate to the objective as he or she believes on reasonable grounds to be necessary to prevent the commission, continuance or completion of an indictable offence or to effect or assist in effecting the lawful arrest of a person committing or suspected of committing any offence. Example A member or PCO uses lethal force on a person to prevent that person from committing an indictable offence that involves causing really serious injury or death because the member or PCO believes on reasonable grounds that it is necessary to use that force for that purpose. The member or PCO may do so before that offence is committed. Self-defence (s.322K, Crimes Act) Section 322K, Crimes Act relates to self-defence. The circumstances in which a person may carry out conduct in self-defence includes the: defence of the person or another person prevention or termination of the unlawful deprivation of the liberty of the person or another person protection of property. Section 322K, Crimes Act states: A person is not guilty of an offence if the person carries out the conduct constituting the offence in self-defence. A person carries out conduct in self-defence if: the person believes that the conduct is necessary in self-defence; and the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them. This section only applies in the case of murder if the person believes that the conduct is necessary to defend the person or another person from the infliction of death or really serious

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Operational_safety_and_the_use_of_force_final
text: carries out the conduct constituting the offence in self-defence. A person carries out conduct in self-defence if: the person believes that the conduct is necessary in self-defence; and the conduct is a reasonable response in the circumstances as the person perceives them. This section only applies in the case of murder if the person believes that the conduct is necessary to defend the person or another person from the infliction of death or really serious injury. Operational response principles The operational response principles represent the role, functions, obligations and goal of Victoria Police. They reinforce that members and PCOs have: a duty to provide a community service under legislation, policy, training and terms of employment a responsibility to perform their duties as safely as possible under legislation, policy, training and terms of employment a goal to perform their duties while minimising all types of harm. The operational response principles provide: a guide for members and PCOs in performing their operational duties clarification of organisational expectations improved operational decision making. The principles are: Service – members and PCOs are obligated to provide a service to the Victorian community, in line with their legislated responsibility. In performing this role, they may be required to perform tasks that may be considered inherently unsafe. Members and PCOs are trained, equipped and empowered to perform such tasks and there is a community expectation that they will do so Safety – while providing a service members and PCOs will, as far as practicable, identify hazards and mitigate risks to themselves and others. This is consistent with the requirements of the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 Harm Minimisation – the goal of policing activities is to minimise harm caused by the actions of police or the actions of others. This is a broader concept that extends beyond the use of force and physical injury. It encompasses human rights, psychological and emotional harm and other impacts on community safety and confidence. Operational safety tool The operational safety tool SAFE TACTICS supports the operational response principles. It: is not an exhaustive list but incorporates a number of tactical considerations increases the focus on harm minimisation and consequence management provides prompts relevant to operational policing. The operational safety tool is designed so that members and PCOs are more agile in their response to the operational environment and are empowered and enabled to make rapid and relevant operational decisions. SAFE TACTICS provides a continuous and non-linear process, meaning that the various steps can and should be revisited regularly throughout an incident. Operational Safety and Tactics Training Operational Safety and Tactics Training (OSTT) When undertaking OSTT, members and PCOs are trained in the use of force. This includes: the application of

title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Operational_safety_and_the_use_of_force_final
text: and PCOs are more agile in their response to the operational environment and are empowered and enabled to make rapid and relevant operational decisions. SAFE TACTICS provides a continuous and non-linear process, meaning that the various steps can and should be revisited regularly throughout an incident. Operational Safety and Tactics Training Operational Safety and Tactics Training (OSTT) When undertaking OSTT, members and PCOs are trained in the use of force. This includes: the application of s.462A, Crimes Act a range of tactics a range of OSE (refer to VPM Operational safety equipment for use of force requirements for specific OSE) for members, the application and importance of the Tactical Options Model (TOM) for PCOs, the application and importance of aspects of the TOM in relation to their issued OSE and training. Tactical Options Model (TOM) The Victoria Police TOM is an organisational visual aid that outlines the various tactical options available to members and PCOs. It includes communication, physical presence, negotiation, tactical disengagement, and cordon and manage, as well as OSE. When considering which tactical option to choose, members and PCOs should be mindful that their goal is to minimise the overall harm caused by their actions or the actions of others. Where the use of force is required, the random arrangement of tactical options encourages members and PCOs to escalate and de-escalate the choice of equipment or tactics in accordance with the direction the incident is taking, the objective and the information available to them. ‘Other weapons/tactics’ in the TOM includes Active Armed Offender option and a vehicle being used as a tactical use of force option (interdiction). For full details of the TOM and access to the TOM Manual, refer to the Victoria Police Learning Hub (VPLH). Specialist support When planning an operation or responding to an incident, there are several support services that may assist in safely managing or resolving the incident, particularly when the incident may be outside the capability of the responding units. These support units include the Special Operations Group, Bomb Response Unit, Critical Incident Response Team, Dog Squad, trained negotiators and other relevant units. Refer to VPM Specialist support for further details. Recording of rationale Members and PCOs must position themselves to make considered and defensible decisions when responding to incidents that may involve the use of force. If force is used, members and PCOs must record the details of the incident and any justification that determined that the use of force was necessary in the circumstances. Once notified, the duty officer or divisional patrol supervisor must: assess the situation and, where practical, attend the scene ensure that proper after care and medical attention has been provided investigate the incident to determine whether the use of any equipment was in line with policy determine if the circumstances meet the criteria for must or should consider suspension of the members OSTT qualification as outlined in VPM Operational safety and tactics training qualifications ensure the relevant Use of Force App report, Incident Fact Sheet and Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) notifications are submitted where appropriate. See VPM OHS Incident management for more information on reporting OHS incidents. Refer to VPM Operational supervision and incident attendance for guidance on the level of supervision required at the incident. Professional Standards Command must be notified in accordance with VPM Complaints and VPM Discipline. Critical incidents The Centre for Operational Safety (CfOS) must be notified where either: the use of OSE has resulted in the death or serious injury of any person where the investigating member believes expert evidence in the area of OSE, tactics or training is required. A Use of Force App report and an Incident Fact Sheet must be submitted where required. Refer to VPM Death or serious injury/illness incidents involving police for instructions relating to the management of any incidents where death or serious injury has resulted from one or more of the following: the discharge of a firearm or use of force by an employee the use of a vehicle by an employee in the course of their duties the person being in the care or custody of an employee attempts to bring a person in custody (e.g. sieges, suicides) an escape or attempted escape from policy custody any police actions or inactions during other policing activities or operations. Reporting use of force Purpose of collecting use of force information Victoria Police collects Use of Force details of incidents where force is used by or against members and PCOs as well as information about pursuits to: identify trends in force used against members and PCOs and operational responses develop strategies to address identified risks, including but not limited to training determine whether operational training and techniques are adequate. Criterion for using Use of Force App reports A Use of Force App report must be submitted where force is used by or against a member or PCO. One Use of Force App report must be completed for each incident where force is used. Where more than two members, PCOs or two other people are involved, submit one Use of Force App report. Do not submit Use of Force reports following OSTT. In circumstances where the Use of Force App is offline, members should continue to complete the Use of Force App report and also complete the ‘Report an Error or Fault’ form via Service Now. The information entered on the Use of Force App must be reviewed and submitted to the supervisor when connectivity is restored. Definitions or actions requiring reporting via Use of Force App Completion and submission of use of force reports Use of Force App reports should be checked by a supervisor prior to submission. Use of Force App reports must be submitted within 24 hours of the incident by the: member or PCO in charge of the incident where force has been used pursuit controller or investigating member following a pursuit member responsible for animal destruction. title: Operational_safety_equipment_VPM_Operational_safety_equipment_final
text: Operational safety equipment Context Members use a variety of tactical options to carry out their roles and functions under the Victoria Police Act 2013. Where members and Police Custody Officers (PCOs) respond to situations that may require the use of force, they must possess a range of skills which will enable them to resolve the situation safely, efficiently and effectively. To increase this capability, members and PCOs are trained in the use of and issued with operational safety equipment (OSE). Members and PCOs are required to carry operational safety equipment that is appropriate for the duties they are performing and for which they have received relevant training. The equipment to be carried must: be proportionate to the threat likely to be encountered have regard to the safety of the member, PCO and the public. Members and PCOs must understand the policy and legislative provisions regarding the use of force which are outlined in VPM Operational safety and the use of force and relevant legislation. Members and PCOs may be called upon to justify the use of force and may need to prove that their actions were reasonable in the circumstances. As part of their roles, Victorian Public Service (VPS) employees may also encounter firearms and other operational safety equipment when performing their duties (e.g., issuing equipment or as a property officer). Where there are concerns for any employees that are consistent with section 9 of VPM Operational safety and tactics training qualifications, assessment and management must be consistent with the suspension, review and reinstatement of a member or PCO’s Operational Safety and Tactics Training (OSTT) qualification. This must include consideration of alternative duties and the removal of access to equipment issue areas and property storage areas. Managers and supervisors are to reinforce safety messages to all employees and ensure awareness of the requirement to remain vigilant and alert to risks at all times. This policy applies to all employees who issue, carry, use or are otherwise responsible for operational safety equipment. For the purpose of this policy the term ’PCO’ includes PCOs and supervising PCOs (SPCO). Policy at a glance This policy includes: member and PCO responsibilities regarding maintaining current OSTT qualifications the responsibilities of supervisors and work unit managers to maintain sufficient supplies of current issue OSE and its safe storage the responsibilities and recording requirements for authorised members accessing and issuing equipment using the Victoria Police Equipment Tracking Management System (ETMS) details of minimum equipment carriage requirements details of the carriage and storage of firearms responsibilities surrounding the use of firearms at training or demonstrations and firing ranges responsibilities of members and PCOs when using OSE, including aftercare provisions. Restraint techniques and positional asphyxia Positional asphyxia or suffocation occurs when the position of a person’s body interferes with respiration, resulting in death. Keep any person who is physically restrained under close observation. Take care to ensure the person is placed in and maintains a position that allows unrestricted breathing. If any restriction or impairment to respiration is observed or suspected, immediately seek medical assistance. Restraint techniques that could impair a person’s unrestricted breathing should only be used when absolutely necessary and for the briefest possible time. text: Purpose This Asset Management policy sets out roles and responsibilities for the management of assets, as defined by either their value or level of importance to operational capability, which are owned or managed by Victoria Police. The purpose of this policy is to detail the expectations of how assets will be managed and to clarify the principles and objectives that should guide development of all asset management strategies and plans. Contents Purpose 1 Contents 1 Definitions 1 Audience 2 Organisational and state context 3 Principles and objectives 4 Responsibilities and procedures 5 Further advice and information 8 Update history 8 Appendix A – The asset lifecycle 9 Definitions Acquisition – Procurement of assets to meet an identified service need, including the assessment of procurement options. Asset – For the purposes of this policy, an asset is an item or thing that has potential value and is the responsibility of Victoria Police. From the perspective of the organisation’s asset register, Victoria Police has over ten thousand owned, high-value assets valued at over $1.5 billion. In addition, Victoria Police owns thousands of other assets not captured on the asset register because they are individually valued at less than $5,000 and leases of high-value assets such as fleet and property. Not all items warrant management under this policy. As such, a value and a capability test are to be used to define when an item is an asset. Value Threshold The Value Threshold relates to the cost of purchase or replacement of an item, thing or intangible asset and applies to: individual items with a replacement value equal to or more than $50,000 individual items required to be or usually purchased in bulk with a total replacement value of equal to or more than $50,000 contracts or leases for goods or services equal to or more than $500,000. Capability Threshold Assets support operational capability. Therefore, in line with Victoria Police’s Capability Planning Framework, an item is considered an asset under this policy if the lack of access or ability to use the item would have a material impact on capability. This definition is irrespective of the Value Threshold. Asset determination – An item will be determined to be an asset, and therefore managed under this policy, if it meets the Value or Capability Threshold detailed above. Asset lifecycle – The series of life stages of an asset, from Planning through to Disposal, that need to be effectively managed to get the maximum organisational benefit out of an asset. Disposal – Treatment of an asset that has either reached the end of its useful life, is considered surplus, or is under-performing. Exempt assets – Some assets are exempt from management under this policy due

title: Org_Policy_Statements_Asset_management_Final
text: meets the Value or Capability Threshold detailed above. Disposal – Treatment of an asset that has either reached the end of its useful life, is considered surplus, or is under-performing. Exempt assets – Some assets are exempt from management under this policy due to being specifically excluded under the AMAF or due to unique custodianship arrangements. These include, but are not limited to, financial assets, cultural collections, artworks and library collections. Financial assets – Get value from a contractual right to ownership claim. Examples include, but are not limited to, cash, stocks and bank deposits. Further information on financial assets can be found in Accounting Standard AASB 132. Intangible assets – are identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance. They are generally long-term resources of an organisation and derive their value from an organisation. Further information on intangible assets can be found in Accounting Standard AASB 138. Operation and maintenance – Management, use and maintenance of an asset to deliver services. Planning – Determination of asset requirements, based on an assessment of both service delivery needs and the capability of the existing asset base to meet these needs. For further information or to request and asset exemption under this policy, contact the ASSET-STRATEGY-MGR PBEA. Principles and objectives The principles for effective asset management for Victoria Police include: assets are aligned to policing needs, with consideration for available resources, legal and technical requirements, and competing needs a whole of lifecycle approach is applied to planning and decision making asset performance is monitored asset management plans for, manages, and mitigates risk and uncertainty the management of assets is responsive to changes in demand, use, or requirement there exists strong accountability and governance frameworks decisions are accurately informed by asset costs, value, condition, utilisation, functionality, capacity (existing and/or required), safety, operational importance and remaining useful life asset management is driven by a continuous improvement and adaptive management approach. The objective of this policy and the associated Asset Management Strategy is to support the Victoria Police’s remit to serve the Victorian community and uphold the law so as to promote a safe, secure and orderly society through the effective and efficient management of assets. This will be accomplished through the achievement of the following five asset management objectives: compliance – assets must be managed and maintained compliant with all legislation, regulations, as well as Victorian Government and Victoria Police policies. Where compliance mandates specific maintenance regimes, these will be built into the appropriate Asset Management Plans (AMPs) and budgets health, safety and wellbeing – assets should provide an environment that promotes and maintains staff health, safety and wellbeing. The service or capability that the asset supports should inform asset management plans and investment decisions presence and visibility – Assets are provided and maintained in a manner which enhances the presence and visibility of operational policing where appropriate.
