title: Witness_protection_VPM_Witness_protection_FINAL_doc
text: Witness protection Context Witness protection is a critical tool for law enforcement when meeting the challenge of serious and organised crime. The ability of a witness to give testimony in a judicial setting or to cooperate with police investigations without fear of intimidation or reprisal is essential to maintaining the rule of law. Legislation and policies are necessary to protect witnesses whose cooperation with police or testimony in a court of law would endanger their lives or those of their families. The Victorian Witness Protection Program (WPP) and Alternate Protection Arrangements (APA) are two separate mechanisms of protection, established by the Witness Protection Act 1991 (the Act), which are administered by the Chief Commissioner of Police. The purpose of the Act is to facilitate the security of persons who are, or have been, witnesses in criminal proceedings in or elsewhere in . Fundamental principles that apply to the provision of witness assistance and protection are: witness protection and assistance is intended to remove or reduce barriers to cooperation in criminal investigations and prosecutions. It should not be provided as a reward or inducement as far as practicable, there should be a clear separation of the investigation and the protective functions of Victoria Police. the decision to protect a witness should be determined primarily by reference to the risk incurred by the person as a consequence of the person’s participation in, or cooperation with, the criminal justice system protection and assistance provided to a witness under the Act should be tailored to the individual circumstances and risk faced by the witness and the community the safety of the witness should take priority over the successful conduct of a prosecution the interest of children involved in, or affected by, the provision of witness protection and assistance should be separately considered and their welfare should be a determining factor in decision making there should be public accountability for the operation of the witness protection and assistance provided under the Act, subject to the need to safeguard: the health and safety of any person the effective conduct of any investigation or intelligence-gathering in relation to criminal activity the overall integrity of the Victorian witness protection program and the provision of alternative protection arrangements under the Act. This Policy outlines ’s approach to witness protection, in line with legislative provisions. Contents Context 1 Contents 2 Scope and application 2 Responsibilities and procedures 2 1. Media 13 Related documents 13 Further advice and information 13 Update history 13 Scope and application This Policy applies to: Officer in Charge and members, Witness Protection Unit (WPU) Superintendent, State Intelligence Division (SID) Detective Inspectors and Investigation and Response (I&R) Inspectors Operational members Responsibilities and procedures Initial action and response Members are to provide immediate assistance and protection, where they identify a threat of death, serious injury or serious intimidation toward a person who has: given evidence in court proceedings agreed to give evidence in court proceedings provided information to assist with the judicial process. An ‘at risk’ person in respect to witness protection may include a: victim witness material witness co-operating co-accused registered human source witness dependant police officer judicial official. In the case of a threat against a police officer, a referral can be considered from the Threats Against Serving Members (THASM) Review Panel. The member who identifies the threat is to notify a Detective Inspector or I&R Inspector who must assess the risk. If deemed suitable for Witness Protection Unit (WPU) assessment and/or referral, the WPU must be immediately notified. The WPU will then undertake an assessment of the circumstances and provide further information and advice. Outside business hours, the WPU response is facilitated through Police Communications, with the approval of the Crime Duty Officer or a Regional Duty Inspector. The Detective Inspector or I&R Inspector can authorise temporary emergency accommodation for the witness to address immediate risk, at the cost of the Region or Command, while WPU are processing the application. This must only occur after initial advice has been provided by the WPU. The Detective Inspector or I&R Inspector is to ensure that the threat against the witness is assigned for appropriate police investigation. It is important that no undertaking is made to a witness which impacts their ability to provide witness testimony. In addition, no commitment is to be made about witness assistance or protection until a WPU assessment has been conducted and a response strategy authorised. Witness Protection Unit (WPU) Responsibilities The WPU, State Intelligence Division (SID), Intelligence and Covert Support Command (ICSC) is responsible for the administration of WPP and APA arrangements. The Officer in Charge of the WPU must: oversee the preparation of a threat-risk assessment for all cases under assessment maintain a Register of Protected Witnesses under Interim Protection Declaration (IPD), WPP or APA coordinate the operation of the WPP and APA respond to requests for assistance from police members and other police jurisdictions ensure offences against the Act are investigated provide secretariat support to the Witness Protection Evaluation Committee (WPEC) and the Witness Protection Oversight Committee (WPOC) prepare a report to the Minister as per Section 20R of the Act assist the IBAC in regards to inspections conducted under 20B of the Act. The Officer in Charge, is to ensure: requests for police assistance are responded to in a timely manner threat-risk assessments are compiled and presented to WPEC as part of the overall case consideration and evaluation process in a timely manner all witness protection policies and guidelines (VPM and WPU local operating procedures) are complied with information shared between agencies is appropriate and authorised in accordance with the Victorian Protective Data Security Standards as set out by the Commissioner for Privacy and Data Protection the integrity and privacy of that information is protected information is used correctly and for the purposes for which it was intended. Threat-risk assessment The WPU will perform a witness protection threat-risk assessment to evaluate the level of threat-risk to a witness. The assessment features two components that rate the threat to the witness and its intensity: threat assessment, which determines the overall threat level. There are two levels; high or low risk assessment, which informs an appropriate response strategy. The threat-risk assessment tool is dynamic and designed to be periodically re-applied to review the case. It is imperative that this assessment is reconsidered when there is any change to the circumstances of the case or if new intelligence is received about the threat. Timely review should assist in identifying if the level of threat-risk has escalated or reduced. If the threat-risk is assessed as high, the WPU will engage with the witness and if they agree, retain responsibility for taking action in respect of witness assistance and protection. Interim protection Interim Protection Declaration (IPD) The Superintendent, SID is the authorised delegate to issue an IPD under s.9C, of the Act. To issue an IPD, the delegate must believe that: further time is required to consider whether to include the witness in the WPP or APA, and the witness or member of the family of the witness, is in urgent need of protection. The delegate may make an IPD with the written consent of the witness to whom the declaration relates. If the witness is under 18 years of age, a parent or guardian of the witness is required to provide the consent. Whilst an IPD is in force, police can provide assistance through necessary and reasonable action to protect the safety and welfare of a witness or the member of a family of the witness. This does not include a permanent change of identity. An IPD: takes effect on the day it is made and remains in force for a specified period, not exceeding 3 months may be extended by giving written notice to the witness, before the original declaration ceases that extension may be for a period not exceeding a further 3 months, with the approval of the Superintendent SID, who may consult the Assistant Commissioner, ICSC. An IPD ceases to be in force when: 3 months expires and no extension is granted the witness signs a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to enter the WPP or APA the witness is notified of a decision not to be admitted to the WPP or APA. title: Workplace_adjustment_VPM_Dogs_in_the_workplace_final
text: Dogs in the workplace Context Victoria Police recognises the value of trained and accredited assistance dogs in assisting people living with certain disabilities to alleviate the effect of their disability, including in their places of work, and the positive effect that engagement dogs have on a person’s mental health and well-being. Victoria Police supports the presence of assistance and engagement dogs where there is a demonstrated need for them. Workplaces have an obligation under anti-discrimination legislation to make necessary reasonable adjustments to accommodate prospective and current employees with a disability. The health, safety and wellbeing of Victoria Police employees is important, and Victoria Police is committed to providing a supportive workplace and assisting its employees with management of their disability or in their recovery (where applicable) along with ensuring employees are not exposed to further risks. This policy sets out the considerations and information required to guide managers and employees in determining how a request for an assistance dog can be accommodated within the workplace. The accommodation of an assistance dog could be a reasonable workplace adjustment for employees with disability. Further information on workplace adjustments is outlined in VPM Reasonable workplace adjustment and Reasonable workplace adjustment practice guide. This policy also sets out the considerations for having engagement dogs in the workplace. This policy is supported by the Dogs in the workplace practice guide. Responsibilities and considerations 7 Related documents 8 Further advice and information 9 Update history 9 Definitions Anti-discrimination legislation – a term that refers to the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth) and the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 (Vic). Assistance dog - any dog which has been specifically trained by an accredited assistance dog provider (such as Assistance Dogs Australia) in any jurisdiction (as determined by Assistance Dogs International) in accordance with the respective federal and state legislative requirements, to assist a person with a disability to alleviate the effect of the disability. Assistance dogs are trained to meet standards of hygiene and behaviour that are appropriate for a dog in a public place. There are three types of assistance dogs: service dogs (trained to assist their owner in ways specific to their needs, including owners with physical, sensory or psychological disabilities including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism and dementia), guide dogs (for people with vision impairment), and hearing dogs (for people with hearing impairment). Disability - as defined in anti-discrimination legislation, disability includes physical, intellectual, psychiatric

text: and behaviour that are appropriate for a dog in a public place. There are three types of assistance dogs: service dogs (trained to assist their owner in ways specific to their needs, including owners with physical, sensory or psychological disabilities including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism and dementia), guide dogs (for people with vision impairment), and hearing dogs (for people with hearing impairment). Disability - as defined in anti-discrimination legislation, disability includes physical, intellectual, psychiatric and immunological impairments, learning disabilities and physical disfigurement. A person who has been diagnosed and is living with PTSD meets the criteria for a disability. Engagement dog - a trained support dog which has been specifically trained by an accredited assistance dog provider to help in stressful situations and have a positive effect on a person’s mental health and well-being. These dogs can otherwise be known as welfare, peer support or therapy dogs and within Victoria Police are used to support a work area or workplace rather than an individual employee. Other dogs - refers to puppies or dogs that may be in training and in the workplace, such as a guide dogs or Australian Border Force detector dogs. Police member - includes police employees on executive officer contracts and employees whose terms and conditions of employment are subject to Victoria Police (Police Officers, Protective Services Officers, Police Reservists and Police Recruits) Enterprise Agreement 2025 or any successor enterprise agreement. Victorian Public Service (VPS) employee: means an employee of Victoria Police whose employment is covered by the Victorian Public Service Enterprise Agreement 2024 or any successor enterprise agreement (including Police Custody Officers and Forensic Officers), or an executive employee of Victoria Police covered by an executive contract of employment. Work area: a work area may refer to any of the following: region, department, division, police service area (PSA), cluster, station, unit or branch. Workplace: a workplace is the location where work duties are undertaken. Scope and application This policy applies to all Victoria Police employees including ongoing, fixed term and casual employees and all contractors. Where this policy refers to an assistance dog, it encompasses service dogs, guide dogs and hearing dogs that fall within the definition of assistance dog. Where this policy refers to the use of engagement dogs across Victoria Police, it encompasses those already in workplaces and any that may be introduced in the future. This policy does not apply to working dogs within Victoria Police, such as those in the Dog Squad or Bomb Response Unit. This policy should be read in conjunction with the Dogs in the workplace practice guide. This policy does not apply to working dogs within Victoria Police, such as those in the Dog Squad or Bomb Response Unit. This policy should be read in conjunction with the Dogs in the workplace practice guide. Assistance Dogs Responsibilities and considerations Overview The presence of an assistance dog in the workplace is supported under anti-discrimination legislation and VPM Reasonable workplace adjustment. An employee’s eligibility for an assistance dog is determined by an independent assessment by an accredited assistance dog provider. An employee is not required to provide additional medical evidence to support having an assistance dog in the workplace but is required to provide documentation from the accredited provider and must request the presence of their assistance dog in the workplace, as per any request for a reasonable workplace adjustment. Prospective VPS employees As part of the recruitment process into Victoria Police, successful applicants with either a permanent or temporary disability and/or accessibility requirements (including any requirement for an assistance dog) should identify any reasonable adjustments they consider necessary to adequately perform the requirements of the role (see VPM Reasonable workplace adjustment), noting applicants should not be treated disadvantageously as a result of their disability. As part of the recruitment process, the hiring manager (or manager in the workplace) of the successful applicant who requires or already uses an assistance dog is responsible for developing a formal plan to accommodate the assistance dog (see Dogs in the workplace practice guide) before the employee’s commencement date with the organisation. As per anti-discrimination legislation, this plan must be developed in discussion with the successful applicant. Considerations for police members Operational policing requires police members to be Operational Safety and Tactics Training (OSTT) qualified. Operational police members could be required to respond to an incident requiring police intervention, including both primary and secondary response duties as defined in VPM Operational safety equipment. Since it is not possible to complete OSTT while accompanied by an assistance dog and because assistance dogs are not trained to be in an operational policing environment, assistance dog arrangements are not possible for police members performing operational duties. In some cases, it may be possible to accommodate an assistance dog in a role that is varied to accommodate the police member’s medical needs. This may temporarily assist the employee with alleviating the effect of their disability, and depending on the disability, may assist with a long-term ability to perform the inherent requirements of their substantive role. In consultation with the police member, consideration may be given to altered duties, an alternative role and/or an alternative location. The time period for

text: to accommodate an assistance dog in a role that is varied to accommodate the police member’s medical needs. This may temporarily assist the employee with alleviating the effect of their disability, and depending on the disability, may assist with a long-term ability to perform the inherent requirements of their substantive role. In consultation with the police member, consideration may be given to altered duties, an alternative role and/or an alternative location. The time period for modified or alternative duties, role or location should be based on medical advice from an appropriate medical professional, with advice sought from the Police Medical Officer (PMO) and/or Police Psychology and if necessary, the injury management consultant (IMC). Where medical advice or the PMO determines that the assistance dog is required on a permanent basis for the police member, the accommodation process outlined in VPM Mobility (members) must be followed. Considerations for VPS employees Existing VPS employees who require an assistance dog are required to follow the process and considerations as listed in this policy and the Dogs in the workplace practice guide. VPM Reasonable workplace adjustment also applies. Depending on their role, in order to accommodate an assistance dog in the workplace, and in consultation with the employee, consideration may be given to altered duties, an alternative role and/or an alternative location. Request process Overview The requirement to accommodate an assistance dog to support an employee in the workplace is a reasonable workplace adjustment under state and federal anti-discrimination legislation. Consideration may need to be given to assessing the employee’s capacity to perform the inherent requirements of their substantive role. This may require assistance from the PMO or an employee’s registered medical practitioner (via the employee and with their consent). Employee requirements Where an employee is deemed eligible for an assistance dog from an accredited assistance dog provider, this will be the primary evidence required to accommodate the dog in the workplace. Where an existing employee qualifies for an assistance dog, they should discuss this with their work unit manager as soon as is practicable, preferably while in the process of obtaining an assistance dog or while planning their return to work. Requests for the use of an assistance dog must be submitted in writing using a General Report [Form 47] via the work unit manager and their Department/Region/Command Head to the Assistant Commissioner, Human Resources Command (HRC). The request should include any relevant supporting documentation including but not limited to: relevant paperwork from the assistance dog provider setting out the training that the assistance dog has received and that the provider organisation is an accredited organisation (e.g. Assistance Dogs International or International Guide Dog Federation), as only dogs from an accredited organisation are

A formal plan should be developed for the assistance dog in the workplace in conjunction with the work unit manager. Further information on the creation of a supporting plan can be found in Dogs in the workplace practice guide. Employees may seek advice from the Business Partnering and Workplace Relations Division (BPWRD) or the Gender Equality and Inclusion Division at any time. The work unit manager should discuss any concerns with the employee prior to making a final comment on their request. The work unit manager’s recommendation (after consideration of how they can accommodate the request), with endorsement from the relevant Department/Region/Command Head and the employee’s written request, should be submitted to the Assistant Commissioner, HRC for final consideration to determine if all relevant matters have been considered. The progression of the request, including the work unit manager’s recommendation, should be communicated to the employee. The outcome of their application should be communicated in writing at the earliest opportunity. BPWRD will provide advice to management and the Assistant Commissioner, HRC in relation to a specific request, including compliance with this policy and other relevant obligations, where requested. Implementation process Overview Requests for the presence of an assistance dog in the workplace should be endorsed and accommodated in line with VPM Reasonable workplace adjustment. See section 2 of Dogs in the workplace practice guide for information on what must be included in the formal plan and the requirements associated with having an assistance dog in the workplace. Employee (owner) responsibilities The assistance dog is the responsibility of the employee. This includes responsibility for all maintenance, care, costs and control of the assistance dog. An assistance dog must wear its special jacket or vest at any Victoria Police site. Assistance dogs must always be on a lead: in common areas within a Victoria Police site when being transported to and from a Victoria Police site while the employee is performing work duties externally to a Victoria Police site. Formal plan A formal plan must be developed between the employee and work unit manager to identify local arrangements for the dog. This must include completion of a risk assessment and building management plan, as well as other considerations, as outlined in the Dogs in the workplace practice guide. The plan must outline what reasonable adjustments will be made to support the employee and their assistance dog in the workplace. This plan must be sent to BPWRD, HRC to be recorded centrally and should be reviewed annually or as required (see section 3.4 below). Review of arrangement A review of the formal plan assessing how well the assistance dog is being accommodated with the employee in the workplace should be scheduled to ensure the needs of Victoria Police, the employee and the assistance dog continue to be met. Reviews should occur at least every 12 months or where there is a change in circumstances. Reviews may also occur, and arrangements amended as required where there may be issues with the dog, or the impact on others. All requests for assistance dogs must be genuinely considered on a case-by-case basis within a reasonable timeframe, whilst exercising positive duty to ensure the prevention of discriminatory practices or behaviours. All requests for assistance dogs must be genuinely considered on a case-by-case basis within a reasonable timeframe, whilst exercising positive duty to ensure the prevention of discriminatory practices or behaviours. Where a manager requires support in the initial assessment of a request for an assistance dog (or where it is likely the request is unable to be accommodated in the workplace), it is recommended that they seek advice from BPWRD on the individual circumstances. Where a request cannot be accommodated, and no alternative arrangements to accommodate the request can be made, a written response must be provided to the employee outlining the reasons for the refusal. Requests must only be refused on unjustifiable hardship grounds (as per anti-discrimination legislation). Refusals should only occur where management have assessed the request in accordance with section 2.2 of this policy and assessed the request to ensure compliance with anti-discrimination legislation. The written response should outline the relevant facts and matters that were considered by management in assessing the application. Where a request for an assistance dog in the workplace has been unable to be accommodated and the employee wishes to seek a review of actions, in accordance with VPM Review of actions (grievance), local issue resolution should be attempted in the first instance. If this is unsuccessful in resolving the review of actions, the employee may submit a review of actions within 28 calendar days of notification of the outcome of the request. Advice can be sought from the Review of Actions Registrar at any stage. Employees retain the right to refer a refused request for an assistance dog to other agencies such as the Fair Work Commission or the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission (VEOHRC). Leave to care for an assistance dog (VPS employees only) The Victorian Public Service Enterprise Agreement 2024 (clause 56) allows VPS employees an entitlement to paid carer’s leave when they are absent from the workplace to care for their assistance dog who is ill or injured. This is part of their overall personal/carer’s leave entitlement. To support the paid carer’s leave request, employees must provide their manager with evidence from a registered veterinary practitioner or a statutory declaration stating the condition of the assistance dog requires the employee’s care or support. These dogs can provide support on an ongoing regular basis or on ad hoc visitation basis, where a need arises. text: Reasonable workplace adjustment Context Victoria Police is committed to employment practices and standards that are fair, equitable and inclusive. Victoria Police is committed to improve its capacity to employ, develop and retain people with disabilities. Reasonable workplace adjustments will depend on individual circumstances and specific requirements. Contents Context 1 Contents 1 Definitions 1 Scope and application 2 Policy 2 Responsibilities and procedures 2 1. General 2 2. Current employees 3 3. Managers and supervisors 3 4. Recruitment 4 5. Police recruitment 5 6. Information handling 5 Related documents 5 Further advice and information 6 Update history 6 Definitions Reasonable workplace adjustment describes any change that is made so that a person with disability can have equality of access, employment and advancement opportunities. It is a term that is often used in employment. Other terms commonly used include: Access: Refers to the ease with which people are able to use services and/or resources. This includes access to buildings, car park spaces, facilities, resources, services and programs, equipment, signs, information, training programs, etc. Disability: Includes physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairments which in interaction with various barriers may hinder full and effective participation on an equal basis with others. Functional capacity evaluation: Assess whether the person is able to perform the inherent requirements of the job based on their level of function. The Victoria Police Medical Advisory Unit may conduct this evaluation in conjunction with specialist units as part of their medical assessment process (e.g. whether the person can put on and take off the equipment belt in an alternate manner). Inherent requirements: Functions that are a necessary part of the job. Unjustifiable hardship: A term used in the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 which describes how to determine whether an adjustment is reasonable. Scope and application This policy applies to all Victoria Police employees requiring reasonable workplace adjustments. This includes all graduates, work experience students and trainees who acquire disability while already employed, or if their current disability requires reasonable adjustments that are not already in place for both temporary and ongoing impairment. This policy also applies to prospective employees with disability applying for all positions with Victoria Police who may require reasonable adjustments. Policy The development of a reasonable workplace adjustment policy ensures that all prospective applicants and current employees have reasonable opportunities to achieve their potential and are not treated disadvantageously as a result of disability. The policy also fulfils requirements of the Victoria Police Accessibility Action Plan 2014-2017 and Victorian legislation. The requirement for reasonable workplace adjustments may be provided for people with disabilities: That occur at any age or stage in life or employment; present at birth, or acquired; that are temporary or in an ongoing capacity; that

title: Workplace_adjustment_VPM_Reasonable_workplace_adjustment_Final
text: applicants and current employees have reasonable opportunities to achieve their potential and are not treated disadvantageously as a result of disability. The policy also fulfils requirements of the Victoria Police Accessibility Action Plan 2014-2017 and Victorian legislation. The requirement for reasonable workplace adjustments may be provided for people with disabilities: That occur at any age or stage in life or employment; present at birth, or acquired; that are temporary or in an ongoing capacity; that may or may not be visible. Reasonable workplace adjustments will take into account all relevant circumstances and balance the benefits, the cost, and the effects on an individual, a workplace and Victoria Police as a whole. Under the Disability Discrimination Act 1992, an adjustment is considered reasonable unless it causes ‘unjustifiable hardship’ to the employer or organisation. Unjustifiable hardship could be in the form of financial cost, an amendment to the physical building that is not possible due to council or other restrictions, or an adjustment that would disadvantage other employees. The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 stipulates that it is lawful for an employer to discriminate against a person on the ground of the person’s disability if the person is unable to carry out the ‘inherent requirements’ of the position or would, in order to do so, require services or facilities that would impose an ‘unjustifiable hardship’ on the employer. For further information on how to apply reasonable adjustments in the workplace see the Guidelines. Responsibilities and procedures General A request for workplace adjustment must be considered in accordance with the following legislation and agreements. Victorian Public Service Enterprise Agreement 2016 Part 1 Clause 7 addresses anti-discrimination and the importance of respecting and valuing the diversity of the workforce by helping to prevent and eliminate discrimination on the basis of physical or mental disability. Clause 47.8 outlines where reasonable adjustments may be used to facilitate return to work. Equal Opportunity Act 2010 Section 20 requires that employers make reasonable adjustments for persons offered employment or an employee with disability. The employer must make reasonable adjustments unless the person or employee could not or cannot adequately perform the genuine and reasonable requirements of the employment even after the adjustments are made. The Equal Opportunity Act 2010 includes limited exceptions where discrimination is not considered unlawful. Refer to the Policy section which discusses reasonable workplace adjustment considerations related to this legislation. Disability Discrimination Act 1992 The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 states that organisations have an explicit duty to make reasonable adjustments. The act now expressly provides that the failure to make ‘reasonable adjustments’ may constitute either direct or indirect discrimination. Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Article 27 stipulates that employers must ensure that ‘reasonable

title: Workplace_adjustment_VPM_Reasonable_workplace_adjustment_Final
text: is not considered unlawful. Refer to the Policy section which discusses reasonable workplace adjustment considerations related to this legislation. Disability Discrimination Act 1992 The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 states that organisations have an explicit duty to make reasonable adjustments. The act now expressly provides that the failure to make ‘reasonable adjustments’ may constitute either direct or indirect discrimination. Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Article 27 stipulates that employers must ensure that ‘reasonable accommodation’ is provided to persons with disabilities in the workplace. Fair Work Act 2009 Division 5 Section 351 addresses discrimination and provides that an employer must not take adverse action against a person who is an employee, or prospective employee, because of the person’s physical or mental disability. Current employees If an employee requires an adjustment, they should discuss this with their manager and/or make a written request and describe: the adjustments they propose; the reasoning, ideally with medical certification, detailing the circumstances and any recommendation. Design of a reasonable adjustment should be made in collaboration with managers and supervisors and may include participation in the medical review process. Managers and supervisors Responsibility Managers and supervisors are responsible for ensuring that the workplace provides every opportunity for employees with disability to participate fully within the workforce. Where a workplace adjustment is required, the manager should provide the adjustment within a reasonable time frame. Initial considerations The following items should be considered when a request for an adjustment is received: notification to the appropriate Injury Management Consultant (IMC); police member referrals to Mobility and Deployment, Medical Advisory Unit; VPS employee referrals to Employee Relations; the proposed adjustment and alternatives; the cost of proposed adjustments; evaluation of any detriment to other employees or operational matters; commencement of planning associated with the implementation of adjustments and review. Existing adjustments Periodic assessment of existing adjustments should be undertaken with the employee to ensure continued success and effectiveness. The impact of disability may fluctuate and managers should address this appropriately. Learning and development Suitable modifications to training programs and online learning may be required to ensure accessibility for all employees. Adjustments may also be required where an employee with disability relocates from their usual workplace to another workplace on secondment. Recruitment Overview The principles of equal opportunity must be followed throughout the recruitment process and ensure that all prospective employees are treated fairly and reasonably with consideration to equal employment opportunity. The recruitment process should be free from barriers which prevent equal opportunity for prospective employees to demonstrate that they are the best person for the job. text: equal opportunity must be followed throughout the recruitment process and ensure that all prospective employees are treated fairly and reasonably with consideration to equal employment opportunity. The recruitment process should be free from barriers which prevent equal opportunity for prospective employees to demonstrate that they are the best person for the job. Considerations When a vacancy arises, before advertising, managers should review the existing position description and consult with Classifications and Review before advertisement. Managers may consider whether full-time work is an inherent requirement of the role or whether work-share, part-time work or other similar adjustments may be considered. It is not unlawful for an employer to deny employment to a person where they cannot meet the inherent requirements of the job. Assessment of applications and interview process Ideally, panel members are informed by the candidate prior to interview of any adjustments that may be required, however there is no obligation on the candidate to disclose their disability prior to interview. During the shortlisting process, if the panel considers that the candidate with disability meets the inherent requirements of the position, they should be offered an interview. At interview, if a disability is disclosed, panel members should ask whether there are any reasonable adjustments that the organisation might arrange to assist the potential employee do their job. Assessment of applicants must be based on the ability to perform the inherent requirements of the position. If the candidate with disability does not meet the inherent requirements of the position, then a clear explanation of this should be outlined in the selection report. Selected candidate requiring reasonable workplace adjustment If the successful candidate has a disability, commence consideration of and planning for reasonable workplace adjustment and where possible, implement changes prior to commencement. Managers can refer to the publication “Manager’s Guide – Disability in the workforce”. Police recruitment Overview The Equal Opportunity Act 2010 allows exemption on the grounds of ‘protection of health, safety and property’ where discrimination is reasonably necessary to protect the health or safety of any person or of the public. This may be relevant for Recruit, PSO or PCO recruitment. The Victoria Police Recruitment website provides prospective employees with information of the entry requirements, including fitness and medical conditions. A self-assessment kit is featured and can be used to assess whether a potential candidate meets the inherent requirements of the role. These conditions also apply to current members that choose to apply for advertised positions. If a police member, PSO or PCO has some doubt of whether they can perform the inherent duties of the advertised position they can contact the Medical Advisory Unit for advice. text: Workplace behaviours Context Victoria Police is committed to providing a safe, inclusive and respectful workplace free from bullying, discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment and victimisation. Victoria Police is continuing to build a workplace culture of respect and adopts a zero-tolerance approach towards inappropriate behaviours, as described in this policy. All employees play an important role in promoting and maintaining a positive and safe working environment and in upholding standards of appropriate behaviour and conduct, both within and outside the organisation. Behaviour that falls short of this standard will be dealt with in accordance with this policy. In accordance with the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth), Victoria Police has positive duty obligations to eliminate sexual discrimination, sexual harassment and victimisation in the workplace. This policy outlines the appropriate and acceptable standards of behaviour in the workplace and supports employees to meet these standards in order to provide a safe, inclusive and respectful workplace for all. Contents Context 1 Contents 1 Definitions 1 Scope and application 8 Legal framework 8 Responsibilities 9 1. Standards of behaviour 9 2. Resolution 10 3. Breach of this policy 10 Related documents 10 Further advice and information 11 Update history 12 Definitions Scope and application This policy applies to all Victoria Police employees during all work-related situations, whether during or outside normal working hours, whether on leave or rostered for duty, and including before and after shifts and breaks. Work-related situations include but are not limited to, situations where people are: in any Victoria Police workplace (including staff rooms and change rooms) in work vehicles at any place where work duties are performed (including on patrol; making inquiries; at public transport hubs; at court; at off-site meetings e.g. at a cafe, private home; at training, conferences and work trips including overnight, residential and meals or social contact during trips) while engaged in work or work-related activities, including dealings with colleagues or members of the public, on or off-site, face-to-face or using Victoria Police information systems, telephone or social media applications and platforms identifying themselves as an employee of Victoria Police or referring to Victoria Police, its employees or operations, including through social media or where they can be identified by others as an employee of Victoria Police at social functions, events and activities organised by or through Victoria Police, such as office parties, dinners, graduation, retirement or Christmas functions. This policy does not remove any obligation which a police member has under the Victoria Police Act to report the misconduct of another police member. This policy does not remove any obligation which a police member has under the Victoria Police Act to report the misconduct of another police member. Legal framework Victoria Police has various legal duties in relation to the health and safety of its employees and others in the workplace: S.21 of the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 provides Victoria Police with a duty to provide and maintain, so far as is reasonably practicable, a working environment for all employees which is safe and without risks to health S.25 of the Occupational Health and Safety Act provides an obligation on all employees of Victoria Police to take reasonable care for their own health and safety and the health and safety of those they work with S.26 of the Occupational Health and Safety Act places an obligation on managers of workplaces to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a working environment for all employees of the workplace which is safe and without risks to health. Failure of Victoria Police or its employees to meet the relevant legal duties may result in: workers' compensation claims WorkSafe prosecutions common law personal injury claims vicarious liability. In the event of any such claims, Victoria Police will be required to prove what steps have been taken to provide a safe working environment in compliance with its legal duties. This may include regular training which has been provided, policies and procedures, and specific actions that have been taken in individual cases to identify and address risks to health and safety. This highlights the importance of creating and maintaining a safe working environment and responding to inappropriate behaviour in a timely and considered manner. Responsibilities Standards of behaviour Employee responsibilities All employees are responsible for their own conduct and must comply with the expected standards of behaviour set out in VPM Professional and ethical standards and the Victorian Public Sector Code of Conduct for Special Bodies. Employees are also expected to adhere to the Victoria Police Values in contributing to safe, inclusive and respectful workplaces. Employees of Victoria Police must not engage in inappropriate behaviours. Inappropriate behaviours will not be tolerated by Victoria Police and action will be taken in accordance with VPM Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution – Procedure. Employees are encouraged, if they feel comfortable and safe, to call out and address inappropriate behaviours before they escalate, including by using interventions and tools set out in VPM Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution – Procedure. Employees are encouraged, if they feel comfortable and safe, to call out and address inappropriate behaviours before they escalate, including by using interventions and tools set out in VPM Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution – Procedure. All employees are responsible for: being familiar with and complying with this policy, ensuring their behaviour is safe, inclusive, respectful and appropriate for the workplace taking steps to prevent inappropriate behaviour from occurring or escalating in their workplace or in connection with work, by: if concerns are raised about their own behaviour, being willing to admit to mistakes, make amends and change their own behaviour, seeking help if needed supporting those who may have experienced inappropriate behaviour and refraining from any form of victimisation supporting the efforts of those seeking to change their own behaviours and of those seeking to create a safe, inclusive and respectful workplace assisting and co-operating in the application of this policy and in any process to address inappropriate behaviour taken under VPM Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution – Procedure. Supervisor responsibilities In addition to their responsibilities as employees, supervisors are responsible for: promoting this policy and the Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution – Procedure providing employees with advice and guidance on the application of this policy and VPM Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution – Procedure, where appropriate taking steps to prevent inappropriate behaviours from arising in the workplace by regularly communicating and reinforcing clear expectations for safe, inclusive and respectful behaviour leading by example, by role-modelling safe, inclusive and respectful behaviour in the workplace being knowledgeable and alert to the kind of behaviour and signs of workplace harm that might indicate a problem exists or is emerging when becoming aware of inappropriate behaviours, responding promptly, sensitively and confidentially in accordance with VPM Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution – Procedure wherever appropriate and avoiding any conflict of interest, assisting individuals to resolve concerns about workplace behaviour informally at the local level. Employees can and should take reasonable steps to raise concerns about inappropriate behaviours even if the conduct in question was not specifically targeted at them. title: Workplace_behaviours_VPM_Workplace_behaviours_reducing_harm_and_resolution_Procedure_final
text: Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution - Procedure Context Victoria Police is committed to reducing workplace harm, including psychological harm that may result from employees behaving inappropriately in the workplace. Any behaviour that has the potential to cause workplace harm to individuals, a team or Victoria Police’s reputation may activate this Procedure. This includes bullying, discrimination, harassment, inter-personal conflict, predatory behaviour, sexual harassment, vexatious complaints, victimisation and workplace incivility. Reasonable management action carried out in reasonable manner is not considered by Victoria Police to be harmful workplace behaviour. VPM Workplace behaviours provides clear guidance about the standard of behaviour expected. VPM Workplace behaviours – reducing harm and resolution – Procedure supports this Policy in remediating workplace harm, sets out the processes to be followed and the options available when employees behave inappropriately. It is aligned with and supports Victoria Police’s commitments under the Mental Health Review and VEOHRC Review, as well as the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004. This Procedure has been developed to help facilitate and guide early intervention and remedial action whenever inappropriate behaviour occurs. It is designed to allow multiple access points and support the people involved to change their behaviour while retaining clear pathways for disciplinary action. Purpose Early intervention is the key to reducing workplace harm. Early intervention includes immediate action to protect and support affected people, as well as providing appropriate assistance to identify and change inappropriate behaviour. This approach recognises that everyone is capable of behaving inappropriately and should be provided with the opportunity to change. It relies on acceptance by everyone that mistakes can often be remedied, and relationships restored. An early response may stop inappropriate behaviours from escalating or becoming entrenched, limit workplace harm and reduce long-term personal leave, unplanned leave and workers’ compensation claims. This approach builds trust, reduces anxiety and supports healthy workplace relationships. Victoria Police employees should take reasonable steps to raise a concern in relation to inappropriate behaviour of others which is contrary to VPM Workplace behaviours and which may affect the performance of their work, their health and well-being, or that of others. This Procedure provides all employees with: information that supports and guides early intervention by supervisors, affected people, colleagues and witnesses and encourages positive changes in behaviours and attitudes; information about the principles, processes, options and outcomes that may be applied to respond to and resolve inappropriate behaviour; and clarity about responsibilities and obligations to ensure the effective and timely resolution of matters, with due regard for the health, safety and well-being of employees. Scope and application This Procedure applies to all Victoria Police employees. This Procedure does not remove any obligation which a police member has under the Victoria Police Act 2013 to report the misconduct of another police member. This Procedure is not intended to deal with complaints involving allegations of misconduct or criminal conduct, and employees should ensure that such complaints are referred to Professional Standards Command (see below Consideration of Professional Standards Command referral). This Procedure does not apply to grievances regarding specific management actions, inaction or decisions that an employee is seeking to contest or review. Employees should refer to VPM Review of actions (grievance). Prevention and early intervention Building safe, inclusive and respectful workplaces Building a positive work environment is an important factor in creating and maintaining a safe, inclusive and respectful workplace free of workplace harm. Everyone plays a critical role in maintaining a positive work environment through behaviours that include (but are not limited to): being courteous and polite, co-operative and patient fair and equitable treatment of everyone acknowledging mistakes early engaging in remedial action promptly. Supervisors also have an obligation to create and maintain safe, inclusive and respectful workplaces. The following points may help supervisors foster a positive working environment: role-modelling appropriate behaviours encouraging help-seeking behaviour ensuring expectations about workplace behaviour, roles and performance are clear providing regular, consistent and constructive performance feedback consulting and involving employees in decision-making and explaining

text: and polite, co-operative and patient fair and equitable treatment of everyone acknowledging mistakes early engaging in remedial action promptly. Supervisors also have an obligation to create and maintain safe, inclusive and respectful workplaces. The following points may help supervisors foster a positive working environment: role-modelling appropriate behaviours encouraging help-seeking behaviour ensuring expectations about workplace behaviour, roles and performance are clear providing regular, consistent and constructive performance feedback consulting and involving employees in decision-making and explaining the reasons for decisions that affect them encouraging and assisting employees to identify and address workplace concerns responding to behaviours that could cause workplace harm regularly checking on the wellbeing of employees and facilitating referrals to support services as required. Indicators of workplace harm Identifying early warning signs of inappropriate behaviour which may cause workplace harm will help supervisors and co-workers to support all employees. In particular, supervisors and co-workers should be alert to changes in behaviours and mood of those around them. Supervisors and co-workers should follow up concerns with conversations. This timely identification will prompt implementation of early intervention strategies. Some of the behavioural and physical indicators may be (but are not limited to): emotional reactions and erratic behaviour disengagement and low morale reduced ability to concentrate increased withdrawal from colleagues such as reduced participation in work activities. Environmental scan for supervisors Supervisors need to have regular conversations with employees and other supervisors about what is occurring in the workplace. If there are concerns about inappropriate behaviour, review the following: number and frequency of unplanned absences or reports of workplace harm relevant information and records including diversity dashboard, incident reports, workers’ compensation claims, staff surveys, absenteeism and staff turnover data work allocations in regards to fairness, overload or lack of role clarity inspect how work is carried out and observe how employees interact with each other, noting any impact on productivity e.g. delays or backlogs. Early intervention strategies Early intervention is focussed on identifying and responding to warning signs and reports of incidents in the workplace. If a supervisor identifies early warning signs that an employee could be impacted by workplace harm, the supervisor is responsible for taking action immediately to address the issues before they develop. Responding early can stop employees from escalating behaviours that may cause workplace harm or further workplace harm. For more information on available interventions, refer to the Intervention Matrix and Intervention Options. Consideration of Professional Standards Command referral Any employee making, receiving or dealing with inappropriate behaviour should, at the earliest possible stage, give consideration to the seriousness of the conduct and whether it is appropriate to refer the matter to Professional Standards Command (PSC). Consideration of Professional Standards Command referral Any employee making, receiving or dealing with inappropriate behaviour should, at the earliest possible stage, give consideration to the seriousness of the conduct and whether it is appropriate to refer the matter to Professional Standards Command (PSC). Complaints involving allegations of misconduct or criminal conduct are not intended to be dealt with under this Procedure and should be referred directly to PSC. Specifically, though "victimisation" is defined in VPM Workplace behaviours and for the purposes of this Procedure as including conduct done in contravention of the victimisation offence in section 173 of the Victoria Police Act, it is not intended that allegations of an offence under that section would be dealt with under this Procedure. Resolution processes An early intervention approach to inappropriate behaviour relies on remedial and restorative actions that aim to minimise workplace harm to all concerned while building interpersonal skills and supporting respectful workplace relationships. To best achieve a sustainable change in behaviours and relationships the selection of interventions is based on the nature of the observed or reported behaviour combined with the willingness and ability of those involved to participate in remedial actions. The intervention will focus on resolving the issues and assisting the parties to minimise the actual or potential harm to themselves, the other participants, their co-workers and the workplace. This Procedure outlines three approaches to resolution that may be used; Direct Feedback, Local Resolution; and Formal Resolution. Where a matter is managed through Local Resolution, the supervisor will act as the case manager. The local case manager can seek advice and support through any of the Support Options. If Local Resolution is unsuccessful or if it is not appropriate, the Formal Resolution process may be engaged. This Procedure has been designed to ensure that inappropriate behaviours may be dealt with by Victoria Police in a manner which causes the least possible workplace harm to participants. Victoria Police encourages employees who have experienced and/or witnessed inappropriate workplace behaviours to, where possible, raise concerns in accordance with this Procedure prior to making a complaint with any external agencies. The external agencies that an employee may seek resolution depending on their situation include: Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission Victorian Civil and Administration Tribunal WorkSafe Independent Broad-Based Anti-Corruption Commission. Principles and key aspects of the resolution process Natural justice principles The processes set out in this Procedure should be conducted in a fair and equitable manner and in accordance with the principles of natural justice. These include that: decision makers act objectively and without bias the process and outcome is as timely as reasonably possible participants are regularly informed of the progress of the processes participants are given the opportunity to explain their situation, and a reasonable opportunity to respond to any and all information raised which may have a reasonable bearing on the matter all relevant information and evidence provided by each participant will be considered before decisions are made participants are given the opportunity to understand the reasons for the proposed actions and of any decision which affects them. What are the complainant’s rights during the resolution process? The complainant has rights to: a support person (See Definition below) obtain their own external advice (at their own cost) be advised of the substance of the respondent’s response as early as possible, with sufficient details to understand and recall the events and circumstances of any counter allegations have the opportunity to respond to any adverse allegations about them made by the respondent not to be victimised for making a complaint confidentiality throughout the process, so far as is reasonably possible. What are the respondent’s rights during the resolution process? The respondent has rights to: a support person (See Definition below) obtain their own external advice (at their own cost) be advised of the substance of the allegations against them as early as possible, with sufficient details to understand and recall the events and circumstances complained of have an opportunity to respond to the allegations confidentiality throughout the process, as far as is reasonably possible. Confidentiality Why is confidentiality important? Confidentiality needs to be maintained and is important to protect the reputation, right to privacy and health and well-being of participants involved in these processes. Information will only be accessible to people with a direct need to know. Can complainants or witnesses remain anonymous? Anonymous complaints can be made and will be progressed under this Procedure if the allegations are serious in nature and sufficient evidence or information is provided to enable the matter to be considered. However, in many situations natural justice principles will mean that the respondent is entitled to be informed of who raised the matter and the substance of the allegations in order to respond fully. However, in many situations natural justice principles will mean that the respondent is entitled to be informed of who raised the matter and the substance of the allegations in order to respond fully. It may be necessary to speak with other employees in the workplace to determine what happened, to afford fairness to those involved and to resolve the matter. What is considered vexatious? Vexatious means a complaint or response to a complaint without substance or merit with the intent to inflict inconvenience, harassment or workplace harm to others. Any person whose complaint or response to a complaint is found to be vexatious may be subject to discipline action. Public interest disclosure In some circumstances a complaint may be considered to be a public interest disclosure. Refer to VPMG Public interest disclosures or contact PSC for further information. Support options Support services There are a range of support options available to all employees to seek advice and support throughout these processes. Support person All participants may access assistance from a support person of their choosing. There must not be any unreasonable refusal by Victoria Police to allow a participant to have a support person present as part of an identified resolution process. Victoria Police will have regard to the most conciliatory and timely option for resolution, when determining participation in any identified process. Who can be a support person? A support person may be a colleague, friend, family member, service professional or union representative but may not be a person holding a current certificate of legal practice, unless they are an employee of The Police Association, Community & Public Sector Union or Victoria Police. A support person must be someone independent to the issue being addressed. What is the support person’s role in the resolution process? A support person may, where requested by the participant: provide moral, practical and emotional support, advice and guidance take notes on behalf of the participant assist the participant to prepare responses or submissions, if required when appropriate to do so (having regard to the capacity of the participant to speak on their own behalf) the support person may, on the participant’s behalf; present information, options and proposals; respond to proposals, or ask questions about the dispute resolution process, but may not question any other participant. The support person must: treat all matters in a confidential manner and agree to follow the principles and procedures as outlined in this Procedure be respectful and courteous towards all people involved in the processes work cooperatively to progress each stage

The support person must: treat all matters in a confidential manner and agree to follow the principles and procedures as outlined in this Procedure be respectful and courteous towards all people involved in the processes work cooperatively to progress each stage of the resolution process without undue or unreasonable delay co-operate with any reasonable request by the supervisor, case manager, facilitator or mediator for the participant to speak on their own behalf declare any conflict of interest to the supervisor. If a conflict of interest exists, the person overseeing the process may request or require the participant to nominate an alternative support person. The supervisor must be notified of the identity of the support person prior to any meetings. The supervisor may refuse to involve the participant’s support person, and may invite that participant to nominate an alternative support person if a support person refuses to adhere to the above requirements. Responsibilities and obligations All employees All employees play a critical role to ensure that inappropriate behaviour in the workplace is addressed and eliminated as far as reasonably practicable. The focus should be on preventing, and where necessary, reducing workplace harm to all and rebuilding constructive working relationships. This requires all employees to: if they feel comfortable and safe, speak up about behaviour they observe that makes them or others uncomfortable ensure they speak respectfully to the respondent and recognise that they may be unaware that their behaviour is having a negative impact on others give the supervisor sufficient information to allow further enquires to be made be prepared to listen carefully and respectfully when told their own behaviour is not acceptable or causing someone distress seek support and guidance in how to achieve sustainable changes in their behaviour in a timely way when their behaviour has been identified as inappropriate actively engage in training and professional development activities related to inappropriate behaviour, workplace harm and working with people who have different ideas and perspectives act professionally, appropriately and honestly at all times throughout these processes, treat all participants with respect and continue to carry out their duties and function to the best of their ability reasonably participate in any resolution process which may involve providing information, participating in meetings, discussions, counselling, interviews and providing statements regarding their version of events ensure all information relating to a matter and the resolution process is kept confidential. This includes keeping concerns raised informally confidential keep details of what has occurred, including notes and any supporting materials ensure reprisal

text: and continue to carry out their duties and function to the best of their ability reasonably participate in any resolution process which may involve providing information, participating in meetings, discussions, counselling, interviews and providing statements regarding their version of events ensure all information relating to a matter and the resolution process is kept confidential. This includes keeping concerns raised informally confidential keep details of what has occurred, including notes and any supporting materials ensure reprisal action is not taken against any person who has made, or may raise a concern, claim or complaint, or who provides information about a concern, claim or complaint report misconduct or criminal conduct to PSC. If an employee does not comply with the requirements to reasonably participate, maintain confidentiality and to avoid reprisals during the resolution process, this may constitute a breach of discipline under section 125 of the Victoria Police Act (for police members) or misconduct under clause 27 of the Victorian Public Service Enterprise Agreement 2024 (for VPS employees), and disciplinary action may be taken. An employee who refuses to reasonably participate in resolution processes may risk having their matter referred to the discipline process and lose any protections afforded by this Procedure. Supervisors Supervisors have a positive duty to eliminate sexual discrimination, sexual harassment and victimisation in the workplace and are key to ensuring that inappropriate behaviour is, so far as possible, addressed and resolved fairly, effectively and with due regard for the health and safety of all employees in the workplace. In doing so, supervisors are required to: take ownership for the effective response to inappropriate behaviour assist in the selection of remedial and restorative intervention programs, where appropriate participate, support and implement remedial and restorative intervention programs, where appropriate refer matters to a higher level supervisor where there is real or perceived bias or conflict of interest proactively address inappropriate behaviour when becoming aware of it ensure the health and safety of everyone involved during any resolution process treat all matters seriously, promptly and confidentially support the Formal Resolution process as required (this may include gathering information, arranging interviews with witnesses, undertaking interviews) monitor and assess the effectiveness of remedial and restorative interventions and programs to sustain behavioural improvement ensure that documentation is recorded and kept throughout the process seek advice, guidance and support during the Local Resolution process from a higher level supervisor, OneLink, Workplace Relations or PSC, if required report misconduct or criminal conduct to PSC. HR Business Partners HR Business Partners take a coaching approach by providing support to Local Area Management on people management matters to enable them to effectively manage their employees. In doing so, HR Business Partners will: provide Local Area Management with practical guidance, advice and support to address inappropriate behaviour through the Local Management Resolution process seek subject matter expertise from specialists in the Human Resources Command (e.g. OneLink, Workplace Relations) to support Local Area Management with local workplace interventions to address inappropriate behaviour ensure that appropriate documentation is recorded and kept throughout the process ensure that Local Area Management implement interventions through the Local Management Resolution process and continue to monitor the situation to ensure the matter has been resolved. OneLink OneLink is a central pathway for employees impacted by workplace harm to access the services they need. OneLink is a confidential service that provides advice, guidance and support to employees about the resolution process. In doing so, OneLink will: help to reduce barriers to reporting workplace harm provide an end-to-end service to ensure matters raised are addressed support employees to choose which pathway is right for them provide advice and information on options available to those seeking advice. Workplace Relations Workplace Relations provides subject matter expertise, including consultation in relation to police respondents and assessments/case management in relation to VPS respondents, in relation to matters including bullying, discrimination, harassment, inter-personal conflict, victimisation and workplace incivility. In doing so, Workplace Relations is required to: assess requests for resolution and consult with Local Area Management about the implementation of an appropriate method of resolution ensure resolution processes are conducted in an efficient manner clarify responsibilities to the people involved in a resolution process ensure everyone involved is kept informed of the progress of a resolution process, where appropriate ensure appropriate documentation is recorded and kept throughout the process monitor the progress of any recommended outcomes arising out of a resolution process and where necessary, escalate the matter if recommended outcomes have not been implemented. Local Area Management Local Area Management (Inspector to Assistant Commissioner) play an important role during the Formal Resolution process. They are responsible for: implementing the outcomes arising from the Formal Resolution process considering and implementing any temporary actions which may be necessary during the course of the resolution process to protect the safety and well-being of any person and the integrity of the process and, where necessary, consulting with Workplace Relations in relation to any proposed action reviewing any temporary actions implemented during

text: Assistant Commissioner) play an important role during the Formal Resolution process. They are responsible for: implementing the outcomes arising from the Formal Resolution process considering and implementing any temporary actions which may be necessary during the course of the resolution process to protect the safety and well-being of any person and the integrity of the process and, where necessary, consulting with Workplace Relations in relation to any proposed action reviewing any temporary actions implemented during the resolution process as necessary communicating, where appropriate, with the parties and Workplace Relations in relation to any temporary actions that have been implemented ensuring that appropriate documentation is recorded and kept throughout the process. Resolution – three approaches Each approach aims to achieve a sustainable resolution and to minimise workplace harm. These approaches recognise that everyone is capable of behaving inappropriately at times and should be provided with an opportunity to change. These approaches do not need to be used sequentially. The three approaches are: Direct feedback – where issues are resolved by providing feedback directly and informally Local resolution – where supervisors work with individuals involved to remedy and resolve concerns at the local workplace level Formal resolution – where an employee or supervisor reports a matter, and a determination has been made to progress formal resolution. The three approaches are set out in more detail in the following sections. Direct feedback The affected person, witness or a supervisor can speak about their concerns directly to the respondent. This is often the simplest and quickest approach. Respondents can sometimes be surprised and unaware of the impact of their behaviour on others. In many instances direct feedback will be effective in halting their behaviour. However, if an employee feels uncomfortable they do not need to attempt direct feedback. If possible and appropriate, the respondent should be given the opportunity and support to change their behaviour. The respondent may be dealing with their own issues and be unaware of how their behaviour, manner of speaking or words are being experienced by others. They may be further distressed by hearing they are causing others discomfort. Consider the timing and location for delivering feedback: approach the person directly find a quiet and private place away from the immediate workplace identify the behaviour considered to be unreasonable and inappropriate be specific about the behaviours and the context ask the person to cease the behaviour encourage the person to seek support and guidance, if appropriate keep a record of this action and of any further inappropriate behaviours. Where direct feedback is not an option or does not effectively resolve the matter, employees are encouraged to speak with their supervisor, Peer Support Officer or contact OneLink for confidential advice, support

text: considered to be unreasonable and inappropriate be specific about the behaviours and the context ask the person to cease the behaviour encourage the person to seek support and guidance, if appropriate keep a record of this action and of any further inappropriate behaviours. Where direct feedback is not an option or does not effectively resolve the matter, employees are encouraged to speak with their supervisor, Peer Support Officer or contact OneLink for confidential advice, support and guidance on the services available. Employees should also lodge a HR Assist Incident Report so that any workplace harm or potential workplace harm is recorded. Local resolution Raising a concern If direct feedback is either not appropriate or does not effectively resolve the employee’s concerns, employees are encouraged to speak with their supervisor in order to resolve the issues locally. When a supervisor becomes aware of inappropriate behaviour they should commence this process. If the supervisor is involved in the matter, the employee should raise their concern with the next person in their management structure, or a trusted senior person. If the next person in their management structure is also involved, or if the employee has concerns about how the matter has been dealt with, the employee may seek advice on formal resolution under this procedure. The matter should be referred to PSC where it involves misconduct or criminal behaviour (see above Consideration of Professional Standards Command referral). If it is inappropriate for local management to resolve the matter through local resolution, refer to formal resolution under this procedure. Resolution process Supervisors should respond to inappropriate behaviour by considering the circumstances of the matter raised and then selecting interventions. Interventions are selected to best achieve sustained changes in behaviours and workplace relationships. See Interventions Matrix and Intervention Options. If a contractor or volunteer is involved, the supervisor continues to be responsible for managing the situation. This may involve contacting the contracting agency or volunteer organisation about whether or not the person can continue in their role. Supervisors are encouraged to seek advice, guidance and support from OneLink, Workplace Relations or PSC, as required. Identify the harms and behaviours. Have conversations with people involved to understand their perspectives of the behaviours and workplace harm. Clarify what the issues and concerns are. Use active listening skills and remain non-judgemental during conversations to obtain a full picture of the work and social circumstances of each person and what happened. Remember that the first person to raise concerns may not know or understand everyone’s perspective or the full circumstances. Take immediate action, to ensure a safe workplace and those involved have suitable professional health and welfare advice and support. This may include recommending: they consult their GP or

Assess each person’s willingness and capacity to engage in intervention programs. Check each person’s state of well-being and consider their ability and willingness to engage in a remedial or restorative program. This includes the affected person/s and respondent/s. The default position is they have an ability to engage so an assessment needs to be undertaken to determine if this has been diminished by current work or personal circumstances. With some support, or after participating in counselling or training, a person’s willingness or ability to engage in a joint intervention such as mediation or workplace conferencing may change. When a person is assessed as not having the ability to engage in a joint interest at that point in time, consider a preparatory step such as counselling or conflict coaching. A straightforward question about willingness to engage is sufficient. Do not attempt to force a person to engage in interventions. Select and implement intervention programs. In consultation with those involved, select and implement intervention programs that support and guide the development of acceptable standards of professional behaviour. The aim is to achieve sustained and stable changes in workplace behaviour and relationships. The Interventions Matrix and Intervention Options will help in choosing programs and interventions. Several interventions can be used simultaneously or sequentially, depending on the nature of the behaviours and circumstances of those involved. Outcomes may include one or a combination of the
