The aim is to achieve sustained and stable changes in workplace behaviour and relationships. The Interventions Matrix and Intervention Options will help in choosing programs and interventions. Several interventions can be used simultaneously or sequentially, depending on the nature of the behaviours and circumstances of those involved. Outcomes may include one or a combination of the following (but are not limited to): offer a clarifying explanation a discussion between the people involved resulting in improved working relationships an apology and acceptance of responsibility for their own behaviour agreed communication protocols a change in work arrangements e.g. changes to rosters, workplace practices or duties a commitment to engage in counselling, conflict coaching, mentoring or similar program a commitment to undertake a behaviour change program or training an undertaking or direction that the identified inappropriate behaviour will stop a review of organisational factors contributing to the issues of concern an agreed timetable for monitoring and review. Reassure the complainant that intervention has occurred and record and monitor behaviours. This may involve setting a timeline to meet the expected standards of behaviour and agreeing on a monitoring schedule to check in on the health and welfare of each person involved and find out if the actions taken have been effective. Resolution occurs when there are sustained and stable changes in behaviour and when the participants behave professionally and respectfully with each other. Advise the respondent when satisfied the matter is resolved. Keep records. It is important that supervisors keep records of inappropriate behaviour and any actions taken to address the matter. This includes: ensuring a HR Assist Incident Report is created and completed (note: the inappropriate behaviours tick box needs to be selected). OneLink will automatically be notified for recording purposes and can also provide support and assistance in dealing with the matter keeping written records of conversations and meetings, detailing the date and time, who was present and the agreed outcomes. What happens if the behaviour continues or the matter remains unresolved following attempts at local resolution? If the inappropriate behaviour continues, the complainant remains unsatisfied or the issue remains unresolved after local resolution has been attempted, the matter may be escalated through the formal resolution process under this procedure. Formal resolution Request for formal resolution If attempts at direct feedback or local resolution have been unsuccessful, or it is not appropriate due to the serious nature of the allegation/s, or the health and welfare of the complainant, a request for formal resolution may be made. Formal resolution Request for formal resolution If attempts at direct feedback or local resolution have been unsuccessful, or it is not appropriate due to the serious nature of the allegation/s, or the health and welfare of the complainant, a request for formal resolution may be made. Anonymous complaints may also be lodged through this pathway. How do I make a request for formal resolution? For confidential advice on submitting a request for formal resolution, employees can contact OneLink in the first instance on 1800 598 846. A request for formal resolution may be made by filling out a TEMPLATE: Chronology for Affected Persons or TEMPLATE: Chronology for Witnesses or Supervisors. The completed Chronology Template should be emailed to ONELINK-WORKPLACE-HARM-MGR. Assessment and triage Victoria Police has a number of areas that assess and triage workplace harm. OneLink is a central pathway that is able to assess and triage requests for Formal Resolution as set out below and in the PROCESS GUIDE: Workplace Harm Triage Process: Receive Chronology Template OneLink will make contact with the complainant to acknowledge receipt of their request for Formal Resolution. OneLink may also make further enquiries with the complainant if the information provided in the Chronology Template is not sufficient to make an assessment of the matter. Assessment OneLink will undertake an assessment of the request for formal resolution to determine whether the matter should be referred through one or more of the following services: the supervisor - the nature of the matter is at a level that local resolution is deemed appropriate HR Business Partners – provide advice, support and coaching to Local Area Management to address matters deemed appropriate for local resolution PSC - the matter concerns misconduct, including potential or alleged criminal conduct, sexual harassment, sexual assault or predatory behaviour Workplace Relations, Human Resources Command - for all other matters relating to bullying, reasonable management action, inter-personal conflict, harassment, discrimination, victimisation, workplace incivility. Consent from complainant OneLink will contact the complainant to seek their consent to progress discussions with one or more of the relevant service/s outlined above. Triage consultation If consent is obtained from the complainant, OneLink will bring the relevant service/s together to triage and seek agreement to refer the request for resolution. Referral OneLink will formally refer the request for resolution to the relevant service/s. Case conferencing Representatives from the relevant service/s may meet in a case conference setting on a regular or ad hoc basis where the matter crosses over different areas or has the potential to be referred to another area because of the nature of the allegation/s. If the answer is yes for VPS employees, or if at any stage during the process the answer becomes yes, Workplace Relations may consider dealing with the matter pursuant to the process in the Victorian Public Service Enterprise Agreement 2024 for managing misconduct. Preliminary enquiry If the matter is to proceed as a formal request under this Procedure, the next step is for the Workplace Relations Lead or Workplace Relations Senior Consultant, or other person appointed with the responsibility (including an external provider), to conduct preliminary enquiries. Where a public interest disclosure is involved, the Workplace Relations Lead or Workplace Relations Senior Consultant will liaise with PSC before progressing any further with the matter and ensure adherence to the relevant provisions under the Public Interests Disclosure Act 2012. The purpose of making preliminary enquiries is to get a clear understanding of the sequence and nature of events to establish whether there is an issue to resolve and if so, whether the matter can be resolved through the provision of support to Local Area Management or if an investigation is required. This may include (but is not limited to): the person appointed to undertake the preliminary enquiry, determining who the relevant parties are to speak to basic fact-finding, which may involve speaking confidentially with relevant parties e.g. affected person, witnesses, supervisors, respondent obtaining relevant documentation or information through a variety of sources, which may include (but is not limited to): a written complaint information provided by a manager and/or supervisor information provided by another person collate any relevant documentary evidence available. Through these steps, the Workplace Relations Lead or Workplace Relations Senior Consultant will be seeking to ensure a support person is allocated to those involved and to determine whether further steps need to be taken by the Workplace Relations Lead or Workplace Relations Senior Consultant making preliminary enquiries, in order to give the matter the best chance of resolving without the need for further action. text: Workplace flexibility Context All positions in Victoria Police may be worked flexibly and Victoria Police offers a range of flexible work options across the organisation. Victoria Police recognises the importance of promoting diversity, gender equity and access to more flexible working arrangement options to assist employees in achieving an appropriate balance between organisational requirements and family and personal commitments, as well as to give employees a meaningful level of control over when, where and how work is accomplished. Along with reasonable workplace adjustments, flexible work options include: part-time employment, support while pregnant in the workplace and upon return to the workplace following the birth of a child, hours of work and flexi-time, variations to rostering, working from alternate locations, and supplementary duties. Other flexible options are available to Victoria Police employees such as: cashing out of Accrued Time Off, deferred salary scheme, purchased leave, study leave, voluntary duties and the transfer from one location to another. As an equal opportunity employer, Victoria Police is committed to employment practices and standards that are fair and equitable. Our employment standards are consistent with the obligations found within anti-discrimination legislation at Federal and State level, including the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth), Age Discrimination Act 2004 (Cth) and the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 (Vic), as well as, the Public Administration Act 2004 and the Victoria Police Act 2013. Victoria Police expects management and employees to work together in a cooperative and consultative manner to achieve the best possible flexible work outcomes. Contents 1. Scope and application Victoria Police is committed to a workplace that is inclusive, fair, respectful and supportive of diversity. Workplace flexibility is applied consistently with our obligations under the relevant Acts (aforementioned) the relevant enterprise agreements and related VPM policies. Victoria Police is required by law to take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate discrimination, sexual harassment and victimisation in accordance with the Equal Opportunity Act and Disability Discrimination Act. This means the organisation and its employees are obliged to take steps to prevent discriminatory practices or behaviours, not just respond to issues or complaints of discrimination when they occur. To meet this requirement: As an employer, Victoria Police maintains a workplace that values the diversity and individuality of its employees and encourages a workplace that is inclusive, respectful and fair; As an employer, Victoria Police must exercise positive duty to accommodate reasonable workplace adjustments so that a person with disability can have equality of access, employment and advancement opportunities (as per VPM Reasonable workplace adjustment); All Victoria Police employees and others covered by this policy are expected to exercise their positive duty by preventing discriminatory practices and encourage behaviours that treat others with dignity, courtesy and respect; and Policy owners must exercise positive duty by taking the necessary steps to eliminate barriers to equal opportunity when reviewing or developing systems, policy, training, infrastructure and equipment in their portfolio. Positive duty refers to the duty of employers under Part 3 of the Equal Opportunity Act to take positive action to eliminate discrimination, sexual harassment and victimisation. Policy Victoria Police is committed to providing flexible work options to assist employees to achieve an appropriate work/life balance, noting the dynamic nature of the policing environment and acknowledging not all types of flexibility will work for every role. As such Victoria Police provides its employees with flexibility in working arrangements, where it can reasonably be accommodated, taking into account the employee’s

Policy Victoria Police is committed to providing flexible work options to assist employees to achieve an appropriate work/life balance, noting the dynamic nature of the policing environment and acknowledging not all types of flexibility will work for every role. As such Victoria Police provides its employees with flexibility in working arrangements, where it can reasonably be accommodated, taking into account the employee’s family and carer responsibilities, disability, religion and culture. This applies to all LGBTIQ employees and family structures such as same sex coupled parents, single parents etc. Work unit managers are expected to consider and apply this policy when managing their workplaces. Workplace flexibility represents cooperation and genuine commitment between employer and employee for mutual benefit. Whilst not all forms of flexibility will be suitable for all roles at particular times or under particular circumstances due to the nature of Victoria Police’s business and having to match resourcing to demands, genuine consideration must be given to the employee’s needs and circumstances, alongside service delivery, rostering requirements, and corporate responsibility. This may require additional discussion with the employee to reach agreement on an alternative proposal that accommodates the employee’s circumstances and still meets the needs of the local unit. Victoria Police notes that flexible work practices also assist in attraction and retention and contribute to increased productivity and efficiency of employees. In accordance with legislation and the principles of merit and equity, Victoria Police applies a standard of ‘equitable’, rather than a standard of the ‘same’. Workplace flexibility Overview Work arrangements should be negotiated co-operatively and should provide, as far as practical, flexibility to meet the needs of both employees and the workplace. Flexible work arrangements and individual flexibility arrangements are defined below and are outlined fully in the relevant enterprise agreement. Decisions about requests for flexible work arrangements must be fair, transparent, documented and comply with relevant legislation, and any applicable enterprise agreement. This policy is to be read in conjunction with the Flexible Working Arrangements Checklist. Care relationship: a person is in a care relationship if they provide care to another person because they have a disability, are older, have a mental illness, or an ongoing medical condition (including a terminal or chronic illness or dementia); or has care of a child under a permanent care order, child care agreement or protection order. Directed change: a temporary change to an employee’s roster or working pattern, made to address a specific operational requirement occurring at the instigation and direction of the employer in exceptional circumstances. Disability: physical, mental health, intellectual, neurological or sensory impairments which, in interaction with various attitudinal and environmental barriers, may hinder full and effective participation in society on an equal basis with others. The Fair Work Act and enterprise agreements provide that employees have the right to request a FWA (including part-time and change in work location) in the following circumstances, namely where the employee: has responsibility as parent or carer of a child who is of school age or younger is a carer within the meaning of the Carer Recognition Act 2010 has a disability is 55 years of age or older is pregnant is experiencing family or domestic violence provides personal care, support or assistance to a member of the employee's immediate family, or a member of the employee's household, who requires care, support or assistance because they are experiencing family or domestic violence. The VPS Agreement provides all VPS employees a right to enter into an IFA in order to meet the genuine needs of the employee and employer. An IFA: does not require the employee to have a protected attribute (for example, a disability, parent/ carer responsibility as with an FWA); must be genuinely agreed to between the employee and employer; varies the effect of clause 38 (Hours of Work) or Clause 39 (Shift Work). The Equal Opportunity Act (s19) provides a right to parents and carers to have their caring responsibilities accommodated where reasonable, and provides that the employer must not unreasonably refuse to accommodate those responsibilities. The Checklist exists as an aid for managers when considering applicable requests for a flexible arrangement. Managers must consider applications carefully and with an attitude of ‘how can we make this work’. Managers must meet and discuss an application with the employee and genuinely try to reach agreement on a change in working arrangements that will reasonably accommodate the employee’s circumstances having regard to: the needs of the employee arising from their circumstances the consequences for the employee if changes in working arrangements are not made any alternative flexibility arrangements that may meet the circumstances of the employee that require flexibility any reasonable business grounds for refusing the request.

Procedures and timeframes Employees should submit their requests for flexible work arrangements in writing (using the relevant form as specified in the policy section or the Flexible Arrangements Application Form, or where that is not possible, by email or general report VP form 47) to their local manager as far in advance of the desired implementation of the requested change as possible to allow due consideration of the request. Applications must include (see Checklist for further guidance): details of the circumstances applicable to the request an outline of the timeframe the circumstances will likely apply (where known) supporting information or documentation to support the circumstances such as medical reports, details of carer or parental responsibilities, and any other information that will assist management consideration of the application, where necessary. A written response to the request (including the particulars of the reasonable business grounds if refusing an application) must be provided by their local management or the relevant Delegate to the employee. Where the request is a FWA, a written response must be provided within 21 calendar days of the manager receiving their written application. This applies regardless of how an employee submits their application, for example if an employee emails their manager with their request and then submits the application form at a later date to formalise the request, the 21 day time period starts from the date of the email. In consideration of the requirement to respond in writing within 21 calendar days, local management must: provide to the Delegate in a timely manner, copies of the application supporting evidence, and local management's assessment of the application if appropriate, convene a meeting with the Delegate for the purpose of considering the application, and/or employee to obtain further information in relation to the application or to discuss the request, and/or alternative flexibility arrangements. Pregnancy in the workplace Overview Victoria Police is committed to providing and maintaining a working environment for all pregnant employees that is safe and without risks to health. So far as is reasonably practical, pregnant employees will be provided with the option to undertake alternative duties where there is risk to the pregnant employee, their pregnancy, colleagues and/or members of the public if they continue their usual role. Denying or limiting access to promotion, secondment, temporary duties, transfers or training on the basis of pregnancy, or potential pregnancy is discrimination and/or adverse action and employees must not be denied or limited access to these opportunities or to any other benefits connected with their employment. Definitions Registered Medical Practitioner: means a registered Doctor of Medicine and includes specialists such as an Obstetrician. Notification and risk assessment Once pregnant, some aspects of an employee’s role may pose risks to the employee and their pregnancy. For this reason, pregnant employees are encouraged to notify their manager of their pregnancy as soon as practicable, taking into consideration that some roles will pose higher health and safety risks to the employee and their pregnancy than others. An employee must provide at least 10 weeks written notice of the intention to take parental leave, including the proposed start and end dates and the expected due date. Notification should include a confinement certificate from a Registered Medical Practitioner confirming the pregnancy and expected due date. The manager is to ensure that the notification of pregnancy is treated confidentially and is respectful of the pregnant employee. Early notification will ensure that a risk assessment can be conducted to determine appropriate duties during the pregnancy to avoid placing the pregnant employee or their pregnancy at risk. An occupational health and safety risk assessment of the employee’s duties should be conducted by the manager, in consultation with the employee, and will be based on advice from the employee’s Registered Medical Practitioner. This will enable an informed decision to be made based on the Registered Medical Practitioner’s advice regarding appropriate duties during the pregnancy taking into consideration identified risks in the work environment. The employee must provide the employer with a certificate from their Registered Medical Practitioner using the ‘Pregnancy

Transfer to a safe job Where an employee is pregnant and, in the opinion of a Registered Medical Practitioner, is fit for work, but it is inadvisable for them to continue at their present work because of illness or risks arising out of their pregnancy or hazards connected with the work assigned to the employee, the employee will be transferred, if reasonably practicable, to an appropriate safe job for the risk period. The safe job may involve working from a different location or may mean modifying the employee's existing role to remove any identified risks. This will depend on the result of the risk assessment and opinion of the medical practitioner. The safe job must involve meaningful duties and be commensurate with the employee’s skills, training and experience. This may include undertaking work from another work unit or the employee working from an alternative work location for a specific period or the duration of the pregnancy. The safe job will not alter the employee’s terms and conditions of employment. The employee will have the same ordinary hours of work as the employee’s present position; or a different number of ordinary hours as agreed by the employee and employer. Where an employee reduces their hours to better cope with their pregnancy, any paid parental leave subsequently taken will be paid at the rate of pay applicable prior the reduction in ordinary hours. If a transfer to an appropriate safe job is not reasonably practicable, the employee may elect, or the employer may require the employee to commence paid no safe job leave for such period as is certified necessary by a Registered Medical Practitioner or until the end of the pregnancy. Lactation breaks Principles Victoria Police is committed to fostering a supportive work environment for employees who choose to breastfeed by: providing appropriate workplace facilities for employees who choose to express breast milk or breastfeed their child providing paid lactation breaks during work hours ensuring all employees’ awareness of breastfeeding policies and facilities seeking to eliminate any unlawful direct and/or indirect discrimination on the grounds of breastfeeding. Employees who choose to breastfeed should be supported in that choice and treated with dignity and respect in the workplace. Definitions Breastfeeding: for the purpose of this policy, this includes the physiological process of milk being produced to breastfeed or express breast milk for an infant or young child. Definitions Breastfeeding: for the purpose of this policy, this includes the physiological process of milk being produced to breastfeed or express breast milk for an infant or young child. Caregiver: a caregiver is a person who assumes responsibility for bringing an infant or young child onto Victoria Police premises with the intent of delivering the infant or young child to an employee for the purpose of breastfeeding. Lactation breaks: paid breaks taken by an employee in consultation with their employer for the sole purpose of enabling an employee to express breast milk or breastfeed an infant or young child off site or at the workplace. Child: generally refers to a child up to school age; however consideration should be given to employee’s individual circumstances and needs for breastfeeding a child. Breastfeeding facilities Workplace facilities should be provided, where practical, for employees who choose to express breast milk or breastfeed their child during work hours. Facilities should be accessible for all, in terms of space, location and security access. The minimum requirements for an appropriate workplace facility include, as far as practicable: a private, clean and hygienic space/room which is suitably signed and lockable appropriate seating, a table or bench to support breastfeeding (and breastfeeding equipment) suitable storage area for any equipment and/or electric breastfeeding equipment a power point for breast pumps and other equipment access in the workplace, to a refrigerator/freezer for storing milk and a microwave access to a sink near the private space/room with hot water for washing hands and equipment nappy change table an appropriate receptacle for rubbish and nappy disposal. It is not appropriate for employees to breastfeed or express breast milk in toilet facilities, nor is it an appropriate location for equipment to be cleaned. Sinks and refrigeration located in a staffroom or kitchen facility should be used. Refer to the Australian Breastfeeding Association website for guidance on storage of expressed milk, if required. Generally, workplace facilities should be used, however consideration should be given to allowing the employee to go home, to a caregiver’s home or accessing a childcare centre if requested. Requests should be assessed on a case by case basis. Part-time Employment Objectives All part-time work arrangements should take into consideration any relevant operational and service delivery requirements, rostering principles and the employee’s individual circumstances. Part-time employees will have the same opportunities as other employees in all aspects of employment, including access to training, professional development, assignments and promotion. Definitions The definitions outlined in section 1.2 of this policy apply to this section. Part-time employment An employee may work on a part-time basis where the employee has been selected for a part-time position which was advertised (employer initiated), or the employee has applied and been approved to convert their existing position to part-time (employee initiated). Employee initiated also applies where a position has been advertised as full-time, but an employee has elected to do this role on a part-time basis. Part-time positions can also be filled with the expression of interest transfer process, see section 1.14. This procedure does not apply to employees being rehabilitated under WorkCover (see VPM Management and return to work of ill/injured employees) or where an employee works on a part-time basis pursuant to a flexible working arrangement. Working-from-home and working remotely Overview Victoria Police aims to provide employment options to maximise workforce flexibility and promote a balance between optimal service delivery and employees’ personal commitments. Victoria Police will be fair and transparent in considering requests by employees to work remotely or work-from-home. Employees granted approval to work remotely or from home will continue to be provided with equal opportunities in their employment. Individual working-from-home or remote work arrangements may be permitted on an ad-hoc or short-term basis or on a more regular basis in line with other flexible arrangement requests and will be reviewed regularly, having regard to both employees’ personal responsibilities and organisational needs. Employees are not to undertake remote of home-based work unless they have obtained approval in accordance with this policy. Where a State of Emergency or State of Disaster is declared, Victoria Police may issue other guidance which may supersede this policy in instances of differing information. Definitions Home-based-work (HBW) location: the area designated by the employee within their home as the work location in which they will perform their home-based-work. This includes areas the employee accesses in their home when taking breaks; such as the kitchen, bathroom, passageways and staircases. Home-based-work (HBW) arrangement: a flexible work arrangement that may be authorised on a short-term basis to help accommodate employees’ occasional and intermittent personal commitments, and emergencies or on a more regular basis to assist with an employee’s personal commitments and to help achieve an appropriate work/life balance. Remote work: refers to a location that the employee has requested to work from that is not the employee’s home and may be an interstate or overseas location. Remote work arrangement: a flexible arrangement that may be authorised, on a short-term basis only, where the employee will be working from another location, other than their home, that may be an interstate or overseas location. Eligibility All employees other than recruits, probationary constables and VPS employees who are within their probationary period are eligible to apply to work-from-home or work remotely. Any exception to this will only be considered in exceptional circumstances or as part of a reasonable workplace adjustment for a current or prospective employee with disability. Applications for a remote work arrangement from an interstate or overseas location will be

Applications for a remote work arrangement from an interstate or overseas location will be considered on a case by case basis only and several factors will need to be considered, including the role performed and whether the role can be performed remotely or not. Information management & security Policy adherence All Authorised Users have a duty and responsibility to ensure that Victoria Police information is protected from harm, unauthorised or inappropriate disclosure. If Victoria Police employees have approval for a remote or HBW arrangement, they must ensure that they continue to adhere to Victoria Police policy. This includes maintaining the confidentiality, integrity and availability of Victoria Police information. To ensure the security of Victoria Police information, Authorised Users who are not Victoria Police employees are not to undertake work at home or remotely. Risks Working-from-home increases the security risks for Victoria Police information including (but not limited to): the potential for people without a ‘need-to-know’ or without an appropriate security clearance to gain access to (or read) official information or other official resources loss of Victoria Police information in transit between the workplace and home viruses or other malicious code being present or being introduced to IT equipment. Refer to the Protective Security Practice Guide – 810 - Working from home securely for further guidance. Security classified information Information that has been assessed as PROTECTED or above is not to be worked on using home-based or remote computer equipment, unless this is done on the Victoria Police network through approved secure two-factor authentication (such as Connect.Police tokens). Refer to VPM Information categorisation, collection and recording for information on security classifications. Hardcopy security classified information must be stored in a container suitable for the classification of the material when not in use. Refer to Protective Security guide – G200 – Assessment and handling of Victoria Police information. If a suitable security container is not available, then the information should not be taken home. Any deviation from these requirements requires approval by the Department Head after seeking advice from the Information Security Manager and the Protective Security Manager, Information Security, Security and Management Services Division. This applies to an approved remote or HBW location. text: Business Continuity Management Context Business Continuity Management (BCM) provides the structure and processes for Victoria Police to identify threats to the organisation’s business through a framework for building resilience and the capacity for an effective response to those threats. Business continuity issues can arise from any event which caused or has the potential to cause major or catastrophic disruption of critical infrastructure, and/or business functions and service delivery of Victoria Police. Under instruction 3.7(1) of the Standing Directions issued by the Minister for Finance in 2018 under the Financial Management Act 1994, Victoria Police is required to have developed, implemented, maintained, reviewed and tested a business continuity planning process. The Chief Commissioner is required to provide annual attestation as to this requirement and provide assurance to the Emergency Management Commissioner (EMC) that Victoria Police is in a state of preparedness to respond to any emergency, including exercising the functions of command, control and co-ordination. The primary objective of BCM is to build organisational resilience by establishing a framework that allows Victoria Police to prevent, prepare, respond to, and recover from any disruption to critical services/functions. Policy at a glance This policy includes: information for employees on the BCM Framework and its key accountability structure direction on business continuity arrangement standard operating procedures for work units, emergency management roles and police operations centres responsibilities involved in business continuity exercising for work unit managers, Local Area Commanders (LACs)/line managers and members responsible for police operations centres response requirements for work unit managers and LACs/line managers during business continuity events and incidents annual BCM and emergency management assurance reporting responsibilities for the organisation and auditing requirements for the BCM Auditor. Business Continuity Planning and Exercising 3 3. Business Continuity Events and Incidents 5 4. Annual Business Continuity Management & Emergency Management Assurance Reporting 7 5. Business Continuity Auditing 9 Related documents 10 Further advice and information 10 Update history 10 Definitions Accountable Manager - the relevant Assistant Commissioner or Executive Director of each region/department/command. Business Continuity Event (Interruption) - A short-term impact on service delivery that does not exceed the maximum tolerable outage. The interruption would not require relocation or activation of the Business Continuity Arrangement Standard Operating Procedure (BCA SOP) and can be managed through local interventions and workarounds. Business Continuity Incident (Disruption) - An emergency or extended interruption, that is preventing, or has the potential to prevent, a work unit from delivering a critical service within the agreed maximum tolerable outage time. Business Continuity Incident (Disruption) - An emergency or extended interruption, that is preventing, or has the potential to prevent, a work unit from delivering a critical service within the agreed maximum tolerable outage time. Business Continuity Management (BCM) Framework – Sets out the structure and arrangements to ensure that all aspects of BCM in Victoria Police comply with relevant standards and practice guidelines, with the aim of strengthening organisational resilience. Executive Accountable Manager – A nominated Deputy Commissioner or Deputy Secretary. Maximum Tolerable Outage (MTO) – The maximum period (identified through a business impact analysis) that Victoria Police (from a single work unit up to state level) can tolerate the disruption of a critical business process, before the achievement of objectives is adversely affected. Scope and application This policy applies to all work unit managers, LAC or line managers, Divisional Managers, Executive Accountable Managers, State Incident Command and Control System (ICCS) functional managers, Municipal Emergency Response Coordinators (MERC), Regional Emergency Management Inspectors and Superintendents (REMI/REMS) and police operations centre (POC) managers. Responsibilities and procedures Key Business Continuity Accountable Positions The following positions have accountability under the BCM Framework. State Business Continuity Manager The State Business Continuity Manager (SBCM) is the Inspector at the State Business Continuity Unit, State Emergency Response Coordination Division (SERCD), State Emergencies and Support Command (SESC). SBCM responsibilities: ensure Victoria Police is compliant with overarching BCM standards and legislation perform SBCM roles as defined in the BCM Framework and associated plans overall management and coordination of the BCM Framework and arrangements for the organisation, including the influenza pandemic plan and the crisis management plan management of BCM in Police Emergency and Event Command (PEEC) application. Executive Accountable Manager The role of the Executive Accountable Manager is to provide strategic direction and advice to Executive Command and the appointed State Police Commander in the response and recovery phases of a major business continuity related incident to Victoria Police. Executive Accountable Manager responsibilities: ensure the Executive Crisis Management Team (ECMT) is prepared and available for activation (refer to crisis management plan) management of state level BCM issues impacting the organisation ensure effective BCM practices for the ECMT maintain oversight of the Annual BCM & Emergency Management (EM) Assurance Reporting. Accountable Manager The Accountable Manager has responsibility for the management of business continuity for their region/department/command. It is recommended that Accountable Managers appoint a Deputy Accountable Manager to oversee and report on BCM activities for the region/department/command. Accountable Manager responsibilities: overall management of significant BCM incidents affecting their region/ department/command

It is recommended that Accountable Managers appoint a Deputy Accountable Manager to oversee and report on BCM activities for the region/department/command. Accountable Manager responsibilities: overall management of significant BCM incidents affecting their region/ department/command support the Police Commander in the development and implementation of response and recovery plans for critical services/functions. Business Continuity Planning and Exercising Business Continuity Arrangements Standard Operating Procedures for Work Units All work units are required to create business continuity arrangements, known as BCA SOPs and review these biannually. A work unit BCA SOP must be completed on the template provided by the State Business Continuity Unit, available in PEEC. Refer to the Business Continuity intranet page for relevant training materials, including ‘how to’ guides, flow charts and videos to assist stakeholders and support BCA SOP development. A work unit may develop and maintain a joint BCA SOP with other like work units, for example: a cluster of one-member stations a division that comprises a number of small work units, i.e. a business management division incorporating a project officer, finance officer, HR practitioner. A joint BCA SOP must adequately reflect the individual arrangements of each work unit. Business Continuity Arrangements Standard Operating Procedures for Emergency Management Roles and ICCS Functions Emergency management is a critical function performed by Victoria Police. The services and functions performed by employees in certain emergency management roles must be included in a BCA SOP. Business Continuity Arrangements Standard Operating Procedures for Police Operations Centres A BCA SOP for POCs is completed by the respective member responsible for each centre and is uploaded to the Advance File Library of BCM PEEC. Business Continuity Exercising Exercising is the method by which BCA SOPs are tested. Exercising provides assurance that BCA SOPs are current, effective, relevant, and understood by employees. Every work unit, MERC and POC that is required under this policy to have a BCA SOP should exercise their BCA SOP biannually (minimum requirement). Exercise scenarios have been provided in the exercise template in BCM PEEC, as well as provision to exercise a custom scenario. Business Continuity Events and Incidents Business Continuity Events (Interruption) If a work unit is impacted by a situation or event that causes a short-term interruption which does not exceed critical service delivery MTOs, work unit employees should utilise workarounds to manage the interruption to ensure critical services are maintained. For example, using mobile phones and diverting incoming phone calls to a neighbouring police station during a telecommunications

text: well as provision to exercise a custom scenario. Business Continuity Events and Incidents Business Continuity Events (Interruption) If a work unit is impacted by a situation or event that causes a short-term interruption which does not exceed critical service delivery MTOs, work unit employees should utilise workarounds to manage the interruption to ensure critical services are maintained. For example, using mobile phones and diverting incoming phone calls to a neighbouring police station during a telecommunications interruption. Business Continuity Incidents (Disruption) If a work unit is impacted by an emergency or extended disruption, which exceeds or has the potential to exceed critical service delivery MTO, the work unit BCA SOP should be activated to maintain service delivery. Annual Business Continuity Management & Emergency Management Assurance Reporting Organisational reporting requirements Each year, Victoria Police through the Chief Commissioner, must provide an annual attestation against Instruction 3.7 (1) of the Standing Directions 2018, issued under the Financial Management Act 1994, and provide assurance to the Victorian Government and to the EMC against two criteria: BCM Attestation - that Victoria Police has developed, implemented, maintained, reviewed and tested a business continuity planning process Emergency Management Preparedness - Victoria Police provides assurance to the EMC that Victoria Police is ‘in a state of preparedness to respond to any emergency, including exercising the functions of command, control and co-ordination’. To enable Victoria Police to provide these assurances, every work unit manager or MERC is required to complete a ‘Business continuity and emergency management preparedness annual assurance report’ in PEEC. This is an annual requirement and is undertaken during the annual assurance cycle in July and August each year. Reports should be completed as early as possible in line with the annual assurance cycle to allow time for approval and auditing. Work unit reporting requirements Municipal Emergency Response Coordinators/Regional Emergency Management Inspectors and Superintendents reporting requirements Division/Region/Department/Command/State reporting requirements Business Continuity Auditing Audit requirements Each region/department/command is required to appoint a unit (i.e. audit and risk unit) or nominated employee(s) to perform the role of business continuity management auditor (BCM Auditor). The auditor should be independent (i.e. not involved in preparing the BCA SOPs or be a participant in the business continuity exercise) and remain impartial. The BCM Auditor responsibilities are: auditing of BCA SOPs and business continuity exercises to assist the Accountable Manager or Deputy Accountable Manager with preparation of the annual assurance regional reports (in PEEC). title: Workplace_management_VPM_Workplace_Standards_final
text: Workplace standards and management Context The Victoria Police mission is to provide a safe, secure and orderly society by serving the community and the law. Victoria Police employees implement this mission through: Frontline operational members providing policing service to the community Employees performing roles that enable and support the provision of these core services. Regardless of their role, when employees perform their tasks professionally, in a timely manner and in accordance with legislative requirements and organisational standards, they contribute to the provision of service excellence to the Victorian community. The most straightforward day to day administrative task, done well, helps Victoria Police to achieve its mission. Managers and supervisors play an essential role in achieving this objective through setting and implementing workplace standards. This role is not simply about ensuring compliance. It is about creating a workplace culture that understands the value of meeting these standards. This policy is intended to: Outline the organisation’s expectations regarding workplace standards and management for managers, supervisors and employees Provide minimum standards for managing workplaces. Contents Context 1 Contents 1 Scope and application 1 Responsibilities and procedures 2 2. Workplace management principles 3 3. Workplace standards and structure 3 4. Communicating workplace standards 4 5. Management continuity 5 6. Workplace inspections 6 7. Function audits 6 8. Workplace managers responsibility 7 Related documents 7 Further advice and information 7 Update history 8 Scope and application This policy applies to all managers and supervisors Responsibilities and procedures Work Unit Managers Work Unit Managers are responsible for the day to day management of their work unit and for ensuring that workplace standards and performance measures are met. This includes: Managing their allocated human, financial and physical resources to support workplace performance and service delivery. They must ensure that these resources are appropriately deployed and managed to support the work unit’s tasks and accountabilities in accordance with policies and guidelines on: professional and ethical standards operational duties and responsibilities people management occupational health and safety information management and security management of finance and physical resources Ensuring that the performance and professional development of their employees is managed in accordance with VPMP Performance and professional management. As stated in this policy, employees must be informed of: the requirements of their job, the standard of performance expected of them; and instances where they are not meeting the required standard Identifying risks or issues that may be impacting upon employee or workplace performance or service delivery and taking action to address them. If there are any risks or issues that cannot be resolved at their management level, or that a higher level of management should be aware of, they must advise the next line manager. Supervisors Supervisors are responsible for: Supporting Work Unit Managers in achieving the required workplace standards Ensuring that employees in their work unit meet the minimum workplace standards. They must speak with and support employees so that they can undertake their role and complete tasks in a professional and timely manner The actions and decisions of employees when they are under their supervision. Local Area Commanders and Senior Managers Local Area Commanders and Senior Managers are responsible for the performance and service delivery of their Police Service Area or Division. They must ensure the workplaces under their control are meeting required workplace standards. If there are any risks or issues that cannot be resolved at their management level or that a higher level of management should be aware of, they must advise the next line manager. Department Heads Department Heads are ultimately accountable for the performance of their Region or Department. They must oversee their Region or Department’s compliance with this policy. Departments and Regions are to document how their function audits and inspections procedures were developed on a risk-basis. Delegation of responsibilities Managers may delegate responsibility for particular functions or activities to employees under their management. However, they are still accountable for the decisions and actions of those employees within the scope of the delegation. Corporate governance Corporate and Workplace Performance Unit, Capability Department is responsible for establishing, overseeing and reporting on workplace management standards across all levels of the organisation. Workplace management principles When undertaking the responsibilities outlined above, managers and supervisors are to apply the following principles: Know your business – clearly understand what is required of you and the employees for which you are responsible be familiar and keep up to date with relevant organisational priorities, legislation, policies and systems focus on key areas that directly relate to providing, enabling or supporting policing services to the community. Aim for high standards – proactively and responsibly manage issues to completion acknowledge that the application and compliance with workplace standards relates to providing, enabling or supporting services to the community ensure that their work units are managed on a continual basis throughout the course of the month continuously improve by identifying and acting on risk at the earliest opportunity with practical solutions that deliver real results. Workplace standards and structure General standards The standards for managing specific functions or activities are documented throughout the Victoria Police Manual (VPM) or in legislation. The Workplace standards and inspections manual provides an overview of the standards that apply to functions or responsibilities that are common to most workplaces across the organisation. Work Unit Managers of workplaces that perform specialist functions or activities that are not included in the VPM must establish suitable standards for these functions. Workplace management structure Managers must establish and document a workplace management structure that is appropriate for their workplace, taking into consideration its functions and applicable standards, risks, size and composition. This may include the establishment of supervision groups, the allocation of portfolios, and/or the allocation of specific roles and responsibilities. Standards for operational work units Operational Work Unit Managers must ensure that their workplace management structure addresses the following high risk areas, which form the basis of managing core frontline policing activities: LEAP / Interpose – ensuring that crime is recorded and that relevant investigations are managed Traffic incident system (TIS) – ensuring that traffic incidents are recorded and that relevant investigations are managed Briefs and justice related processes – ensuring that required standards and timeframes are met Property – ensuring that seized and found property is appropriately recorded, stored and disposed of Correspondence – ensuring that required standards and timeframes are met Persons in police care or custody – ensuring management systems / records address risk and support the safety of both persons in care or custody and police members. The Workplace standards and inspections manual details the standards that apply to the management of these functions. Communicating workplace standards Standard Operating Procedures Managers must develop Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that document how the workplace they are responsible for is to operate and any specific standards that apply. SOPs: Are only to reflect local arrangements and must not replicate, replace or be inconsistent with any requirements in the VPM Must contain sufficient information to support employee

title: Workplace_management_VPM_Workplace_Standards_final
text: Workplace standards and inspections manual details the standards that apply to the management of these functions. Communicating workplace standards Standard Operating Procedures Managers must develop Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that document how the workplace they are responsible for is to operate and any specific standards that apply. SOPs: Are only to reflect local arrangements and must not replicate, replace or be inconsistent with any requirements in the VPM Must contain sufficient information to support employee induction, ongoing workplace management, business continuity and handover of roles and responsibilities, including – the established workplace management structure and workplace inspection system (see s.5) any specific standards or requirements that apply to the workplace how any specific portfolios are managed specific delegations that apply to the workplace’s manager or employees Must be approved by the next line manager. See VPMP Policy development and advice on developing local SOPs. Induction Managers must ensure that any employee that starts work in their workplace is provided with an induction which includes safety and the expected standards for that workplace. Management continuity Conduct of structured handover Before transferring, commencing leave or other extended absence from a workplace, managers and portfolio holders must conduct an appropriate handover with the employee assuming their role. The handover must be recorded and address how the workplace and/or portfolio area is managed, management expectations and any issues or risks that apply to the workplace/portfolio. Handover content A suggested check list to assist a structured handover process is available as an appendix to this document. As workplaces within Victoria Police differ, this list is not exhaustive and may vary according to the workplace. Topics to be covered in a handover process include: Staff welfare, OHS and personnel issues Rostering, flexible working arrangements and leave (including stay in touch plans, where relevant) Training and professional development Operations, projects and tasks Stakeholder management issues Business continuity planning/emergency management Relevant contact details. Information security All information included in handover documents should be managed with appropriate sensitivity and confidentiality to assure against unjustified discrimination. Handover documents will generally include personal information (defined as ‘sensitive’ in Schedule 1 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014) and/or health information (as defined in the Health Records Act 2001) and therefore: The documents must be given the protective marking of Sensitive: Personal Need to know principles apply; copies (electronic or physical) are to be kept to a minimum and must be stored so that can only be accessed by people with a need to know the information. Workplace inspections Purpose All workplaces must conduct workplace inspections. The purpose of workplace inspections is to mitigate risk and assess the effectiveness of the workplace management systems by: verifying whether the required workplace standards are being met identifying any areas of non-compliance or risk and taking relevant remedial action. Approval Department / Regional level approval of workplace inspection procedures is required. This can be in the form of a set of risk based common procedures to be adopted in all core policing Divisions, PSA’s and work units. Requirement Having regard to the Workplace standards and inspections manual, Work Unit Managers must in consultation with their line manager, establish a risk based inspection system that reflects the functions in their workplace. Work Unit Managers who are responsible for functions that are not included in the Workplace standards and inspections manual, must ensure that appropriate inspection standards are established, particularly where the functions are high risk. The workplace inspection system must be documented in local SOPs and must include: frequency of inspections items and records to be inspected verification process recording and reporting requirements process for addressing issues that may arise. Conduct and reporting Work Unit Managers must ensure that workplace inspections are conducted in accordance with the established system. They must report the outcome of inspections to their line manager in accordance with the schedule in the Workplace standards and inspections manual. Line managers must review workplace inspection reports. They must ensure that any risks to workplace performance are identified and that action is taken regarding them. Function audits A function audit is a risk based process to proactively test the progress of a particular function, item or area of management or reactively resolve problems that have been identified through the workplace inspection, verification or risk management processes. Senior Managers and Local Area Commanders must consider the need to conduct function audits in their workplaces to address specific risks in their workplaces. They may direct areas (such as Regional Risk and Audit Teams) or employees to undertake audits. Benchmarking information such as the provided by the “Harper Station Books Application” compliance scores and PALM property gauges provide an indicator of management effectiveness and should be used to inform the tasking of audit resources to high risk areas and work units. A compliance audit is to be conducted within three months of the function audit. Where, at a Departmental or Regional level a determination is made not to conduct function audit/s,

Workplace managers responsibility At the start of each financial year the workplace manager will: Analyse the workplace inspection reports for the previous 12 month period. Identify any risks coming from the workplace inspection reports. Develop a local risk mitigation strategy to reduce or eliminate any identified risks. Report, through line management to the Department Manager on the workplace inspections highlighting the identified risks and confirming the action that has been taken or will be taken to reduce or eliminate the risks. Where no risks have been identified, a report must still be generated.
